## Summary
Computer Use on Windows can enumerate WeChat and QQ windows and read accessibility text, including currently displayed messages and file names, but window screenshot capture repeatedly times out. Clicking a freshly observed accessibility element also fails because capture geometry is unavailable. This blocks a desktop workflow that requires navigating chat history.

## Environment
- Windows 10 Pro, version 10.0.19045, build 19045.
- Installed app package: OpenAI.Codex_26.1007.2314.0_x64.
- Bundled Computer Use plugin: 26.1007.21434.
- Graphics devices reported by Windows: Intel UHD Graphics 630 (driver 31.0.101.2115), OrayIddDriver Device, GameViewer Virtual Display Adapter. Their presence is recorded for diagnostics; no causal relationship has been established.
- Target apps and Computer Use helper run in the active local console session.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Open WeChat or QQ on an unlocked Windows desktop.
2. Initialize the bundled @oai/sky client in node_repl.
3. Select an actual returned window using sky.list_apps()/sky.list_windows() and sky.get_window().
4. Activate the window, refresh its Window object, and call sky.get_window_state({window, include_text:true, include_screenshot:true}).
5. Refresh window selection and retry the capture.
6. Read accessibility text with include_screenshot:false. Try clicking the chat-history button with an element index from that fresh observation.

## Actual behavior
Screenshot calls repeatedly return:
```
FrameArrived timed out: timed out waiting on channel
window capture timed out: timed out waiting on channel
```
Clicking a freshly observed control returns:
```
coordinate input geometry is unavailable
```
Window enumeration and accessibility-only text reads succeed. Activation and some keyboard navigation work, but reliable history-search navigation could not be established.

## Expected behavior
Return a screenshot and usable geometry for the selected visible window so Computer Use can safely navigate search and history controls.

## Troubleshooting performed
- Refreshed window selection and rehydrated Window objects.
- Activated and maximized target windows.
- Reset JavaScript execution sessions and retried initialization.
- Restarted helper processes.
- Restarted/reinstalled the desktop app and rebooted Windows; capture errors persisted afterward.

The user reports that this desktop workflow previously worked. The first failing version and root cause have not been established. An earlier sandbox startup/file-lock error was observed, but command execution now works and the ongoing capture failure remains; these are not asserted to have the same cause.

## Related reports
Symptoms overlap with #52754, #52993, #53137, and #53145. A shared root cause has not been confirmed.

Please investigate the Windows capture pipeline and advise a supported diagnostic or recovery procedure. This report contains technical symptoms only; no customer messages, financial files, raw session transcript, account identifiers, or credentials are attached.

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1029.61003 (build 24614), verified from the installed app Info.plist

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.6; uname -mprs: Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

The desktop app's built-in instructions cause the assistant to decline Schedule-based monitoring of a task running in an external web system, even though the official documentation explicitly describes checking long-running operations until they finish.

**Scope: the monitored task belongs to an external web system. It is not a Codex session, thread, subagent, or Codex task.** Codex would only periodically check its status and report or continue the user's authorized follow-up when the external operation finishes.

The app-provided Automations instructions include:

> Do not create an automation to track a specific job or task through a milestone, failure, or completion.

The following sentence directs the assistant to keep checking in the current task when asked to watch a run or task to completion. Neither sentence explicitly limits the restriction to Codex's own tasks.

In a fresh local chat, the assistant discovered the native automation_update tool (including thread-attached heartbeat support), but declined to create this kind of schedule because it interpreted the built-in restriction as also covering external-system tasks. Clarifying that the task is external did not resolve that interpretation.

This is an instruction/documentation conflict observed before scheduling, not evidence of a scheduler backend rejection or a missed scheduled execution. No tracking schedule was created during this investigation.

Official documentation, checked on November 5, 2026:
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/automations?surface=app#schedule-a-task-inside-a-chat

It explicitly lists “checking a long-running operation until it finishes” as a use case for a schedule in an existing chat. It also describes minute-based follow-up intervals, preserved chat context, and prompts with reporting and stopping conditions. The documented deployment-follow-up example appears to fit this external-system use case.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence on one installation; not independently reproduced on another installation:

1. Ask a local Codex chat whether it can use Schedule to follow a task running in an external web system until it completes.
2. In a fresh chat, check whether automation_update is available. It is discoverable here.
3. The assistant declines to create the monitoring schedule, citing the built-in prohibition on tracking a specific job or task to completion.
4. Clarify that the monitored task is external, not a Codex session/thread/task. The assistant still interprets the generic wording as applying to it.
5. Compare the built-in instruction with the linked official Scheduled tasks documentation.

Suggested minimal prompt for maintainers (a generalized example, not a verbatim transcript):
“Every five minutes, return to this chat and check the status of the task in the external web system. Notify me on completion or failure and stop the schedule. This is not a Codex task or session.”

The relevant tool was discovered, but its create operation was not called. This report does not establish whether the backend would accept that schedule.

### What is the expected behavior?

Please clarify and align the runtime instructions, tool guidance, and public documentation for external-system monitoring.

- If the prohibition is intended only for tracking Codex's own running tasks, explicitly scope it that way and allow user-requested monitoring of tasks in external web systems through the documented existing-chat Schedule flow.
- If external-system tasks are also intentionally prohibited, explain that boundary in the documentation and provide the supported alternative for periodic checks without keeping one conversational turn continuously active.
- Ensure a fresh chat does not refuse a documented use case merely because “job or task” is ambiguous.

A useful regression case would request monitoring of a harmless external task with an explicit completion/stop condition, separately from any test involving Codex's own task lifecycle.

### Additional information

Read-only inspection located the exact restriction in the installed application archive:

- App version: 26.1029.61003, build 24614 (read from Info.plist).
- Archive: /Applications/ChatGPT.app/Contents/Resources/app.asar
- Member: .vite/build/early-bootstrap-339-a1c76730c29ac8b1.js
- The Automations text is held in the minified sX constant and included by the instruction builder inside <app-context>.
- The caller getProjectAwareDeveloperInstructions() is in .vite/build/early-bootstrap-45-628adb74a9c47df1.js.

These are build-specific packaged identifiers, not a claim about the upstream source-file layout. The restriction was found in the app bundle, not introduced by project AGENTS.md or a user skill. No installed files, configuration, or schedules were modified to test it.

issues.body:
### Environment

Codex desktop for Windows, installed package version `26.1111.2228.0`. Windows 10 22H2 x64, build 19045. SumatraPDF is the Windows default PDF reader.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Have Codex return a clickable link to a large local PDF in its final response.
2. Left-click the filename once.
3. While waiting for the first page, try to continue using the chat.

### What happens

The click immediately opens a right-hand preview tab, and Codex can stall for a long time before the PDF is usable. An accidental click is enough to interrupt work in the chat. The user reported this during normal use. Exact file size and stall duration were not measured.

### Expected behavior

Keep the chat responsive while the first page loads. Please also let users choose what a normal click on a local PDF does: preview in Codex, open in the system default reader, or ask each time. In the latter two modes, the choice should take effect before Codex starts loading the PDF. The existing context menu helps with deliberate opens but cannot prevent an accidental left-click from starting the preview.

### Investigation lead

In this Windows build, the bundled PDF preview panel accepts a Base64 data URL, decodes its payload into a byte array in the renderer, then passes that array to PDF.js via `getDocument({ data, worker })`. It requests page 1 after the document promise resolves. That path requires the whole encoded payload before first paint. Profiling the time to first page and renderer responsiveness on a large local PDF would help establish how much of the stall occurs during file transfer, decoding, and first-page rendering. A range-capable local file source may be worth testing.

Related: #58367 describes lag while navigating PDFs on macOS. This report concerns the initial click and wait for page 1 on Windows.

prs.title: Defer Git worktree status until the turn starts
prs.body:
Defer Git worktree status until the turn starts

## Why

A turn interrupted during setup can be discarded before it runs. Starting
the worktree scan during setup can spend time scanning for a turn that
will never send a model request.

## What changed

Collect `HEAD` and remote URLs in the background after turn setup, and
start the worktree status scan only after the turn is admitted to run.
Model requests use the latest available Git metadata while collection
continues, and later requests can include the worktree status once it
is available.

Use shared background Git root discovery for the memory extraction
change probe and pass the resolved root into the probe.

## Testing

Regression tests cover requests proceeding while status is blocked,
later requests carrying the updated `HEAD`, remote URL, and dirty
status, and an interrupted wake skipping the worktree scan.

issues.title: Assess the impact of AST-aware file reads, search, and mapping

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: kind/customer-issue
labels.description: Issues that were reported by customers

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

This is one such subtask (also including fixing a broken build) that could be delegated to a subagent such as the generalist to outsource the fix and return to the main agent with a working build. 

Considerations/Objectives:
- Investigate getting the model to use the generalist in subtasks such as this
- evaluate if calling is consistent and provides enough feedback back to the main agent to prevent any hallucinations of state (does the generalist let the main agent know what changes it had to make / if the fix couldn't be fixed without further changes)
- Does the main agent provide enough context for the generalist to successfully accomplish its tasks? Or could this require a way for the main agent to share more context?
- Add behavior evals to see if the behavior is followed consistently.

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

labels.name: priority/p3
labels.description: Backlog - a good idea but not currently a priority.

labels.name: area/agent

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: fix(core,cli): parse PowerShell commands asynchronously to prevent UI spinner freeze
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes a multi-second UI freeze on Windows where the Thinking spinner and elapsed-time counter stop updating before the Shell tool panel appears when Gemini CLI validates or executes PowerShell commands.

## Details

- **Root cause:** PowerShell AST command parsing (`parsePowerShellCommandDetails` in `packages/core/src/utils/shell-utils.ts`) used blocking `child_process.spawnSync('powershell.exe', ...)` without per-invocation caching, stalling the Node.js event loop up to 14 times (~200–500ms per spawn) across policy evaluation, taint/build-file checks, confirmation generation, Windows sandbox checks, and React UI renders.
- **Scoped async parsing (`@google/gemini-cli-core`):**
  - Added `CommandParseCache` + `AsyncLocalStorage` (`shell-parse-cache.ts`) to reuse completed parses (including `null` failure results) and deduplicate concurrent in-flight parses within a single `PolicyEngine.check()` or `ShellToolInvocation` lifecycle without introducing an unbounded process-wide cache.
  - Added non-blocking `parsePowerShellCommandDetailsAsync` (`child_process.spawn` with `windowsHide: true` and `stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe']`) and async shell helpers while preserving all existing PowerShell AST and command-substitution fallback safeguards.
  - Updated `PolicyEngine`, `Scheduler`, `ShellToolInvocation`, `untrustedContextTracker`, and Windows sandbox safety checks to parse asynchronously and share cached results across validation, `ProceedAlways` policy updates, and execution.
- **Non-blocking UI (`@google/gemini-cli`):**
  - Precomputed optional `hasRedirection` on `exec` confirmation details so `ToolConfirmationMessage` and `useGeminiStream` (`AUTO_EDIT` transitions) avoid synchronous re-parsing.
  - Updated `useTurnActivityMonitor` to resolve unconfirmed PowerShell redirection checks asynchronously via `hasRedirectionAsync` instead of calling `hasRedirection` synchronously during React render.
  - Updated `useExecutionLifecycle` (`!` Shell Mode) to fast-path non-`gemini` and obvious interactive `gemini` commands in-process and disambiguate remaining PowerShell commands via `isInteractiveGeminiCommandAsync`.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30249

## How to Validate

1. Run the targeted unit and integration test suites (verifying scoped cache isolation, 15ms timer responsiveness during simulated PowerShell startup latency, and zero `spawnSync` calls across Core and CLI UI):
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/shell-parse-cache.test.ts src/tools/shell-powershell-parsing.integration.test.ts
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/ui/hooks/powershellUiParsing.test.tsx src/ui/hooks/useGeminiStream.test.tsx
   ```
2. Run full preflight validation:
   ```bash
   npm run preflight
   ```
3. On Windows PowerShell, start Gemini CLI interactively and ask the model to run:
   ```powershell
   Get-ChildItem | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name,Length,LastWriteTime
   ```
   as well as a redirected command (`Get-ChildItem > out.txt`), and confirm the Thinking spinner and elapsed-time counter remain smooth and responsive before and during the Shell confirmation prompt.

prs.title: feat(core): add configurable per-tool-call timeout (tools.callTimeout)
prs.body:
## Summary

Adds a `tools.callTimeout` setting (seconds, default `0` = disabled) that caps
the wall-clock duration of a single tool call. When the deadline passes, the
tool's `AbortSignal` fires and the call ends as a recoverable
`TOOL_CALL_TIMEOUT` error, so the model can change its approach instead of the
CLI waiting indefinitely.

This builds on @officialasishkumar's work in #27423 (his commit is kept as-is
with his authorship, rebased onto current `main`). The follow-up commit
addresses the review points raised in #3375 and a couple of others I found
along the way.

## Details

Enforced centrally in `ToolExecutor`, so it covers shell, MCP, web fetch and
every other tool through the same cooperative-abort path as Ctrl+C. For shell
commands that means the existing abort handler kills the process group, not
just the promise.

Changes on top of #27423:

- **No `AbortSignal.any`.** It needs Node >= 20.3, but `engines` allows 20.0,
  and it gives no way to detach from the parent signal. The derived signal is
  now built by hand (as `shell.ts` already does). The listener on the caller's
  signal is removed in `finally`, so nothing builds up on a long-lived signal.
- **No spurious abort on success.** The previous `finally` called
  `deadlineTimer.abort()`, which aborted the signal handed to the tool even
  when the call had finished normally. Now the timer is just cleared.
- **Timeout vs. user cancellation** is decided by which one fired first, using
  a flag set only by the timer. A timer that comes due after the user has
  cancelled cannot turn a cancellation into a timeout.
- **Very large values are clamped.** Node's `setTimeout` fires after 1ms
  for delays above 2^31-1 ms (about 24.8 days), so a "basically never" value
  like `9999999` would have timed out every call at once.
- **Subagent invocations (`Kind.Agent`) are exempt.** They already have their
  own budget (`maxTimeMinutes`, default 10) with a graceful wrap-up turn.
  Hard-killing them at, say, 60s would throw away all of the subagent's work.
  The tool calls a subagent makes still go through `ToolExecutor` and are each
  capped. Happy to drop this if maintainers would rather the setting apply
  literally everywhere.
- **Test mocks updated.** The shared mock configs in
  `packages/cli/src/test-utils/mockConfig.ts` and
  `packages/a2a-server/src/utils/testing_utils.ts`, and the one in
  `scheduler_hooks.test.ts`, had no `getToolCallTimeout`. On current `main`
  that made 5 a2a-server E2E tests and 1 core scheduler test fail.
- Rebased onto `main` and regenerated the docs and schema with
  `npm run docs:settings`.

## Related Issues

Fixes #3375
Supersedes #27423

## How to Validate

1. In `~/.gemini/settings.json`:
   ```json
   { "tools": { "callTimeout": 5 } }
   ```
2. Ask the CLI to run `sleep 30`.
3. After about 5s the call ends with "Tool execution timed out after 5
   seconds…", and `pgrep -f "sleep 30"` shows nothing left running.
4. With the setting unset or `0`, behavior is unchanged.

```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/scheduler/tool-executor.test.ts src/config/config.test.ts
npm run docs:settings -- --check
```

New unit tests cover: the timeout firing (for tools that reject and for tools
that resolve with partial output, like shell), the disabled path, user
cancellation before and during execution, no abort or leftover listeners after
a normal completion, clamping of very large values, and the subagent
exemption.

I also checked locally (macOS, Node 22) with a real `ShellTool` running
`sleep 37` through `ToolExecutor` with a 2s limit. The call returned
`TOOL_CALL_TIMEOUT` after about 2.1s, and `pgrep` found no `sleep 37` process
afterwards, so the process group is killed, not just the promise.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed)
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Noted breaking changes (if any): none, opt-in and off by default
- [ ] Validated on required platforms/methods:
  - [x] MacOS
    - [x] npm run

prs.title: fix(core): stop overriding core.sshCommand with an empty string
prs.body:
## Summary

`getSafeGitEnv()` (and the sandboxed shell defaults) set `core.sshCommand` to an empty string. Git executes that config value, so any operation that needs SSH fails before ssh is even attempted:

```
error: cannot run : No such file or directory
fatal: unable to fork
```

`GIT_SSH_COMMAND` was already set to a BatchMode ssh command, but the empty `core.sshCommand` config override takes precedence over it and breaks the operation.

## Reproduction

```console
$ git remote add origin ssh://localhost/nonexistent/repo.git
$ GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=core.sshCommand GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0= git fetch origin
error: cannot run : No such file or directory
fatal: unable to fork
```

Without the override the same command reaches ssh instead (`Host key verification failed.`).

## Fix

Pin `core.sshCommand` to a real, non-interactive command instead of an empty string:

- `getSafeGitEnv()` uses the command it already computed for `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, so the config override and the environment variable can no longer disagree, and BatchMode handling (including plink) is unchanged.
- The sandboxed shell defaults use the inherited `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, falling back to `ssh -o BatchMode=yes`.

Keeping the override (rather than dropping it) means a `core.sshCommand` in the user's gitconfig still cannot bypass the non-interactive setting.

`core.fsmonitor` and `core.hooksPath` are deliberately left empty: Git does not execute those values, and an empty `core.hooksPath` keeps repository hooks disabled. `core.editor`/`sequence.editor` are also unchanged, since they only matter for operations that would otherwise open an interactive editor.

## Tests

- New unit test: `core.sshCommand` always matches `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` and is never empty (default env, custom `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, plink).
- New integration test: `git fetch` against an SSH remote with the sanitized env must not report `cannot run` / `unable to fork`. Both new assertions fail before the fix.
- Updated the two existing assertions that pinned the empty override.
- `packages/core`: `gitUtils.test.ts` 18/18, `shellExecutionService.test.ts` 93/93, `tsc --noEmit`, eslint and prettier clean.

Fixes #30328

prs.body:
Fixes #30205

Title: ci(triage): apply only labels the repository defines, and only issue numbers from dedup

Summary

The issue triage automation takes the model's answer and writes it to the
issue. This change adds a check at each of the three write points so that
only expected values reach the GitHub API:

1. .github/workflows/gemini-automated-issue-triage.yml, Apply Labels step:
   the returned label must be one of the area/ labels the model was given
   (steps.get_labels.outputs.available_labels). Anything else fails the
   step with a clear message instead of being applied.
2. .github/scripts/apply-issue-labels.cjs (used by the scheduled triage):
   the repository's label list is fetched once; names not in it are
   dropped with a warning before addLabels. Entries whose issue_number is
   not a positive integer are skipped.
3. .github/workflows/gemini-automated-issue-dedup.yml: the comma-separated
   list is filtered to numeric items before the comment is built.

Why

Model output should be treated like any other untrusted input to a step
that holds an issues:write token. Today a label name that is not on the
allowed list, or a non-numeric item in the duplicate list, is passed
through as is. These checks make the automation behave the way the prompts
already describe.

No behaviour change for valid output. Three files, 74 lines.

prs.title: fix(cli): report hook-blocked prompts over ACP
prs.body:
## Summary

Over ACP, a prompt blocked by a hook came back as an empty `end_turn` with no `session/update`, so the client couldn't tell the prompt was denied or why. ACP now sends the reason as an `agent_message_chunk`, matching the `Agent execution blocked: ...` text that non-interactive mode and the TUI already show.

## Details

`GeminiClient` yields `AgentExecutionBlocked` with the hook's reason, but the event `switch` in `Session.prompt` (`packages/cli/src/acp/acpSession.ts`) had no case for it, so it fell through to `default` and was dropped. The new case uses `systemMessage` when present and falls back to `reason`, the same rule as `nonInteractiveCli.ts` and `useGeminiStream.ts`. The stop reason stays `end_turn`.

This also covers `AfterAgent` blocks, since they yield the same event.

`AgentExecutionStopped` is also unhandled in this switch. I left it out to keep this PR to what the issue asks, and I'm happy to follow up separately.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30114

## How to Validate

1. `npx vitest run src/acp/acpSession.test.ts` in `packages/cli`. The new test `should tell the client why a hook blocked the prompt` fails without the change and passes with it. `npm run preflight` passes for `packages/cli` on macOS. Two tests fail in `a2a-server` (`workspace_trust.test.ts`) and `core` (`shellExecutionService.test.ts`) on my machine, and they fail the same way on `main` without this change.
2. Manually: add a `BeforeAgent` hook that exits 2 with a reason on stderr (the repro in #30114), start `gemini --acp`, and send a prompt that triggers it. The client should get an `agent_message_chunk` reading `Agent execution blocked: denied by policy` before the turn ends.

prs.title: fix(core): quote IDE CLI path for cmd.exe in /ide install on Windows
prs.body:
## Summary

On Windows, `/ide install` fails with "Failed to install VS Code companion extension" whenever the editor CLI is in a folder whose name has a space. The "Do you want to connect VS Code to Gemini CLI?" prompt runs the same command, so it fails too. VS Code's default install folders always contain a space (`...\Microsoft VS Code\bin\code.cmd`), so IDE integration cannot be set up automatically on a standard Windows install. This PR quotes the CLI path for `cmd.exe` so the install command runs.

## Details

- **Root cause.** On Windows, the installers in `packages/core/src/ide/ide-installer.ts` run `code.cmd`, `positron.cmd` or `antigravity.cmd` with `spawnSync(commandPath, args, { shell: true })`. `shell: true` is required, because Node refuses to spawn a `.cmd` file directly (`EINVAL`, see #9995). But Node then does not quote the command. It joins the command and the arguments with spaces and runs `cmd.exe /d /s /c "<joined text>"`. `cmd.exe` cuts the path at the first space and reports `'...\Programs\Microsoft' is not recognized as an internal or external command`. The non-zero exit is caught and shown only as the generic failure message.
- **Fix.** A small `runCompanionInstall()` helper quotes the command path and arguments on Windows with the existing `quoteCmdArg()` from `utils/editor.ts`. That is the helper `openDiff` started using in #29753. On macOS and Linux nothing changes: no shell, no quoting. The three installers (VS Code and Firebase Studio, Positron, Antigravity) now call this helper instead of three identical `spawnSync` blocks.
- **No change for paths that already work.** `quoteCmdArg()` leaves paths without spaces or special characters as they are, so working installs (for example Scoop) behave exactly as before.
- **Left as is.** On Node 24, passing arguments together with `shell: true` still prints the `DEP0190` deprecation warning. That already happens today, and also in `openDiff`. Building the command line by hand to avoid it would be a separate change.
- **Tests.** The existing Windows tests expected the unquoted call, which is exactly the call that breaks in `cmd.exe`. They now expect a quoted path. New tests cover:
  - the per-user VS Code install path;
  - the default-location fallback used when `code` is not on `PATH`;
  - Positron on Windows;
  - a space-free path that must stay unquoted;
  - macOS passing a path with spaces unquoted, because it uses no shell.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30245

Earlier Windows reports of the same symptom (#12528, #15622, #17033) were closed without a root cause.

## How to Validate

1. Run the unit tests:

   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/ide/ide-installer.test.ts --coverage.enabled=false
   ```

   All tests pass.

2. Show that the new tests catch the bug. Put back the old source, run the tests again, then restore the fix:

   ```bash
   git checkout HEAD~1 -- packages/core/src/ide/ide-installer.ts
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/ide/ide-installer.test.ts --coverage.enabled=false
   git checkout HEAD -- packages/core/src/ide/ide-installer.ts
   ```

   With the old source, 5 tests fail: two VS Code paths with spaces, the default-location fallback, Positron and Antigravity. The space-free path and macOS tests pass on both versions.

   I ran steps 1 and 2 with Node 22 (the tests mock the Windows platform): with the fix all 25 installer tests pass; with the old source the 5 new Windows tests fail. Prettier, ESLint and `npm run typecheck` also pass.

3. Manual check on Windows, with VS Code in its default folder:
   1. Run `npm run build`.
   2. In VS Code's integrated terminal, inside the repository folder, run `npm start`.
   3. Run `/ide install`.

   Before this change: "Failed to install VS Code companion extension..." (reproduced with Gemini CLI 0.68.0 on Windows 11, see #30245). After: "VS Code companion extension was installed successfully.", and IDE integration connects.

4. Optional check of how the failure happens (Windows, plain Node): run the repro script in the linked issue. It shows `spawnSync(path, args, { shell: true })` on a `.cmd` inside a folder with a space exiting with status 1 ("...is not recognized..."), and the quoted path running.

prs.title: fix(core): keep the synthetic binary ack so injected audio/video stays in its own turn
prs.body:
## Summary

With Gemini 3 models, `read_file` on audio or video fails with 400 "Requests ending with a model turn are not supported" when using Code Assist (Login with Google). The binary injection from #26352 sends the media in its own user turn behind a synthetic model ack. Because that ack is a thought-only part, thought stripping drops it. The media then coalesces into the `functionResponse` turn, which is the shape the API rejects. This PR keeps the ack as a plain-text model turn when history is sent.

## Details

- In `stripThoughts` (both copies), `scrubHistory` and `scrubContents`, a synthetic binary ack turn becomes `model[text: "Binary content received. Proceeding with analysis."]` instead of being dropped. The `!isSyntheticBinaryAckTurn` exclusions are removed because those branches can no longer be reached for the ack.
- The recorded history keeps the thought ack, so nothing changes in the UI. Sessions recorded before this change are also fixed on resume, because the conversion happens when the request is built.
- The `historyHardening` test that expected the merged `[functionResponse, inlineData]` turn now expects the three-turn shape. A new `GeminiChat` test checks the request a modern model receives. Both new assertions fail on `main` and pass with this change.
- Images and PDFs are unaffected, since they stay nested in `functionResponse.parts`.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30229

## How to Validate

1. Unit tests:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/historyHardening.test.ts src/core/geminiChat.test.ts
   ```

prs.title: feat(acp): support session/close so clients can release a session
prs.body:
## Summary

ACP clients can now release a session with `session/close`. Today the method fails with `-32601 Method not found`, because `GeminiAgent` does not implement `unstable_closeSession`, the handler the SDK routes `session/close` to. As a result, every session holds its config, chat and MCP connections until the `--acp` process exits. This brings an explicit close in line with how the agent already releases sessions in `loadSession` and on shutdown.

## Details

- `AcpSessionManager.closeSession(sessionId)` removes the session from the map, then awaits `session.dispose()` and logs a failed disposal. This is the same order and error handling `loadSession` uses when it replaces an existing session. Because the id is forgotten first, a `session/load` of the same id that follows keeps the session it creates.
- An unknown id gets `-32602 Session not found`, like `cancel`, `prompt` and `setSessionMode`.
- `initialize` now advertises `sessionCapabilities: { close: {} }`, so clients can see the method is supported.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30231

## How to Validate

1. Unit tests:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/acp/acpSessionManager.test.ts src/acp/acpRpcDispatcher.test.ts
   ```
   The three new assertions fail on `main` and pass here: the advertised capability, routing through the session manager, and closing a session even when its disposal throws.
2. Over stdio against `gemini --acp`, send `initialize`, `session/new`, `session/close`, and then `session/prompt` on the closed id:

   | Build | `sessionCapabilities` | `session/close` | `session/prompt` on the closed id |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | main `e5d88fb2c` | `null` | `-32601 Method not found` | answers, so the session is still alive |
   | this PR | `{"close":{}}` | `{}` | `-32602 Session not found` |
3. Two sessions in one `gemini --acp` process (this PR, `-m gemini-3-flash-preview`), closing only the first:

   | Step | Result |
   | --- | --- |
   | `session/new` × 2 | two distinct ids |
   | prompt A "remember APPLE", prompt B "remember BANANA" | both `end_turn` |
   | `session/close` A | `{}` |
   | `session/prompt` A | `-32602 Session not found` |
   | `session/prompt` B "which word?" | `end_turn`, "BANANA", so B keeps its history |
   | `session/close` A again | `-32602 Session not found` |

prs.title: fix(core): avoid blocking PowerShell parsing during shell checks
prs.body:
## Summary

Avoid blocking the Node.js event loop while parsing PowerShell commands during shell policy checks, confirmation, and execution preparation on Windows.

Synchronous PowerShell startup and AST parsing can freeze the Thinking spinner and elapsed time before the Shell panel appears. This change moves those parsing operations to asynchronous process execution.

## Details

- Reuse complete parse results and in-flight promises within a single policy-check recursion or Shell invocation.
- Preserve the existing PowerShell AST parser, Bash fallback safeguards, and raw PowerShell redirection checks.
- Parse child commands independently instead of synthesizing results from parent AST nodes.
- Prepare command and stripped-wrapper forms before confirmation and execution helpers consume them.
- Await the internal taint-risk check in the scheduler.
- Introduce no process-wide cache or new parser timeout.

Standalone synchronous APIs remain supported. Existing sandbox-internal synchronous parsing and parser-process cancellation limitations are outside this change.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30249

## How to Validate

### Automated checks

From the repository root:

```powershell
npx vitest run --root packages/core src/utils/shell-utils.test.ts src/utils/untrustedContextTracker.test.ts src/policy/policy-engine.test.ts src/policy/policy-engine.powershell.test.ts src/policy/policy-updater.test.ts src/tools/shell.test.ts src/scheduler/scheduler.test.ts src/scheduler/policy.test.ts src/policy/shell-safety.test.ts src/policy/shell-substitution.test.ts src/config/config.test.ts --coverage.enabled=false --maxWorkers=2

npm run typecheck
npm run build
```

Results on Windows 10 Pro with Node 24.14.1:

- 769 related tests passed in an isolated checkout.
- 22 additional policy integration, AppRig, and modelSteering tests passed.
- 192 deterministic comparisons against the original policy engine produced identical policy results.
- Full ESLint, type checking, and build passed.

### Manual validation

Run npm start and ask Gemini to execute this exact command through run_shell_command:

Get-ChildItem | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name,Length,LastWriteTime

Verify that the spinner and elapsed time continue updating during the transition from Thinking to the Shell panel. Repeat within the same session and after restarting the CLI.

The scoped implementation was manually retested without observing the original freeze. This was not a controlled performance comparison on the originally affected machine.

### Validation limitations

The local full suite is not entirely green. Previously failing files were compared with unmodified base e5d88fb2c using separate checkouts and dependencies:

| Selected historical failures | Base passed / failed | This branch passed / failed |
|---|---:|---:|
| core | 389 / 36 | 387 / 38 |
| CLI | 86 / 18 | 86 / 18 |
| a2a-server | 3 / 1 | 3 / 1 |

Common failed assertions and primary errors match. The two additional core failures also reproduce on the base in a focused rerun. They are unchanged inode tests whose ino + 1 assumption fails when NTFS inode values exceed JavaScript's safe-integer range.

No new regression was identified in the compared tests. No security checks were relaxed or tests skipped.

Full preflight was attempted, but its YAML lint command stopped because the Windows shell could not find grep. The equivalent YAML check passed through Git Bash, and remaining static checks were completed separately. Overall preflight is not claimed passing; upstream CI and platform validation remain necessary.

prs.title: fix(core): keep a tier alias's config when the tier resolves to its first model
prs.body:
## Summary

A custom alias defined on a tier (`flash-lite`, `flash`, `pro`) now keeps its `generateContentConfig`. Previously, `applyModelSelection` re-resolved the config whenever the selected model's name differed from the resolved name. For a tier the selected name is always the concrete model, so every request used that model's stock settings: temperature 1, thinking HIGH, and no output cap. The alias's own settings were silently ignored, even though no fallback had happened.

## Details

- `applyModelSelection` now re-resolves only when the selected model differs both from the resolved name and from the head of that name's policy chain (`resolvePolicyChain(config, model)[0]`). That head is the model the tier resolves to, so it is the model the alias config was written for.
- A real availability fallback, where the pick is some other model in the chain, still takes that model's config exactly as before.
- Aliases on concrete models are unaffected, because for them the chain head is the model itself.

## Documented behavior

[Advanced Model Configuration](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/cli/generation-settings.md) (`docs/cli/generation-settings.md`) describes behavior that `main` does not follow for an alias on a tier:

- **Step 1: Alias Resolution.** The docs say the requested model string is looked up in the alias map, its `extends` chain is merged, and *"this results in a base `ResolvedModelConfig`."* On `main`, that config is thrown away whenever the selected model's name differs from the resolved name. A tier alias such as `flash-lite` always resolves to a different, concrete name, so the request is re-resolved under that name and gets that model's stock settings.
- **Overrides.** The docs say an override's `match.model` *"matches the requested model name or alias."* The re-resolution uses the concrete model name, so an override that matches the alias, or the tier name, does not apply either.
- **The docs' own example.** The `precise-mode` example (`extends` a chat alias with `temperature: 0.0`) depends on this too. If the model it ends up on is resolved or promoted to another name, `temperature: 0.0` is dropped the same way.

This PR makes the runtime match the documented resolution. The alias's resolved config is kept unless an availability fallback moves the request to a different model in the chain. Only that fallback, which the docs do not describe as a config change, takes the other model's config.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30238

## How to Validate

1. Unit tests:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/availability/
   ```
   The new test fails on `main`. It defines `my-lite` on `flash-lite` with `temperature: 0.2` and `maxOutputTokens: 256`, then checks that the selected concrete model keeps both. The existing fallback test still passes.
2. Add this to `settings.json`:
   ```json
   "modelConfigs": { "customAliases": { "my-lite": { "modelConfig": {
     "model": "flash-lite",
     "generateContentConfig": { "temperature": 0.2, "maxOutputTokens": 256 } } } } }
   ```
   Then run `gemini -m my-lite -p "Reply with the single word ok."` with a local proxy via `CODE_ASSIST_ENDPOINT` that records `generationConfig`:

   | Build | `model` | `generationConfig` |
   | --- | --- | --- |
   | main `e5d88fb2c` | `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` | `temperature: 1`, `thinkingLevel: HIGH`, no `maxOutputTokens` |
   | this PR | `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` | `temperature: 0.2`, `maxOutputTokens: 256` |

prs.title: fix(acp): truncate large tool outputs for the model like the CLI does
prs.body:
## Summary

ACP now bounds large tool outputs for the model the same way the CLI does. `Session.runTool` runs tools without the scheduler, so it never reached `ToolExecutor.truncateOutputIfNeeded` and sent a large shell or MCP output whole. One `seq 1 60000` call cost 369k input tokens over ACP, compared with 60k once the CLI's rule is applied. Outputs larger than the context window failed the turn.

## Details

- `ToolExecutor.truncateOutputIfNeeded` is now public. Its `call` parameter is narrowed to what the method reads: `request`, plus an optional `tool` for the MCP check. Scheduler call sites are unchanged.
- `Session.runTool` calls it on `toolResult.llmContent` before converting the result to a function response. Both the recorded history and the response sent to the model use the bounded content. ACP therefore gets the same threshold (`getTruncateToolOutputThreshold()`), the same saved file under the project temp `tool-outputs/` folder, the same head and tail text, and context-management distillation when that is enabled.
- The `tool_call_update` sent to the client still carries the full display content. Only what the model receives changes.
- The `acpSession` test config gains the fields the shared method reads. Without them, a tool call in those tests would quietly take the error path.

## Related Issues

1. Unit tests:

prs.title: fix(acp): run parallelizable tool calls together like the CLI scheduler
prs.body:
## Summary

ACP now runs the independent tool calls of a turn together, as the CLI's `Scheduler` does. The ACP prompt loop awaited each call before starting the next, so a turn with several searches, fetches or shell commands took as long as all of them added up. In one turn with four `sleep 3` shell calls, everything finished at 12.1 s on `main` and at 3.0 s with this change.

## Details

- The loop in `Session.prompt` batches each run of consecutive calls with `isParallelizable`, the predicate the `Scheduler` uses. Edits, `update_topic`, and calls marked `wait_for_previous` still run alone and in order.
- Each batch runs with `Promise.allSettled`, so every call that was started has settled before an error is thrown, just as the scheduler waits for the calls it started. `runTool` already turns tool errors into error responses.
- Responses are appended in the model's call order, so the next request is the same as before. Only the timing changes.
- Permission requests for calls in one batch can now reach the client together, as they do in the CLI.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30235

## How to Validate

1. Unit tests:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/acp/
   ```
   The new `acpSession` test fails on `main`. It sends two parallelizable calls and one `replace`, then checks three things: the first two start together, the edit starts only after both finish, and the responses keep call order.
2. Over stdio with `gemini --acp -m gemini-3.8-flash`, ask for four independent calls in one response, `sleep 3 && echo A` through `D`, approve each permission request, and time each `tool_call` from `in_progress` to `completed`:

Updates `esbuild` from 0.25.0 to 0.28.2
Release notes

Sourced from esbuild's releases.

v0.28.2

  • Fix tree shaking bug due to TypeScript import alias (#4507)

    This release fixes a bug that could cause esbuild to incorrectly tree-shake imports that are used in a TypeScript type alias under certain circumstances. Affected code uses a TypeScript-specific import assignment and looks something like this:

    import Base from './dep.js';
import Alias = Base.SomeType;

  • Fix CSS minification bug involving & (#4497)

    This release fixes a bug where esbuild's CSS minifier incorrectly removed a & when it was unsafe to do so. Here is an example:

    /* Original code */
.a .b {
  & .b:not(& .c) {
    color: red;
  }
}

    /* Old output (with --minify) */
    
.a .b{.b:not(& .c){color:red}}
    

    /* New output (with --minify) */
    
.a .b{& .b:not(& .c){color:red}}

    This should match <span class="a"><span class="b"><span class="b">yes</span></span></span> but not <span class="a"><span class="b">no</span></span>. The old output incorrectly matched both.

  • Avoid overwriting input files without --allow-overwrite (#4484)

    For example: esbuild input.js --outfile=input.js tells esbuild to overwrite input.js with the output of running esbuild on it. This was supposed to already be prevented by default, but it accidentally regressed in version 0.17.0 and apparently didn't have any test coverage. The error message was being printed but the input file was still being overwritten. Oops.

    This release puts the original behavior back. With this release, esbuild should now actually avoid overwriting input files unless --allow-overwrite is explicitly present. This is done by not writing out any files when a build error is encountered.

  • Fix incorrect code generated when using top-level await (#4498)

    Previously esbuild could generate code containing a syntax error in complex scenarios involving top-level await used in a dependency cycle. The problem was a missing async on one or more module wrapper closures. With this release, esbuild now uses a fixed-point iteration algorithm to correctly annotate all dependencies in the cycle as needing an async module wrapper.

  • Fix a minification bug with lowered logical assignment operators (#4508)

    This release fixes a bug that could cause esbuild to generate incorrect code for logical assignment operators when lowering them to an older target environment. Specifically the lowering process requires duplicating the left-hand side, but esbuild incorrectly failed to count the duplicate as a new usage when the left-hand side is an identifier. That then caused the minifier to believe that the left-hand side was only used once and could attempt to incorrectly inline an initializer into the first usage. This bug has now been fixed:

    // Original code
function foo() {
  let x
  bar(x ||= {})

Changelog

Sourced from esbuild's changelog.

Changelog: 2025

This changelog documents all esbuild versions published in the year 2025 (versions 0.25.0 through 0.27.2).

0.27.2

  • Allow import path specifiers starting with #/ (#4361)

    Previously the specification for package.json disallowed import path specifiers starting with #/, but this restriction has recently been relaxed and support for it is being added across the JavaScript ecosystem. One use case is using it for a wildcard pattern such as mapping #/* to ./src/* (previously you had to use another character such as #_* instead, which was more confusing). There is some more context in nodejs/node#49182.

    This change was contributed by @​hybrist.

  • Automatically add the -webkit-mask prefix (#4357, #4358)

    This release automatically adds the -webkit- vendor prefix for the mask CSS shorthand property:

    /* Original code */
main {
  mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat
}

    /* Old output (with --target=chrome110) */
    
main {
    
mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat;
    
}
    

    /* New output (with --target=chrome110) */
    
main {
    
-webkit-mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat;
    
mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat;
    
}

    This change was contributed by @​BPJEnnova.

  • Additional minification of switch statements (#4176, #4359)

    This release contains additional minification patterns for reducing switch statements. Here is an example:

    // Original code
switch (x) {
  case 0:
    foo()
    break
  case 1:
  default:
    bar()
}

Updates `express` from 5.1.0 to 5.3.0
Release notes

Sourced from express's releases.

v5.3.0

Highlights

🐞 Bug fixes

  • Fixed HTTP header conflict between Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding in res.send - by @​YuryShkoda in #4893

    Fixed the behavior of res.send() to prevent conflicts between Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding HTTP headers in responses. The Content-Length header in res.send() is now only added when a Transfer-Encoding header is not present, complying with the HTTP specification that states both headers should not coexist in the same response. ETag generation is unaffected by the presence of a Transfer-Encoding header - by @​cuishuang in #7459

  • Upgrade qs to ^6.16.0, which fixes CVE-2026-2391 (GHSA-w7fw-mjwx-w883), CVE-2026-82417 (GHSA-4mjr-xmp4-gh2g) and CVE-2026-82562 (GHSA-x5fp-wj9c-mxmx): arrayLimit bypasses in comma parsing and a denial of service via an attacker-controlled isBuffer - by @​davetashner in #7057 and #7478, and @​cyphercodes in #7305

  • Upgrade proxy-addr to ^2.0.8, which fixes CVE-2026-90711 - by @​lazerg in #7474

🚀 Improvements

  • Allow conditional revalidation for QUERY requests. req.fresh previously only validated freshness for GET and HEAD requests, so QUERY responses never returned 304 despite a matching validator. Since QUERY is a safe, idempotent, and cacheable method that supports conditional requests, it is now included in the freshness check - by @​Cherry in #7366

    // QUERY /reports with If-None-Match: "12345"
app.query('/reports', (req, res) => {
  res.set('ETag', '"12345"');
  res.send(results); // now responds 304 Not Modified
});

  • Improve HTML structure in res.redirect() responses when HTML format is accepted by adding <!DOCTYPE html>, <title>, and <body> tags for better browser compatibility - by @​Bernice55231 in #5167

  • When calling app.render with options set to null, the locals object is handled correctly, preventing unexpected errors and making the method behave the same as when options is omitted or an empty object is passed - by AkaHarshit in #6903

    app.render('index', null, callback); // now works as expected

  • Upgrade content-type to ^2.0.0, bringing a faster parser (~1.5x quicker Content-Type parsing/formatting in res.send()) along with a behavior change: res.send() now keeps any existing parameters when adding the charset and no longer throws on a Content-Type that fails to parse. type-is is upgraded to ^2.1.0 as part of the same change - by @​blakeembrey in #7234

    res.set('Content-Type', 'text/plain; foo=bar').send('hey');
// -> Content-Type: text/plain; foo=bar; charset=utf-8

  • The default error handler now logs the full error object instead of only its stack trace, so nested details such as Error.cause and library-specific properties (e.g. Sequelize's parent/original) are no longer swallowed - by @​Nitin-Mohapatra in #6464

  • Upgrade content-disposition to ^2.0.1, which changes the Content-Disposition header emitted by res.download(), res.attachment(), and res.sendFile(): file names that are valid HTTP tokens are no longer wrapped in quotes. This is equivalent per RFC 6266, but applications asserting on the exact header bytes should update their expectations - by @​blakeembrey in #7233

    res.attachment('user.html');
// before -> Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="user.html"
// after  -> Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=user.html

Updates `esbuild` from 0.25.0 to 0.28.2
Release notes

Sourced from esbuild's releases.

v0.28.2

  • Fix tree shaking bug due to TypeScript import alias (#4507)

    This release fixes a bug that could cause esbuild to incorrectly tree-shake imports that are used in a TypeScript type alias under certain circumstances. Affected code uses a TypeScript-specific import assignment and looks something like this:

    import Base from './dep.js';
import Alias = Base.SomeType;

  • Fix CSS minification bug involving & (#4497)

    This release fixes a bug where esbuild's CSS minifier incorrectly removed a & when it was unsafe to do so. Here is an example:

    /* Original code */
.a .b {
  & .b:not(& .c) {
    color: red;
  }
}

    /* Old output (with --minify) */
    
.a .b{.b:not(& .c){color:red}}
    

    /* New output (with --minify) */
    
.a .b{& .b:not(& .c){color:red}}

    This should match <span class="a"><span class="b"><span class="b">yes</span></span></span> but not <span class="a"><span class="b">no</span></span>. The old output incorrectly matched both.

  • Avoid overwriting input files without --allow-overwrite (#4484)

    For example: esbuild input.js --outfile=input.js tells esbuild to overwrite input.js with the output of running esbuild on it. This was supposed to already be prevented by default, but it accidentally regressed in version 0.17.0 and apparently didn't have any test coverage. The error message was being printed but the input file was still being overwritten. Oops.

    This release puts the original behavior back. With this release, esbuild should now actually avoid overwriting input files unless --allow-overwrite is explicitly present. This is done by not writing out any files when a build error is encountered.

  • Fix incorrect code generated when using top-level await (#4498)

    Previously esbuild could generate code containing a syntax error in complex scenarios involving top-level await used in a dependency cycle. The problem was a missing async on one or more module wrapper closures. With this release, esbuild now uses a fixed-point iteration algorithm to correctly annotate all dependencies in the cycle as needing an async module wrapper.

  • Fix a minification bug with lowered logical assignment operators (#4508)

    This release fixes a bug that could cause esbuild to generate incorrect code for logical assignment operators when lowering them to an older target environment. Specifically the lowering process requires duplicating the left-hand side, but esbuild incorrectly failed to count the duplicate as a new usage when the left-hand side is an identifier. That then caused the minifier to believe that the left-hand side was only used once and could attempt to incorrectly inline an initializer into the first usage. This bug has now been fixed:

    // Original code
function foo() {
  let x
  bar(x ||= {})

... (truncated)

Changelog

Sourced from esbuild's changelog.

Changelog: 2025

This changelog documents all esbuild versions published in the year 2025 (versions 0.25.0 through 0.27.2).

0.27.2

  • Allow import path specifiers starting with #/ (#4361)

    Previously the specification for package.json disallowed import path specifiers starting with #/, but this restriction has recently been relaxed and support for it is being added across the JavaScript ecosystem. One use case is using it for a wildcard pattern such as mapping #/* to ./src/* (previously you had to use another character such as #_* instead, which was more confusing). There is some more context in nodejs/node#49182.

    This change was contributed by @​hybrist.

  • Automatically add the -webkit-mask prefix (#4357, #4358)

    This release automatically adds the -webkit- vendor prefix for the mask CSS shorthand property:

    /* Original code */
main {
  mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat
}

    /* Old output (with --target=chrome110) */
    
main {
    
mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat;
    
}
    

    /* New output (with --target=chrome110) */
    
main {
    
-webkit-mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat;
    
mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat;
    
}

    This change was contributed by @​BPJEnnova.

  • Additional minification of switch statements (#4176, #4359)

    This release contains additional minification patterns for reducing switch statements. Here is an example:

    // Original code
switch (x) {
  case 0:
    foo()
    break
  case 1:
  default:
    bar()
}
