prs.title: fix: finish a half-switched Git update instead of reporting it current
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On a Git checkout install that runs from releases, an update can fail after it switched the release link but before any Gateway started the new release. The next `openclaw update` then treated that never-started release as the one serving. If the target was that same release it reported "already current" and the Gateway stayed on the old build. If the target was newer, it recorded the never-started release as the new trial's fallback, so a candidate that failed to start fell back to a build that had never run. Each attempt also left another full build on disk.

## User Impact

User impact: the next plain `openclaw update` repairs a half-switched Git install. If the target is the release already placed, the update finishes its activation without rebuilding. If the target is newer, the fallback stays the release that last served and the superseded release is removed. Nothing manual is needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Root cause: `updateGitRelease` (`src/infra/update-runner-git-release.ts`) used the release link as the running release (`running = slot`), and `publishGitRelease` recorded whatever the link named as the trial's `previous`. The link records what the next start should load, not what serves. After an update fails between the switch and the restart, the link names a release whose trial is still armed with `attempts: 0`. The trial record's `previous` is the release that served.

Competing hypothesis: the false `already-current` came from the tree comparison or from `beforeRuntimeVerified`. Falsifier: with the same leftover and the same tree comparison, reading the serving release from the trial record turns the RED case green, and no change to the comparison is needed. The new runner tests fail on the base for exactly this reason (`expected 'skipped' to be 'ok'`, trial `previous` = the never-served release).

Why the link was used: #199706 uses it so the serving release is found even when the CLI runs from the preserved checkout. That still holds. The link's release is used whenever there is no trial or the trial has passed, and also when a process holds a lease on it (it may be serving).

The fix has one owner: `readGitReleasePlacement` in `src/infra/git-release.ts` reads the trial record and the leases and returns:
- `serving`: what serves;
- `fallback`: the release that last passed a trial;
- `unserved`: the placed release, if any.

It uses only the existing trial fields and lease files. The runner then:
- **Builds on the serving release.** `before`, the already-current check and failure recovery use `serving`, not the link.
- **Target is the placed release:** the match is checked in `beforeCandidate`, which every candidate reaches after local-commit replay and before install or build. The target is admitted through the caller's normal inspection hook first, which is also where the CLI observes the service it will restart. The runner then reuses the placed release and keeps its armed trial. The normal restart, verification and trial settlement follow.
- **Target is newer:** `supersedeUnservedGitRelease` puts the link back on the fallback, which also clears the stale trial. The new release then goes on trial with the fallback as `previous`. The placed release is removed only when a reread just before the switch shows the launcher never counted a start, and no lease is held at removal. A release that may have served is left to the normal 24 h collection.
- **Serving release is the target:** the link goes back to it, the placed release is discarded, and the result is `already-current`.
- **Collection keeps the fallback,** even when the link left it more than 24 h ago. Before this, a fallback older than 24 h could be collected while it was still the trial's `previous`.
- **Result note:** a `git-release-placement` note names both releases and says what the update did.

There is no new config key, stored field, schema or protocol, and no retention rule change. The only removal is of the placed release this same path created, never started, and now supersedes.

Update behavior: this runs in the installed updater, which for a Git checkout is the checkout's own build. An updater built before this change keeps the old behavior until the checkout runs a build with it.

**A safe fallback.** A back-out must always land on a working Gateway. The fallback must therefore be a build of the commit that serves right now, present and intact: its `build-info`, build and runtime stamps, entry and Control UI must verify against the commit its worktree has checked out.
- **Normal case:** the trial's `previous` is that build. In a conversion leftover, the Gateway still runs the plain checkout through the old service definition, and `previous` is the first release built from the commit the checkout's `dist` serves.
- **What serves in the leftover:** nothing has started the placed release (the launcher counted no start and no process holds its lease). So the Gateway serves either `previous` (a launcher-backed install) or the checkout at `previous`'s commit (conversion). Either way, `previous`'s commit is the serving commit.
- **`previous` present but incomplete:** the update rebuilds that commit as a new release, as the conversion does for its first release. It verifies the rebuilt release and makes it the fallback before anything else switches; the placed release is then superseded as usual.
- **`previous` gone:** the runner has no record of the serving commit. The checkout's `dist` is not proof that the service runs it. So the update switches nothing and ends as a retryable failure, `git-release-fallback-unavailable`, with `serviceRestartSafe: false`. The message says the Gateway keeps serving, not to restart it into the release link, and to run `openclaw triage` so an agent can rebuild a fallback from the serving commit.
- **Why the gone case can still happen:** with this change, collection keeps the fallback, so a fixed updater never removes it. It can still be gone if an older updater's 24 h collection removed it.
- **Never a fallback:** a release that has never run is never recorded as the fallback, unless a process is running from it right now, in which case it is what serves.

This fix is also what lets an install leave the state that shipped `8f80fe08` updaters create after #201327. They fail in their own process with a false "Agent database migration did not finish" and leave this same half-switched leftover. The next update from an updater with this change finishes or supersedes it.

## Evidence

**Owner tests (real Git worktrees, the real `publishGitRelease`, and the real launcher process for the back-out):** `src/infra/update-runner-git-release.test.ts` has 8 new cases. All 8 fail with the base production files and pass at the head; the 4 existing cases pass on both.
- the placed target is activated without a build, and the target is still admitted through the caller's inspection hook;
- a newer target falls back to the serving release, the never-served release is removed, and after two failed candidate starts the launcher serves 1.0.0 again;
- a release the launcher started, or one leased by a running process, is kept and never becomes the fallback (the leased one is reported as serving);
- a `--no-restart` leftover is discarded when superseded;
- a serving target puts the link back;
- an incomplete fallback is rebuilt from the serving commit and becomes `previous`;
- a missing fallback changes nothing and refuses with the triage route.

**End to end, through the real `openclaw update`** on isolated macOS launchd Git release-mode installs. Each install has its own profile, state directory and port, and a synthetic config with no channels, providers or credentials. Upstream is a local bare repository with three target commits:
- `t1` and `t2` change only a docs file;
- `t2bad` makes `startGatewayServerCore` throw at start, standing in for the observed out-of-disk boot refusal.

The installed updater is the checkout's own build: base `3eee09d9b462` for RED, the PR head `6917f1fb32f5` for GREEN.

The leftover is made by a real first update to `t1`, killed the moment `releases/.trial` appears. The result is the incident's shape:
- the link names the `t1` release, which never served;
- `.trial` is armed (`attempts: 0`) with the first release as `previous`;
- the service still runs the checkout through its old definition.

Each cell restores that leftover from an APFS clone, then runs one plain `openclaw update --channel dev --yes`. Downtime is the Gateway port polled every 0.5 s.

| Cell | Code | Result | Time | Downtime | Releases on disk after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **RED (a)** target = placed `t1` | base | `skipped: already-current`, exit 0 after a full duplicate build. The Gateway still serves the checkout build; the link and `.trial` are unchanged. The update was silently dropped. | 214 s | 0 s | 2 (8.4 GB) |
| **RED (b)** target `t2` | base | Reports "updated … (from 7138ac46)", the never-served build. The unit tests show the trial's `previous` was that build. The never-served release is kept. | 266 s | 21.7 s | 3 (13 GB) |
| **GREEN (a)** target = placed `t1` | head | Note: "…has not passed its trial… finishes activating it instead of rebuilding it". No candidate build (validating 20 s vs about 170 s). The unit is rewritten to the launcher, the Gateway serves the `t1` build (`3b380a69`), the trial is settled. Exit 0. | 133 s | 17.5 s | 2 (8.4 GB) |
| **GREEN (b)** target `t2` | head | Note: "…It never started, so this update removed it." Result "from 6917f1fb", the serving build. The Gateway serves `t2`, the trial is settled, exit 0. | 247 s | 13.8 s | 2 (8.4 GB) |
| **GREEN (c)** target `t2bad` (fails both starts) | head | The never-served `t1` was removed, and `t2bad` went on trial with the serving release as `previous`. It failed twice, and the launcher switched back. Afterwards the Gateway serves the fallback release's build of `6917f1fb` (a working Gateway), the link names it, and no trial is left. Exit 1 `build-id-mismatch`, with "Your Gateway is still serving 2026.11.5; nothing to restore". | 261 s | 35.7 s | 2 (8.4 GB) |
| **GREEN (d)** fallback release made incomplete (its `dist/.runtime-postbuildstamp` removed), target `t2bad` | head | Note: "…its fallback … does not verify as a complete build. This update rebuilt the commit it was built from (6917f1fb32f5) as release …". The update first rebuilt and verified the serving commit as a new release, put the link on it, and removed the never-served `t1`. Then `t2bad` went on trial with the rebuilt release as `previous`. It failed twice, and the launcher switched back. Afterwards the Gateway serves the rebuilt release's build of `6917f1fb` (a working Gateway), the link names it, and no trial is left. Exit 1 `build-id-mismatch`. The incomplete release is kept because it served. | 475 s | 33.3 s | 3 (13 GB) |

The RED cells show both failure modes on base. In (a) the update reports current while the Gateway stays on the old build. In (b) a never-served build becomes the fallback, and builds pile up: three full builds and 13 GB after one retry. The GREEN cells show each is fixed through the shipped entry point.

GREEN (a) also exposed a real defect in an earlier revision of this PR, fixed here. Reusing the placed release skipped the caller's target inspection hook, so the CLI never observed the service and printed "Gateway service management skipped". The reused path now runs that hook first (regression assertion in the owner test).

None of the cells hit the known false `post-update-failed` from the schema-bump state-database handoff; the targets carry no schema bump.

Recordings (raw terminal captures, sanitized, 3x speed with idle time capped at 1 s). Full raw logs are not attached because the Crabbox artifact store rejected the upload from this machine (`http 401`).

Owner tests, RED (base production files) then GREEN (head):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/29948943-6325-4365-8c72-0772adc6cccb

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/59384d9c-9a2b-44f9-88c1-f02cf4740fe6

End to end, RED (a), RED (b), GREEN (a), GREEN (b), GREEN (c), GREEN (d):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ae36aedc-d58f-4652-8d94-1713cdcdad21

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5ddc9a54-2aac-40d8-8142-6ee9900d3e09

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fc24c354-cdc3-4575-a35e-66f92617f302

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/070c531c-02b1-48f9-a0e2-a88205c70174

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/462ce9f7-58d4-4525-ba19-a06c0fb522cc

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7d888ab4-929b-4e32-8489-b3fa5a4ebd79

<details><summary>Checks</summary>

- `OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/update-runner-git-release.test.ts src/infra/git-release.test.ts src/cli/update-cli/update-command-verification.test.ts src/infra/package-release-retention.test.ts`: pass (the launcher cases skip under Bun, so they were run under Node)
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`: pass
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on the touched files: pass
- `pnpm check:baseline-ratchets --base 2183caf789cb --no-merge-base` (the merge base): all ok, net test lines +279
- `pnpm check:docs`: pass
- PR CI on `6917f1fb32f5`: green. The `PostgreSQL conformance (1/4)` failure on the first head was `server-database-engine-cron.postgres.test.ts` failing with ECONNREFUSED on a Gateway port. That code is untouched here, and the same shard passed on the next two heads with no change in that area.
- `git diff --check`: clean
</details>

Test file audited in full: `src/infra/update-runner-git-release.test.ts`.
- The target-selection mock now builds the selected revision, calls `beforeCandidate` before building as the real preflight does, and registers the real preflight's cleanup.
- The recovery mock compares real paths, because the running root is now the release path, not the link path.
- Nothing was removed.

Independent review: a fresh read-only reviewer (Opus) checked the diff against the behavior contract. Fixed:
- a failed switch back to the fallback no longer continues (it fails the update);
- the "never started" check is reread right before the switch;
- the placed release is reused before the build, not after it;
- a leased link release counts as serving;
- lease reads use the resolved prefix;
- `--no-restart` and missing-fallback messages are accurate;
- the reuse decision rereads the link;
- one release-ID helper;
- tests: keep-list ageing in the reuse case, no-build and message assertions, the pending case, and a launcher timeout.

`autoreview` does not run on this machine.

## Not proven

- A fallback that is gone is handed to an agent (`openclaw triage`) and is not repaired automatically. The runner has no record of the serving commit. Reading it from the serving Gateway's build ID is a possible follow-up.

- A start that begins in the instant between the reread and the link switch could still see its release removed. The launcher counts the start before loading the release, and the lease is rechecked at removal, so the window is a few milliseconds.
- When the target carries local commits, the placed-release match runs after replay, so the replay itself is repeated (no install or build).
- Platforms: macOS launchd only.

All end-to-end cells ran at head `6917f1fb32f5`. Nothing was pushed after them.

prs.title: fix: let Git installs update across a database schema change
prs.body:
Related: #199706

## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw update` on a Git checkout install that runs a Gateway service fails whenever the new version changes a database schema. The update builds and selects the new release, then stops with `Agent database migration did not finish: … expected schema 43, found 42`, and the Gateway keeps serving the old build. Every later update fails the same way, so the install is stuck on its current build.

## User Impact

User impact: a dev-channel Git install can update across a schema change again. The Gateway restarts into the new release and upgrades its state when it starts, as the release layout intends.

No config or migration action is needed for installs that pick this up.

Installs already on a build that has this failure run the old updater, so they cannot receive this fix through `openclaw update`. Recovering those installs is not covered here.

## Why This Change Was Made

A Git release update never stops the Gateway and never runs Doctor: the Gateway that boots from the new release upgrades state. The post-activation state check still required the candidate schema to be applied before the restart. That can only hold for the in-place and package paths, which migrate during the update. The check now leaves a Git release's state alone.

#200578 moves every Git install onto releases and does not change this check, so the same failure would reach those installs too.

## Evidence

Observed on a Linux dev-channel Git install with a systemd user Gateway service, updating across agent schema 42 → 43:

- Fetch, build, release placement and the release smoke check all passed.
- The run then recorded an `openclaw doctor` step with `durationMs: 0`, exit 1 and the "migration did not finish" message for each agent database, and finished `failed` with reason `openclaw doctor`.
- `gateway recovery verification` reported a build mismatch: the old Gateway process had never stopped.

Added a regression test at the state-inspection seam with real SQLite fixtures: a Git release whose candidate schema is ahead of the stored state is no longer reported as a failed migration, and the database bytes are unchanged.

Gaps:

- The test and type check were not run locally (the worktree has no installed dependencies); CI is the proof for both.
- No end-to-end release update across a schema change was run with this change. Behaviour after the restart (start-time upgrade of large state inside the verification window) is not proven here.

Autoreview on the diff: no findings at P2 or above.

Size: production +6 −2, tests +23.

prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Session recall can return a transcript match after a conversation becomes private or the reader's membership is removed while the search is running. The other session-search routes already check current disclosure facts when publishing their responses.

## User Impact

Recall no longer publishes hits or page metadata from an invalidated sharing snapshot. This does not change the authority lifetime of already-admitted agent or automation work.

## Why This Change Was Made

Publish the complete recall response inside the existing prepared-row callback. Reuse the same visibility decision for worker filtering and final publication, and use the projection's existing sharing revision to discard stale pages and their counts together before one retry. Both Gateway and embedded callers now use that publication boundary.

No new permission policy, manager, cache, schema, or configuration is introduced. A scope that changes again during the retry asks the caller to retry instead of returning stale or partial metadata.

Main was integrated at `949e51dff17c0e1c4cc37f82af8ac5942c0f67e1` to resolve the conflict with merged #201490. Its candidate-batch preparation is preserved inside the shared authorization owner: one preparation per worker batch and one fresh final disclosure snapshot, not per matching key.

## Evidence

The real authenticated WSS Gateway regression fails on the original production code by returning the private transcript snippet after membership removal. It passes with this change and also verifies that the next request remains denied. Authentication, RPC dispatch, transcript search, and sharing writes are real; only the completed worker-read timing is controlled. No model/provider call is needed for this read-only endpoint.

- After conflict resolution, all 75 focused search-scope, inventory-privacy, and embedded-caller/history tests pass, including upstream batch/singleton equivalence across physical owners and both sharing-revocation metadata regressions. The four-file run took 127.21 seconds including compilation.
- The actual WSS membership-revocation test passes again in the documented network-isolated Linux runner (54.04 seconds including transformation). Its complete isolated runtime build also passed (154.1 seconds). The host's automatic runtime-preparation separation check was refused; the supported isolated route was used without bypassing that guard.
- Core, Gateway-method test, agent-tool test, and root E2E TypeScript checks pass; scoped type-aware production lint, test lint, formatting, and diff checks pass.
- Independent Codex autoreview through P2 is `scoped-clean` on the complete integrated candidate against main `949e51dff17c0e1c4cc37f82af8ac5942c0f67e1`, committed unchanged as `3b67c579f6f38f88dfd760b8b5cdb651bc6d410a`. No findings. The reviewer assessed supplied source/evidence; test execution was performed separately. Updated exact-head CI and landing gates remain pending.

- Benchmark caller follow-up for [CI run 44427434900, job 135237801255](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44427434900/job/135237801255): reproduced TS2741 and the actual benchmark's missing-callback runtime failure. The script now supplies the required publication callback and preserves its existing historical `--owner-ref` comparison mode; no production safeguard was made optional. The full scripts typecheck, 15 focused owner tests, type-aware lint and formatting pass. Both current and historical owner ABIs complete five-sample, ten-iteration allocation measurements with independent result assertions; this verifies the measurement path, not a performance-improvement claim. Independent Codex P0–P2 review of this follow-up is `scoped-clean`, committed unchanged as `44db084d25dfc2a12f83fb9ab6db4da224114360`. Updated exact-head CI remains required.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction, prior proof, and scope</summary>

Both native sharing-revocation regressions are red before the repair and green afterward, including stale count/truncation metadata. Initial validation also passed all 60 focused search and embedded-caller/history tests. Independent Codex autoreview through P2 was `scoped-clean` for the initial candidate against base `71ee55620d0786d4078dfa41c3527488c4a7cad4`, committed unchanged as `387f53bfef6f4574da21e36682060be8db95e3b5`. Local ClawSweeper was unavailable; hosted review when ready remains with the owning workflow.

CI follow-up: [run 44416183120, job 135197897380](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44416183120/job/135197897380) exposed an obsolete `sessions-list-privacy` rejection expectation. The identical failure reproduces on the original base production code and published head. #201334 intentionally retains named-role policy for an admitted request; the corrected test proves that request completes and a fresh request excludes the newly forbidden row and transcript. No production authority behavior changed in this follow-up. Its 28 focused cases and static checks passed, with independent Codex P2 review `scoped-clean` for the delta from `7b1190514ffad1fae3d8d7f790ad25fbfcea42d4`, committed as `d9c6e7fafa396cba683eaecf63299f12dcfccd73`; that repair remains in ancestry unchanged.

`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-search-scope.test.ts src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.test.ts src/agents/tools/embedded-gateway-stub.history.test.ts src/agents/tools/sessions-list-privacy.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`

The WSS proof uses the same E2E file via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs --isolated-image <verified-local-image-sha256> run --config test/vitest/vitest.e2e.config.ts test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/session-recall-publication.e2e.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`. The runner verified its image/runtime/browser prerequisites, disabled networking, and confirmed container cleanup.

Against integrated main, runtime production grows by 58 net lines, the benchmark caller adds 8 net lines, and tests grow by 175. Most of the visible owner diff moves unchanged authorization logic so both boundaries reuse it. The conflict adjustment adds no manager, fixture, schema, or production policy and preserves upstream batching.

A separate baseline audit observed two existing `operator-run-cancellation.test.ts` assertions expecting immediate device revocation after receiver admission, contrary to the intentional #201377 lifetime policy. This PR does not change that owner or restore continuous revocation; no broad CI-green claim is made.

prs.title: ci: test stable client sources against candidate Gateway
prs.body:
Related: #200555

## What Problem This Solves

Existing mobile release E2E builds candidate clients against a published Gateway. This adds the reverse direction: **stable-release-source rebuild compatibility** against the candidate Gateway. It does not claim the current public mobile store build or exact store-distributed binary.

## Implementation

- Resolve the latest published stable repository release once, pin its tag and commit for both platforms, and restore that selection on reruns.
- Build native clients only from the separate stable-source checkout. Keep qualification harness/fixtures at qualification commit Q and the isolated Gateway checkout/build at candidate commit C; C and Q may differ. Verify and record all three identities.
- Reuse the existing iOS/Android E2E and Gateway preparation owners. Ordinary mobile-release qualification retains its existing direction.
- Add an independent `stable-release-source-compatibility.yml` child and integrate it through existing Full Release Validation dispatch, immutable plan, receipt, coverage, reuse, summary, and terminal-policy owners. Require the verifier and both native jobs to succeed; missing, failed, skipped, or cancelled evidence cannot pass. Historical plans retain their original child inventory.
- Preserve pairing/chat/relaunch assertions. Separate synthetic utility traffic from primary iOS chat requests rather than weakening the strict request count. Android Wear uses the existing controlled transport boundary, not real phone-to-watch delivery.
- Revalidate the frozen stable release tag/SHA against the canonical published release before dependency execution. Check out the verified SHA and check the actual client HEAD before building. Prepare the Gateway toolchain from Q before checking out C or the stable client; preserve C/Q independence.

## Native Runtime Evidence — November 18, 2026

Both runs succeeded with identical independent identities:

- Stable client: `v2026.11.5` / `e13cf15ece9bbd969b7362927c315362c90c97ff`
- Candidate Gateway C: `d0e329fe21686a79c84e104c49c0efa5a02a285a`
- Qualification harness/workflow Q: `db6905d3eb8e20994009f57a64e3d1de0cf9a453`

**iOS:** https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44302633973

- Both native UI tests passed: pairing/chat/relaunch and keyboard/transcript-follow behavior.
- Exactly three primary provider requests; all expected first, second, and relaunch messages received; cleanup confirmed.
- Downloaded proof records `status: passed`, `complete: true`, exact C/Q/client identities, and candidate-source Gateway.
- Artifact `ios-release-e2e-stock-44302633973-1`, ID `14427218623`, SHA-256 `9b6e468f3f370b40ab76c59df507b6730fd2adcd820161e056d78fa8618ebf8e`.

**Android:** https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44302638044

- Phone/Wear initial chat, relaunch, phone-restart recovery, long reply, and reader phases passed.
- All eight expected provider markers occurred exactly once; cleanup confirmed; stable client checkout clean.
- Downloaded proof records `status: passed` and exact C/Q/client identities. Instrumented debug APKs are explicitly identified as source rebuilds.
- Artifact `android-release-e2e-44302638044-1`, ID `14429305012`, SHA-256 `f463439353faac2c1d09639c285a145e65cd22e8f7aceecd5eee83147469ca13`.

These runs prove native compatibility at the listed C and exercise the distinct-C/Q harness path. They do not qualify every Gateway change at Q as C, and they predate the latest CI/security repair; they are not exact-head native proof for that repair.

## Earlier Validation

- Native boundary suites: **179 tests passed**; selector/workflow suites: **16 passed**.
- FRV owner suites: **365 passed**, with **12** focused role-policy regressions. Missing-verifier reproduction accepted by baseline policy and rejected by the fixed policy.
- Earlier required macOS/workflow siblings: **1,430 tests passed** across eight files.
- Runtime build, affected scripts/test/tooling typechecks, targeted lint/format, and workflow actionlint/security/repository guards passed. Empty token environment variables were unset for the workflow security check.
- Docs listing, two-page MDX validation, internal-link audit (16,753 links, zero broken), and diff checks passed. Earlier dependency setup gaps were resolved.
- Fresh independent review found and prompted repair of the C=Q restriction; that review reported no blocking findings and independently passed 105 tests.

## CI Repairs and Latest Focused Validation

- Repair PR-caused fixture failures: isolate inherited `GITHUB_SHA` in the selector test, update FRV child/page inventories, and preserve real Android module exports in partial mocks. Consolidate duplicate tests without dropping admission and evidence boundaries.
- Repair stable-client provenance before execution: verify the frozen named published release and immutable SHA, fail closed on malformed/missing/moved pins, use the verified checkout output, and assert actual checkout HEAD. Prepare shared toolchain actions against Q before independent source checkouts. No job-level `cache-mode`, validator bypass, or CodeQL suppression was added.
- **25 selector/workflow tests passed** across two files, including eight real CLI subprocess cases. The final workflow assertion pass separately passed **8 workflow tests**. The named-release and moved-tag regressions failed on the previous baseline before the fix.
- Targeted typecheck, lint, format, workflow actionlint/security/repository guards, docs listing, and diff checks passed. A live canonical-release CLI check accepted the correct frozen tag/SHA and rejected a mismatched SHA.
- The test-line ratchet passes with **1,068 net added test lines**, the normal 400-line allowance, and the exact **668-line per-change allocation** in `config/test-lines-allocations/201151-stable-client-compatibility.txt`; the shared allowance is unchanged.
- Fresh independent review found no blocking defect in the latest repair. Its suggested CLI coverage and checked-out HEAD ordering assertions were added and passed afterward.
- The latest broad macOS/workflow sibling batch hit the **300-second timeout** and ended with SIGTERM / compiled-subprocess exit 143. The iOS file completed with 124 tests passing, but the broad batch is **not a passing gate**. Earlier broad results above are prior-head evidence only.

## Remaining Security and Hosted Admission / Scope

Keep this PR **draft**. The latest repair does **not** establish that all CodeQL findings are resolved: candidate C still supplies install/build code executed on the same runner and can affect later Q tooling, workspace/environment, and cache capabilities. Stable-client provenance and Q-first setup do not sandbox candidate execution. This is an explicit unresolved candidate-code execution / CodeQL risk, not an inherited-only or scanner-only claim. Candidate admission that preserves C/Q independence, or genuine execution isolation, requires a separate disposition. No new exact-head CodeQL result is claimed here.

Native proof is complete only for the identities above; the new combined child/FRV hosted dispatch-and-receipt path remains **unexecuted**. GitHub returned HTTP 404 because `stable-release-source-compatibility.yml` is not registered on the default branch. Existing registered native workflows were used for the successful native runs. No default-branch mutation or merge was performed.

A repository release is not evidence of the currently public App Store/Play build. Store-to-source mapping, exact Play-signed installable APK/splits, physical-iOS external automation, real Wear Data Layer delivery, and desktop coverage remain outside this claim. Store credentials and physical devices are not prerequisites for the implemented source-rebuild lane.

prs.title: fix(agents): keep silent replies in replay so the session prefix stays append-only
prs.body:
## Problem

A silent reply (`NO_REPLY`) was dropped from model replay by row-local normalization (`normalizeAssistantReplayMessage` in `replay-history-sanitization.ts`). The next user turn then sat directly after the silent turn's user message. On routes that merge consecutive user turns at the stream boundary (`mergeConsecutiveUserMessages` in `attempt-tool-call-replay-sanitization.ts`), the next request merged the new user turn into the already-sent one. The sent prefix changed, so the prompt cache broke.

- Bedrock Converse merges every adjacent user pair (`preserveContextBoundaries: false`), so every turn after a silent reply breaks the cache there.
- Chat Completions (the unowned fallback policy) merges adjacent plain user turns. Gateway turns that carry a runtime-context block are kept apart, so this route breaks only for user turns without that block.
- OpenAI Responses and direct Anthropic Messages do not merge. They are not affected.

Found by the randomized prefix suite: bedrock seed 1 breaks at step 22 (`silent` then `user`, after a `modelSwitch`). Message 38 is the silent turn's user message, and it is rewritten. The model switch is not part of the cause. It only happens to come first in that journey.

## Fix

This ports 0191111b26aa onto the current replay sequence. The replay code was split into row-local and sequence steps after that commit.

- Row-local normalization no longer drops silent replies.
- `normalizeReplaySequence` drops a visible silent reply only when the next non-custom row is an assistant turn. That turn never merges into it, which keeps #99620 intact. A silent reply before a user turn, or as the newest row, stays. Replay is append-only again.
- The payload-free compaction replay uses the same rule through a `silentReply` source fact. The array path and the fact path give the same result, as the existing mixed-history parity test shows.

Accepted edge case: a silent reply that is the newest row stays in replay. If the next stored row is an assistant turn with no user turn between them, the silent reply is then dropped. This changes the prefix once. It is rare, visible and recoverable.

This PR supersedes the silent-reply part of draft #198201. That draft also carries a worker-pin fix, which this PR does not touch.

## Evidence

**Red on base, green on head.** The new test `attempt-tool-call-replay-sanitization.test.ts` › "keeps the %s request append-only after a silent reply" runs `normalizeMessagesForLlmBoundary` and then the stream wrapper for two consecutive requests.
- On merge base 428d2047b766, it fails for both `bedrock-converse-stream` and `openai-completions`: the second request has `[quiet, next]` merged into message 2.
- On this head, it passes for both.

**Randomized prefix suite, bedrock seed 1.** This is the harness from the prompt-cache branch, run locally and not committed. It uses a real Gateway and a fake Bedrock transport.
- Base 428d2047b766: one break, `{"step":22,"kind":"user","change":"message 38 ..."}`.
- Head: passes (183 s).

**Real route, before/after.** This used an isolated scratch Gateway (`env -i`, random port) on OpenAI Responses (`gpt-6.1-sol`, with a switch to `gpt-6-astra` and back). Turn 5 replied a real `NO_REPLY`. Each value is the provider-reported `cacheRead` for that request:

| request | 1 | 2 | 3 (switch) | 4 (back) | 5 (silent) | 6 (after silent) | 7 | 8 | total read |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | 0 | 3490 | 0 | 4005 | 5040 | 5565 | 6046 | 6567 | 30713 |
| head | 0 | 3496 | 0 | 4006 | 5033 | 5556 | 6045 | 6562 | 30698 |

As expected, Responses does not merge user turns, so it shows no break on base and no regression on head. The break needs a route that merges user turns. No Bedrock credentials were available for a real Bedrock run, so the Bedrock proof uses the fake transport above. The Bedrock cacheRead gain is unmeasured on a real route.

**Gates**
- `pnpm tsgo:core` passed.
- `pnpm check:test-types` passed.
- oxlint and oxfmt are clean on the changed files.
- `ocx test src/agents/embedded-agent-runner` + `session-tool-result-guard.transcript-events.test.ts`: 1465 passed, 1 failed. The failure was `run.shared-integration.test.ts` › timeout cancellation, on a heavily loaded host. That file passes alone on head.
- Touched test files pass on head.

**Size:** production code +28/-5 (3 files); tests are updated where they asserted the old drop (`replay-history.test.ts`, `exact-compaction-replay.test.ts` Google marker case, `attempt-prompt-context.test.ts` shrink case).

**Local review:** first head flagged a per-silent-row history copy (`slice`); fixed in cd54752 with an index walk.

prs.title: fix(gateway): bind loopback caller conversation tool-policy assertion
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #201195. When a session runs through a CLI runtime (tools reached via the OpenClaw MCP bridge), `github_read` always fails with:

```
GitHub reading requires an active github_read tool invocation.
```

The check in `src/gateway/server-methods/tools-github.ts` requires `caller.assertToolAllowed`, but the loopback caller identity built by `createAdmittedGatewayToolCallerIdentity` carried no `assertToolAllowed` assertion. Direct-RPC callers (inside the Gateway's own agent loop) get that assertion from `agent-tools.caller.ts`; MCP-bridged calls never did.

## Solution

Bind the loopback caller's effective conversation tool-policy assertion in `src/gateway/mcp-http.ts`'s `createCallerIdentity`. The loopback grant already carries the `conversationToolPolicy` that filtered the served catalog; this wires it through the same standard path so tools that re-assert the active invocation's policy can verify it. Plugin-id and `group:plugins` allowances expand through the served catalog's own plugin ownership (`expandPolicyWithPluginGroups` + `buildPluginToolGroups`), matching the catalog pipeline rather than introducing different policy semantics at invocation.

This preserves the existing authority model:
- Direct-RPC refusal is unchanged.
- If the conversation policy denies the tool, it never appears in the served catalog (already filtered at construction), and the bound assertion also rejects it.
- No policy means "allow all not denied" — matching the catalog's own default, so an admitted permitted GitHub read now passes instead of being rejected unconditionally.
- Plugin-group allowances (`"github"`, `"group:plugins"`) expand to concrete tool names exactly as the catalog pipeline does.

## Impact

Behavioral fix for a real user fault: permitted GitHub reads through the MCP bridge from a CLI runtime now work. No new options, config, or persistence. ~12 production lines.

## Evidence

- Root cause chain verified at source (ClawSweeper's `source-repro`): rejection at `tools-github.ts:73` when `caller.assertToolAllowed` is absent; loopback identity at `mcp-http.ts` lacks the assertion; working sibling at `agent-tools.caller.ts:82` supplies it.
- Collision check: no open PR touches `src/gateway/mcp-http.ts`, `src/agents/tools/gateway-caller-context.ts`, `src/gateway/server-methods/tools-github.ts`, or `src/agents/tool-policy-match.ts`; no open PR claims issue #201195.
- Regression (red/green): new `src/gateway/mcp-http.loopback-caller-policy.test.ts` fails on base (`assertToolAllowed` is `undefined` → `expected 'undefined' to be 'function'`) and passes with the fix. Plugin-group expansion is covered separately: with `allow: ["github"]` the base assertion rejects the admitted `github_read` (red), and the fix accepts it (green). Full `mcp-http.test.ts` suite: 63 passed, no regressions.
- Review finding addressed: the [P2] readonly `McpLoopbackTool[]` parameter now passes the mutable array to `buildPluginToolGroups` (head `785af5e3`); scoped `tsc` typecheck of the changed files is clean.
- Containerized end-to-end attempt (Docker `ubuntu:24.04`, Node 24, pnpm 12.15.0; a scripted claude-cli child speaking real MCP JSON-RPC over the loopback bridge; real `api.github.com` fetch of issue #201195), run as a 4-variant matrix on head `785af5e3`:

  | Variant | Conversation policy | Served loopback catalog | `github_read` call |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `plugin` | `allow: ["github"]` | `[]` | `Tool not available: github_read` |
  | `concrete` | `allow: ["github_read"]` | `[]` | `Tool not available: github_read` |
  | `none` | (no policy) | 37 core tools | `Tool not available: github_read` |
  | `native` | `allow: ["github"]`, realistic native tool surface | `[]` | `Tool not available: github_read` |

  Reading: with no policy the bridge serves 37 tools, so the grant→`toolsAllow`→catalog chain works end to end in the harness. But `github_read` is absent from the CLI loopback projection even unrestricted, so the call fails at "Tool not available" before it can reach the policy assertion this PR fixes. In the reported production scenario `github_read` *is* served — the user's error came from the tool's own policy assertion — so the remaining gap is harness fidelity of this qa-lab lane (plugin tools are not projected into its CLI bridge catalog), not the policy path changed here.
- **Real behavior proof (shipped-run)**: isolated Gateway in a container (Ubuntu 24.04), genuine Claude Code CLI runtime as the agent backend (`agentRuntime: { id: "claude-cli" }`), conversation policy `tools.allow = ["github"]`, production `github_read` through the loopback MCP bridge. Full detail and red/green trajectories in [this comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201228#issuecomment-7001240050):
  - HEAD `785af5e3`: `tool.call github_read` → `tool.result ok`; agent replies with the exact title of #201195. Gateway log: 0 occurrences of the rejection string.
  - BASE `f7c68043` (merge-base, identical environment): `github_read` ×3 and `github_search` ×1 all rejected; agent reports the Gateway error verbatim: `GitHub reading requires an active github_read tool invocation.` — the exact #201195 production failure.
- An earlier containerized harness experiment (scripted MCP client over the loopback bridge) reached only catalog lookup because that scaffolding does not project plugin tools into its CLI catalog; it is superseded by the shipped-run proof above.

prs.title: fix: avoid repeated provider preparation during model fallback
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Choosing a fallback model repeatedly prepares provider plugins just to read each candidate's shared rate-limit state. Long fallback chains repeat config normalization, auto-enable preparation, and registration-key calculation before every run, even when the config and registry have not changed.

## User Impact

Fallback selection uses substantially less CPU and memory. Candidate ordering, account selection, rate-limit gates, and reload behavior stay the same. No configuration changes or migration are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Normal reply fallback runs before candidate-level model-runtime acquisition, so the existing prepared-snapshot route map does not cover this outer health read. The selected plugin registry's existing load context now retains normalized candidate routes per captured config, only when the caller uses the metadata owned by that registry. Scoped inspections selecting another inventory retain the existing resolution path. This preserves plugin-derived model IDs, endpoints, and headers; account eligibility and current rate limits are still read on every run. Config publication, registry replacement, and existing context rebinding select fresh facts. Mutable setup inputs retain the existing uncached behavior.

The production delta is +35 lines for this lifecycle-owned projection; there is no new global or request-keyed cache. Existing prepared-snapshot consumers continue to carry their routes directly.

## Evidence

The executable synthetic plugin regression fails on the base with 18 auto-enable calls across three warm six-candidate runs; the fix makes zero auto-enable, config-normalization, registration-key, or model-normalization calls. Differential tests preserve candidate ordering, skipped-attempt records, and final-attempt eligibility as all six routes become saturated, including plugin transport rewrites. Config republication and registry replacement select fresh routes. Interleaved inspection inventories with different transport endpoints cannot borrow each other's routes.

Five alternating before/after pairs, each with 500 measured runs after 100 warmups, using 48 plugin entries, three executable providers, one configured channel, and six fallback candidates:

| Per warm fallback run | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Main-thread CPU | 5.345 ms | 0.149 ms |
| Process CPU | 6.171 ms | 0.243 ms |
| Owner wall time | 5.281 ms | 0.122 ms |
| Sampled allocation | 10.727 MB | 0.276 MB |
| Allocation beneath activation preparation | 8.096 MB | 0 |

Cold first-run wall time was 85.4 ms versus 81.0 ms. The final A/A control showed a 2.3% CPU shift and 0.21% allocation shift; the improvement is well beyond that variation. Timing, allocation, and work-count passes ran separately. This synthetic metadata/health path does not access session databases or enumerate workspaces.

Reproduce with `node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/model-fallback-activation-inputs.ts --flow registry-runner --config published --iterations 500 --warmup 100`, adding `--allocation` or `--counts` in separate processes.

35 focused tests passed, covering fallback activation, prepared and registry-owned routes, shared rate-limit and sticky behavior, plugin load context, and prompt-prefix stability. Codex autoreview is clean through P2. The changed modules have no Control UI imports.

`pnpm check:changed --base 67aacbb676e55db620f56fbdb5132726d69ff512` passed on the final patch, including all guards, typechecks, and lint. Final staged Codex autoreview is clean through P2. There are no unresolved local failures.

## CI qualification

Final-head CI run [44467659599](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44467659599) completed with one inherited failure: `checks-ui-e2e (1/2)`, the Plugins first-visit asset bound (57 assets versus a limit of 56). Every other selected job passed, including all Node shards and `security-fast`; the aggregate gate is red because of that UI case.

The same case fails on the exact CI main parent `43ed271df4a1bc109d8fe07c502985f40c116d6a`. Attribution is [37e7af19884b4](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/37e7af19884b4a92667fc3be816eab64ad904c5b), [#201620](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201620): its security-audit Tooltip import adds an asset. The immediate parent `3b0b7e23f65fd` passes the same focused case; the introducing commit fails identically. This is a main regression requiring a separate owner repair, not a passing CI result. The entire UI tree and relevant test/build inputs are unchanged between the tested main parent and this PR merge.

Reproduction at each unmodified checkout: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.ui-e2e.config.ts --configLoader runner ui/src/e2e/route-asset-requests.e2e.test.ts -t 'bounds plugins ready-window asset requests' --maxWorkers=1`.

The scoped maintainer instruction permits pinned-head admin landing for exact-parent reproduced, commit-attributed inherited failures with green local proof. The native workflow retains that evidence. ClawSweeper reviewed final head `aab9b17faa964` with zero findings and zero open items.

prs.title: fix(macos): complete OpenClaw ID sign-in inside the app
prs.body:
Related: #144596 (the same popup-host boundary affects session navigation; this PR fixes account sign-in only).

## What Problem This Solves

“Sign in with OpenClaw ID” in the Mac app can do nothing, while the same local Gateway works in a browser. The web flow reserves a popup that the Mac host discards, and an external browser cannot return the sign-in through the app’s separate browser storage.

## User Impact

User impact: local OpenClaw ID sign-in has an app-owned login window and returns to the original Control UI account menu, without moving the chat into an external browser.

**Draft: native compilation, the real WebKit regression, live issuer compatibility, and before/after Mac screenshots are pending the reporter’s isolated Tart/GitHub Actions run. This is not a verified Mac fix or ready-to-merge claim.** Both the Mac app and its Gateway-served Control UI need this change. Browser cookies/tokens are not imported: an existing Safari/Chrome login does not automatically authenticate the app.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing Gateway PKCE and code-redemption owner. A reply-capable native bridge presents the Gateway-issued authorization URL in an unprivileged WebKit window and returns the matching callback to the initiating app document. The Control UI then redeems the code and stores its account through its existing owner.

The login window shares the app’s website data store but receives none of the dashboard’s native handlers or injected scripts. Requests are limited to the current dashboard main frame and its callback path; close, document replacement, and timeout settle the pending presentation. Generic popup/link policy, remote device-grant admission, and native claw-enrollment sign-in are unchanged. No configuration, schema, or dependency changes.

Simplification/test audit: removed two redundant mocked popup-helper call-shape checks. Retained independent unsafe-URL, account/menu, sign-out, and browser geometry contracts. Added the native WK transport regression rather than treating synthesized storage events as native sign-in proof.

## Evidence

- Follow-up `0098679b5d71078a259b3915ca4f9b0b651acb84`: fixed the Swift compilation error reported from the [isolated macOS build](https://github.com/jjjhenriksen/openclaw/actions/runs/44468842162) by spelling the identity check `message.world === WKContentWorld.page`. Jacqueline reports a minimal type-check passes with that spelling. Verified that the published follow-up is exactly one replacement line and keeps the check intact; `git diff --check` passes. **A fresh full macOS build, WebKit tests, screenshots, and live sign-in results on this new head are still pending.**
- The two new client-routing cases fail on the unchanged production source at base `428d2047b766fcf0e8d426c1d967b0c8697b8625`, then pass with the change. They verify account storage after a native reply and no external-browser fallback on cancellation. This is client-contract proof, not Mac runtime proof.
- 50 focused tests across external URL, account menu, and account/sign-out suites pass (latest Vitest duration 2.69 seconds; wrapper 3.57 seconds).
- UI typecheck, targeted type-aware lint, TypeScript/Markdown formatting, native i18n verification, documentation link audit (0 broken links), and `git diff --check` pass.
- Added `DashboardOpenClawIDSignInTests`: real DashboardWindowController/WK message transport, an HTTP issuer fixture, actual callback navigation, cancellation, source/callback rejection, and absence of privileged bridges in the login page. **Not compiled or run in this Linux workspace.**
- Local Auto Review was attempted for the complete candidate against the base above but timed out without a report. No clean independent-review result is claimed.

[Thorough Tart, GitHub Actions, red/green, and full-app testing directions](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/0098679b5d71078a259b3915ca4f9b0b651acb84/docs/platforms/mac/openclaw-id-sign-in-testing.md). The full-app checklist includes browser-already-signed-in, persistence, cancellation/retry, dashboard lifetime, network failure, and unchanged browser behavior. A live identity provider rejecting embedded WebKit remains a failed acceptance check; no user-agent spoofing or policy relaxation is proposed. Screenshots and live results remain outstanding.

### Contributor credit

Reported by Jacqueline Henriksen; implementation and test directions prepared at her request.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/94894fe8-9030-45b9-af97-31c42c2d07c0)

## Worked on by

prs.title: fix(windows): consult netstat after an empty PowerShell listener census
prs.body:
Closes #195492

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: on Windows, `readWindowsListeningPidsResultSync` treats a successful but empty PowerShell `Get-NetTCPConnection` census as an authoritative "no listener" result and never consults its netstat fallback. A live listener that CIM omits is then reported as a free port, and consumers can clean up a healthy Gateway.

## User Impact

When PowerShell returns no listener, the reader now asks netstat before reporting an empty census. A listener that only netstat sees is returned. A port is reported empty only when both native collectors see nothing, and a non-empty PowerShell result is still trusted without a second query.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Only short-circuit on a non-empty PowerShell census.
- On an empty census, run the existing netstat fallback and union both observations.
- Preserve the previous result if netstat itself fails after PowerShell succeeded, so the fallback cannot make the reader less available.

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/infra/windows-port-pids.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 4/4 passed: empty-PowerShell/netstat-listener, non-empty PowerShell, both empty, and PowerShell failure.
- Red-on-base: reverting only `windows-port-pids.ts` makes the empty-census case return `{ ok: true, pids: [] }` instead of the netstat listener.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` clean; oxlint clean on both files.

prs.title: feat: share an agent as a template from the agent menu
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Turning an agent into a shareable template starts from chat today, so you have to open that agent's main session and know what to ask. The agent menu already lists every agent, but each row only offers Settings, and that Settings icon draws a box on hover that the neighbouring sidebar actions no longer use.

## User Impact

User impact: hovering an agent in the agent menu now shows a Share button next to Settings. Clicking it opens that agent's main session and sends "Create a shareable template of yourself", so the agent starts preparing its template for review. Both row actions now brighten on hover instead of drawing a box.

Share appears only when Templates is turned on and the connection is allowed to create template drafts, the same conditions as the existing Create template action.

## Why This Change Was Made

Template creation already works from an ordinary chat request, so Share sends that request as a normal message in the agent's main session and then opens the session. It does not create a draft itself. If the message cannot be sent, the menu stays where you were and an error toast offers a retry.

The two row actions share one style so they stay consistent, and the hover rule now changes only the icon color.

## Evidence

Hovering the Research row in the agent menu, dark theme. Before is `main` at 29f26872924, after is this branch. Both use the real Control UI build with the same synthetic mocked Gateway data.

### What was checked

- A browser test in the sidebar interactions suite hovers each row action and checks that the background stays transparent while the icon color changes, reaches Share then Settings with Tab, clicks Share, and checks that exactly one `chat.send` goes to `agent:research:main` with the message, no template draft is created by the UI, the session opens, and the message is visible in the transcript. prs.title: fix: keep empty chats free of message-loading placeholders
prs.body:
Fixes #201479

## What Problem This Solves

Opening a new empty chat can show message-loading bubbles even though no saved messages exist. This also affects chats opened during Template setup and makes an empty conversation look as though it is waiting for old messages.

## User Impact

Empty chats stay clear. Existing chats with confirmed saved messages keep their loading skeleton until those messages arrive. When history presence is unknown, the conversation stays neutral; history requests, drafts, and composer readiness are unchanged. No configuration change or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The loading flag describes several startup operations, not whether saved messages exist. The existing transcript writer and bounded metadata backfill expose an optional `hasMessages` fact. Empty sessions get that fact during ordinary row preparation, before publication; legacy preview enrichment remains optional. Data-free boot and route shells remain neutral.

Pending-history lifecycle remains separate from bubble presentation, so loading saved history does not announce it as a new reply. A presented pane without any observed row can discover metadata for a concrete, non-global chat, including on mobile without a sidebar roster. This optional lookup accepts only a present row and cannot clear or replace facts already accepted through history or another reader. Unresolved and global targets retain their existing history-admission ordering. Queued Stop refreshes and authoritative row retirement retain their original behavior.

prs.title: fix(macos): treat failed port inspection as unknown, not free
prs.body:
Closes #190152

## What Problem This Solves

macOS `PortGuardian` asks `lsof` which process is listening on a port. `lsof` can fail in ways that say nothing about the port: missing from `PATH`, exceeding the 5 second probe deadline (for example on a wedged SMB/NFS mount), or exiting non-zero for an unrelated reason. The old code folded all of those into "no listener", and every caller treated the port as free. Three symptoms:

* `gateway install --force` / launchd repair overwrote a Gateway that was started by hand, because the "is the owner ours?" guard was skipped when the probe returned nothing.
* `ManagedNodeGatewayMigration` decided the existing service was absent and took the port over.
* The child-start path skipped the attach step and spawned a second Gateway on a busy port, producing the repeated start failures and the Onboarding screen that claims nothing is listening.

Reproduced by pointing `PATH` at an `lsof` stub that sleeps past the deadline, or by removing `lsof` entirely: the port reports idle while a real listener is bound.

## Why This Change Was Made

A missing answer is not a negative answer, so the probe now has three outcomes. `PortGuardian.inspect(port:)` returns `PortInspection`:

* `.free` — `lsof` ran, exited 1, and printed nothing, exactly what `lsof` does when no process matches. This is the only case that may be read as "the port is idle".
* `.owned(Descriptor)` — the listener was parsed successfully.
* `.unknown` — timeout, pre-flight failure, unexpected exit code, or unparseable output.

`lsof` runs with `-b` so a stuck mount cannot block the probe, and the shell call goes through `ShellExecutor.runDetailed` because the old `run` threw the exit code away, which is how "exit 1, nothing matched" got confused with "exit 2, lsof is unhappy".

Every consumer handles `.unknown` explicitly and conservatively: persistence ensure returns `.skipped` instead of reinstalling, repair collects no evidence from an undecided probe, the attach path fails with "Could not determine whether port X is free" and never spawns a child on a port it could not inspect, and migration raises "the existing owner was preserved". The diff is +432/−99 over eight files, 187 of those insertions being regression tests; it cannot shrink further because the tri-state has to reach every place that read `nil` as "free".

One deliberate deviation: for `.unknown` the readiness publisher keeps the existing `isCurrentGatewayReadiness` check rather than `canPublishGatewayReadiness(instance: nil)`. The latter is always false for `.child` starts and would pin a failed child start in `.starting`; the old predicate keeps today's behaviour without claiming anything about port ownership.

## User Impact

* Failing probes no longer cause a Gateway to be replaced, migrated, or started twice; the app waits for the next probe instead of acting on a guess.
* Healthy machines are unchanged: a successful `lsof` with no match is still `.free`, so install, repair and start paths behave exactly as before.
* Debug diagnostics and Onboarding stop claiming "nothing is listening" when the probe failed; they report the port could not be inspected.
* Trade-off, accepted on purpose: an inconclusive probe during migration records one failed attempt and retries next launch, instead of stealing a running service.
* Everything touched lives under `apps/macos/`: no shared package, CLI or protocol surface changed.

## Evidence

Proof branch `fix/macos-portguardian-inconclusive-190152` @ `349b0ec7dc6` (rebased on `main` `999e873a916`), run through a throwaway `proof/190152` workflow on a hosted `macos-26` runner (Xcode 26.6, Swift 6.3.3, Node 24, pnpm 12.15.0, repo-pinned SwiftFormat 0.63.1 / SwiftLint 0.65.1 via `lint-swift.sh` + `format-swift.sh`). That job patches one unrelated, pre-existing build break at job time (`OpenClawChatUI/ChatMediaVideoAttachment.swift` uses `VideoPlayer` without an availability guard and does not compile on hosted runners); the patch is never committed and is not in this diff.

```
Build complete! (1000.13s)                    # swift build --build-tests
✔ Test run with 8 tests in 1 suite passed after 6.376 seconds.    PortGuardianDiagnosticsTests
✔ Test run with 91 tests in 1 suite passed after 22.144 seconds.  GatewayProcessManagerTests
0/440 files require formatting, 6 files skipped                    swiftformat (0 errors)
```

`swiftlint` reports one `type_body_length` warning on `GatewayProcessManager`; upstream's wrapper treats size limits as advisory under Actions, so the job stays green.

Input variant → observed output (executed, not asserted by inspection):

| Probe input | Result | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `lsof` absent from `PATH` | `.unknown`, `isListening == true` | `a missing lsof is unknown instead of a free port` |
| `lsof` stub sleeping 8 s, real listener bound | `.unknown` after 5.5 s (killed at the deadline) | `an lsof timeout stays unknown within the probe deadline` |
| `lsof` exit 2 | `.unknown`, never "idle" | `a failing lsof never reports the port as idle` |
| real `lsof`, loopback listener | `.owned`, pid == test process | `real lsof reports a loopback listener as owned` |
| real `lsof`, unbound port | `.free` | `real lsof reports an idle port as free` |
| classification matrix (timeout / pre-flight / exit 1 / exit 2 / unparseable) | `.inconclusive` except exit 1 with empty output | `listener classification keeps failed probes undecided` |
| undecided probe during persistence ensure | only `status` runs, no `install` | `defers persistence when port inspection is inconclusive` |

Not covered: upstream's `xcode-27` runner (unavailable to a fork) and Windows/Linux (every changed file is macOS-only).

prs.title: fix(plugins): surface dropped prompt-build context
prs.body:
Supersedes #118555 (auto-closed for inactivity; branch re-merged with current main).

## What Problem This Solves

Plugins use `before_prompt_build` to add context that can determine what an agent does next. When that contribution is lost, the prompt looks exactly as it would if the plugin had nothing to report — the plugin's block is simply absent. An agent whose work queue arrives through the hook therefore cannot distinguish "no ready work" from "the ready-work block was dropped", and silently does nothing.

On `main` the loss is operator-log-only. `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-prompt-helpers.ts` wires `before_prompt_build` through a `logHookFailure` that warns and returns `undefined`, and the caller treats `undefined` identically to "contributed nothing"; `src/agents/harness/prompt-compaction-hook-helpers.ts` does the same for the harness and the authorized phase. Per-handler losses inside the chain reach only `handleHookError` in `src/plugins/hooks.ts`, with no callback that lets a caller observe a discarded contribution.

## Why This Change Was Made

When a contribution is dispatched and then lost, the runtime appends one bounded, redacted `<dropped_plugin_context hook="before_prompt_build">` marker to the turn's `appendContext`, naming the affected plugin and a fixed reason code (`handler-failed` or `dispatch-failed`).

Existing policy is preserved: prompt-build hooks stay fail-open, surviving contributions still reach the prompt, error details stay in operator logs and never enter model context, and authority-only handlers are reported only by the authorized phase that can run them. Raw plugin identities are counted before labels are sanitized and truncated, so display collisions cannot understate the loss count. The marker lists at most five entries, is capped at 640 bytes, and accounts for omissions with `+N more`. Failures *before* dispatch (history load, hook-context assembly) are deliberately unmarked: nothing was dropped, and telling the agent to re-read context that never existed is the same misleading instruction the marker exists to prevent.

The two prompt-build dispatch phases were extracted into `src/plugins/hooks-prompt-build.ts` and `src/agents/cli-runner/hook-prompt-build.ts` to stay under the line-cap ratchet. The CLI helper returns `ResolvedPromptBuildHookResult | undefined`, the contract `prepareCliTurnPromptContext` requires, so the extraction does not narrow the caller's static type.

### Changed during this re-merge — one sub-behavior removed

Upstream retired the prompt-build re-entrancy guard in `0301614ddd9` ("refactor(plugins): simplify transient cleanup bookkeeping (#174872)"), which deleted `AsyncLocalStorage` and `beforePromptBuildDispatch` from `src/plugins/hooks.ts`; `runBeforePromptBuild` now dispatches unconditionally. The branch's third reason code, `nested-prompt-build`, therefore has no premise left. Rather than resurrect the retired guard, this merge **removes** that reason code, its 2 unit tests and proof scenarios [4] and [8], which are marked RETIRED in the proof header with the remaining scenario numbers left stable. The docs reference and the proof script's "WHAT IS REAL" description no longer promise nested-prompt-build suppression or a surviving re-entrancy guard.

## User Impact

Agents can distinguish "the plugin had nothing to add" from "the runtime lost the plugin's context", which prevents false empty-queue conclusions, without exposing exception text, credentials, endpoints, or plugin-authored prompt injection. No configuration or public plugin SDK change.

## Evidence

Measured on this head, `1650afd3378e5acad1021962802bc0f2d637ab87`, today (2026-11-13).

### Real behavior proof — real dispatcher, real CLI/harness/embedded prompt assembly

Command (exactly, from the branch worktree):

```
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/proof-prompt-build-drop-marker.ts
```

Key lines of the real output (`EXIT 0`, 46 assertions; full capture below):

```
[1] healthy contribution reaches the prompt and adds NO marker
  ok  healthy: block present in assembled prompt
  ok  healthy: no drop marker (marker is not unconditional)

[2] throwing handler: reason code only, healthy plugin survives
[plugins] [hooks] before_prompt_build handler from proof-beads failed: bd ready --json failed in /repo: AUTH_TOKEN=*** https://internal.invalid/v1/queue
  ok  throw: marker names proof-beads with a fixed reason code
  ok  throw: no error-derived text reached the prompt
  ok  throw: healthy plugin's contribution survives

[9] CLI consumer end to end: prepareCliRunContext prompt
  ok  cap/cli: overflow summary counts the 25 unlisted drops
  ok  cap/cli: marker is 516 bytes, within the 640-byte cap

[11] CLI boundary asymmetry: a pre-dispatch failure is log-only, never marked
[agent/cli-backend] cli prompt-build hook preparation failed: Error: pre-dispatch preparation failed: AUTH_TOKEN=*** https://internal.invalid/v1/queue
  ok  pre-dispatch: the CLI prompt still opens with the untouched base ask
  ok  pre-dispatch: no drop marker — nothing was dispatched, so nothing was dropped
  ok  post-dispatch: a real dropped contribution still yields exactly one marker
  ok  post-dispatch: the marker names the plugin whose contribution was actually lost

All runtime assertions passed. (46 checks)
```

**What is real:** `createHookRunner` and `initializeGlobalHookRunner`/`getGlobalHookRunner` with production options (the real dispatcher, the real per-hook timeout, the real `handleHookError` fail-open path); all three production prompt consumers — `resolveAgentHarnessBeforePromptBuildResult`, `resolvePromptBuildHookResult`, and `prepareCliRunContext` driven end to end so the CLI scenarios assert on `params.prompt`, the exact string handed to the backend; the real `createEmptyPluginRegistry`/`setActivePluginRegistry` activation seam; and real `prepareSystemAgentRunAdmission` admission via `withTestRunAdmission`, so the CLI path's live-authority assertions run.

**What is stubbed or constructed:** the hook registration records (same `{pluginId, hookName, handler, priority, timeoutMs}` shape the loader produces), the CLI backend descriptor, and an on-disk temp session file. Nothing between a handler and the assembled prompt is stubbed. The capturing logger in scenario [6] is an instrument, not a stub.

### Installed-plugin + provider-boundary proof: previously green, now blocked by main on Linux

`scripts/proof-118555-installed-plugin-provider-request.ts` (also committed here) installs each fixture through the real `installPluginFromPath`, loads it with the real `loadOpenClawPlugins` through the loader's real conversation-hook consent gate, and asserts on the **stdin of a real spawned provider process** reached through `runCliAgent`. On PR #118555 it passed 26 assertions and failed on pristine `origin/main` at the "exactly one loss notice" assertion — the silent drop this PR fixes, observed at the provider boundary.

Re-run on this head today it no longer reaches the provider boundary, for a reason that is not about this PR: current `main` added `acquireLinuxChildSubreaper` (`src/process/supervisor/linux-child-subreaper.ts:39`), which refuses child ownership when the owning process has source-loader hooks. Every `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs` proof is such a process, so the spawn is rejected before the recorder starts:

```
  ok  healthy-only: loader registered before_prompt_build for every INSTALLED fixture (1)
  ok  healthy-only: the installed plugin's CLI backend is the resolved provider
[process/supervisor] spawn failed: runId=proof-118555-healthy-only reason=AggregateError: Linux child ownership requires a process owner without source-loader hooks
PROOF FAILED after 2 checks: AggregateError: Linux child ownership requires a process owner without source-loader hooks
```

The two assertions that do run still confirm the installed plugins loaded off disk, passed the consent gate, and that the installed plugin's CLI backend was the resolved provider. The marker assertions beyond that point are unverified on this head.

### Built shipped-CLI capture on an isolated identity — healthy, failing, overflow

This is the entry-point run the review asked for: the **built production CLI**, plugins installed
through the real `openclaw plugins install` CLI, and the three cases captured off the **bytes the
runtime sent to a model provider over HTTP**, not off an in-process return value.

What the binary is: `<openclaw-build>/dist` + `openclaw.mjs`, a real production build reporting
`OpenClaw 2026.11.3 (59fa16a)`. That is **a build of our fork's `integration` branch, which contains
this PR branch merged**, not a build of this PR alone. Across this PR's production files the build and
this head are identical except for one file, `src/agents/cli-runner/prepare.ts`, which the build has
**3 insertions / 20 deletions** ahead of this head — and both hunks belong to *other* open branches that
also touch that file (`fix/native-capture-warm-refusal-e2m1` contributes `refuseNativeCapture(...)`;
`fix/zai-agent-sdk-setup-entry` contributes the `resolveApiKeyForProviderCore` backend-auth fallback).
Neither hunk is in this PR's diff, and **every line this PR changes is byte-identical in the build**,
including all of `src/plugins/prompt-build-drop.ts`, `src/plugins/hooks-prompt-build.ts`,
`src/agents/cli-runner/hook-prompt-build.ts`, `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-prompt-helpers.ts`
and `src/agents/harness/prompt-compaction-hook-helpers.ts`. Verified with
`git diff --stat origin/integration origin/fix/prompt-build-drop-marker -- <this PR's production files>`.

Isolation: every run got a fresh `HOME`, a fresh `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, a fresh `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`,
its own workspace, and its own loopback port (18911-18913). Nothing touched `~/.openclaw`, the operator's
config, or the Gateway on 18789.

Per scenario the harness: writes fixture plugin packages in the shape npm ships; installs each one with
`node openclaw.mjs plugins install <dir> --force --accept-capabilities` (real CLI, real install root —
`Installing to /tmp/cap197114-run/<scenario>/state/extensions/<id>…` / `Installed plugin: <id>`);
writes operator config granting `plugins.allow` plus `hooks.allowConversationAccess`; then runs one real
turn with `node openclaw.mjs agent exec --config … --state-dir … --model stub/stub-model "latest ask …"`.

```
node <openclaw-build>/openclaw.mjs plugins install <fixture-dir> --force --accept-capabilities
node <openclaw-build>/openclaw.mjs agent exec --config <tmp>/openclaw.json \
  --state-dir <tmp>/state --cwd <tmp>/work --model stub/stub-model \
  "latest ask from the operator: summarize the ready work"
node assert-captures.cjs
```

**1. Healthy** — one installed plugin contributes, nothing is dropped. The first user message the provider
received begins with the plugin's block and the operator's own ask, and carries no marker:

```
[Fri 2026-11-13 14:08 MST] HEALTHY-CTX-FROM-cap-healthy

latest ask from the operator: summarize the ready work
```

**2. Failing** — a healthy plugin and a throwing plugin, both installed through the CLI. The healthy block
survives, and this exact text arrived inside the provider's HTTP request body:

```
<dropped_plugin_context hook="before_prompt_build">
The runtime dropped this turn's before_prompt_build contribution from cap-failing (handler-failed).
That context is MISSING from this prompt, not empty — do not read its absence as "nothing to report" (for example, an empty task or work queue). Re-read anything you need from its source before acting.
</dropped_plugin_context>
```

The thrown error's message (`ready-work query failed: sk-FIXTURE-SECRET-…`) appears **nowhere** in the

  "main": "index.mjs",
  "activation": { "onStartup": true },

`stub-provider.cjs` — the only stub: a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint that records every request body:

```js
// Minimal OpenAI-compatible stub model endpoint.
// Records every request body it receives, then answers with a fixed completion.
// Usage: node stub-provider.cjs <out-dir> <port>
const http = require("node:http");
const fs = require("node:fs");
const path = require("node:path");

const outDir = process.argv[2];
const port = Number(process.argv[3]);
fs.mkdirSync(outDir, { recursive: true });
let seq = 0;

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  let body = "";
  req.on("data", (chunk) => {
    body += chunk;
  });
  req.on("end", () => {
    seq += 1;
    const slug = req.url.replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9]+/g, "_");
    fs.writeFileSync(
      path.join(outDir, `req-${String(seq).padStart(2, "0")}-${req.method}${slug}.json`),
      body || "{}",
      "utf-8",
    );
    if (req.url.includes("models")) {
      res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" });
      res.end(JSON.stringify({ object: "list", data: [{ id: "stub-model", object: "model" }] }));
      return;
    }
    res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" });
    res.end(
      JSON.stringify({
        id: "chatcmpl-stub",
        object: "chat.completion",
        created: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000),
        model: "stub-model",
        choices: [
          {
            index: 0,
            message: { role: "assistant", content: "STUB-OK" },
            finish_reason: "stop",
          },
        ],
        usage: { prompt_tokens: 10, completion_tokens: 2, total_tokens: 12 },
      }),
    );
  });
});
server.listen(port, "127.0.0.1", () => {
  fs.writeFileSync(path.join(outDir, "stub.ready"), String(port), "utf-8");
  console.log(`stub provider listening on 127.0.0.1:${port}`);
});
```
