prs.title: feat(gateway): opt-in Cloudflare Access JWT verification for trusted-proxy auth
prs.body:
Closes #200361

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: in the documented Cloudflare Access setup, any process that can reach the Gateway from a trusted proxy address can claim any email (with a garbage or unsigned `cf-access-jwt-assertion`) and be admitted as that user, including `operator.admin`.

## User Impact

User impact: operators can set `gateway.auth.trustedProxy.cloudflareAccessJwt` so the Gateway admits a Cloudflare Access request only when its assertion is signed by their Access team for their application. Forged identity headers are refused. The setting is off by default and existing configs behave exactly as before.

```json5
trustedProxy: {
  userHeader: "cf-access-authenticated-user-email",
  requiredHeaders: ["cf-access-jwt-assertion"],
  allowLoopback: true,
  cloudflareAccessJwt: {
    issuer: "https://example.cloudflareaccess.com",
    audience: "your-application-aud-tag",
  },
}
```

## Why This Change Was Made

With the setting on, trusted-proxy admission verifies `cf-access-jwt-assertion` before trusting the user header:

- RS256 only, against the team's keys from `<issuer>/cdn-cgi/access/certs`. Keys are read with a 64 KB limit and fetched on demand: again on the first request after ten minutes, or for an unknown key id, at most once every 30 seconds per issuer. A failed fetch keeps the last good keys.
- `iss` must equal `issuer`, `aud` must contain `audience`, `exp` is required, and `exp`/`nbf` allow 60 seconds of clock skew.
- The user comes from the signed `email` claim. The user header must match it (case-insensitive), because other code still reads that header.
- Failures have distinct reasons: `trusted_proxy_access_invalid`, `trusted_proxy_access_user_mismatch`, `trusted_proxy_access_keys_unavailable`. They are documented in the trusted-proxy troubleshooting list.

Things reviewers should weigh:

- **Hand-written RS256 on `node:crypto`.** Verification is about 60 lines over `createPublicKey` and `crypto.verify` with `alg` pinned to RS256. The only JWT library in the repo (`jose`) belongs to the OpenAI plugin, and adding it to core would be a new core dependency. Happy to switch if maintainers prefer `jose` in core.
- **New config key** `gateway.auth.trustedProxy.cloudflareAccessJwt` (`issuer`, `audience`), with labels, help text and the regenerated config baseline. The issuer pattern is shared with `cloudflareAccessOidc.issuer`.
- **Fails closed with enterprise browser delegation.** Delegated identities are not Access emails, so delegated requests are refused while verification is on. The docs say so, and a test covers it.
- **Service-token JWTs have no email.** Nodes that pass Access with a service token send no user header, so they keep the existing `trusted_proxy_user_missing` outcome before any JWT work, then authenticate with their own credentials. A service-token assertion paired with a forged email header is refused as a mismatch.
- **Translations not regenerated.** The new config labels and help text are English only. The UI translation memory (`ui/src/i18n/.i18n/*.tm.jsonl`) is left to the normal i18n job.

## Evidence

- **Regression tests** (`src/gateway/auth.test.ts`, `src/gateway/trusted-proxy-delegation.test.ts`): forged unsigned assertion, another key's signature, another application's `aud`, expired assertion, forged user header, verified user admitted, service-token request, certs endpoint down, last good keys kept with one fetch per backoff window, and delegation refused. On `main` the forgery and delegation cases fail because the requests are admitted (`ok: true`). With this change, all pass.
- **Forgery harness over the Control UI HTTP surface** (the same requests as the issue): with the setting on, a garbage assertion, an unsigned JWT, a JWT signed by another key under the team's key id, and a valid assertion with a forged email header all get HTTP 401 with no operator config in the response. A correctly signed assertion gets HTTP 200. With the setting off, the forged requests are admitted, as on `main`.
- **Upgrade from latest stable, shipped Gateway, clean macOS VM** (macOS 26.6 guest, Node 24.21): `openclaw@2026.11.4` installed from npm ran the documented Cloudflare config (`docs/gateway/cloudflare-access.md` step 3) and admitted all three forgeries sent with curl from the same host. The same state was then upgraded to this branch (built from its `git archive`) with `openclaw doctor --fix` (exit 0). `gateway.auth`, `trustedProxies` and the MCP config were kept byte for byte, and with the setting off the branch behaves like stable. `openclaw config set gateway.auth.trustedProxy.cloudflareAccessJwt ...` was accepted and hot-applied; after it, all three forgeries got HTTP 401 with no operator config in the response. The third forgery names a key id from a real Access team's live `/cdn-cgi/access/certs`, so the Gateway fetched those keys and rejected the signature. Team name redacted.

  <details><summary>Guest transcript (redacted)</summary>

  ```text
  ##### 1. stable 2026.11.4 Gateway, forged requests (04:02:57Z)
  gateway stable pid=2165 ready after 8s
  [garbage assertion] HTTP 200, operator-only MCP config in response: yes
  [forged unsigned JWT] HTTP 200, operator-only MCP config in response: yes
  [real team key id, attacker signature] HTTP 200, operator-only MCP config in response: yes

  ##### 2. upgrade the same state to this branch: doctor --fix, then Gateway with the setting off (04:03:08Z)
  ```

prs.title: fix(cli): request scopes a session-only device grant covers
prs.body:
Related: #199692

Depends on #199693. This branch is stacked on it, so until #199693 merges the diff also shows its commits.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a device paired with only `operator.sessions.write`, as the multiplayer guide recommends for guests, can't use `openclaw gateway call` or `openclaw tui`. The CLI asks for `operator.read` and the TUI for admin, read, write and approvals, so every connect becomes a scope-upgrade request for the admin.

## User Impact

User impact: a session-only guest can list, read and create its sessions from the CLI and use the TUI within its grant. Once the TUI has stored the grant with a device token, its connections and `gateway call` file no upgrade request. Behind trusted-proxy auth the Gateway issues the TUI no device token and `gateway call` stores none, so there each connection is refused once with a scope-upgrade request and then works within the grant. #199699 removes that refusal as a Gateway opt-in.

Devices whose grant holds the general scope are unchanged, and a device that needs a real upgrade (for example `operator.read` to `operator.admin`) still files one.

In the TUI, a session-only device gets no command list or pending approvals, because those need `operator.read` and `operator.approvals`.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Where the client learns its grant:**
- `gateway call` projects its least-privilege scopes through the stored device grant with the existing `projectOperatorScopesForMethod`. It narrows only when the method's session-scoped alternative still authorizes the call.
- The TUI connects within a stored grant that holds `operator.sessions.*` and none of its default scopes, unless `--token` or `--password` is given.

**A device approved before it ever connected:** it has no stored grant, so its first request can exceed it. The Gateway's scope-upgrade refusal already reports `approvedScopes`, and the client uses that:
- The gateway client gains an opt-in `fitScopesToApprovedGrant` hook that reconnects once within the reported grant, which the TUI uses.
- `gateway call` retries once with the session grant.
- The TUI stores the device token it receives with the grant, so its later connections, and `gateway call` reading that stored grant, fit it. `gateway call` keeps its read-only storage mode on the retry and stores nothing.

Until a grant is stored, each connection still files that request first, because nothing tells the client its grant before it asks. Behind trusted-proxy auth nothing is stored, so that holds for every connection. The opt-in Gateway change in #199699 removes it.

**Moves:** two moves keep the touched files within the line-cap ratchet without changing behaviour:
- CLI scope selection, including the existing `sessions.create` cwd escalation retry, moves to `src/gateway/call-scopes.ts`.
- The gateway client's host-dependency defaults move to `packages/gateway-client/src/client-host-deps.ts`. `client.ts` re-exports their types, so the package API is unchanged.

**Docs:** `docs/start/multiplayer.md` and `docs/cli/tui.md` describe the guest behaviour and when the first-connect request remains.

## Evidence

- **New tests:**
  - `src/gateway/call.stored-grant-scopes.test.ts` 5/5. A session-only grant reads with `operator.sessions.read`; a read grant and a method without a session scope keep their request; a refused request retries with the reported grant and keeps read-only storage on both attempts (this case fails without the read-only fix); a grant that can't serve the method does not retry.
  - `packages/gateway-client/src/client.approved-grant.test.ts` 3/3, against a real WebSocket server that refuses with a scope upgrade: reconnects once within the reported grant; pauses without the hook, or when the hook keeps the request.
  - `src/tui/gateway-chat.connection.test.ts` 16/16, adding session-only, read, `operator.pairing` and `--token` grants.
  - Without this change, the session-only, retry, `operator.pairing` and `--token` cases fail; the keep-behaviour cases pass on both.
- **Existing tests:** `call.test.ts` 91/91, `client.test.ts` 95/95, `client.handshake.test.ts` 22/22, `client.device-auth.test.ts` 25/25, `reconnect-policy.test.ts` 19/19, `tui.test.ts` 51/51.
- **Static checks:** typecheck, lint and format are clean.
- **Restack onto #199693's pairing hint:** this branch now sits on `a675d1b23b7`, which adds the `openclaw gateway call` hint for an unpaired edgeAuth device and keeps an explicit `--url` in it. `git range-diff 3411a94ae50..48d8e528f08 a675d1b23b7..74994fa1a99` shows this branch's two commits unchanged, and the runs below were made at `48d8e528f08`, before the restack. On `74994fa1a99`: `call.edge-auth.test.ts` 6/6, `call.stored-grant-scopes.test.ts` 5/5, `call.test.ts` 91/91, `gateway-chat.connection.test.ts` 16/16, `client.approved-grant.test.ts` 3/3, typecheck clean, line-cap ratchet OK. On `71857425b24`, the same two commits on #199693's first hint commit: `client-bootstrap.auth.test.ts` 6/6, `client.test.ts` 95/95, `tui.test.ts` 51/51.
- **Live run** at `48d8e528f08` (built with `pnpm build:runtime`): a loopback Gateway with `gateway.auth.mode: "trusted-proxy"`, behind a small TLS proxy standing in for Cloudflare Access (it answers 302 unless the request carries `Cf-Access-Token`, then injects the identity headers). The guest config has only `gateway.remote.url` and `gateway.remote.edgeAuth`: no token, no password, no stored device token. `--tls-fingerprint` is there only because the test proxy uses a self-signed certificate. The output is trimmed, and IDs and ports are from throwaway test state. The admin approves only `operator.sessions.write`. The Gateway has `narrowToDeviceGrant` off, as it is by default and as it is without #199699.

- **Upgrade from 2026.11.3, stored credentials kept:** the same loopback trusted-proxy setup, starting on the published `openclaw@2026.11.3` package for both the Gateway and the guest. prs.title: fix(outbound): keep gateway-executed CLI send transcript writes in the gateway process
prs.body:
Closes #199155

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a scripted `openclaw message send` can write into a resident Gateway session from the CLI process, causing the next agent turn to fail with stale session state or a transcript sequence collision.

## User Impact

Gateway-executed sends appear once in destination history, and the resident agent can subsequently append user, tool-result, and assistant messages. No configuration, migration, or dependency changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Every Gateway `send` now uses the existing message-action runner and confirmed-message owner. Delegating callers write neither destination history nor session routing after the RPC. This covers direct plugin handlers and authenticated transport callers with the same ownership rule. Model-authored sends retain caller-owned retry semantics.

The cleanup removes the parallel Gateway transcript recorder and `callerRecordsDestinationHistory` flag. The runtime reproduction also caught a second foreign write: the CLI repeated the route commit after Gateway acceptance. Removing that duplicate write fixes the resident follow-up without weakening SQLite conflict detection or adding retries.

## Evidence

- **Real process-boundary proof:** rebuilt CLI → isolated resident Gateway → synthetic loopback channel/model. CLI exit 0; transport executed in the Gateway PID; one platform send and one destination row after same-key replay. The subsequent resident agent turn executed a tool and completed successfully. Its ordered transcript sequences were CLI message **9**, user **10**, tool call **14**, tool result **15**, assistant **18**; all **19 rows** had unique, increasing sequences. Runtime e2e: **1 passed**, 15.03s wall time.
- **Regression:** the original direct-send path failed destination-history persistence. The repaired handler-boundary suite passes **4 cases**: text, multiple media filenames, location-only content, and receipt-confirmed thread routing, each with replay and a subsequent append.
- **Focused checks:** Gateway handlers **78 passed**; outbound payload/action contracts **77 passed**; send/mirror/session-entry regression set **57 passed**; Zalo delivery consumer **3 passed**.
- **Build/static checks:** `pnpm build:runtime`, core and affected messaging/root/Gateway-method test typechecks, touched-file lint/format, `git diff --check`, and line-cap/test-line ratchets pass.
- **Independent review:** read-only OpenClaw reviewer using `openai/gpt-6.1-sol`, P0–P2 coverage of the complete local candidate against `e4f55593741ed56f9bac9196847bb079f25c8d75`; no production correctness findings. Its test-budget finding is addressed. Local Codex CLI/helper review was unavailable; this was a narrative subagent review, not helper-enforced isolation or structured attestation.

The change removes 86 net production lines against that base. Test growth is 529 lines: the handler payload/thread cases and separate-process resident-owner proof catch different failures. The 129-line allocation above the ordinary 400-line allowance records that necessity. The final fixture-only relocation into existing test support preserves coverage and passes the affected handler/type/lint checks.

Limits: platform and model endpoints are synthetic, not live Telegram or a paid provider. Local proof is not a cross-platform claim. Exact-head PR CI has since passed; captured output and the CI run are included below.

## Captured behavior proof (November 18, 2026)

These are excerpts from the retained local execution logs, not reconstructed expected output. Boilerplate, local filesystem paths, and unrelated diagnostics are omitted. All transport/model I/O used isolated synthetic loopback fixtures; no live provider or production state was used. The passing candidate was subsequently committed as `df590f89492ae62b5d20cf7438dcb5ddc7eaf501`; final fixture-only movement was separately validated.

The runtime test asserts the transport process is the resident Gateway, exactly one delivery/history row remains after same-key replay, and the actual subsequent user → tool call → tool result → assistant flow appends in unique increasing sequence order. The JSON above is emitted by that execution after its assertions.

### Exact-head CI

[CI run 44272834010](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44272834010) completed **successfully** for `df590f89492ae62b5d20cf7438dcb5ddc7eaf501` after maintainer approval. prs.title: fix(android): keep large file downloads from timing out after 20 seconds
prs.body:
Closes #193282

## What Problem This Solves

On Android, a file or audio attachment that takes longer than 20 seconds to download fails, even when data keeps arriving. The 20 second limit covers the whole call, including the body. Files can be up to 100 MB.

## User Impact

Large attachments open on slow links. A stalled download still fails after 20 seconds without a byte.

## Why This Change Was Made

The buffered download applies a fixed 20-second OkHttp read timeout. Each read gets the idle budget, so healthy transfers can continue past 20 seconds overall. A server that keeps sending occasional bytes can still hold the call open for a long time.

## Evidence

The regression uses the production `GatewaySession` download path, real OkHttp, and a local HTTP server.

- Healthy transfer: the server sends 24 chunks one second apart. The test requires byte-for-byte equality and an elapsed time over the original 20-second whole-call budget.
- Stalled transfer: the server sends 1 KiB, then waits 30 seconds before the second chunk. The test requires a `SocketTimeoutException` within 19.5–25 seconds.

| Run | Result |
| --- | --- |
| PR merge base `f7257f2c6688` with the revised regression | Healthy transfer fails during the response-body read with `InterruptedIOException: timeout` from OkHttp's whole-call timer. |
| Fixed code with the revised regression | All 21 tests in `GatewaySessionCustomHeadersTest` pass. The regression takes 43.2 seconds. |
| Android `:app:ktlintCheck` | Passes. |

The emulator evidence below is from the original PR revision, which used the same 20-second download read timeout. The follow-up removes the test-only constructor parameter and exercises the fixed policy directly.

### Real app run (Android 36 emulator, Gateway built from upstream main)

I built the play debug app from main and from this branch. A small proxy sits between the app and a real Gateway. It adds one chat message with a 30 MB `big-report.pdf` attachment and answers `artifacts.download` with a ticketed URL. It serves that URL at 1.2 MB/s, so the whole download takes about 26 seconds, but bytes arrive all the time. In the app I open Chat and tap **Open** on the file.

| Run | What the proxy log shows | What the app shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| main, 30 MB at 1.2 MB/s | `app closed the download connection after 22487040 bytes`, 20 s after the request | "Could not download. Try again or reconnect..." |
| this PR, same file and speed | `finished sending 31457280 bytes` (about 28 s) | the PDF viewer opens `big-report.pdf` |
| this PR, stalled link (1 KB, then nothing) | `app closed the download connection` 20 s after the request | the download fails after the 20 s idle limit |

The stalled case still fails fast on this PR, so the stall guard stays. The PDF viewer is blank because the proxy sends filler bytes, not a real PDF.

I did not use a real agent to send the file, because the test Gateway has no model. The proxy only supplies the attachment and the download. The app code that handles the tap, the `artifacts.download` call and the OkHttp download is the shipped code.

Screenshots (main, then this PR, then this PR with a stalled link):

| main, after 20 s | this PR, the file opens | this PR, stalled link |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ![main fails at 20 s](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jondihaynes/openclaw/proof-android-2026-11-04/media-download-timeout/main-slow-t37s.png) | ![this PR opens the file](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jondihaynes/openclaw/proof-android-2026-11-04/media-download-timeout/branch-slow-t45s.png) | ![stalled link still fails](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jondihaynes/openclaw/proof-android-2026-11-04/media-download-timeout/branch-stall-t45s.png) |

Recordings, proxy logs and the scripts are in [this folder](https://github.com/jondihaynes/openclaw/tree/proof-android-2026-11-04/media-download-timeout/): `rec-main-slow.mp4`, `rec-branch-slow.mp4`, `rec-branch-stall.mp4`.

prs.title: fix(agents): agents fail to reach another agent by its display name
prs.body:
Related: #140203

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: an agent cannot reach another agent when it uses that agent's display name instead of its agent id.

## User Impact

User impact: when an agent sends to or spawns a display name such as "Nova", the error now names the correct agent id. The agent retries with that id and the call succeeds.

`agents_list` now also shows `identity.name` when an agent has no `name`. With a spawn allowlist, agents see `main` as "Nova" and use `main` from the start.

Agent ids stay the only routing key. A display name never routes a call. No config or default changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Many setups keep the id `main` and give the agent a display name. Other agents know only the display name. They pass it as `agentId`, and the call fails with `Agent "Nova" not found`. Nothing in the error tells the agent the correct id.

The change adds one helper in `src/agents/identity.ts`. It finds the agent whose `name` or `identity.name` matches the unknown `agentId`. The match ignores case. The helper adds a hint only when exactly one reachable agent matches. Hidden or denied agents never appear in the hint.

- `sessions_send` adds the hint to both "not found" errors. The existing session access check decides which agents the requester can reach. That check reads `tools.agentToAgent`, the per-agent `tools.agentToAgent.send` list and `tools.sessions.visibility`.
- `sessions_spawn` adds the hint to the target policy error. The spawn allowlist decides which agents the requester can reach.
- `agents_list` and the Gateway agent list use one shared rule for the display name: `name`, then `identity.name`.

## Evidence

Live tests on a local Gateway with a real local model (Ollama `gemma4:12b`). Each setup uses an isolated home and two agents. `main` has `identity.name: "Nova"`. `mark` has no name. `tools.agentToAgent` allows `main` and `mark`. Each trial sends one message to `mark`.

### Round 1: no spawn allowlist

Message: "Ask Nova what 2+2 is. Use agents_list first, then sessions_send." `agents_list` lists only `mark` on both builds, because it lists spawn targets.

| Build | Trial | First `agentId` | Error text | Recovered |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| main `b0966db` | 1 to 3 | `nova` or `Nova` | `Agent "Nova" not found. Run openclaw agents list to see configured agents.` | No, 0 of 3 |
| This branch | 1 to 3 | `nova` or `Nova` | `Agent "Nova" not found. Did you mean agent id "main" (Nova)? Run openclaw agents list ...` | Yes, 3 of 3. The retry with `main` returned "4". |

![Before: main sends to nova and gets a plain not-found error](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jondihaynes/openclaw/proof/agents-list-identity-name/proof/agent-name-hint/before-main.png)

![After: the error names main and the model retries with main](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jondihaynes/openclaw/proof/agents-list-identity-name/proof/agent-name-hint/after-branch.png)

### Round 2: `mark` has `subagents.allowAgents: ["*"]`

| Scenario | Build | `agents_list` shows | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "Ask Nova ... use agents_list, then sessions_send" | main `b0966db` | `mark`, `main` | 0 of 3 recovered. Each send to `Nova` failed with the plain error. |
| same | This branch | `mark`, `main` named "Nova" | 3 of 3 sent to `main` on the first try and returned "4". No hint was needed. |
| "Start a sub-task on Nova using sessions_spawn" | main `b0966db` | `mark`, `main` | 0 of 2 reached `main`. One spawn to `Nova` failed. One model spawned a child of `mark` with no `agentId` and called that a success. |
| same | This branch | `mark`, `main` named "Nova" | 2 of 2 spawned on `main` on the first try. |
| "Use sessions_spawn with agentId Nova. Do not call agents_list." | main `b0966db` | not called | 0 of 3 recovered. Error: `agentId "nova" is not in the configured agent registry (allowed: main, mark)` |
| same | This branch | not called | 4 of 4 recovered. Error: `... (allowed: main, mark). Did you mean agent id "main" (Nova)?` The retry with `main` was accepted and returned "4". |
| "Use sessions_send with agentId Nova", with `mark.tools.agentToAgent.send: []` | This branch | not called | 3 of 3 got the plain error with no hint. `mark` cannot send to `main`, so the hint stays silent. |

In the send-denied trial that told the model to use `agents_list` first, the model never sent to "Nova". So it shows no hint result. The three direct send-denied trials above cover that case.

![Before: agents_list shows main without a name, and both sends fail](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jondihaynes/openclaw/proof/agents-list-identity-name/proof/agent-name-hint/base-agents-list-no-name.png)

![After: agents_list names main as Nova, and the model sends to main directly](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jondihaynes/openclaw/proof/agents-list-identity-name/proof/agent-name-hint/head-send-direct-to-main.png)

![After: two spawns fail, the hint names main, and the spawn on main succeeds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jondihaynes/openclaw/proof/agents-list-identity-name/proof/agent-name-hint/head-spawn-hint-recovery.png)

### Tests

Each new case fails without its fix and passes on this branch:

- `src/agents/tools/sessions.test.ts` "suggests only a sendable agent id": unique name and non-Latin name get the hint. A shared name, agent-to-agent messaging off, an empty per-agent `send` list and `self` visibility get no hint. An explicit `send` grant under `agent` visibility gets the hint.
- `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-target-policy.test.ts`: a hint for an allowed agent. No hint for an agent outside the allowlist.
- `src/agents/tools/agents-list-tool.test.ts`: `name` first, then `identity.name`.

Consumer tests pass: `src/gateway/agent-list.test.ts`, `src/agents/identity.test.ts`, `src/agents/openclaw-tools.subagents.sessions-spawn.allowlist.test.ts`, `src/agents/subagents/spawn/acp-spawn.test.ts` and `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn.test.ts`. `pnpm tsgo:core`, the `agents-tools` test typecheck lane, `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` pass on the changed files.

Gap: the hint reads names from config only. An agent with a name only in its workspace `IDENTITY.md` gets no hint. The Gateway agent list has the same limit.

prs.title: feat(gateway): connect approved trusted-proxy CLI and TUI devices within their grant
prs.body:
Related: #199692

Depends on #199698. This branch is stacked on it, so until #199698 merges the diff also shows its commits.

## What Problem This Solves

A device approved for fewer scopes than its client requests, such as a team guest approved for only `operator.sessions.write`, can't know its grant before it connects. Its first connection after approval therefore always files a scope-upgrade request, for scopes the admin already decided not to give.

## User Impact

User impact: with the new opt-in `gateway.auth.trustedProxy.narrowToDeviceGrant`, an approved CLI or TUI device behind the trusted proxy connects within its grant from the first connection. No upgrade request is filed and no audit entry is written. The TUI also keeps a device token, as the CLI already does. When named operator roles are enforced, a human operator identified by the proxy still receives no device token, as before; their CLI and TUI connect within the grant on every connection without storing it.

The option defaults to `false`, so existing Gateways behave exactly as before.

With the option on, `openclaw security audit` reports a new warn-level finding, because the TUI's token, like the CLI's, authenticates a direct Gateway connection without the proxy identity until the device is revoked.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Existing mechanism:** the Gateway already narrows a same-key scope upgrade to the paired grant, with no pairing request or audit entry, for browser and native UI clients when `trustedProxy.deviceAutoApprove` is enabled. This change gives that lane to CLI and TUI devices under its own option.

**Which connections it applies to:** same-key operator devices that authenticate through the trusted proxy and send no browser `Origin`. For those:
- A request that exceeds the grant connects with the intersection, and the hello reply reports the resulting scopes. That is how a newly approved device learns its grant.
- A connection never receives more than the grant. A request that includes `operator.admin` overlaps every grant, because admin implies every operator scope, so it connects within the grant.
- Only a request that shares no scope with the grant, such as `operator.pairing` alone against a session-only grant, still files the upgrade.
- Browser clients and new device enrollment are unchanged.

**TUI device token:** trusted-proxy auth treats the TUI like the Control UI and issued it no device token. Under the option it gets one, so it keeps the grant between runs. With the option off, its default, nothing changes. Named-role human operators stay tokenless either way.

**New audit finding:** `gateway.trusted_proxy_narrow_to_device_grant` (warn). `deviceAutoApprove` already reports a warn finding; this option reported nothing. The finding and `docs/gateway/trusted-proxy-auth.md` tell the admin to keep the proxy as the only Gateway ingress, and to remove a device with `openclaw devices remove <deviceId>` when its user's access ends.

**Config-surface budget, 2654 to 2655:** the option adds one boolean key, so the core count in `docs/.generated/config-baseline.counts.json` grows by exactly one. It has to be an option rather than a default because it changes which connections file upgrade requests and which clients hold device tokens; existing admins rely on both. No existing key fits: `deviceAutoApprove` also auto-approves new device enrollment, which an admin who only wants guests to stay within their grant should not have to accept. No other config is added.

**Docs:** `docs/gateway/trusted-proxy-auth.md` gains a section for the option, its config reference entry and the audit checklist line. The section says that the option is off by default and that named-role human operators get no device token. `docs/start/multiplayer.md` points guests' admins to it. `docs/cli/tui.md` marks the TUI's trusted-proxy behavior without a device token as the default and links the option.

## Evidence

- **Server tests:** in `src/gateway/server.auth.trusted-proxy-device-autoapprove.test.ts` 20/20:
  - An approved session-only TUI connects within its grant and receives a device token, with no pending request and no upgrade audit line.
  - The same holds for a CLI requesting `operator.read`, which connects with `operator.sessions.read`.
  - With the option off, the TUI still files the upgrade.
  - Without the Gateway change, the TUI and CLI cases fail; the option-off case passes on both.
- **Audit test:** `src/security/audit-gateway-exposure.test.ts` 27/27, with the finding present only when the option is on. Without the finding, the new case fails. `audit-gateway.test.ts` 8/8.
- **Config tests:** `zod-schema.gateway-auth.test.ts` 57/57, `doc-baseline.integration.test.ts` 10/10, `configure.gateway.test.ts` 16/16. Typecheck, lint and format are clean.
- **Rebased on current `main` with #199693's pairing hint:** this branch is now on `main` at `3a3eed8695e` and includes `5ce6d65f695` and `49d8da05cf6`, #199693's `openclaw gateway call` hint for an unpaired edgeAuth device, which keeps an explicit `--url`. `git range-diff 987c04a0086..465d5ab0c3c origin/main..1c9cb58e474` shows all ten commits unchanged except the regenerated config baseline hashes in the gateway commit (the core count is still 2654 to 2655). The live run below was made at `4cce58081cc`, before the restacks. On `1c9cb58e474`, after a clean install: `server.auth.trusted-proxy-device-autoapprove.test.ts` 20/20, `audit-gateway-exposure.test.ts` 27/27, `audit-gateway.test.ts` 8/8, `zod-schema.gateway-auth.test.ts` 57/57, `doc-baseline.integration.test.ts` 10/10, `configure.gateway.test.ts` 16/16, `call.edge-auth.test.ts` 6/6, `call.stored-grant-scopes.test.ts` 5/5, `call.test.ts` 91/91, `gateway-chat.connection.test.ts` 16/16, `client.approved-grant.test.ts` 3/3, typecheck clean, config baseline check and line-cap ratchet OK.
- **Live run** at `4cce58081cc` (built with `pnpm build:runtime`): a loopback Gateway with `gateway.auth.mode: "trusted-proxy"`, behind a small TLS proxy standing in for Cloudflare Access (it answers 302 unless the request carries `Cf-Access-Token`, then injects the identity headers). The guest config has only `gateway.remote.url` and `gateway.remote.edgeAuth`: no token, no password, no stored device token. `--tls-fingerprint` is there only because the test proxy uses a self-signed certificate. The output is trimmed, and IDs and ports are from throwaway test state. The admin approves only `operator.sessions.write`, and the Gateway has `narrowToDeviceGrant: true`. The branch includes #199693 and #199698, rebased on current `main`.

Then the Gateway host and both guests move to this head (`1c9cb58e474`) with the same state, run `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive`, and the admin sets `narrowToDeviceGrant: true`. guest2's first TUI start asks for the default scopes with no device token, connects within its grant with no upgrade request, and its second start and `gateway call` use the device token it received. guest1 keeps working with the token 2026.11.4 stored. prs.title: feat: offer Sign in with ChatGPT first when connecting OpenAI
prs.body:
Closes #201406

## What Problem This Solves

Someone connecting OpenAI for the first time is steered to Codex login. Codex login (device code) is the only OpenAI sign-in shown up front in first-run Model Setup and macOS onboarding, and the first OpenAI choice in `openclaw onboard`, Settings → Models and the Android app; Profile → Connected accounts and `openclaw models accounts login openai` list Codex browser login first. Codex login runs on the Codex backend, where the models a user sees depend on the Codex version OpenClaw reports. Sign in with ChatGPT uses the documented public OpenAI API for the same ChatGPT plan, but it sits under "More sign-in options" or below both Codex logins.

## User Impact

Every setup surface lists Sign in with ChatGPT first, with Codex login (device code) right after it and still shown up front, since it needs no localhost callback when the Gateway's browser runs on another machine:

- `openclaw onboard`, Settings → Models → Connect provider, macOS onboarding, the macOS/iOS chat sign-in sheet and Android: Sign in with ChatGPT, Codex login (device code), Codex login (browser), API key.
- First-run Model Setup: still alphabetical by provider, with a provider's options kept together, so OpenAI shows Sign in with ChatGPT and then Codex login (device code).
- Profile → Connected accounts and `openclaw models accounts login`: each provider's methods follow the same order as the other pickers; providers keep their order.
- The OpenAI docs list Sign in with ChatGPT first, and it is the first tab in Getting started.

Nothing changes for anyone already signed in:

- Saved profiles, routes, auth order and the selected model are untouched; there is no migration.
- `openclaw models auth login --provider openai` without `--method` still runs Codex browser login.
- `/login openai` and `/login codex` in chat still use Codex device code.
- Choosing the Codex runtime in setup (the detected "Codex" option, and automatic setup, which installs the Codex plugin) still signs in with Codex login.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pickers order sign-ins by the OpenAI manifest's `assistantPriority` and `onboardingFeatured`. Sign in with ChatGPT becomes featured with the lowest OpenAI priority; Codex device code stays featured right after it.

On main, two surfaces ignore that order. First-run Model Setup sorts its rows by label across providers, which puts "Codex login (device code)" under C, above "Sign in with ChatGPT" under S; it now sorts by provider and keeps each provider's rows in the Gateway's order. The Connected-accounts catalog lists methods in manifest order; it now orders each provider's methods by the same priority. The manifest order itself is unchanged, because saved Codex profiles from older releases are labeled by it.

Codex runtime setup must start Codex login even though it is not first, and option order or kind cannot tell which OpenAI choices are Codex login. Provider auth choices get an optional `agentRuntimeLogin` field (documented in the manifest reference). OpenAI sets it to `codex` on its two Codex login choices, and both Codex setup paths start the first marked choice.

The Control UI first-run card (automatic setup) still prepares Codex and offers Codex login. It moves to Sign in with ChatGPT together with the change that makes the OpenClaw harness the default for new installs.

## Evidence

Isolated Gateways with empty state and no credentials in a macOS VM, main (`6018bc9`) against this PR (`f5a3cd0`). Each pair uses the same page, viewport and crop. The Gateways sit behind a local identity proxy with a made-up person, so Profile → Connected accounts can render.

**First-run Model Setup** (`/settings/model-setup?firstRun=1`, the up-front sign-in section):

| main | this PR |
| --- | --- |
| ![First-run Model Setup on main: Codex login (device code) is the only OpenAI sign-in up front](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d22b7301ca1143ec24db19f73a3a911704ce4e47/images/2026/11/dbe3a900-0e84-4269-828b-b78f57e9eb2f.png) | ![First-run Model Setup with this PR: Sign in with ChatGPT, then Codex login (device code)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d22b7301ca1143ec24db19f73a3a911704ce4e47/images/2026/11/fc653aee-fd36-4322-8d29-469382155942.png) |

**Profile → Connected accounts → Add account → OpenAI → Sign-in method:**

| main | this PR |
| --- | --- |
| ![Connected accounts on main: Codex login (browser), Codex login (device code), Sign in with ChatGPT, OpenAI API Key](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d22b7301ca1143ec24db19f73a3a911704ce4e47/images/2026/11/599d9c50-fa18-412a-8afa-d641ec7c69e1.png) | ![Connected accounts with this PR: Sign in with ChatGPT, Codex login (device code), Codex login (browser), OpenAI API Key](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d22b7301ca1143ec24db19f73a3a911704ce4e47/images/2026/11/9e147ec1-c58d-4796-a02e-772130ba38e8.png) |

`openclaw models accounts login` reads the same catalog.

**Automatic setup still offers Codex login.** `openclaw.setup.auto` (what the Control UI first-run card calls) on empty Gateways installs the Codex plugin and returns `needs-sign-in` with `openai-device-code` ("Codex login (device code)") on both main and this PR. That run also goes through the detected-Codex setup path.

**An existing user keeps their login and model.** A user of the latest release (2026.11.5) with a saved Codex login and `openai/gpt-6-astra` selected; then this PR's build runs `doctor --fix` and the Gateway on the same state. Before and after are identical:
- the saved Codex login profile;
- the selected model `openai/gpt-6-astra`;
- setup reports setup complete, with the current model and "Saved Codex login (browser) sign-in".

The login is made up (synthetic tokens), written through the release's own OAuth credential writer. This runs the new build on the old state, as an update does after installing, without packaging the build for `openclaw update`; this PR changes nothing in update or Doctor. The automatic-setup and existing-user runs used `e8e97dd`, which differs from this head only in sign-in ordering and Codex device code's featured flag.

**Tests that fail without the fix:**
- Model Setup keeps a provider's sign-ins together in Gateway order: fails with label sorting.
- The Connected-accounts catalog orders methods by priority and keeps provider order: fails with manifest order.
- Codex setup selection: the automatic-setup tests list Sign in with ChatGPT first and an unmarked OpenAI device-code option ahead of Codex. With the old first-match rule 3 of 19 fail, with a device-code-only rule 5 of 19 fail, and with the marker all 19 pass.

A contract test loads the bundled manifests and checks that only `openai` and `openai-device-code` are marked as Codex login.

**Tests run (all pass):** OpenAI manifest, automatic setup, plugin contract registry, setup auth options, provider auth choices, login options, auth choice prompts, `/login` command, configure prompts, Codex setup authority, Model Setup view, page, first-run and state, Profile model accounts, account-connect worker, catalog and control plane. Core and UI typecheck, lint and format are clean.

**Not covered here:** a real Sign in with ChatGPT login.

prs.title: fix: redact known secrets from config-write errors
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A refused settings update can repeat a known secret embedded in the selected config path. Conflict responses bypass the diagnostic redaction already used by neighboring config-write errors.

## User Impact

User impact: config-write conflict diagnostics mask known secrets while retaining the refusal reason and appropriate recovery guidance. Permissions, write behavior, raw logs, and normal config-path visibility are unchanged. No migration or user action is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Apply the existing diagnostic redactor at the shared conflict-response owner. This is privacy hardening for trusted operators, not a new access-control boundary or a guarantee that paths are hidden.

## Evidence

- A real isolated Gateway/WebSocket regression fails on base a90c5419b779df517ea3c3ea0bee0b37e87f85ac because a registered synthetic secret reaches the response. With the fix, the secret is masked, the file stays unchanged, and useful nonretryable guidance remains.
- The regression and existing retryable/nonretryable controls pass: 3 tests. Regression time: 23.55s before, 22.96s after; fixed command including preparation: 76.38s.
- Separate core and gateway-server test-shard typechecks pass, as do focused lint, formatting, and git diff --check. No build/package boundary changed; no full build was run.
- The filesystem regression skips Windows because file symlinks require platform-specific privileges. No external provider calls were used.
- Independent native-agent source review at P0–P2 found no actionable findings in the complete transferred semantic change against base a90c5419b779df517ea3c3ea0bee0b37e87f85ac. The source owner/caller review was separate from implementation; tests were not independently rerun. Managed Auto Review failed with a missing handoff response file and produced no report; no Auto Review pass is claimed.

- Publication transfer verification: both changed source files match the tested implementation SHA-256 values exactly; the production owner, refusal producer, redactor and Gateway harness match between the implementation base and publishing checkout. The publishing checkout reran all 3 focused cases successfully (79.47s wrapper). Remote readback confirmed the original two-file redaction diff; the current branch additionally includes the separately attributed CI test correction below.

### Separate-process behavior proof

Executed the published head 70e877ac9038435b01d5370f6c166cd0d8e734d3 and baseline b413b8e1966780121c211abbf3f91adb5c173afa in separate compiled Gateway processes, with actual authenticated WebSocket requests through production GatewayClient. This is distinct from the committed in-process regression. The synthetic credential became known through normal gateway.auth.token environment SecretRef resolution: no test-only redaction-registry injection or mocked config handlers.

Sanitized observation summary from the retained process/RPC/file receipts:

```text
                         base b413b8e       head 70e877ac
separate Gateway process true               true
authenticated RPC        succeeded          succeeded
ordinary write on disk   debug              debug
config.patch marker      present            absent
config.set marker        present            absent
config.apply marker      present            absent
all refusal codes        INVALID_REQUEST    INVALID_REQUEST
recovery guidance        retained           retained
inappropriate retry      absent             absent
all refusal target bytes unchanged          unchanged
repaired-path write      info persisted     info persisted
owned process cleanup    confirmed          confirmed
```

The client verified target bytes independently with SHA-256 before and after each refused write. The head target retained hash 81f1b404bb150a74cc5a688d9746d0dc4b1462451da891572e6f723294ff584f. Both process scenarios exited 0: baseline 4.076s and head 4.616s, excluding preparation. Successful writes before refusal and after restoring the regular file demonstrate that authorized functionality still works. Both owned Gateway processes terminated and cleanup was independently checked.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction and evidence binding</summary>

From the exact-source detached worktree, the same private scratch driver launches the repository's separately compiled Gateway harness and uses the real production bootstrap:

```sh
PROOF_EXPECT_MASKED=1 \
PROOF_SOURCE_HEAD=70e877ac9038435b01d5370f6c166cd0d8e734d3 \
PROOF_OUTPUT_DIR=<owned-private-output> \
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
  src/gateway/server.config-conflict-process-proof.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

The baseline uses PROOF_EXPECT_MASKED=0 and its full SHA above. Identical driver SHA-256: bce7809fe4f4e4b942452999eed9b5ad749a690fdc676d94cb956193d71cef81. Compiler manifests bind executed config-response source to each clean tracked checkout; only the untracked proof driver differs from the tracked source. Private receipt SHA-256 values: head 82350a84c1753ae4cd096523267ffe61c4d03e33b0b3efba2787803a5494da37; baseline 0bcc1afcd9e6759a088652a102bb9cb8a1bb4a0e468e5e39f311b894652a5e31. These identify retained local evidence, not independently hosted attestations.

No credentials, raw logs, private endpoints, external model calls or production state are included here. This qualifies the source-built Linux separate-process behavior, not packaged-release or Windows behavior. Initial dependency/schema setup attempts did not produce behavioral verdicts; disposable proof installations resolved them without reinstalling shared dependencies. The redaction production source and regression remain unchanged by the later CI-only test correction; this process proof retains its exact original head binding.

</details>

### CI correction and current-head qualification

At Mitchell's request to make this PR's CI pass, this branch now includes the exact existing test-only correction from [d9c6e7fafa39](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/d9c6e7fafa396cba683eaecf63299f12dcfccd73), developed with @vincentkoc in [#201502](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201502). No recall-production changes from that PR are included.

The stale assertion expected a named-role change to cancel an already-admitted inventory. #201334 deliberately fixes role policy for that request. The corrected case verifies both halves: the admitted request returns its permitted rows, and a fresh request excludes the newly forbidden row and transcript. Existing cancellation, draft, lifecycle, physical-store and disclosure-negative controls remain intact. No production authority, permission, skip, ignore or retry policy changed.

- Full corrected privacy file: 14/14 passed; role-policy and run-authority controls: 51/51 passed (65 total, 66s wall).
- Agents-tools test typecheck, targeted typed lint, formatting and diff checks passed.
- Local proof ran on b413b8e1966780121c211abbf3f91adb5c173afa plus the exact canonical test delta; that test and its inspected owners match the previously tested CI base. It is not labeled a new hosted-CI pass.
- The published update b67090700ab75e9426eeadb369d3255d76a60b3f changes only that test (+9/-4); its corrected file blob is 9144eaaba24a0fc8073093834a068ca7cfe68e95, identical to the canonical correction. The redaction production file and redaction regression are byte-identical to the reviewed/proven version.
- Current-head [CI run 44436325601](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44436325601) passed on b67090700ab75e9426eeadb369d3255d76a60b3f. The [canonical CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44436325601/job/135270868105) completed successfully at 01:33 UTC on November 19; its complete log confirms all selected jobs succeeded, with RELEASE_FAST_LANE=false and ALLOW_KNOWN_MAIN_RED=false. Unselected platform jobs remain explicitly skipped. The prior failure below is historical. The separate-process redaction evidence remains bound to 70e877ac, with unchanged production/proof inputs, rather than being relabeled as a rerun at the new commit.

### Prior-head CI failure attribution

The previous-head [checks-node-changed job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44422618807/job/135220019573) failed in the unchanged sessions-list role-enrichment test, and its dependent CI gate was red. Those results are retained as prior-head evidence.

The test ran on merge 7dc0e3ce13576fb9d339045accecaf3956858baf, whose parents are main 07baab52b4147001e9b6060ea4371d383aabd683 and PR head 70e877ac9038435b01d5370f6c166cd0d8e734d3. Its delta from main is only this PR's two files. An independent bounded control on canonical main ancestor b413b8e1966780121c211abbf3f91adb5c173afa reproduced the same line-328 “promise resolved instead of rejecting” assertion in src/agents/tools/sessions-list-privacy.test.ts (1 failed, 13 deselected; 55s). That test and its five inspected session/role-authority owners are byte-identical across the control, CI base and tested merge. The failure occurs without the redaction change. The subsequent test-only correction above reuses the canonical repair; no blind CI rerun was used.

Limits: this is source-equivalence plus a focused ancestor control, not a full exact-base/shard replay. The repository failure classifier could not run because its gh executable was unavailable. The retained CI log is a bounded tail.

Contributor credit: Mitchell Etzel. The CI expectation correction is reused from @vincentkoc’s existing work in #201502.

prs.title: fix: preserve subagent outcomes across Gateway interruptions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A Gateway restart can interrupt a completion-required subagent and silently retire its outcome, especially when the requester has already finished its turn. Separately, a transient failure before a direct completion is consumed can leave its input cancelled, making the scheduled retry fail permanently against the same input.

## User Impact

User impact: requesters receive the interrupted child's “Gateway stopped” outcome after startup, and direct completions can retry transient failures before consumption. Intentional Stop and already-completed work retain their existing replay protection. No configuration or schema changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Shutdown now uses the existing terminal completion owner instead of intentional quiet-kill settlement. It captures the error and defers cleanup, preserving the required delivery obligation through restart. Direct completion turns now use the same processing receipts and safe cancelled-input retry as private and batched completions.

The production change is seven net lines: an explicit error outcome with deferred cleanup, and inclusion of direct completions in the existing receipt classification. No new retry loop, cache, or state owner. Requester-run turnover and source-owner guards are handled separately in #195275 and are untouched here.

Related: #198905, #199488, #199868, #201460, #195275.

## Evidence

Real-Gateway restart regressions fail on the exact base and pass with this change: a running child reports its shutdown error to both a yielded requester and an already-finished requester; a recovered completion survives a transient access-policy failure and reaches the requester on retry. The assertions require the actual child outcome, so a generic restart prompt cannot satisfy them.

244 lifecycle/worker/restart-collector tests and 74 Gateway receipt, queued-registration and swarm-close tests pass. All 18 real-Gateway restart and completion-custody cases pass, including announcement crashes, private completions, busy requesters and stale settle wake recovery. `pnpm check:changed` passes, and isolated Codex review is clean through P2. Synthetic scale proof uses a 43.35 GiB database, 10,800 sessions, 4,300 runs and 62,000 files (1.116 GB), on APFS. Five interleaved A/A/B timing groups give shutdown-owner wall medians of 628/652/650 ms and CPU medians of 970/981/1002 ms; the unchanged A/A controls include a 1767 ms outlier, so no speedup is claimed. Three separate allocation-sampling groups show main-isolate allocation of 14.54/14.56/18.00 MB, about 24% extra for preserving canonical completion custody. Every candidate run retains 16/16 required outcomes; both base controls retain 0/16. Imports, fixture setup and hydration are outside timing. Allocation excludes worker heaps; CPU includes workers. This measures terminal settlement, not total restart downtime or btrfs behavior. The committed probe reproduces the measurement.

The generic historical “agent run aborted” message alone does not identify its aborting predicate. This change fixes the independently reproduced obligation and retry defects; it does not claim to establish that historical predicate.

## CI attribution

Exact-head CI run [44431185416](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44431185416) has one inherited failure: `src/gateway/chat-goal-created-authority.e2e.test.ts` times out waiting for provider cancellation after `users.setRole`. It reproduces on CI’s exact main parent `b7bf9150fa20bfe93cfe6a64b79c4f0f5ec4ce4e`. The unchanged test passes on `b400e8deed133ac0fa084072424fe1285f162952` and fails on its immediate successor `ad550e953a9bcd81a424de087afed5823454ec97` (#201377). That change fixes authority for an admitted recovered continuation but leaves this test expecting mid-request role revocation. This is a main test-contract regression requiring follow-up, not dismissed as noise. This PR changes neither the failing test nor its recovery-authority owner. All other CI jobs pass or skip, including security-fast; all 18 restart cases also pass in CI. Local focused proof and `pnpm check:changed` are green. ClawSweeper’s final-head review has zero findings and zero open items. Landing uses the explicitly authorized inherited-failure exception; CI is not described as fully green.

prs.title: fix(gateway): work started by a cron run dies when the parent run ends
prs.body:
Closes #185961

## Decision for maintainers: cron reassignment

**Behavior change:** with this PR, children spawned by a cron-root run keep running after the parent run returns, **including when that cron job is later reassigned or deleted**. Today they die when the parent returns, whether or not anything was reassigned. That is the reported bug, and the reason the issue asks where the child's lifetime should start.

- Children still stop on `/stop`, on aborting the parent with its descendants, and on a reset of the requesting session (the existing requester-wide subagent cleanup), the same as children of a main session.
- The cron root's own session stays fenced, which is what #161085 protects: a child writes only to its own session, and its completion report runs as a new run in the cron key with its own fresh fence.
- If children should also stop when the cron job is reassigned, each child would need to hold a cron-root lease for its whole life. This PR does not add that; I'm happy to follow up if you prefer that design.

Jobs a cron-root run starts with the cron tool (`action: "run"`, second fix below) need no decision: the started job is admitted as its own cron run in the cron run queue, and an isolated job runs in its own `:run:` session, which takes no cron-root lease or request fence. Dropping the caller's fence only stops the job inheriting a fence that ends with the caller's run; it changes no lifetime policy.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: work started by a run in a cron job's base session (`agent:<id>:cron:<job>`) fails with "Guarded request authority is no longer active" once that run ends:

- sub-agents it spawns die, and their completion reports never reach the cron session;
- a job it starts with the cron tool (`action: "run"`) that outlives the tool's wait (60 s by default) fails on its first provider request after the parent returns.

## User Impact

User impact: children spawned from a cron-root run keep working after the parent run returns, and their results are delivered back to the cron session, the same as children of a main-session run. Jobs a cron-root run starts with the cron tool finish normally even when the parent run ends first.

## Why This Change Was Made

A stable cron root fences its own provider requests for the life of its run (#161085): the run's prompt executes inside `withGuardedFetchRequestAuthority`, which marks the fence inactive when the run returns. `sessions_spawn` runs inside that prompt and launches the child through the in-process `agent` dispatch. The child's queued work captures the async context, so the child, and later its completion-report turn, inherit the parent's fence and fail on their first provider request after the parent returns.

The in-process `agent` handoff (`withInProcessGatewayDispatch`) already starts accepted autonomous runs outside two caller-owned scopes, the caller's transcript writer and its operator tool authority, because they "must not retain the caller's … authority after that invocation closes". This change adds the caller's request fence to that list, through `runOutsideGuardedFetchRequestAuthority` in `fetch-request-authority.ts`. The child then establishes its own fences when it runs, like any other run.

The cron job launch (`launchCronRunQueueResult` in `src/cron/service/run-queue.ts`) has the same gap: it already drops the caller's operator tool authority because "the launch owns its lifetime beyond the request acknowledgement", but a `cron.run` from a cron-root run's tool call launches the job inside that run's fence. The launch now also starts outside the caller's request fence, through the same helper; the job then sets up its own fence when its agent turn runs.

The request store can also carry a per-request egress check (`beforeRequest`). A run installs it only around its own provider stream call (`attempt-stream-settle.ts`), not while tools execute, so none is active when `sessions_spawn` hands off and none is dropped.

## Evidence

On unchanged `main`, both the mock-model Gateway runs and the live runs with a real Anthropic model show the reporter's exact error chain: the child's next provider request fails with "Guarded request authority is no longer active", the completion-report turn into the cron session fails with the same error, and the Gateway logs `Subagent announce give up (permanent_failure)`. With this change, the child finishes and its report reaches the cron session in both.

### Gateway regression (built Gateway process, local mock model)

`test/gateway-cron-root-subagent-spawn.e2e.test.ts` (new, one case) starts the built Gateway with a local OpenAI Responses mock. An `agent` request on `agent:main:cron:child-lifetime` spawns one child with `sessions_spawn`; the child's provider replies are held until the parent's `agent` request has returned. The case requires the child's second provider request and the report turn into the cron session to both arrive. Tool search is off so `sessions_spawn` is a direct tool, as in the existing `cron-isolated-spawn-only-child-delivery` QA scenario. Unchanged `main`, Gateway log (ids shortened):

```
[diagnostic] lane task error: lane=subagent:agent:main:cron:proof-job error="Guarded request authority is no longer active." taskKind=spawn sessionKey=agent:main:subagent:3966…
[diagnostic] lane task error: lane=main error="Guarded request authority is no longer active." taskKind=turn sessionKey=agent:main:cron:proof-job runId=announce:v1:…
[agents/subagent-announce] Subagent completion direct announce failed for run e0da64e0… err={"name":"GatewayClientRequestError","message":"Guarded request authority is no longer active.",…}
[warn] Subagent announce give up (permanent_failure) run=e0da64e0… requester=agent:main:cron:proof-job
```

Mock-model Gateway runs of this scenario: unchanged `main` failed 4 of 4 with the chain above (the child never reaches the model); with this change 9 of 9 passed. Those counts come from a longer local version of the test; the committed case is that scenario trimmed to its core assertions (the committed case waits on the child's own run with `agent.wait`: on unchanged `main` it fails as soon as that run ends with `status: "error"`, 1 of 1; with this change it passes 2 of 2 in about 20 s).

### Live run (real Anthropic model)

Same built Gateway with `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5`, reached through a local recording proxy that holds the child's first reply until the parent's `agent` request has returned. The parent was asked to spawn one child and reply `SPAWNED`. The child was asked to read a file and reply `LIVE-CHILD-OK`. Three runs on each side, cron key `agent:main:cron:live-child-lifetime`: `main` failed 3 of 3 as below; with this change 3 of 3 completed and delivered the report (in two of them the child answered with a sentence instead of the exact marker word, but its run finished and the report arrived). Excerpts from the first pair:

Unchanged `main`: the model's reply to the child's first request (a `read` call) arrives, then the child's second request fails inside the Gateway before it leaves, and the report turn fails on the fence:

```
response role=parent tools=[sessions_spawn] … response role=parent text="SPAWNED"
parent run returned status=ok
response role=child status=200 tools=[read]
[model-fetch] error provider=liveproxy api=anthropic-messages model=claude-sonnet-5-5 elapsedMs=0 sessionKey="agent:main:subagent:4f9c…" requestNumber=2
[diagnostic] lane task error: lane=main error="Guarded request authority is no longer active." taskKind=turn sessionKey=agent:main:cron:live-child-lifetime runId=announce:v1:…
[warn] Subagent announce give up (permanent_failure) … requester=agent:main:cron:live-child-lifetime
```

With this change:

```
parent run returned status=ok
response role=child status=200 tools=[read]
response role=child status=200 text="LIVE-CHILD-OK"
response role=report status=200 text="The live-child task finished successfully and returned exactly LIVE-CHILD-OK. …"
[agent] run announce:v1:agent:main:subagent:1978…:b355… ended with stopReason=stop
```

No "Guarded request authority" line in that Gateway log.

### Job started with the cron tool (one-off Gateway run, not committed)

Same built Gateway and mock model. A cron-root `agent` run creates a job with the cron tool and starts it with `action: "run"` and a 1 s wait; the mock holds the job's provider replies until the parent's `agent` request has returned. Unchanged `main`, the job's `cron` `finished` event, 62 ms after the parent returned:

```
{"action":"finished","status":"error","completionStatus":"failed","error":"Guarded request authority is no longer active.",…}
```

With this change the job finishes with `status: "ok"` after two provider requests, 5 of 5 runs (about 17 to 20 s each, mostly Gateway startup). This stays out of the committed tests: the unit case below covers the same contract without a second Gateway boot.

**Unit (cron launch):** `src/cron/service.run-queue.test.ts` › `starts a manual run outside its caller's request fence` runs `cron.run(id, "force")` inside a request fence and requires the job runner to see none. It fails on `main` (the runner sees the caller's fence) and passes here.

**Agent handoff:** this was an extra assertion in the existing launch case of `server-plugin-in-process-dispatch.authorization.test.ts`. `main` removed that whole suite in #198943 (consolidating redundant coverage), so the case left with it. The handoff stays covered end to end by the Gateway case below, whose spawned child crosses that dispatch boundary and fails on `main` without this change.

**Consumers:** 17 related test files (every `server-plugin-in-process-dispatch.*` suite, `server-plugin-subagent-runtime*`, `subagent-spawn.in-process-gateway`, `subagent-announce-completion-delivery`, `fetch-guard.authority`, `attempt-execution-phase`): 164 of 164 pass. One fork-transport timeout under a loaded host passed 3 of 3 on rerun; that test reads through `sessions.get`, not the changed `agent` path. For the cron launch: `src/cron/service` and `service.run-queue.test.ts`, 536 of 537 pass on current `main` plus this PR; the one failure (`ops.gateway-mutations.test.ts` › `leaves durable state unchanged when its caller is revoked during validation`, a 10 s `cron.add` timeout) fails the same way on unchanged `main`, 3 of 3.

Test lines are net +139 against `main`, within the per-PR allowance (the earlier allocation record is removed): one root-cause unit test that reuses `service.run-queue.test.ts`'s service and command-job helpers (+26, fails on `main`) plus one Gateway case (113 lines, which also waits for the report's committed chat event and checks it in the cron session's `chat.history`, reusing the shared Gateway test-instance and mock-model helpers) for the report turn into the cron session, which no unit layer reaches; ClawSweeper's review of the issue asked for exactly this regression. The Gateway case takes about 22 s, mostly Gateway startup; the cron-tool path is shown by a one-off Gateway run in the body instead of a second committed Gateway case.

After merging current `main` on 18 Nov (`16c28ff6acc`): #177296 wrapped the autonomous `agent` dispatch in `withoutGatewayToolCallerIdentity`; the merge nests it inside this change's `runOutsideGuardedFetchRequestAuthority`. On an isolated Linux test machine `service.run-queue.test.ts` and the Gateway case pass, and `pnpm check:changed` passes in full.

**Stopping a detached child** (existing coverage, rerun on this change): `subagent-control.accepted-stop.test.ts`, `subagent-control.commands.test.ts` and `subagent-announce.requester-settle-cancel.test.ts` pass (92 tests with the launch test). Locally, aborting the child (`sessions.abort`) or resetting the cron root (`sessions.reset`) after the parent returns stopped the child before its next provider request (2 of 2 each; the child sent no further request).

**Operator revocation** (one-off proof run, not committed): the cron-root parent was started by an operator connected with its own device. After the parent returned, an admin revoked that device's operator token (`device.token.revoke`), then the held child was released. 2 of 2 runs on this change; the child never reached the provider:

```
02:42:55.560 [gateway] device token revoked device=8483… role=operator
02:42:55.582 [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=subagent:agent:main:cron:child-lifetime error="Session turn no longer owns controller admission" taskKind=spawn runId=100e39c3…
agent.wait → {"status":"error","stopReason":"rpc","providerStarted":false}; provider requests from the child: 0
```

**Checks:** `pnpm check:changed` on the change: typecheck, format, lint, line-cap, test-line, assertion and mock ratchets pass. Its remaining failures do not involve this change: Knip reports unused exports in untouched files (`extensions/knowledge/src/conversation-access-view.ts`, `src/gateway/worker-environments/workspace-manifest-comparison.ts`, `src/state/openclaw-agent-execution-cleanup.ts`), and the SQLite worker ratchet could not run on the test host (`rg` missing).

Proof artifice: the Gateway runs use a local mock OpenAI Responses server (or, for the live run, a recording proxy in front of the real model) that holds the child's or job's replies until the parent's `agent` request has returned; operator revocation was triggered by an admin call; unit tests run inside a hand-made request fence.

Not tested: a cron job woken by `sessions_send`, and the CLI-runtime (`claude-cli`) parent path. Both reach the child through the same `agent` handoff. For the cron-tool path: a started job whose target is the main session (it queues behind the caller's turn, so on `main` it always starts after the fence has closed; the change covers it the same way, but no run shows it), `runMode: "due"`, and a real model.

Follow-up, not in this PR: `runOutsideOperatorToolGatewayAuthority` has other callers. Chat dispatch, channel startup and plugin services start with no request fence. Session maintenance can run inside a cron-root turn; whether its work can outlive that turn is not traced here.
