prs.title: fix: report the same cancellation when a queued steer is replayed
prs.body:
Related: #200533, #176084, #201094

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Discussion, implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/813619ca-7b77-4818-841b-a84729db8e92) — follow-up for the two CI blockers below.

## What Problem This Solves

After a CLI caller successfully cancels a queued steer, resending its message ID can return a cached abort response or say the input was cancelled because it failed. The response depends on when the Gateway finishes writing the cancellation receipt.

## User Impact

A withdrawn steer now reports the same cancellation on replay, including while the receipt is still being written. The original turn continues and the caller can send the message again with a new ID.

## Why This Change Was Made

An exact `chat.abort` targeting an injecting chat input records `user-stop` for that chat. Replay checks the durable cancellation first, then the admitted cancellation for the same chat, ahead of the response cache. The separate `userInitiated` presentation flag retains its existing meaning.

The follow-up also fixes two stale tests after #201334. Losing access rejects the next admission, but does not cancel already-started work. A stale Stop connection still closes without cancelling that turn. These test fixes do not change production authorization.

## Evidence

- The original pre-cleanup regression returned `in_flight`. With the fix, replay reports `INVALID_REQUEST` with `chat-input-cancelled` and `user-stop`, both before and after durable settlement. All six steer FIFO cases passed in [hosted CI on the original fix](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44389272826/job/135103170380); the steer runtime and regression are unchanged in the follow-up.
- Both stale device assertions failed on bare `main` and in the incoming PR merge. The cross-device test waited 90 seconds for an abort that should not happen. After correction, 80 focused tests passed on `2394fca92d6a57`, and the isolated real Gateway product test passed in 19.8 seconds on identical code. Independent source review found no remaining findings.
- Prior [session-identity ratchet](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44389272826/job/135103169655), [first failure on an unrelated PR](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44257752988/job/134644348510), and [hosted CI for the reviewed follow-up](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44434872778).

prs.title: fix: avoid full sandbox checkouts when lockfiles change
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Starting a sandboxed session after a lockfile change rebuilds the entire source template, even when a valid prepared generation is available. A three-file commit can therefore write more than a gigabyte of unchanged source before the session starts.

## User Impact

Lockfile changes now use the same independent-generation refresh as other source changes. Unchanged source and dependencies are cloned with copy-on-write sharing; installation still runs against the selected frozen lockfile. Existing readers retain their original generation. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The sandbox caller already supplies refresh, retains commits, and permits refresh while readers use the previous generation. Its callback nevertheless rejects any changed `pnpm-lock.yaml` before cloning. Remove that redundant rejection and let the existing installer reconcile dependencies. Attribute changes still rebuild because checkout transforms can affect unchanged blobs. Production delta: **−2 lines**, with no new cache, state owner, or option.

## Evidence

The owner regression fails on the parent: a three-file advance rewrites all six fixture files. The fix writes three, avoids another `createTemplate`, keeps the previous generation's HEAD and lockfile intact while a reader holds it, installs updated dependencies, and preserves attribute-triggered rebuilds. **53 focused tests pass** across template, checkout, custody, and retained-generation suites (146.5 s wrapper wall; the changed owner suite remains in its existing worker-backed integration shard).

Native Linux/Btrfs proof uses 62,000 payload files (~1.1 GB), a three-file commit, 5,000 retained dependency files, and an independent physically allocated 35 GiB synthetic SQLite file with 5,000 rows. Two A/A controls precede five serial counterbalanced pairs. Acceptance: source content writes scale with changed files, old generations remain intact, and selected source/dependency output remains correct.

| Git checkout metric | Before median / p95 | After median / p95 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `wchar` | 1,105,978,742 / same B | 5,977,063 / same B |
| Charged `write_bytes` | 1,299,126,623 / 1,299,896,671 B | 6,038,223 / same B |
| Write syscalls | 124,086 / same | 93 / same |
| Wall | 4.717 / 6.186 s | 0.167 / 0.229 s |
| CPU | 2.587 / 3.276 s | 1.924 / 2.069 s |

All 81.92 MB of retained dependency data remains shared with zero exclusive bytes. Native refresh reports zero content rescans and preserves the sampled unchanged file's stat identity inside its new snapshot. Git still traverses and serializes the whole index; this eliminates unchanged source-content writes, not every O(tree) operation. A/A checkout controls were 9.556/3.642 s, so timings show substantial storage variability; byte counts are deterministic. Five samples make nearest-rank p95 the maximum.

Full-owner APFS runs use real sandboxed pnpm and include manifest preparation and the final session clone. Two A/A controls precede five counterbalanced pairs; all verify source, installed local dependency, and source-derived hook output.

| Full-owner metric | Before median / p95 | After median / p95 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Lock advance wall | 13.152 / 22.935 s | 13.431 / 15.897 s |
| Lock advance process CPU | 2.204 / 2.767 s | 2.162 / 2.289 s |
| Lock advance main-thread allocation | 63.384 / 70.566 MB | 63.968 / 77.537 MB |
| Same-commit wall | 1.752 / 3.947 s | 1.714 / 1.889 s |
| Same-commit main-thread allocation | 6.995 / 11.065 MB | 10.148 / 12.174 MB |

Full-owner median latency is effectively flat (+2.1%); the demonstrated benefit is lower write volume, not a general startup-speed claim. A/A lock-advance controls were 17.188/14.689 s. Process CPU excludes external Git/Docker/guest CPU; allocation covers only the main thread. Seed medians also varied despite identical cold-build code (33.878/24.135 s), reinforcing the timing limit. Same-commit allocation increased by 3.15 MB median; a separate resumed-process CPU/heap profile found the unchanged cache-hit path mostly idle, with sampled retained allocations in shared state/worker/process infrastructure. That profile does not causally explain the total allocation difference; it remains a reported measurement limitation. No hidden samples or extra cache were introduced. The Btrfs probe isolates the Git sequence and storage occupancy, not concurrent Gateway traffic. Its first cleanup exposed an open synthetic SQLite handle after all samples completed; the workload now closes it explicitly, and the container, loop reference, and backing image were cleaned up.

Reproduction: `scripts/perf/sandbox-template-commit-measure.ts --lock-change` and `scripts/perf/sandbox-template-git-refresh-measure.py --lock-change --database-gib 35`, using the documented synthetic fixture and frozen owner modules. No production data is used.

Local validation: `pnpm check:changed` completed all constituent gates; its initial formatting and test-resource naming failures were corrected and the targeted format/core-lint checks pass. All type, unused-export, script-lint, boundary, schema, and import-cycle gates passed. The final held-reader regression was rerun after cleanup changes (pass, 25.83 s wrapper wall). Independent Codex autoreview of the full local diff plus the unchanged checkout, installer, cache, filesystem, and Git-pack owners is **scoped-clean through P2**. Hosted Codex review completed on `89c678a` with no findings. Exact-head [CI run 44431986964](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44431986964) passed. [ClawSweeper final-head review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201546#issuecomment-6996454303) reports zero findings and zero open items. Landed through `scripts/pr` as `895091c987878103a8d76b5de3db004e691fe831`.

prs.title: fix: let remote Codex app-servers use library skills instead of an unreadable Gateway path
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

With a remote Codex app-server (`appServer.remoteWorkspaceRoot`), the skills list shown to the model gives each Skill Library skill a location in the Gateway's state directory (`<state>/skill-library/<id>/revisions/<rev>/SKILL.md`). The model reads skills with Codex's own file tools on the remote machine, where that path does not exist, so the read fails and the skill is silently not followed.

## User Impact

User impact: on a remote Codex app-server, library skills are listed with a pointer to `skills_read` (which reads the pinned revision on the Gateway) instead of a path the model cannot open. When `skills_read` is not offered, library skills stay listed by name and description with a note that their instructions cannot be read on this machine, instead of a broken path. Local app-servers (a child of the Gateway) and every other placement are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Codex extension passes the core skills catalog through as is. When the app-server is remote, it now finds the Skill Library entries by name (from the snapshot's resolved skills) and replaces their `<location>` line with a `<location_note>`: one that names `skills_read`, or, without `skills_read`, one that says the instructions cannot be read on this machine.

Library skills that a remote-exec placement has already copied into the worker workspace keep their location: the snapshot lists them at that copy, under `remoteWorkspaceRoot`, where the app-server can read them.

Entries are matched by name, not by path: the rendered catalog shows home-compacted paths (`~/.openclaw/...`) while the snapshot keeps canonical ones. The change adjusts the rendered catalog rather than re-rendering it, because the catalog is built and budgeted in core before the harness runs; re-rendering it in the extension would duplicate that budget and path compaction.

Without `skills_read` the options were inlining each SKILL.md body, dropping the entry, or keeping it with a note. Inlining would read every pinned body from Gateway disk on every turn (the catalog keeps only a content hash) and grow the prompt with instructions the turn may never use. Dropping hides a skill the user pinned. The note is one line per entry and tells the model, and through it the user, why the skill cannot be followed. Other skill sources keep their locations.

Accepted limits: only SKILL.md is reachable this way. Supporting files of a library skill are still not delivered to a remote app-server; that would need a copy step and is left for a follow-up.

## Evidence

A new fake app-server test runs a full attempt with a library skill and a workspace skill and checks the developer instructions sent on `thread/start`, for a remote app-server with `skills_read`, a remote one without it, a remote one whose library skill was already copied into its workspace (no `skills_read`), and a local one. The catalog in the test shows the library skill at a home-compacted path while the snapshot keeps the canonical path, as production snapshots do. (The production snapshot builder is core code that extension tests cannot import without a new SDK export, so the test reproduces its output shape.)

- With the fix: all four cases pass; the existing skill-read bridge tests (`dynamic-tool-skills.test.ts`) still pass.
- On `main`, and on this PR's first head (which matched by path), the two Gateway-path remote cases fail (the compacted Gateway path is still listed). On the previous head (which rewrote every library entry), the copied-skill case fails (its readable location was replaced by the note).
- `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` on the touched files, `pnpm tsgo:extensions` and `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test`: clean.

<details><summary>Commands</summary>

Run on a remote test VM from a snapshot of `main` (c5ef395ba72) plus this change:

```
CI=true pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.remote-skills.test.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-skills.test.ts --maxWorkers=1   # 7 passed
git checkout HEAD~1 -- extensions/codex/src/app-server/attempt-context.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt-context.ts
CI=true pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt.remote-skills.test.ts --maxWorkers=1   # fails on main and on earlier heads, see above
```

</details>

This patch has not been run against a live remote app-server and model. The problem itself on a real install, with the catalog listing the Gateway path, `cat` failing with ENOENT on the remote machine, and `skills_read` by name working once the tool is allowed: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw-enterprise/pull/6509#issuecomment-6994445016

prs.title: fix(exec): let owner-started background commands schedule follow-ups when they finish
prs.body:
Related: #177510

## What Problem This Solves

A background command started by an owner can finish, wake the same chat, and then be refused when it tries to create a follow-up automation. Another human message was needed to restore the owner's authority.

## User Impact

Owner-started commands can schedule follow-ups from their completion turns without another message. Non-owner commands, other chats, and unrelated system events do not acquire owner authority.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Continue the starting turn's owner decision under its captured operator source and tool restrictions; command output remains untrusted.
- Bind that continuation to the same chat key, preserving the continuation contract from #200191. Transcript rotation during compaction does not change ownership.
- Remove the added transcript-ID reset fence: transcript IDs identify physical storage, not chats. Existing chat-key admission and lease mechanisms govern occurrence lifetime. Goal successors keep only live requester/operator authority, independent of the settled completion event, preserving #187069. Ownership revocation is still checked before execution and tool effects.
- Preserve existing scheduler, hook, and durable-restart behavior. This addresses the owner-only gate, not general `toolsBySender` matching in the related issue.

## Evidence

- Stock source with the regression test: 1 failed, 3 passed. Patched requester/same-chat tests: 5 passed.
- Real process-to-completion suite: 29 passed, including owner/non-owner turns, original guest scope and revocation, cron continuations, and reset routing.
- Isolated Control UI: an owner starts `sleep 5`; six seconds later its completion resumes the chat and creates the requested one-shot automation without another human message. `openclaw automations list --json` on that Gateway then showed the stored `at` job targeting the same session.
- Post-merge scoped validation on `153765819b95ca483923b7249b75b67690476c9b`: requester 5/5, Goal continuation 63/63, process-to-wake 29/29 (97/97 total). The rotation regression also asserts owner authority survives compaction.
- `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-session-identity-ratchet.mts --base origin/main --no-merge-base`: passed (1613 files, 6408 grandfathered pins). `git diff --check`: passed. No repository-wide typecheck was run.

AI-assisted (OpenClaw agents). Redacted session log and stored-job check: https://gist.github.com/Marvinthebored/a99536a0a0bfe4e7285cff5e310a7ed7

prs.title: fix(onboard): wait for a freshly started Gateway with --skip-health
prs.body:
Closes #201394

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw onboard --install-daemon --skip-health` starts a fresh Gateway service, then makes one 1.5 s probe and reports the healthy service as unreachable because it has not started listening yet.

## User Impact

Interactive onboarding now waits with the normal Gateway startup timing whenever it started or restarted the service, even with `--skip-health`. `--skip-health` still skips the health RPC, but no longer hides the Control UI link, suggests a restart, or drops the TUI into local mode for a Gateway that is still starting.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Treat a freshly started or restarted Gateway as a startup wait even when `--skip-health` is set.
- Do not re-probe that started Gateway with the single short probe after the wait.
- Keep the existing single-probe behavior for skipped/failed installs and reused Gateways.

## Evidence

- `pnpm test src/wizard/setup.finalize.trusted-proxy.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 6/6 passed, including the real-finalizer `--skip-health` regression.
- Red-on-base: running the same regression against `ee37dd3`'s finalizer fails because the short probe path runs instead of the startup wait.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` clean; oxlint clean on both changed files.

- Interactive PTY proof (real `openclaw onboard --classic --flow quickstart --install-daemon --skip-health`, isolated `--profile`, provider redacted):
  - **Before** (same dist built from the unmodified docs branch): `Installed systemd service: …openclaw-gateway-onboard-proof4.service` followed by `│ Gateway: not detected (connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:19797) │` and `Gateway not detected yet. The managed systemd did not become reachable after setup… Retry the managed service`, while the service was already `active (running)`.

prs.title: fix(process): spawn broker exits when an unbuffered command hits EMFILE
prs.body:
Closes #151671

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the Gateway's spawn broker exits when a streaming command (`buffer: false`, which is what the exec runner, the agent's bash, grep and find tools, and `open-path` pass) fails with `EMFILE` or `ENFILE` at spawn time, taking every other command the broker was running down with it.

#150975 made the raw `spawn` path survive descriptor exhaustion. The execa path has the same hole one layer up: Node returns a child without `stdio` on `EMFILE`/`ENFILE` and emits the error on the next tick; execa 10 reads `subprocess.stdio` outside its own spawn `try/catch`, throws `TypeError: subprocess.stdio is not iterable`, and abandons the child with no `error` listener. `startBrokerExeca` never gets a child to attach to, so the deferred spawn error is an unhandled `error` event and the worker dies with exit code 1 without running `shutdown()`. Buffered execa never reaches that point because its output socket fails first with a normal `EMFILE`.

## User Impact

User impact: an unbuffered command that hits `EMFILE` inside the broker now fails on its own with `code: EMFILE` (the same error the raw path reports since #150975), and the broker, the commands it is running, and their callers are unaffected. Before, that one failure ended the broker: every in-flight command got `Spawn broker exited; command outcome is unavailable`, the host terminated their processes, and the broker restarted. No behavior change for buffered commands, raw spawns, or any non-descriptor failure (`ENOENT`, `EAGAIN`); Linux only, since the broker only runs there.

## Why This Change Was Made

The child execa abandons is unreachable from the broker (execa throws before returning it), so the guard catches what that child does next instead. The `execa()` call is wrapped; when it throws synchronously, `adoptAbandonedSpawnError` installs a one-shot `uncaughtException` listener for the current tick window (removed when it fires or on the next immediate). The child's deferred `spawn` error with `EMFILE`/`ENFILE` is thrown to the caller in place of the TypeError; anything else that reaches the listener is re-raised on the next tick after the listener is gone, so unrelated uncaught exceptions keep Node's default fatal handling. The window is the next tick because that is exactly when Node emits the queued spawn error (`process.nextTick(onErrorNT, ...)` in `lib/internal/child_process.js`), and the listener is registered synchronously in the same tick as the throw.

The new test is the unbuffered execa twin of the #150975 regression: `prlimit --nofile=3:` on the broker, one `host.spawnExeca(argv, { buffer: false })`, `EMFILE` on both `ready()` and `result`, broker pid unchanged, limits restored, a following command succeeds, descriptor count balanced.

Execa itself should treat a streamless subprocess as an early error (attach the listener, return `handleEarlyError`); that is an upstream issue I will file separately, and this guard stays correct with or without it.

## Evidence

All runs on Linux (Fedora 44, kernel 7.1.10), Node v24.21.0, execa 10.0.1, against the real broker worker process through `createSpawnBrokerHost()`, the harness #150975 used for its own proof. "main" is unmodified `main` at efe55d71621 (also reproduced on b63010de72a); "fix" is this branch, rebased onto 6188881e052 to resolve a conflict with #159578 (both added code at the end of `execa-worker.ts`; the fix itself is unchanged). The gates below were re-run on that base from a fresh clone (kernel 7.2.6).

Reproduction on main, broker stderr captured (host.ts temporarily inheriting stderr, then restored byte-identical):

```
caller:   Error: subprocess.stdio is not iterable            (ready() and result)
broker:   node:events:505
              throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event
          Error: spawn /home/.../node EMFILE
              at ChildProcess._handle.onexit (node:internal/child_process:287:19)
          code: 'EMFILE'
          exit code 1
host:     next command: SpawnBrokerError "Spawn broker request delivery failed", caused by write EPIPE
```

Same through the product boundary: `spawnCommand(argv, { buffer: false, stdout: "pipe", stderr: "pipe" })` inside `runWithSpawnBroker(host, ...)`, the path `src/process/exec-runner.ts` takes for every streamed command: rejected with the TypeError, broker gone.

| probe (broker at `prlimit --nofile=3:` unless noted) | main | fix |
|---|---|---|
| execa `buffer: false` | TypeError; broker exits; next command EPIPE | `code: EMFILE` on `ready()` and `result`; broker alive; fds 22 -> 22; next command ok |
| `spawnCommand({ buffer: false })` via `runWithSpawnBroker` | TypeError; broker alive after: false | `code: EMFILE`; broker alive after: true |
| a `sleep 30` in flight when the above happens | broker gone, sleep terminated by the host's lost-child cleanup, its close resolved with no exit event | broker alive, sleep still running under the same broker pid |
| raw spawn (the #150975 case), raw with an `ipc` slot, raw with one free descriptor | `EMFILE`, alive | unchanged |
| execa buffered output | `listen EMFILE` from the output socket, alive | unchanged |
| fork failure (`prlimit --nproc=1:`), raw and execa | `EAGAIN`, alive | unchanged |
| missing executable through execa `buffer: false` (no limit) | `ENOENT`, alive | unchanged; the guard does not engage |

Broker deaths per unbuffered `EMFILE` spawn: 3 of 3 on main, 0 of 5 on the branch. In-flight commands lost: 1 of 1 vs 0 of 1.

Guard contract under real Node (the function copied verbatim into a script): a real streamless child from `spawn()` at `nofile=3` (`child.stdio` is `undefined`) is adopted as `EMFILE` with `syscall: spawn ...`, 0 listeners left, process alive; an unrelated `RangeError` thrown in the same window still exits the process with code 1 and its own stack; no error in the window returns the original TypeError after one immediate; a non-TypeError passes through untouched.

Tests and gates:

- New test on `main` with only the test applied: `expected Error: subprocess.stdio is not iterable { ...(4) } to match object { code: 'EMFILE' }`. On the branch: passes. Guard removed again (planted failure): same failure; restored: file hash equals the committed blob.
- New test on 6188881e052 with only the test applied: the same `subprocess.stdio is not iterable` failure. On the branch: passes.
- `src/process/spawn-broker/`: 22 files, 96/96 (79 in the process shard, 17 in unit-fast), plus five repeated runs of `spawn-failure.test.ts` and one `--sequence.shuffle` run of the directory (seeds 1790635200800 and 1790635211456).
- Test cost: the new test runs in 184 ms; `pnpm test src/process/spawn-broker/spawn-failure.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` takes about 28 s wall, almost all of it transform.
- `pnpm test:changed`: 9/9, exit 0. `node scripts/check-changed.mjs`: exit 0. `oxfmt`, `oxlint`: clean.
- `pnpm check` on 6188881e052: every step passes except `lint`, which fails on four `max-lines` errors in files this PR does not touch (`node-launch-adapter.test.ts`, `session-create.ts`, `missing-configured-plugin-install.repair.ts`, `config-env-vars.ts`), identical on `main`. The two changed files lint clean.
- Fresh environment: `git clone`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm build` (exit 0), the three spawn-failure tests 3/3 from that checkout.

Release check: v2026.9.4 (2026-09-11) has no spawn broker; the broker arrived with #150564 on 2026-09-17 and #150975 followed the same day. `main` only.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction recipe</summary>

```ts
// vitest, Linux, next to spawn-failure.test.ts
const host = createSpawnBrokerHost();
await host.ready();
execFileSync("prlimit", ["--pid", String(host.pid), "--nofile=3:"]);
const run = host.spawnExeca([process.execPath, "-e", "process.exit(0)"], { buffer: false, reject: false });
await run.child.ready().catch((e) => console.log(e.message)); // main: "subprocess.stdio is not iterable"
// main: the broker process is gone within the same tick; any further host.spawn(...) fails with
// "Spawn broker request delivery failed" (write EPIPE). fix: e.code === "EMFILE" and the broker is alive.
```

</details>

### Review guide

`execa-worker.ts`: the existing `execa(...)` ternary moves into a `start` closure so its inferred type is kept, one `try/catch` around the call, and two new functions at the bottom (`isDescriptorSpawnError`, `adoptAbandonedSpawnError`). `spawn-failure.test.ts`: one new `it`, a line-for-line twin of the #150975 test with `spawnExeca` and `buffer: false`.

### Not in this PR

- Execa upstream: a streamless subprocess should become an early error inside execa; filed as sindresorhus/execa#1262.
- The raw spawn path (#150975) and the buffered execa path are unchanged; both already survive.
- The host's recovery behavior after a broker loss (terminate lost children, restart) is unchanged; this PR removes one way of getting there.

### Checklist

- [x] Reproduced on a clean build of `main` through the broker API and through `spawnCommand` before changing code
- [x] Regression test fails on `main`, passes on the branch, on the real broker process
- [x] `pnpm test:changed`, `check-changed`, `oxlint`, `oxfmt` green
- [x] `pnpm check` green on the rebased branch apart from the four `max-lines` errors already on `main`
- [x] Allow edits from maintainers enabled



## Maintainer verification

[Independent current-main/candidate real-broker proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/151672#issuecomment-5927801152): main loses the broker and concurrent command; candidate surfaces EMFILE, completes the other command, and runs a later command on the same broker. The regression fails on current main and all three focused cases pass on this head. No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

prs.title: fix: clear stale cold-session markers after a Gateway restart
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Gateway restarts repeatedly retry obsolete recovery markers on old sessions whose transcripts are in cold storage. Each attempt fails before it can clear the marker, so the same errors and startup work return after every restart.

Related: #200924

## User Impact

Obsolete markers on sessions with no recorded yield wait settle once without restoring their cold transcript. Live interrupted main sessions and committed child-result continuations retain their existing resume behavior. No schema change, data migration, configuration change, or operator action is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Restart discovery intentionally includes retained modern and legacy markers so recovery can either resume or settle them. The committed requester-settle check introduced in #200924 read transcript input before deciding whether the session had a yield wait to override. A retained cold input identity therefore threw inside the entry-replacement planning callback, before the metadata write could commit; the write itself does not require transcript hydration.

Resolve the existing wait first, then inspect committed input only when there is a wait to override. The existing recovery owner clears obsolete markers. Production growth is four lines for the conditional; no new owner, cache, fallback, or scan is introduced.

## Evidence

The real SQLite regression fails on base `bf7681df7893a12ae9788e37995cb4bee5e0d60d` and passes with the fix for archived, done, killed, failed, and unset-status sessions. Its retained transcript identity points to an unavailable cold archive. The first restart clears the marker, the second does not retry it, and neither dispatches a turn or restores the archive.

The restart, yield, and scope suites passed 56 tests. The five cold cases are consolidated in the existing scope suite, which passes all 17 cases. The real Gateway `announcing-crash` completion-recovery scenario passed with a synthetic Responses provider. This is Gateway transport/restart proof, not a live external-provider test. `pnpm check:changed` passed, including full core lint, core/test/script type checks, and database worker/dialect ratchets. Final Codex autoreview found no actionable P2+ findings.

The exact cold-marker path also passed through two actual `pnpm openclaw gateway run` starts on the final built head. A separate private synthetic fixture contained 30 cold markers (30 sessions, 90 transcript events). Both `/startupz` responses reported `started`. The first startup summary was `resumed: 0, skipped: 30`, all `marker-not-current-or-legacy-ineligible`; the second summary was `[]`. Persisted markers went 30 → 0 → 0. Archive descriptors, target cold input bodies, event counts/sequence bounds, and run IDs remained unchanged. Neither startup logged `SessionTranscriptColdError` or `SQLite session write failed`; both Gateways shut down cleanly. Background cold archival was disabled in this fixture to keep unrelated maintenance from changing hot sibling payloads. The deliberately unavailable archives can produce unrelated usage-cache warnings; no archive restoration is claimed. This is behavior proof, not the scale timing run.

Performance acceptance recorded before measurement: two fresh-context owner passes over 30 stale cold cycles in 10,000 synthetic sessions, a populated approximately 35 GiB SQLite database, and 62,000 workspace files. Five counterbalanced A/B and A/A pairs, separate allocation sampling, zero candidate cold errors or dispatches, all markers cleared after the first pass, and none selected on the second. All measured candidate passes cleared all 30 markers on the first restart and selected none on the second; no turn was dispatched.

The benchmark's direct cold-navigation call only prepares the explicitly selected synthetic fixture before measurement. Its narrow database inventory classification records that offline caller; runtime callers remain under the archive mutation worker. Measurements use macOS/APFS; btrfs is not covered. No production data was copied.

| Metric (median / p95) | Base | Fix |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Two-restart harness wall (ms) | 391.04 / 404.12 | 251.99 / 418.56 |
| Process CPU, including workers (ms) | 514.42 / 553.51 | 326.29 / 404.75 |
| Main-thread CPU (ms) | 128.76 / 132.20 | 69.71 / 91.01 |
| Host-isolate sampled allocation (MiB) | 37.81 / 38.47 | 24.14 / 24.47 |
| First restart owner wall (ms) | 207.60 / 232.69 | 162.55 / 569.61 |
| Second restart owner wall (ms) | 159.29 / 171.96 | 66.83 / 74.02 |
| History-worker tasks, two restarts | 246 | 36 |
| Cold errors, two restarts | 60 | 0 |
| Markers remaining after first / second restart | 30 / 30 | 0 / 0 |

Five counterbalanced pairs; each sample averages three two-restart iterations. Individual owner-wall rows use 15 passes per arm and exclude fixture verification. CPU/allocation and combined wall include the same exact-row verification in both arms. Allocation was measured separately, samples collected by minor/major GC included, host isolate only. p95 uses nearest rank. First-use worker initialization was excluded from paired warm measurements. These are recovery-owner measurements, not complete Gateway readiness.

A/A timing controls (both arms run base): wall 383.49 / 408.44 versus 386.89 / 398.14 ms; process CPU 501.90 / 517.17 versus 516.70 / 530.46 ms; both arms exactly 246 history-worker tasks. A/B host load was 12.96–13.66 and A/A 11.74–12.52 on a 32-CPU host. Median wall and process CPU fell by about 36% and 37%, versus less than 1% wall and 3% CPU drift in A/A. One candidate first-pass outlier (569.61 ms) raised candidate p95, so a tail-latency improvement is not established. Separate allocation A/A was 37.65 / 38.44 versus 37.63 / 38.36 MiB, less than 1% median drift; allocation fell about 36% in A/B.

Reproduce with `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/session-read-transactions-fixture.mjs --root <fixture> --sessions 10000 --events 1000000 --target-events 1000 --body-bytes 36500`, then `node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/restart-resume-measure.ts --root <fixture> --baseline <base-owner.ts> --output <new-report.json> --resume --cold-stale --iterations 3`; add `--control` for A/A or `--allocation` for separate allocation sampling. A separate `node --cpu-prof` run captures profiles without contaminating the timing table.

Initial CI found two scheduler-capacity failures when the cold regression occupied a new standalone test file (78 planned jobs versus a 77-job limit). Consolidating it into the existing scope suite fixed both exact failing cases locally without changing any capacity limit. Production code is unchanged. A later fixture audit found the shared archive filename caused INSERT OR IGNORE to retain only one of 30 descriptors. The benchmark now gives each session a unique archive name and ignores only an existing session ID. All measurements above were rerun with 30 verified descriptors; the earlier figures are superseded. The correction passed Codex review.

prs.title: fix: show a plugin page that opens directly or after a reload
prs.body:
Fixes #201511

## What Problem This Solves

When a plugin page is opened by direct link or reload (`/plugin?plugin=<id>&id=<page>`) and the plugin has selected a workspace replacement that calls `mountDefault(...)`, the page area can stay empty. There is no error and no "Retry view" card. Opening the same page from the menu works, so the blank page is easy to hit and hard to explain.

## User Impact

User impact: plugin pages that are opened directly or after a reload render their content instead of staying blank. Pages opened from the menu, and pages that are moved after they mount, behave as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The routed page is built inside the workspace the replacement mounts, and that subtree can settle before it is inserted into the document. The plugin view only starts a mount while its host is connected, so it skipped the mount and nothing ever tried again. The view now remembers a skipped initial mount and finishes it when its host connects. The pending mount is dropped when the view is unmounted or replaced, so registration changes, disposal and error recovery work as before. Moving an already mounted page keeps the plugin's state and does not mount it a second time.

## Evidence

The new test in `ui/src/plugins/control-ui-surface.test.tsx` renders a routed `pages` contribution into a container that is not yet in the document. It checks that the plugin's `mount` is not called while the host is detached, then appends the container and checks that `mount` runs once with a connected container and renders its content. It also moves the page and checks that it is not mounted again and not disposed.

- Without the change, the new test fails: `expected "vi.fn()" to be called once, but got 0 times` after the container is appended.
- With the change, `control-ui-surface.test.tsx` and `control-ui-view.test.tsx` pass (22 tests). The new test takes about 10 ms.
- `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check` are clean on the changed files.

Not run here: the browser-based native plugin UI end-to-end flow, `pnpm tsgo:ui`, `pnpm check:changed`, and a check in Chrome or Safari on iPhone with a real plugin, because the full dependency install could not complete in this environment. The regression test reproduces the detached-then-inserted order directly rather than going through a real workspace replacement.

prs.title: fix: keep a doubtful killed-update recovery on the repair path
prs.body:
Related: #200866, #200994, #201009

## What Problem This Solves

When an `openclaw update` is killed, the next plain `openclaw update` settles what the killed update left behind without asking for `openclaw update repair`. In a few doubtful states it settled when it should have stopped and named repair:

- A source checkout's new build could have the same version and build ID as the build it replaced, which is possible with an explicitly configured build ID. The update then treated it as still running the old build and rolled the killed update's plugin changes back over the new code.
- Checking a source checkout ran `git status` in a way that can download objects in a partial clone, even during `--dry-run`.
- An installation with 99 older update runs was always told that "other update history also needs repair".
- After a machine restart, a container sharing the host's process namespace could settle automatically, although the docs say containers keep the repair path.

## User Impact

User impact: in the first, second and fourth states the next update now stops and names `openclaw update repair`. It leaves the reserved recovery, the killed run's status and the config file unchanged, and it never fetches Git objects to decide. Routine update history no longer blocks the automatic settlement.

Update behavior: these checks run in the updater that is already installed, so published updaters keep their current behavior until they have updated past this change. Nothing new is stored. The checks read the existing update history, recovery records and checkout.

## Why This Change Was Made

Every change is at the owner that decides whether this update may settle a killed update's recovery (`inspectInterruptedUpdateRecovery` and its Git gate `inspectGitActivation`), or at the restart rule's owner (`ranInEarlierHostBoot`):

- **Same build ID.** Settlement tells the original core from the candidate only by version and build ID, so the Git gate refuses when both match.
- **Partial clones.** Checkout inspection uses the repository's read-only Git environment (`gitReadOnlyEnvironment`, which sets `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH`). It also denies every transport with `GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL=`, because older Git ignores `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH`. The worktree hydration code uses the same pair. A partial clone that is missing an object then fails the check locally and refuses instead of fetching.
- **History page.** The "other history" check now uses repair's own rule (`inspectNewerRecoveryHistory`). A full page counts as doubtful only when it ends after the killed run.
- **Containers.** `ranInEarlierHostBoot` now also requires the existing `isContainerEnvironment()` detector to report no container. The detector cannot see a container that leaves no runtime marker, and the doc comment says so.
- **Docs.** `--no-restart` stops the update only while the killed update's Gateway stop is still outstanding. The same-build-ID refusal and the container exclusion are now documented.

The killed-run process test file (1165 lines) is split into four suites over one shared fixture module, with every case kept: settlement and finishing, refusals, the restart rule, and source checkouts. The restart suite adds a case where only the current process runs in a non-host PID namespace, because the base case, with both sides in the same non-host namespace, still passed with the current-side check removed.

### Review findings and decisions

- **"An unacknowledged abandoned run at row 101 is invisible once a full page reaches back before the killed run." Not changed, now with a test.** Every reader of that history reads the same newest-100-row page: the plain update, `openclaw update repair` (`listUpdateRuns({ limit: 100 })` picks the abandoned runs it finishes and acknowledges) and Doctor's "remains abandoned" notes. The new process test runs both entries on the same state: a killed update, 99 older routine runs, and an unacknowledged abandoned run older than all of them. Both finish and acknowledge the killed run with one finalization run, and both leave the older run byte-for-byte unchanged. Refusing for that run would send the operator to a repair that leaves exactly what caused the refusal, so every later update would be refused. The base refused this state only because it refused every full page. The work that run could still owe is installation-wide (Doctor, plugin convergence, Gateway restoration), and the finalization of the killed run performs it. Making older abandoned runs visible past the page would be a change to repair, Doctor and the update together, not to this check.
- **"A damaged `dist` can pass the Git activation check, so the recovery cohort is cleared before repair. Record and compare the dist artifact identity." Rejected by maintainer decision.** `openclaw update repair` settles the same recovery with the same function (`settleInterruptedUpdatePluginCohort`) and has no Git gate at all. The activation record is written only after activation finishes, so a kill during activation already refuses. A recorded digest would also send a developer who rebuilt `dist` after the kill to manual repair for no reason.
- **"If Doctor fails during the finishing stage, a second update no longer sees the unfinished repair." Real, not fixed here; follow-up in progress.** The first invocation still refuses and names repair when finishing fails, as before. A separate read-only design check is looking at whether the existing owed-step rows can carry the obligation. Two rules that inferred it from existing history were tried in this PR and removed because each misfired (one blocked updates after an unrelated failed repair; the other broke when a dry run recorded its row in between).
- **"The case where both processes use a non-host PID namespace adds no distinct guard coverage." Kept.** It is the only case that fails if the restart rule compared the recorded namespace with the current one instead of checking each against the host's.

## Evidence

**What ran through the shipped CLI, and on which SHA.** One installed-package Docker run exists: `package-installed-recovery-live-gateway` passed (608 s) on a package built from `29f83d6a1a0`, the first version of this change, not the current head. In it a real `openclaw update` is killed after stopping a real managed Gateway, a plain `openclaw update` finishes it and the Gateway serves the installed version, a second killed update is refused by `openclaw update --no-restart` with a message naming repair, and `openclaw update repair` restores the Gateway. That lane does not reach the refusals this PR changes (same build ID, partial clone, container after restart, full history page). **No installed-package run exists on the current head.** A rerun on the head and new cells for the changed refusals were planned, but the shared Docker host was held by other jobs for most of this session and the work was stopped; the new cell's only attempt failed before its first command for an undiagnosed reason, so it was removed from this PR rather than left half-done.

**What is fixture-only.** Every changed refusal is proven by process tests: a real child `openclaw update` process reserves its plugin recovery, writes config and is SIGKILLed, then the real `updateCommand` (or `updateRepairCommand`) entry runs to admitted execution with real recovery stores, SQLite and Git. Doctor's child process, plugin installs and the managed service are stand-ins. The restart rule is exercised by injecting the recorded and current boot identities and the container detector; the source-checkout cases use a real Git repository with fixture build files.

**Red on base, green on head (process tests).** Four tests fail on `origin/main` 7ce2d10eced with this PR's tests copied in, and pass on this head:

| Behavior | Base | Head |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Checkout build has the same version and build ID as the one it replaced | settles; plugin changes rolled back over the new code | refuses and names repair; checkout and recovery unchanged |
| Partial clone with a staged change needing a blob only the remote has (`--dry-run`) | `git status` downloads the blob | refuses; the blob is still missing |
| Killed run plus 99 older successful runs (one full page) | "Other update history also needs repair" | settles, finishes and proceeds |
| Machine restarted; update runs in a container sharing the host PID namespace | settles | refuses: the lease store cannot prove the processes gone |

Controls passing on both sides: a full page ending after the killed run still refuses; the shared non-host PID namespace case still refuses; only-current-process-in-non-host-namespace refuses.

New in this revision: `update-command-killed-run-refusals.process.test.ts` runs the full-page case through both `openclaw update` and `openclaw update repair` with an unacknowledged abandoned run older than the page. Both finish and acknowledge the killed run with one successful finalization run, repair runs no update, and the older run is left byte-for-byte unchanged. On base the `openclaw update` variant fails with "Other update history also needs repair"; the repair variant passes on both, which is the point: repair cannot clear what a refusal would cite.

Recordings (raw terminal captures of the process tests, from the previous revision; the tests they show are unchanged):

RED, base 7ce2d10eced (`Tests 4 failed | 4 passed`): https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8aa9ac7f-1bdf-481e-858f-e65fcc57716c

GREEN, head bc4ab058379 (`Tests 8 passed`): https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f0c8e3d5-1678-454e-b5b2-1d96f0f8d430

Full raw logs are not attached because the Crabbox artifact store rejected the upload (`http 401`).

**Checks on this head.** The four killed-run suites and `test/scripts/docker-e2e-plan.test.ts` pass; `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:core:test` pass; test-lines ratchet against the merged main is within allowance; `git diff --check` is clean. Earlier on this branch: `eager-import-closure` and `update-restart-module-outcome` (24 tests) pass, oxlint and `pnpm check:docs` pass. Autoreview does not run on this machine. A fresh read-only reviewer audited the new tests; its findings on the process test (assert that repair runs no update) were applied, and its findings on the Docker cell no longer apply because the cell was removed.

**Rating.** ClawSweeper (GPT 6.2 Sol) rated the previous head F overall / F proof / C patch after three rounds. What held it down: no shipped-CLI proof of the changed paths on the reviewed build (still true), and the row-101 history finding (now answered with the test above). No rating round was run on this head; the rating no longer gates this PR.

**Not proven.**
- Any installed-package run on this head, including the changed refusals through the shipped CLI.

Each real checkout update builds the candidate in a fresh worktree (install, full build, Control UI build, candidate validation); a cell needs three such builds and a red/green pair six. prs.title: fix: stop calling a busy Gateway lock or a Git update's Doctor start data at risk
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Two update failures were recorded as "Keep the Gateway stopped: data at risk" with no evidence that anything had been written:

- Doctor could not take or inspect the Gateway lock (the lock was held, its inspection timed out, or the lock record could not be read). Doctor refuses before it opens any writer, yet the refusal said `gateway-state-unverified`, even before the update had changed anything.
- A Git (in-place checkout) update marked the run `state-migrated-no-rollback` at the moment it was about to start Doctor, so any later Doctor failure, missing UI assets or HEAD mismatch inherited that mark.

`openclaw update repair` then refuses to start the Gateway for that run.

## User Impact

User impact: a lock timeout or busy Gateway lock is now a deferred, retryable refusal, and a failed Git update keeps "do not roll back code" without claiming data at risk; the update result no longer tells the user to keep the Gateway stopped in those cases. A live owner that the state lock cannot exclude (a legacy 2026.6.33 Gateway, or a lock owner in another process namespace) and an unrestored partial config publication still stop the Gateway, as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

Invariant: "data at risk" needs evidence (a writer that may still run unexcluded, an incomplete migration, a partial restore). A held, timed-out or unreadable lock is contention or "could not verify".

- **Classifier (P1-1), `classifyDoctorMaintenanceRefusal`.** A `GatewayLockError` is deferred only when it shows contention or a failed check: the lock record could not be read, could not be verified, or its inspection deadline expired (these throws are now a typed `GatewayLockInspectionError`), or a coordinated state owner holds the lock (`GatewayStateOwnerContentionError`). Every other lock failure keeps `gateway-state-unverified`: a live or unreadable legacy lock (`LegacyGatewayLockError`), an owner in another process namespace, an interrupted database port (`DatabasePortRecoveryError`), a live owner lease, an owner whose identity cannot be verified. The update applies this classifier in `createUpdateCommandFailureResult`, so the same lock timeout before mutation keeps the original recovery instead of a risk. The lock error classes moved beside `GatewayLockNamespaceError` in `gateway-lock-payload.ts` (re-exported from `gateway-lock.ts`) to keep `gateway-lock.ts` under its line cap.
- **Git legacy (P1-3), `update-runner-git.ts`.** Before Doctor the runner still records `serviceRestartSafe: false, reason: state-migration-started` (code rollback stops there), but no `dataAtRisk`. Doctor's own refusal still sets one; after the runner returns, the update's post-activation inspection measures the schema and sets `state-migrated-no-rollback` when state did move.

History: the GatewayLockError mapping came from #155389 ("defer safe Doctor refusals") as a blanket class; the legacy-lock case it protects is kept explicitly (`doctor-health.legacy-update.test.ts` still passes unchanged). The Git pre-Doctor mark came from #172784, which labeled every "cannot roll back" as data at risk.

Not changed here, and why:
- The Doctor database preflight catch (`assertDoctorMaintenanceReady`, any error → `incomplete-migration`, P1-1 second half). The preflight reports a held recovery store and a failed read through the same untyped "readiness could not be verified" error, so the catch cannot tell them apart. Narrowing it needs a typed cause from `openclaw-database-preflight.ts`; I left it for a follow-up rather than guess.
- Other classifier classes (stop uncertainty, schema refusals) and pre-mutation refusals generally: an unreadable state database detected before mutation is real damage and stays marked (`update-cli.preactivation-inspection.test.ts`).

## Update behavior for published updaters

Doctor runs from the candidate, so a fixed candidate classifies lock refusals correctly even under a `v2026.11.5` or `v2026.10.33` parent; the parent's own classifier still maps a raw `GatewayLockError` it receives through its own code. The Git runner fix runs in the updater, so it applies from the next update driven by a fixed version. Marks shipped updaters already recorded are left to the guidance/repair owner (`verification.recovery.dataAtRisk`, `finalize:data-at-risk`).

Paths: the classifier is shared by package, Git legacy and Git release Doctor runs, standalone `openclaw doctor --fix`, and every trigger (CLI, `update.run`, auto). Git release does not use the in-place runner. Package installs never had the pre-Doctor mark.

## Evidence

Behavior checked with real failures:

- **Lock.** A real `GatewayLockError` from the lock reader (`readActiveGatewayLockIdentity` with an unreadable owner lock record) classifies as deferred `admission-unavailable`; the update failure result keeps the recovery it had. Base: `data-at-risk / gateway-state-unverified`.
- **Git legacy.** The real Git runner test (real git repository, Doctor fails after writing state) for `doctor-failed`, `doctor-threw`, `head-error`, `head-mismatch`, `ui-missing`: no `dataAtRisk`, rollback still not attempted, candidate checkout and migrated state kept. Base: `state-migrated-no-rollback`.
- **Still at risk:** a real lock owner in another process namespace (unknown namespace record, real lock reader); `doctor-data-at-risk` (Doctor's own `unreadable-state` refusal) in the same Git test; an unrestored partial config publication; a live legacy Gateway lock (`doctor-health.legacy-update.test.ts`, unchanged, passes); the explicit ownership refusal in `update-command-invalid-config.test.ts`; pre-mutation unreadable state in `update-cli.preactivation-inspection.test.ts`.

Terminal recordings (raw output, idle gaps capped at 1 s, 3x speed). Base/red: product code at `3eee09d9b46` with this PR's tests; the branch was then rebased onto a newer `main` whose range does not touch the runner, classifier, legacy lock or their tests. Head/green: `b215bea124e`.

- Base / red, Git runner:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2fdfb3f0-a4ff-4887-ba3c-9900b31eeef9

- Base / red, lock classifier:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cbde44e1-55c3-4aad-8cc1-870e73a0f43c

- Head / green (both, plus the legacy-lock control):

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6417b71e-9303-43ef-a6f5-72aa29296c91

Full raw logs are not attached because the artifact store rejected uploads from this machine.

<details>
<summary>Commands and results</summary>

- Red, base product code with the head tests: `update-runner-git.test.ts -t "retains the candidate after migration starts"` → 5 failed, 1 passed (`doctor-data-at-risk` control); `doctor-maintenance-inspection.test.ts` → lock case failed (`data-at-risk` instead of `deferred`), config control passed.
- Green, head: same cases pass, plus the legacy-lock control.
- Affected files, all pass: `doctor-health.legacy-update`, `doctor-maintenance-inspection`, `doctor-maintenance.agent-schema`, `update-runner-git`, `doctor-sqlite-maintenance-lock`, `update-command-invalid-config`, `doctor-maintenance.contention-wait`, `doctor-maintenance.migration-refusal`, `doctor-maintenance.schema-preflight`, `update-command-fresh-doctor`, `startup-client-credentials`, `update-cli.preactivation-inspection`, `gateway-lock.namespace` (13 files, 309 tests).
- `pnpm tsgo:core:all`: pass. oxlint on touched files: pass. `git diff --check`: clean.
</details>

Test files audited in full: `update-runner-git.test.ts` (one expectation changed: the five non-refusal Git failures no longer expect the pre-Doctor mark), new `doctor-maintenance-inspection.test.ts`. No case removed.

Review: `autoreview` does not run on this machine. A fresh independent reviewer read this diff and the contract. Fixed from its findings: the first version deferred every non-legacy lock error, which also covered an interrupted database port and a live owner lease seen after taking the state lock; the classifier now defers only typed inspection failures and coordinated contention, and a namespace-owner case was added. Not taken: classifying a bare (unwrapped) namespace error as at risk, which would add a mark that base does not set.

## Not proven

- No installed-package Docker run for these two items; the Docker cell for this work went to the sibling PR's restart case. A real lock-inspection timeout during an update Doctor was not reproduced end to end; the proof uses the real lock reader and classifier.
- A Git legacy update end to end through `openclaw update` was not run; the proof is the real runner with a real repository.
- The Doctor database preflight catch (above) is unchanged.

Steps this change still leaves to a person, and why:
- A deferred lock refusal leaves Doctor maintenance pending; the existing finalize path records "Doctor and plugin maintenance remain pending" and the next update or `openclaw update repair` retries it. No new manual step.
- A live legacy or other-namespace Gateway still stops the update: the updater cannot safely stop a process it cannot identify. The guidance names `openclaw gateway status --deep` and `openclaw doctor --fix`; routing that through `openclaw triage` is the guidance owner's change.

prs.title: fix: stop marking data at risk when a migrated update's restart fails or a rollback cannot read the schema
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After an update that migrated state, any later failure was recorded as "Keep the Gateway stopped: data at risk (state-migrated-no-rollback)", even when the new version's Gateway had already been started and the failure was only a restart that did not become ready. The same happened when an automatic rollback could not read the database schema, or had no schema baseline (PostgreSQL state): the run said "data at risk (rollback-state-unverified)" although nothing had been restored and the new version was still installed. `openclaw update repair` then refuses to start the Gateway for that run, and the managed-service helper leaves it down.

## User Impact

User impact: a migrated update whose restarted Gateway fails readiness, or whose rollback cannot verify the schema, now ends as a recoverable failure that names `openclaw update repair` and `openclaw gateway status --deep`, and repair can start the installed Gateway. Real risks still stop it: a schema newer than the previous version, a partial restore, preserved config edits, an unknown active install root, and every risk a Doctor or migration owner records.

## Why This Change Was Made

Invariant: "data at risk" needs evidence (a forward schema, a partial restore, an unsettled writer, an owner's refusal). A failed read, a missing baseline or a failure that happens after the new version took over is not evidence.

- **Blanket stamp (P0-2).** `finishUpdate` keeps the migrated rollback block only until it starts the candidate Gateway. Before that, a failure still refuses code rollback and the candidate admission still runs, as today. After the start, the candidate owns the migrated state: later failures (restart readiness, deferred plugin convergence, Windows task, post-activation inspection) carry their own reason and only risks their own owners record. Fixed at the owner, `update-command-post-update.ts`: the block is released in a `finally` around the candidate restart, so a restart that throws after starting the candidate is covered too. The stamp in `completeUpdateCommandResult` is unchanged and no longer applies after the start. The skipped-rollback ledger step then says the started candidate owns the migrated state.
- **Rollback default (P1-2).** `rollbackFailedUpdate` no longer starts with `dataAtRisk = rollback-state-unverified`. A schema read that throws before restoration, or a missing PostgreSQL baseline, refuses rollback with reason `rollback-state-unverified` and no risk; the candidate stays installed and final recovery may start it. Kept as risks, each with its evidence: unknown active root, a newly created database the previous version cannot open, databases restored but not re-verifiable, config restore failing after the package was restored, forward schema, operator config edits.

History: the default and the stamp came from #172784, which made `dataAtRisk` the only "keep stopped" signal and labeled "cannot roll back" as a risk so the previous behavior (never restart) was preserved. Restarting the installed candidate was not considered there; candidate admission (`admitInstalledGatewayRecovery`) already treats `state-migrated-no-rollback` as safe for the candidate before a start.

Not changed (owned elsewhere): `inspectActivatedUpdateState`, recovery guidance text, `update repair`, the stored mark, and the helper's exit 79.

## Update behavior for published updaters

The installed updater runs first. For a migrated update the post-start code runs in the candidate's migrated-finalize worker, so a fixed candidate applies item 1 even under `v2026.11.5` and `v2026.10.33` parents. Item 2 runs in the updater itself, so it takes effect from the next update driven by a fixed version. Marks that shipped updaters already recorded are left to the guidance/repair owner; they key on `verification.recovery.dataAtRisk`, the `finalize:data-at-risk` step and the `state-schema-verification` step.

Paths: package (npm link and pnpm/bun swap) and Git legacy both reach `finishUpdate`; Git legacy rollback uses the same `rollbackFailedUpdate`. Git release mode never takes this rollback and has no migrated worker, so it is unaffected. CLI and managed-handoff triggers reach the same code; on the handoff path an unsafe result still exits 79 and leaves the Gateway down (separate item, P1-4), but the run is no longer marked at risk, so `openclaw update repair` can start it.

## Evidence

Behavior checked at the owners with real failures (real `rollbackFailedUpdate` with real schema reads; real `finishUpdate` with the migrated block from the fixture):

- **Item A.** A migrated update whose started candidate fails readiness (`blocked`), or whose restart throws after starting the candidate (`blocked-throw`), no longer rolls back, records no `dataAtRisk`, writes no `finalize:data-at-risk` step, and its recorded next action names `openclaw update repair` and `openclaw triage` without "data at risk". Base: reason `state-migrated-no-rollback` and the risk mark.
- **Item B.** Rollback whose schema read fails (agent database unreadable) or that has no baseline refuses with reason `rollback-state-unverified` and no risk; the rendered guidance has no "Keep the Gateway stopped". Base: `dataAtRisk: rollback-state-unverified`.
- **Negative controls, still at risk:** forward shared schema (`state-migrated-no-rollback`, with "Keep the Gateway stopped" in guidance); config that cannot be restored after the package was restored (`rollback-state-unverified`); a migrated failure before any candidate start (ownership change, `state-migrated-no-rollback` in the recorded guidance); the existing `preserves a named Doctor risk` test (`unreadable-state` kept). The schema-change table now asserts the risk for every refusal row (unknown root, newly created store the previous version cannot open, forward schema, operator edits), which no test checked before.

Recordings (terminal, this Mac, raw output, no re-typing):

Base/red: product code at `3b03d9c6c4f` with this PR's tests. Head/green: `8ceae53538f` (the PR head; the branch was rebased once onto a newer `main` whose range touches no update finalization, rollback, recovery or guidance file). Idle gaps capped at 1 s, 3x speed.

- Base / red: 6 failed, 4 passed (the 4 are the controls that must stay at risk, plus none of the new cases).

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/90205d99-583a-490d-bc8d-c5b49d34aa18

- Head / green: 9 passed, 1 failed (the macOS setgid case, identical on base).

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/976b4e45-e2a1-49e4-b7d4-f48ca83e8875

Full raw logs are not attached because the artifact store rejected uploads from this machine.

End to end: an installed-package Docker cell (published 2026.11.5 updater → this candidate, port taken during the restart) is queued behind the shared Docker lock; results will be added here.

<details>
<summary>Commands and results</summary>

- Red: product code at base, tests from the head, `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/update-cli/update-command-rollback.test.ts src/cli/update-cli/update-command-post-update-repair.test.ts -t "<the cases above>"` → 6 failed, 4 passed. Failures: `schema-read-denied`, `no-baseline`, `blocked`, `blocked-throw`, Windows `healthy=false` (rollback called), plus `excludes a competing config writer` (see below).
- Green, exact head: same command → 9 passed, 1 failed (`excludes a competing config writer`).
- `excludes a competing config writer … expected 504 to be 1528` fails identically on base: a setgid directory mode check that does not hold on macOS. Not caused by this change.
- Full files `update-command-rollback.test.ts`, `update-command-post-update-repair.test.ts`, `update-command-post-update-recovery.test.ts`, `update-command-migrated.test.ts`: all pass except that same setgid case. `update-command-post-update.test.ts`, `update-command-database-rollback.test.ts`, `update-command-legacy-finalize.test.ts`, `update-command-recovery.test.ts`, `update-command-migrated-windows.test.ts`, `update-cli.preactivation-inspection.test.ts`: pass.
- `pnpm tsgo:core:all`: pass. `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs <touched files>`: pass. `pnpm check:baseline-ratchets --base <base> --no-merge-base`: all ok. `git diff --check`: clean.
</details>

Test files audited in full: `update-command-rollback.test.ts`, `update-command-post-update-repair.test.ts`. Changes to existing tests: the `blocked` row now expects no rollback and reason `readyz-unhealthy` (it had asserted the stamped reason this PR removes); the Windows plugin-activation restart mock now reports the start it performs, as the real restart does, so it no longer exercises the old stamped path. No case was removed.

Review: `autoreview` does not run on this machine. A fresh independent reviewer read the diff and the contract. Fixed from its findings: release the block in a `finally` (restart that throws after a start), keep the risk for a post-stop recheck after a database restore, check the unknown root before the missing baseline, assert the risk in the schema table, a truthful skipped-rollback step, the Windows mock. Not taken: Git release successor restarts do not call `onGatewayStartAttempted`; a Git release does not migrate before its restart, so it reaches finalization without a migrated block (left as is, see Not proven).

## Not proven

- A restored database whose recheck read fails was not reproduced; the mark is kept by code reading only.
- Git release: not exercised; it has no updater rollback and normally no migrated block. If `inspectActivatedUpdateState` sets one (being changed by another PR), the successor restart path does not signal a start, so item A would not apply there.
- Handoff triggers (`update.run`, auto, CLI inside the Gateway tree): unsafe recovery still exits 79 and leaves the Gateway down until `openclaw update repair` (separate item). The run is no longer marked at risk, so repair starts it.
- Linux host: unit proof ran on macOS.

Steps this change still leaves to a person, and why:
- After a post-start readiness failure, the update does not restart the candidate a second time in the same run (the restart was already attempted and failed). The recorded next action names `openclaw triage` (agent-assisted) and `openclaw update repair`; the next plain `openclaw update` is no longer blocked by a risk mark. Automatic retry of the start belongs to final recovery and the helper exit path (P1-4), not this change.
- Genuine risks still stop: they need a decision about data the updater cannot make. Their guidance text is owned by the guidance/repair worker.

prs.title: fix(subagents): yielded parents lose subagent results when their run turns over
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A subagent waiting in `sessions_yield` can lose its children's results when its run ends or another follow-up becomes the latest run in the same session. An accepted settle turn can be cancelled before consuming the results, or consumed results can be recorded as undelivered. Turnover before acceptance can also remove the pending wake without delivering its findings.

## User Impact

Completed children keep their delivery to the waiting session across ordinary run turnover. A requester model failure preserves results already committed to its transcript and shows the turn's error. Reset, explicit Stop, session replacement, and closed completion owners still prevent stale effects. No configuration, schema, or migration changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The settle producer was treating requester-run currency as authority for the entire delivery lifetime. The existing acceptance flag now ends that run-currency check. Before acceptance, ordinary turnover re-arms the existing pending obligation instead of consuming it. Session identity, cancellation, prepared findings, child ownership, and batch closure remain checked by their current owners.

This integrates and simplifies Josh Lehman's original repair. It adds seven production lines, reuses existing state, and removes a redundant terminal condition. The final proof replaces duplicate scaffolding without a test-budget allocation change.

## Evidence

An isolated real Gateway, WebSocket client, actual agent runtime, `sessions_spawn`, `sessions_yield`, `sessions_send`, registry persistence, and `write` tool exercise four children finishing behind a busy requester. A second follow-up changes requester-run selection. Every child has a recorded waiting state and mailbox blocker before release. The only scripted boundary is the local model provider.

All four scenarios pass: normal turnover delivers all four results and writes the marker; a requester model error still delivers all four results and records a visible failure; reset and explicit Stop prevent the pending write. The base owner fails the same scenario with captured `ok` results left pending after its wake disappears. The pre-acceptance replacement regression also fails on base and keeps the wake pending with this repair.

Focused proof: 56 tests pass (40 dispatch, 12 cancellation, 4 real-Gateway cases). The combined local command took 138.61 seconds; the Gateway file took 65.56 seconds on the loaded host. Its queue ordering, persisted delivery facts, and real tool revocation require this product boundary. The final change adds 362 net test lines.

`pnpm check:changed --base bf7681df7893a12ae9788e37995cb4bee5e0d60d` passes, including typechecking, lint, formatting, dead-export scans, and repository guards. Codex autoreview of the final diff found no actionable P0–P2 findings. The exact final Gateway regression fails on that base owner and passes with this repair.

[CI run 44427305860](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44427305860) completed successfully on `fb2e6eb3cb574a6588b354afffb0d6b01a1f1140`, including the aggregate CI gate. ClawSweeper reviewed that exact head with zero findings and zero open checklist items. Large synthetic-fixture measurements are complete; results are below.

The original live incidents are not replayed; all proof data and model responses are synthetic.

Related: #194798.

<details>
<summary>Inspectable terminal evidence from the isolated Gateway</summary>

Base owner at `bf7681df7893a12ae9788e37995cb4bee5e0d60d`, final regression file:

```text
FAIL  |gateway-server (gateway-server-parallel)| src/gateway/server.subagent-settle-turnover.product.test.ts > a runner's settle wake survives a queued follow-up turnover; revocation after acceptance: none
AssertionError: expected { status: 'pending', …(2) } to match object { status: 'delivered' }
(6 matching properties omitted from actual)

- Expected
+ Received

  {
-   "status": "delivered",
+   "status": "pending",
  }
```

Repaired owner, same final regression:

```text
✓ |gateway-server (gateway-server-parallel)| src/gateway/server.subagent-settle-turnover.product.test.ts > a runner's settle wake survives a queued follow-up turnover; revocation after acceptance: none 53732ms
```

The complete four-scenario Gateway run (before only the mechanical Vitest timeout-options correction) produced:

```text
✓ |gateway-server (gateway-server-parallel)| src/gateway/server.subagent-settle-turnover.product.test.ts > a runner's settle wake survives a queued follow-up turnover; revocation after acceptance: none 23891ms
✓ |gateway-server (gateway-server-parallel)| src/gateway/server.subagent-settle-turnover.product.test.ts > a runner's settle wake survives a queued follow-up turnover; revocation after acceptance: requester reset 8969ms
✓ |gateway-server (gateway-server-parallel)| src/gateway/server.subagent-settle-turnover.product.test.ts > a runner's settle wake survives a queued follow-up turnover; revocation after acceptance: explicit stop 9627ms
✓ |gateway-server (gateway-server-parallel)| src/gateway/server.subagent-settle-turnover.product.test.ts > a runner's settle wake survives a queued follow-up turnover; revocation after acceptance: model error 9986ms
```

These scenarios run the real Gateway and tools against a synthetic model endpoint. Runtime assertions wait for all four persisted child rows to be `waiting` with a mailbox blocker before releasing the busy requester; then require all four captured `ok` results to become `delivered`. The model-error case also requires one visible failure card, while reset and Stop require no write effect. No production data or user transcript is included.

</details>

### Synthetic scale measurement

Synthetic owner measurements use a 42.7685 GiB agent database, 5,000 seeded sessions (1,958 populated transcripts), 6,000 retained runs, and 62,000 tracked inventory files totaling 1.116 GB. The benchmark adds 36 requesters and 144 child records, restoring 6,144 resident runs. This is APFS; no production data was copied.

Five fresh-process A1/A2/B cycles were run separately for timing and allocation, with six warmups and 30 measured four-result batches per process. The table is the median of each arm’s five process medians. It covers the real settle owner, session/registry reads, and dispatch transition write; model/transport work and final delivery persistence are outside the measurement. CPU includes worker threads; allocation is main-thread V8 sampling at 1 KiB.

| Arm | Wall ms/batch | Process CPU ms/batch | Sampled JS bytes/batch |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Base A1 | 5.962 | 12.365 | 1,884,784 |
| Base A2 (A/A control) | 6.278 | 25.257 | 1,885,816 |
| Repaired B | 6.239 | 16.441 | 1,876,756 |

Candidate measurements lie within the observed baseline variation across runs. Host CPU noise is large (baseline process medians 12.145–40.131 ms), so no speedup is claimed. All baseline invocations reject the turnover with zero findings delivered; repaired invocations retain all four findings. These owner measurements supplement the separate real-Gateway behavior proof.
