prs.title: fix: shorten sandbox freezes when importing pull requests
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Importing a repository into a workspace can freeze its sandbox for several seconds while pull request preparation verifies that the workspace is pristine. The frozen phase included a settled canonical snapshot and two full filesystem manifests.

## User Impact

The sandbox keeps running during canonical verification. In the synthetic 62,000-file workload, median pristine pause falls 62% and total guest pause falls 53%. Dirty files, staged-only edits, unexpected history, and projection differences still prevent an unsafe initial import. No configuration, schema, or migration changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The guest writes the projection; the Gateway owns the canonical checkout under its reconciliation lease. Move the canonical snapshot and manifest into the existing source-preparation lease, where the guest is running. Bind the prepared view to the accepted baseline so a checkpoint between phases causes a retry before integration. The final comparison retains the paused guest manifest. Git tree equality cannot replace raw filesystem equality, including authored empty directories.

The pristine phase now captures one full manifest instead of two, and performs zero settled canonical snapshots instead of one. Total capture work and the earlier per-entry Git batching remain unchanged. Production code grows by 13 lines to carry the prepared manifest and baseline identity across the existing phases.

## Evidence

The pause-placement regression fails on the parent and passes with this change. All 83 focused publication tests pass, including dirty and staged-only edits during preparation, unexpected history, projection mismatch, and a checkpoint that changes canonical bytes without changing Git HEAD. `pnpm check:changed` passes. Independent Codex review found no actionable P0–P2 findings. [ClawSweeper reviewed this exact head with zero findings and zero open items](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201410#issuecomment-6989495494).

Five interleaved A/A/B groups used 62,000 synthetic files / 1.10 GB, 512 MiB of synthetic Git history, a real Docker guest heartbeat, and the registered publication owner. Every sample verified final contents. No samples were discarded. Each arm below has five samples; p95 is the nearest-rank estimate, which is the maximum at this sample count.

| Metric, median / p95 | A first (n=5) | A repeat (n=5) | B (n=5) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Pristine pause (s) | 9.78 / 24.64 | 10.06 / 13.85 | 3.74 / 5.61 |
| Total pause (s) | 12.19 / 26.82 | 12.38 / 18.03 | 5.76 / 7.80 |
| Longest pause (s) | 10.86 / 25.51 | 10.98 / 16.14 | 4.48 / 6.43 |
| Heartbeat gap (s) | 10.81 / 25.48 | 10.97 / 16.07 | 4.45 / 6.40 |
| Owner elapsed (s) | 122.22 / 218.16 | 126.28 / 200.62 | 107.81 / 189.84 |
| Node-process CPU (s) | 32.56 / 47.02 | 35.48 / 42.26 | 32.73 / 37.52 |
| Guest CPU (s) | 23.05 / 42.64 | 23.87 / 29.53 | 22.17 / 28.51 |
| Main V8 allocation (MB) | 791.43 / 796.19 | 794.90 / 796.80 | 805.42 / 806.27 |

Against all ten baseline controls, median owner elapsed falls 13.2%, Node-process CPU falls 4.5%, and guest CPU falls 6.6%. Main-isolate allocation rises 1.5% (about 12.2 MB). Host contention produced large baseline and candidate outliers, retained above. The frozen source and committed candidate match byte for byte. A separate CPU/allocation profiling pass failed before reaching pristine verification because Git ran out of disk space during fetch; the Docker daemon then became unavailable during cleanup. Its partial profiles are excluded. A separate completed diagnostic profile used the same real Git, publication, and reconciliation owners with the harness’s supported simulated guest; contents verified, and its timings are excluded. The main isolate was predominantly idle waiting for workers and Git, with canonical-path selection the largest named application CPU frame. The ordinary-sample CPU and V8 allocation counters above remain valid.

The workload is `scripts/perf/github-publication-pause-measure.ts`, run serially against frozen parent and candidate source roots with `--native-image` set to the installed Node 26 image. CPU includes Node worker threads but excludes host native Git subprocess CPU; guest CPU is measured separately. Allocation is the main V8 isolate's exact counter. The host filesystem is APFS through the container runtime, not btrfs. The agent database is small and synthetic: this workload does not cover a 35 GiB database or thousands of sessions. No production data was used.

[Exact-head dispatched CI passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44381867118). [Normal ready-PR CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44386096377) failed in Git setup for three Node jobs because the upstream Git PPA returned HTTP 503; no tests ran in those jobs. CodeQL and security review passed. Other tested lanes, including UI, typechecks, lint, and docs, passed. After the package endpoint recovered to HTTP 200, only the failed jobs were retried in attempt 2 at the unchanged PR head; attempt 2 and the aggregate CI gate passed. Both successful CI runs cover the unchanged reviewed head `f031e939a47a73fe091cfaf72d11e537361699f9`.

Two additional projection authority tests fail on exact parent `3da0bc802e100faebc8352f7398fea89410def27`, introduced by #201334 (`04cb8179ccd66c88f2b32eb8bca8c53d2e8b9cb5`): “rejects canonical checkpoint writes after original operator authority ends” and “denies guest filesystem writes after role revocation and a late involvement receipt.” They still expect mid-request role revocation after that change made authority fixed per request. These are separately reported main test regressions, not passing proof or a CI waiver for this PR.

prs.title: feat(matrix): answer an attachment and the text typed with it as one turn
prs.body:
Related: #161505

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the agent replies to a bare attachment and then separately to the user's question when a Matrix client without caption support (for example Element Web) sends the file and the typed text as two messages.

## User Impact

Operators can set `channels.matrix.mediaHoldMs` (or `accounts.<id>.mediaHoldMs`) so a captionless attachment waits briefly for the sender's next text and both are answered in one turn. Default `0` keeps today's behavior. When enabled, an attachment sent on its own is answered only after the wait (maximum 60 s). A held attachment keeps its place in the durable inbound queue, so a Gateway restart delivers it again instead of dropping it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The hold sits between Matrix durable ingress (#176491) and the room message handler. A captionless attachment is buffered in the plugin SDK keyed inbound debouncer (keyed by room and thread); its delivery returns `deferred`, so the attachment keeps its own ingress claim while the room lane stays free for the text. The sender's next plain text joins it and becomes the attachment's caption, the same shape caption-capable clients already send, so existing caption handling produces one turn. The merged turn runs under `fanInChannelIngressLifecycles` of both claims: adoption, deferral, failure and abandonment settle both together, and a turn the handler drops before adoption still consumes both claims. Nothing is re-claimed and nothing is replayed. Any other message in the conversation (another sender, a second attachment, a poll, a location, a reaction), a control command, or the deadline dispatches the held attachment alone first; the debouncer holds the keyed lane until that turn is admitted, so a following `/stop` cannot overtake it. Control commands are recognised with the handler's own normalisation (route, mention patterns, display name) through one shared helper the handler now also uses. Voice messages and captioned attachments are never held. When the monitor closes, held claims are handed back (`onCancelled`) instead of starting turns, and a claim the drain aborts is dropped silently. The setting is Matrix-only, following the triage note that a global queue setting would widen the immediate-media policy to channels that don't need it.

Rebased onto main after #176491. Findings from the first review: the keyed lane is now held through admission (debouncer flush lifecycle); no synthetic replay claim exists any more (each event keeps its durable claim); command normalisation is shared with the handler; polls and locations flush the hold; encrypted double emission and cold-start history no longer reach the hold (ingress deduplicates by event id and skips historical rows before dispatch); the account-level override is bounded like the top-level field.

Second review round (Codex on `92913c1b5a`): an event the server already bundles a replacement for now bypasses the hold like redactions and edits (never folded, never held), and media without `filename` whose body is a single-line file name with an extension (pre-MSC2530 clients, for example `vacation photo.jpg`) is held as captionless; the handler's own caption heuristic is unchanged. Tests added for both. Third round: a reaction's thread is only known after its target is fetched, so a reaction now releases every attachment held in its room before it is dispatched, instead of being keyed at room level; test added. Fourth round: a text joins a held attachment only if its server timestamp is within the hold window of the attachment's (a replay after downtime drains old events back to back); the hold's command check reads the runtime's live config snapshot like normal ingress and uses the canonical `isControlCommandMessage` predicate, so bare abort triggers such as `stop` release the attachment first; tests added. Fifth round: a reaction also waits for attachments already on their way to a turn (flushed but not yet admitted) before it is dispatched, and a claim that cannot be reopened on close is logged rather than left as an unobserved rejection; tests added. Sixth round: the hold is measured from the attachment's server timestamp, so a replay after a restart keeps the original deadline (and an attachment already past it is not held at all) instead of starting a new window; a reaction releases held attachments only when the reaction handler could act on it (it targets one of the bot's own messages), never for a reaction to the held attachment itself or to another user's message; tests added. Seventh round: an attachment replayed after an outage longer than the hold still waits for the companion text that is already queued behind it in the lane (`readLaneBacklog`), so recovery stays one turn; when the reaction target lookup fails, ordering is preserved (the hold is released) rather than skipped; key-verification traffic bypasses the hold like the handler ignores it; the encrypted scenario also asserts no second reply; tests added. Eighth round: the hold reads reaction targets with the handler's own `extractMatrixReactionAnnotation` (a reaction without an explicit `rel_type` is recognised), and the expired-replay companion check applies the same ignored-event predicate as the classifier (edits, bundled replacements, verification traffic, the bot's own events never count as companions); tests added. Ninth round: the hold now uses the reaction handler's own preflight (`resolveMatrixReactionMayStartWork`: approval target, notification mode, target ownership, lookup failure preserves order), and the command check routes by the same effective thread as normal ingress (`resolveMatrixThreadRouting`); tests added.

Tenth round (ClawSweeper on `025c5c3d961`; the ninth-round commit above already covered its reaction-preflight and thread-routing findings): the two recovery cases the earlier body listed as known limits are now handled. (1) Encrypted companions: an expired replayed attachment decrypts queued companion ciphertext through the same local SDK path ingress uses for each delivery (`hydrateEvents`) before it judges it. Ciphertext that cannot be decrypted yet (late room key) still counts when its envelope fits (same sender, within the hold by server time, same thread relation, which stays in clear): the attachment then waits one hold window, and the text is checked again by the normal join rules when the lane delivers it decrypted, so a wrong guess costs at most that bounded wait. (2) Partly admitted catch-up batches: Matrix sync admission now shows each sync batch to the hold (`onSyncBatch`) until every event in it is durable, so an expired attachment that the drain delivers before the rest of its batch is admitted still finds the text that follows it. Nothing in the durable-ingress contract changes: no stored payload, ordering or claim behaviour differs, and nothing runs when `mediaHoldMs` is 0. Also fixed: the previous head's CI failure (`index.test.ts` runtime mock lacked `getOptionalMatrixRuntime`, which the shared reaction preflight's approval-reaction state reads). Tests added for each case, plus two live scenarios (below).

Rebuilt on current main (`ac13a7e0c13`, 2026-10-24) as one commit: main moved the Matrix config UI hints into `config-schema.ts` (the `mediaHoldMs` hint moved with them), inlined the reaction handler's notification mode (now one helper the handler and the hold share), and slimmed the QA scenario contract (`{ details }` executions, no actor cursor bookkeeping); the scenarios follow it.

Eleventh round: rebased on current main (`1f7035c15f3`, 2026-11-07) as one commit, `f31c19123c5`. Main now includes #192585 (`c2cb56c665e`), the core fix for #192522, which is the error the previous evidence recorded for `matrix-media-hold-command-ordering` (`ReplaySafeTranscriptConflictError` when a `/status` arrives while a turn on the same session is still preparing). Nothing in the hold changed since the tenth round. Other changes: the index test runtime mock passes the real module through (`importOriginal`) and overrides only `getMatrixRuntime` / `setMatrixRuntime`, so the mock-exports ratchet accepts it and its baseline entry is pruned; the total test-lines ratchet gets an allocation for the 1049 test lines this change adds (`config/test-lines-allocations/matrix-media-hold.txt`: `media-hold.test.ts`, the ingress sync-batch case, the runtime mock); generated config metadata and docs baseline are regenerated on this base. The command-ordering result on this base is in Evidence: it now passes most runs but still fails intermittently in core, with a different error.

The bound the setting advertises, no attachment waits longer than `mediaHoldMs` past its own server timestamp (or one window after a recovery replay), holds in every case.

Config surface: `channel` count 4003 -> 4005 for the two bounded `mediaHoldMs` fields (top-level and per-account).

## Evidence

Exact head `f31c19123c5`, on main `1f7035c15f3` (2026-11-07), run on a throwaway Linux x86 box.

- `pnpm exec vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-matrix.config.ts extensions/matrix`: 129 files, 1190 tests pass (includes `media-hold.test.ts`, 33 cases).
- `pnpm exec vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-database-workers.config.ts extensions/matrix/src/matrix/monitor/ingress.test.ts`: 5/5.
- `vitest.extension-qa.config.ts` over the scenario catalog, coverage report, scenario selection, live scenario timeouts and the Matrix live-transport units: 53 files, 422 tests pass.
- `pnpm check:baseline-ratchets --base 1f7035c15f3`: all nine pass (max-lines, assertion-safety, database-dialect, timeout-race, mock-exports, test-lines, config-docs, plugin-inventory, database-worker). `pnpm config:channels:check` and `pnpm config:docs:check` clean; `pnpm build` and `pnpm tsgo:extensions` clean; oxlint, oxfmt and `pnpm lint:docs` clean; the pre-commit hook ran and passed.
- Data model: nothing stored changes. No ingress payload, SQLite, session or migration change; the two `mediaHoldMs` keys are optional and additive; nothing new runs when `mediaHoldMs` is 0.
- **Live behaviour proof (QA Lab Matrix lane, real Tuwunel homeserver + real Gateway + the real Matrix plugin, `--provider-mode mock-openai`)**: `pnpm openclaw qa matrix --provider-mode mock-openai --concurrency 1 --scenario …`, **7 of 7 pass** on the exact head in one run (report below). The mock provider answers the image prompt with the image's colours only when the image reached that turn, so a colour reply proves one turn.
  - `matrix-media-hold-attachment-then-text`, `-standalone-timeout`, `-restart-recovery`, `matrix-e2ee-media-hold`, `matrix-media-hold-outage-catch-up`, `matrix-e2ee-media-hold-outage-catch-up`: PASS.
  - `matrix-media-hold-command-ordering` (DM, hold 8 s): PASS in that run, but **not reliably**. Because the 10-24 failure was 3/3, I ran it ten times per tree on the same box (for this head, the run above plus nine runs of this scenario alone; three on the rebuilt 10-24 code):

    | Tree | Runs | Pass | Fail | Core error in the failed runs |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | this head `f31c19123c5` (main `1f7035c15f3`, includes #192585) | 10 | 9 | 1 | `SessionWorkStartChangedError: Persisted user turn changed before replay admission. Retry the turn.` |
    | this head with only #192585's production change reverted (20 lines in three files; local only) | 10 | 10 | 0 | none |
    | this head with `mediaHoldMs: 0` in the scenario (hold off; local only) | 10 | 10 | 0 | none |
    | the 10-24 code rebuilt on its 10-24 base `ac13a7e0c13` (local only; the 10-24 head is no longer fetchable) | 3 | 2 | 1 | `ReplaySafeTranscriptConflictError: SQLite transcript changed while preparing rewrite` |

    Both failed runs show the sequence recorded on 10-24: the `/status` reply arrives, then the attachment's turn, which the hold dispatched before the command, dies before its reply, and the room gets "OpenClaw couldn't finish this request". The gateway lines from the failed run on this head:

    ```text
    [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=main durationMs=947 error="Persisted user turn changed before replay admission. Retry the turn." errorName=SessionWorkStartChangedError taskKind=turn sessionKey=agent:qa:main
    [model-fallback/decision] model fallback chain stopped: reason=local_runtime_coordination candidate=mock-openai/gpt-5.6-luna errorName=SessionWorkStartChangedError
    Embedded agent failed before reply: Persisted user turn changed before replay admission. Retry the turn.
    ```

    My reading: #192585 fixed the 10-24 error (#192522) for `/status`, but the delivered `/status` exchange is still mirrored into the transcript through the shared command mirror (`mirrorDeliveredReplyToTranscript` -> `recordDeliveredCommandExchange`), and when that write lands between the attachment turn's replay preparation and its admission, admission refuses the turn. That is the mechanism #194303 (open) reports for `/stop`; #194451 (open) covers other directives on the older error. So the race is in core and not specific to Matrix, but the hold makes it likelier, because it dispatches the released attachment and the command back to back. With these counts I cannot say whether #192585 changed the rate for this flow. I have not changed the hold for it: the plugin has no signal for "this turn has passed replay admission" beyond adoption, which it already waits for. If maintainers prefer, the hold could keep the releasing command back until the attachment's turn has replied; that makes the command's reply slower, and a `/stop` sent while an attachment is held would then not stop that attachment's turn.
- Not run: a hand-driven Element Web session (the lane drives the same Matrix client API Element Web uses); the upgrade-survivor lane was not re-run this round (no stored data or migration changed since its 2026-10-19 pass).

prs.title: fix(config): prevent PostgreSQL startup failure during backup recovery
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a PostgreSQL-backed Gateway can fail to start when recovering a valid backup after its active configuration unexpectedly shrinks.

## User Impact

Users can restart the Gateway and recover the retained settings without the “PostgreSQL connections must run in a worker” failure. Recovery retains its source, backup-selection and lease-ownership checks. No schema or storage-format change is introduced.

## Why This Change Was Made

Prepared recovery now uses the existing asynchronous backup validator. The final durable lease-ownership read uses existing engine-store admission while remaining synchronous immediately before filesystem effects. Expired or revoked ownership still refuses recovery.

## Evidence

Exact PR head: `f4f3b0cf1fcfbba16b8d19038300844f8b3cee05`.

- [Independent disposable Gateway proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/193596#issuecomment-6664220296): clean exact-head worktree, Node 24.22.2, pnpm 12.15.0 frozen install and runtime build, PostgreSQL 16.15 / pgvector 0.8.7. A real Gateway accepted 13,269 bytes, then cold-recovered from an 873-byte active config with the retained backup. Ready in 7.37 seconds; clean shutdown; restored coach/bootstrap roster and preserved clobbered snapshot. Subsequent real local tool requests returned 401 without authentication, 200 for authenticated session_status and 404 for policy-disallowed read.
- [Official stable upgrade and retained-data proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/193596#issuecomment-6665250290): stable 2026.11.1 → exact-head SQLite upgrade and explicit native Doctor migration → supported PostgreSQL state-family port → actual cold backup recovery → another restart. Public RPCs preserved the same session ID, message ID, history, label and thinking preference. Recovery logged `size-drop-vs-last-good:13915->1179`; the state anchor matched the port manifest and PostgreSQL schema.
- 23 async-recovery tests and 34 PostgreSQL recovery/lease/SQLite tests pass. Regressions cover the failing cold metadata path, expired/revoked leases refusing filesystem changes, and ordinary main-thread PostgreSQL reads remaining forbidden. Production types, scoped typed lint and the worker-boundary ratchet pass.
- [Latest exact-head ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/193596#issuecomment-6663467986): sufficient real proof, no actionable findings, ready for maintainer review.

Stable used SQLite for shared state and agents; the proof does **not** claim a stable PostgreSQL-state upgrade. Only shared state was ported; agent/session storage remained SQLite. Doctor completed with two Skill Workshop policy-inspection findings, disclosed in the evidence. Live inference/channel behavior and broad exact-head hosted CI remain unqualified.

Downstream source `149ae747c2dc53310ee7c71ba89f2864a7f5a8b8` has byte-identical production fixes and passed the full package build, matching build-info, sequential root/Mattermost packs, archive checks, installed pair and actual Linux full-plugin-installer. Separate prelaunch authoring work is tracked in #193636; normal recovery restoring its accepted backup roster remains intentional.

This recovery fix can land independently of #193636. I checked OpenClaw main at `8ae6b3852f97`: both recovery gaps are still present, and none of the files in this PR have changed on main since its base.

[Hosted CI after marking ready](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43044906589) failed its bundled UI shard. The real-Gateway home-read-only test received `UNAVAILABLE` from `chat.metadata` while preparing metadata for the main agent. Attribution to this PR is unverified. The focused cold recovery and upgrade results above still apply to their recorded scenarios.

prs.title: improve: reduce PostgreSQL agent removal latency
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Removing an agent incurs repeated avoidable database work when the gateway uses PostgreSQL, increasing single-agent removal latency.

## User Impact

Agent removal spends less time checking deletion authority. A delayed check also refuses journal ownership changes before returning to its caller. There is no public RPC, configuration, or schema change.

## Why This Change Was Made

`agentDeletion.assertCurrent` currently opens a write transaction even though it only checks authority. Use the existing lease verifier and deletion-journal predicate without that transaction, retaining live operation admission and a final durable lease verification. After the worker reply, the lifecycle owner checks its existing live lease and committed-journal authority before resolving. Retire, fence, finish, rollback, and purge mutations retain their guarded transactions and final-effect checks.

## Evidence

Current-main applicability checked at `83fd655f3fa`. The worker still performs the repeated guarded PostgreSQL write transaction. Native template provenance changes an adjacent import. The retained regression covers journal replacement during the final authority read.

### Upstream `agents.delete` on PostgreSQL

Built the upstream source tree that became `7a83bcd4768dfde3f991f5f3385c4b9e17ff6cfb` (base `3120ab41d8c828a78e045e97d6897b4da53bbadd`) with `pnpm build:docker`. Exercised the real loopback Gateway WebSocket RPC against disposable PostgreSQL 17, with seven synthetic agents and one seeded session/message per agent. Each deletion requested `deleteFiles: true`.

| Measurement | Original authority transaction | Optimized authority check |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Median warm RPC latency | 9,241.65 ms | 7,784.57 ms |
| Median SQL statements observed during RPC | 840 | 695 |
| Cold first RPC | 9,484.88 ms | 7,924.05 ms |

**15.8% lower median latency in this workload.** Both variants removed the target from the roster, refused writes from its old session, removed its workspace, kept the surviving agent writable, and allowed recreation with empty active history.

This is a controlled operation toggle, not two pristine checkout builds: both variants use the same built upstream tree and the new final host fence; the baseline restores only `agentDeletion.assertCurrent` to its original `guarded(..., () => undefined)` handler. No batch RPC or downstream `agents.detach` endpoint is involved in these measurements.

The final pair ran sequentially after local build/check/review work completed. Each boot performed six deletions; the first cold call was excluded from the five warm samples. A loopback TCP relay injected 5 ms in each database direction only during the measured RPC. SQL totals include fixture background statements observed during the RPC. These are synthetic local measurements, not production RTT or a production speedup guarantee. The full reported 25–40 second production delay remains unexplained.

<details>
<summary>Raw warm output</summary>

```text
original ms:  9309.24, 9151.42, 9110.64, 9301.61, 9241.65
optimized ms: 7831.06, 7784.57, 7599.33, 7803.42, 7739.55
original SQL calls:  840, 844, 840, 840, 849
optimized SQL calls: 695, 699, 694, 695, 695
```

</details>

### PostgreSQL final-effect custody proof

Used the same upstream `agents.delete` RPC and source tree in a separate disposable runtime, with a diagnostic pause immediately before the existing purge call. After the gateway reached that pause, a fixture client changed exactly one PostgreSQL authority row, then released the pause. Instrumentation added no authority check or alternate cleanup path. Trace probes watched the existing purge commit, archive publication, and Trash boundaries.

```text
expired lease:
  agents.delete -> OPENCLAW_STATE_LEASE_LOST (lease loss: expired)
  original session retained; retirement archive rows = 0
  original workspace and agent anchor retained
  destructive-boundary trace = []

superseded journal operation_id, same lease retained:
  agents.delete -> Agent traveler0 deletion no longer owns database cleanup.
  original session retained; retirement archive rows = 0
  original workspace and agent anchor retained
  destructive-boundary trace = []
```

The positive deletion run above proves the ordinary path reaches cleanup; these negative runs prove revocation is rejected before that cleanup. They exercise revocation before the first purge, not every possible instruction-level interleaving. The temporary diagnostic harness is not part of this PR.

### Delayed-reply regression and checks

Extended the existing real-worker late-reply test to commit journal handoff, completion, or rollback after the worker read and before reply delivery. All three cases **failed on the original PR head** because the promise resolved successfully. With the existing final journal guard checked before resolution, all four cases (including scope closure) pass. This protects the lifecycle result boundary after the worker's database read or transaction has ended.

- **47 lifecycle and deletion-cleanup tests pass**; 78.30 s wrapper wall time, 44.71 s Vitest duration. The changed lifecycle file runs 22 cases, with 12.76 s summed test-body time. It uses real worker admission and commit publication; no new production test seam or sleep was added.
- Core typecheck, type-aware lint of the three touched source/test files, formatting, and `git diff --check` pass.
- Fresh independent local Codex autoreview of the complete candidate: no actionable P0–P2 findings. An initial sandboxed invocation could not reach the service; the completed public-source review is the result reported here.
- [Current-head CI passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/41531539590) on `7a83bcd4768dfde3f991f5f3385c4b9e17ff6cfb`, including all three PostgreSQL conformance shards and the aggregate `openclaw/ci-gate`.
- [ClawSweeper follow-up review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/191463#issuecomment-6589024083) reviewed the same head: no findings, proof sufficient, ready for maintainer review; the previous security and merge-risk attention items are cleared.
- The dedicated 22-line test allocation covers net growth from the three newly reproduced stale-journal reply cases; it does not change the shared test budget scalar.

<details>
<summary>Focused validation commands</summary>

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/agent-lifecycle-registry.test.ts src/state/agent-deletion-cleanup.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo
node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig tsconfig.core.json src/agents/agent-lifecycle-registry.ts src/agents/agent-lifecycle-registry.test.ts src/state/agent-deletion.worker.ts
pnpm exec oxfmt --check src/agents/agent-lifecycle-registry.ts src/agents/agent-lifecycle-registry.test.ts src/state/agent-deletion.worker.ts
pnpm build:docker
git diff --check
```

</details>

prs.title: fix(usage): Usage tab double-counts prompts that older Codex runs mirrored twice
prs.body: Closes #140464 ## What Problem This Solves Fixes: the Usage tab counts one prompt as two user messages when the transcript holds a prompt that an older Codex app-server run mirrored a second time. ## User Impact User impact: Usage message counts and the session message list show each prompt once, including sessions recorded before upgrading. Token and cost totals were already correct and do not change. ## Why This Change Was Made Codex app-server turns on releases such as 2026.9.2 annotated the admitted prompt with `mirrorIdentity` and `mirrorSourceFingerprint`, then mirrored a second user row with the same pair. Main no longer writes that row, but retained transcripts keep it and the Usage reader counts every user row. The rollup now skips a user row whose mirror identity and fingerprint match the previous counted user row, and `loadSessionLogs` applies the same rule. The key is kept next to `lastUserTimestamp` in the rollup and in the partitioned checkpoint, so a pair split across incremental refreshes still counts once. `USAGE_COST_ROLLUP_VERSION` goes from 13 to 14, so every cached count is rebuilt. Prompts with the same text but different identities still count separately. ## Evidence - Upgrade from v2026.10.2 on a real Gateway, with the Codex app-server against QA Lab's mock OpenAI provider. One isolated cron agent turn on v2026.9.2 wrote the reported pair, and a control session sent the same text as two turns. v2026.10.2 then ran `openclaw doctor --fix` (agent database v19 to v24) and its Gateway on that state, followed by this branch's doctor (v24 to v26) and Gateway on the same state. On v2026.10.2 the cron session's `sessions.usage` showed user 2 and total 3, and its session logs listed user, user, assistant. On this branch it showed user 1 and total 2, and the logs listed user, assistant. The control session stayed at user 2 and total 4, `usage.cost` stayed at 264 tokens, and the Usage rows cached at version 6 were rebuilt. - On that upgrade, `chat.history` for both sessions matched what v2026.10.2 read, and this branch's doctor left the config byte-identical. One more prompt sent to the control session through this branch's Gateway took it to user 3 on the next incremental refresh, and the cron session stayed at user 1. That turn's model call failed outside the QA harness, so it has no reply. - New tests in the worker refresh file (full scan, pair split across a cached refresh) and the session cost usage test file (logs) fail on main and pass here, and a same-text control passes on both. Keying on the fingerprint alone fails the control. The split refresh test restores the checkpoint and partitions through `partitionUsageCostRollup` the way the worker does, and leaving `lastUserMirrorKey` out of the partitioned checkpoint fails it with a count of 2 instead of 1. - The 58 Usage-related test files pass, 544 tests, with the PostgreSQL usage partition test run against PostgreSQL 17. prs.title: fix(postgres): chat history slows under concurrent reads
prs.body:
Closes #188956
Related: #197313, #190001 (#197313 tracks the repeated read snapshots inside each history page, which #190001 addresses)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: on PostgreSQL, `chat.history` requests queue behind two history workers when several clients load history at once, so tail latency grows with concurrency while the CPU sits mostly idle.

## User Impact

User impact: concurrent `chat.history` on PostgreSQL waits much less for a history worker. Re-measured on current `main` (medians of 8 interleaved runs per build): at 8 concurrent clients p50 drops from 19.6 to 12.02 ms, p99 from 54.31 to 31.76 ms, and throughput rises from 378.1 to 622.95 requests/s; at 32 clients p99 drops from 163.13 to 103.1 ms. Single-client p50 is unchanged; single-client p99 rose from 15.08 to 17.07 ms over all runs (14.87 to 15.13 ms in the quieter block). SQLite keeps its current lane size.

Cost, measured on the same runs (medians of 8 runs per build):

- Memory: during concurrent history reads the Gateway runs up to two more transcript isolates (about 57 MiB of heap each). Peak transcript-worker heap rose from 334.1 to 453.6 MiB and peak Gateway RSS from 2,764.9 to 3,153.1 MiB. The extra isolates retire after the pool's existing idle timeout: 45 s and 100 s after load both builds ran the same number of transcript isolates with about the same heap (45 s: 229.4 vs 242.8 MiB; 100 s: 223.8 vs 227.8 MiB). RSS at 100 s was 2,106.1 vs 2,324.7 MiB.
- PostgreSQL connections: backends for the runtime role peaked at 23 on base and 25 with the change; both were back to 13 after 100 idle seconds. Each extra history isolate can retain up to two idle transports for three minutes; the documented budget (`isolates × (active + 2)`) now notes up to four history isolates.

**Decision for review:** should PostgreSQL history use up to four workers, accepting the cost above? This revises the two-worker reader cap from #167295 and #169110 for one lane on one engine.

- (a) Accept four workers for PostgreSQL history (this PR). Cost: up to two more isolates (about 120 to 124 MiB of worker heap and about 320 to 390 MiB of peak RSS across the two benches below) and two more peak backends, only while history load is concurrent; single-client p99 from 15.08 to 17.07 ms over all runs (14.87 to 15.13 ms in the quieter block). On a host whose CPU is already saturated by other work, the extra workers did not help p99 (see Evidence, block 1).
- (b) Keep two workers. PostgreSQL history keeps queueing: 5.57 ms of queue wait per worker request at 8 clients, 13.34 ms at 16.
- (c) Make the larger lane opt-in with a setting. No default cost, but it adds a config surface for an internal pool size, and the default keeps the queueing.
- (d) A cap of eight. Measured on an older `main` (see Evidence): lower queue wait at 16 clients, at about two and a half times the extra memory and with more backends.

Recommended: (a). The extra workers exist only on PostgreSQL agent stores and only under concurrent history reads, they retire through the existing idle timeout and cleanup owners, and SQLite, transcript search and every other lane keep the current cap. The memory bound stays fixed (at most four history isolates on any host), and the latency it buys is the symptom #188956 reports.

## Why This Change Was Made

On PostgreSQL a history worker spends most of a request blocked in `Atomics.wait` on bridge replies, so sizing the lane like a CPU-bound reader leaves requests queued while CPU is free. The history lane on PostgreSQL agent stores now gets two workers per CPU above one, capped at four (two on a two-CPU host). Transcript search, the other transcript lanes, and every SQLite lane keep the existing reader size from #167295 and #169110. No new setting.

The database engine is installed during boot, after the lane module is imported, so the history pool now resolves its size on first use instead of at import. Production code: +47/-7 lines ignoring whitespace (the pool options block is re-indented inside the first-use constructor); tests +117; docs +9/-4.

Scope: this closes #188956 (the queueing in front of the history workers). The transaction round trips inside each page are #197313, addressed by #190001; the two touch different files and are measured separately.

## Evidence

Evidence files: https://github.com/etzelm/openclaw/tree/assets/pg-r2-l3d-history-reader-lane-evidence/current-main-2026-11-07 (paths below are relative to it; method, host and store in `README.md`). The earlier bench on `31866655fd6` stays at the root of the same branch.

Acceptance rule: through a running Gateway on PostgreSQL, at 8 or more concurrent clients, queue wait per worker request and p50 drop, throughput rises and p99 at 8 clients drops; single-client latency holds; the memory and backend cost is reported, and the extra isolates retire once history load stops.

- **Tests** on this head merged into current `main` `078033289a3`: a per-engine sizing table (`src/infra/worker-pool-sizing.test.ts`) and a lane test that installs the engine after importing the lane, as boot does (`src/config/sessions/session-history-lane-sizing.test.ts`: PostgreSQL 4, SQLite 2, search 2). Both pass, as do the consumer suites for the transcript lanes, the search worker, reconcile readiness, the chat history worker and worker-pool preparation: 12 files, 161 tests (`tests/unit-head.log`). On `main` the sizing table fails because the resolver does not exist, and the PostgreSQL lane case gets 2 instead of 4 while the SQLite case passes (`tests/unit-base-red.log`). `pnpm check:changed` on the merged head passes every check except two repo-wide audits that fail the same way on plain `main` `078033289a3`: changelog attributions (bot credits in `CHANGELOG/` files) and the dead export scan (`scripts/lib/control-ui-gesture-probe.ts`, `src/process/command-reservation-census.ts`) (`tests/check-changed.log`, `tests/base-changelog-attr.log`, `tests/base-deadcode.log`). CI on `987348094eb` was green.
- **After merging `main` `4a0e45492b8`** (head `3e55cf3ef68`): `main` dropped the history worker's `prewarmHistory` option (#198512), so the lazy pool no longer passes it; sizing is unchanged. The sizing table, the lane test and the consumer suites above plus the prewarm and history worker lifecycle suites pass: 14 files, 169 tests. One test in `session-transcript-worker-lanes.test.ts` (`releases pressure subscriptions after native settlement and rearms reopened lanes`, added on `main` by #197510) fails on this head and on plain `main` `4a0e45492b8` alike, 3 of 3 runs each on a macOS arm64 host. `pnpm check:changed` passes every step except the dead export scan, whose findings are all in files this PR does not touch.
- **Closed-loop `chat.history` bench on current `main`**: base `main` `078033289a3` vs this head merged into it, both built with `pnpm build`. A fresh Gateway on PostgreSQL 17.11 per run, seeded through its own RPCs with 200 sessions (170 sessions across 6 agents with 2 to 4,675 messages each, plus 30 imported Claude CLI sessions with tool rows hidden between visible turns). Limit 100, 45 s per arm, 16 runs (8 per build) in two interleaved blocks (base head head base base head head base). No run was dropped. Medians over all 16 runs (`bench/block-all/medians.tsv`; every run in `bench/block-all/arms.tsv`; raw scrapes in `bench/runs/`):

| arm | p50 / p95 / p99 ms | p99 range | requests/s | queue wait per worker request | handler mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 client, base | 6.09 / 10.69 / 15.08 | 12.85 to 51.11 | 156.4 | 0.0 ms | 5.19 ms |
| 1 client, fix | 6.00 / 11.02 / 17.07 | 11.9 to 106.71 | 154.4 | 0.0 ms | 5.27 ms |
| 8 clients, base | 19.6 / 31.82 / 54.31 | 28.99 to 161.47 | 378.1 | 5.57 ms | 19.46 ms |
| 8 clients, fix | 12.02 / 19.64 / 31.76 | 20 to 230.82 | 622.95 | 1.23 ms | 10.1 ms |
| 16 clients, base | 37.66 / 54.15 / 88.16 | 58.52 to 200.55 | 411.8 | 13.34 ms | 37.21 ms |
| 16 clients, fix | 24.6 / 42.92 / 66.77 | 45.72 to 499.74 | 606.65 | 6.73 ms | 23.41 ms |
| 32 clients, base | 71.04 / 96.61 / 163.13 | 90.84 to 421.36 | 431.7 | 28.54 ms | 72.43 ms |
| 32 clients, fix | 48.48 / 84.22 / 103.1 | 66.74 to 578.74 | 634.25 | 17.02 ms | 47.23 ms |

Queue wait is `openclaw_worker_queue_wait_seconds{kind="sessionTranscript"}`; handler mean is `openclaw_gateway_rpc_handler_seconds{method="chat.history"}`. The host is shared, and the wide p99 ranges come from runs under other load, so the two blocks are also reported separately:

- Block 2 (`bench/block-b2/`, started only below a 1-minute load of 12; arms at load 4 to 25): p99 at 1, 8, 16 and 32 clients 14.87 / 30.47 / 68.2 / 115.94 ms base vs 15.13 / 25.1 / 64.69 / 88.53 ms fix; p50 at 8 clients 18.11 vs 11.73 ms, throughput 431.6 vs 651.05 requests/s. At 16 clients p99 is about even while p50 drops from 35.98 to 24.6 ms.
- Block 1 (`bench/block-b1/`, load 6 to 55): p50, throughput and queue wait improve at 8, 16 and 32 clients as above, but p99 does not improve consistently: 69.65 vs 73.11 ms at 8 clients, 147.19 vs 113.72 ms at 16, 198.87 vs 281.24 ms at 32. The worst fix tails are `pg-head-r1` (the highest 1-minute load in the bench, 37 to 55) and `pg-head-r2` (load 25 to 33, started with 25% of host memory free); the other two fix runs in the block have p99 21.7 and 36.16 ms at 8 clients. When the host's CPU is already saturated, extra workers add little.

- **Moved the wrong way**: memory and backends (see User Impact: +120 MiB peak transcript heap, +388 MiB peak RSS, +219 MiB RSS 100 s after load, +2 peak backends); single-client p99 15.08 to 17.07 ms over all runs (14.87 to 15.13 ms in block 2; p50 6.09 to 6.00 ms over all runs, 5.71 to 5.94 ms in block 2; single-client p95 10.69 to 11.02 ms over all runs) and 19.35 to 33.27 ms in block 1 (driven by `pg-head-r2`, single-client p99 106.71 ms); single-client throughput 156.4 to 154.4 requests/s over all runs (163.6 to 155.65 in block 2); and in block 1, under the heaviest host load, p99 at 8 clients 69.65 to 73.11 ms and at 32 clients 198.87 to 281.24 ms. In the pair bench on current `main`, single-client p95 12.75 vs 10.47 ms (+22%), p99 21.33 vs 12.85 ms and throughput 136.4 vs 159.0 calls/s (-14%) (`pair-bench/medians.tsv`). These are part of the decision above.
- **Memory and connections** (`bench/block-all/memory-medians.tsv`, per run in `memory.tsv`): see User Impact. Heap and isolate counts come from the Gateway's worker metrics, sampled by the 30 s diagnostic heartbeat; RSS and backend counts are sampled every 2 s.
- **SQLite**: the lane size is unchanged by construction (the resolver returns the existing reader size for every non-PostgreSQL agent engine; covered by the sizing table and lane test). The earlier bench on `31866655fd6` measured SQLite p50, throughput and transcript isolates unchanged; not re-measured here.
- **Cap of four vs eight** (earlier bench on `31866655fd6`, 3 runs each, `bench/medians.tsv` and `bench/memory-medians.tsv` at the branch root, rows `base-a`, `fix4` and `fix8`): eight gave 0.07 ms queue wait at 8 clients and 1.66 ms at 16, at +325 MiB peak transcript heap, +974 MiB peak RSS and 27 peak backends over `base-a`, against +120 MiB heap, +382 MiB RSS and 25 peak backends for four (`fix4` over `base-a`).

- **Pair bench on current `main` `82210a2bbdb0`** (`pair-bench/`): four builds from one `main` (`main`, `main` + #190001, `main` + this PR, `main` + both), four runs each in interleaved order, PostgreSQL 17.11, closed-loop `chat.history` at 1, 8, 16 and 32 clients. Gate results on the same `main`: unit 12 files / 162 tests pass with this PR (the new sizing and lane tests fail on plain `main`); with both PRs unit 28 / 386 and PostgreSQL conformance 15 / 165 pass. Medians of 4 runs, this PR vs `main`: at 8 clients p50 13.84 vs 19.65 ms, p99 26.26 vs 46.48 ms, 555 vs 385 calls/s, queue wait per worker request 1.06 vs 5.28 ms; at 16 clients p50 29.21 vs 41.94 ms, 507 vs 362 calls/s; at 32 clients p50 58.09 vs 79.41 ms, p99 88.81 vs 199.78 ms, 545 vs 372 calls/s. At 1 client p50 is 6.31 vs 6.01 ms and p99 is noisier (12.12 to 60.43 ms across runs vs 11.74 to 23.23 ms on `main`; the two highest runs had the highest arm-start load of this build's four runs, 13.1 and 17.9 in `pair-bench/arms.tsv`). Cost: peak Gateway RSS 2789 vs 2468 MiB (+321 MiB), peak transcript worker heap 456 vs 332 MiB (+124 MiB), peak transcript workers 8 vs 6, peak PostgreSQL backends 23 vs 21; 100 s after load, 4 workers vs 3 and the same 13 backends. With #190001 as well, p50 is the same at 16 and 32 clients (29.57 and 58.06 ms) but p99 is higher (81.27 vs 67.81 ms, 128.55 vs 88.81 ms). At 8 clients the pair has p50 15.21 ms, p99 55.06 ms and 480.2 calls/s: p99 is above this PR alone (26.26 ms) and also above `main` (46.48 ms), and throughput is below this PR alone (555.25 calls/s) in all four paired runs (`arms.tsv`), so host load does not explain it. The cost comes from #190001 on this dense-page store (history worker time per request 3.741 vs 3.229 ms at 8 clients, `pair-bench/worker-time.tsv`) and is reported there.

### Gaps

- The bench store is synthetic, written through the Gateway's own RPCs, because `main` does not admit a `pg_restore` of a production store. Its shape follows the production bench in #188956.
- Shared host: the p99 tails in block 1 are dominated by other load (per-arm load in `arms.tsv`). Two fix runs (`pg-head-r2` in block 1, `pg-head-r8` in block 2) started while another job held most host memory; both are kept.
- At 16 clients and above the four-worker lane queues again (6.73 ms per worker request at 16, 17.02 ms at 32). A cap of eight removes most of that at a higher memory cost.
- Memory figures needed one measurement-only line, applied identically to both builds: the diagnostic heartbeat publishes its memory sample every 30 s instead of only after agent activity (`scripts/instrument-*.diff`). Isolate counts and heap cover every transcript lane, not only history, and 30 s sampling can miss the exact peak. RSS was watched for 100 s after load here; the earlier 300 s pair on `31866655fd6` (`bench/runs/pg-*-idle-r1` at the branch root) showed no lasting RSS difference with the same isolate count (1,676 vs 1,745 MiB at 300 s).
- Transcript search on PostgreSQL also blocks on bridge replies and keeps its two-worker cap; not measured here.
- The bench host is shared (1-minute load 4.2 to 13.8 at run start, `pair-bench/run-order-and-load.txt`, and 3.8 to 22.2 at arm start, `pair-bench/arms.tsv`). Tails at 1 and 8 clients move with that load; medians at 8 or more clients do not. Idle retirement past 100 s was not sampled in the pair bench; the earlier bench above covers it.

prs.title: fix: show earlier attachments in Session files
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Opening Files in a long chat could show only the recent uploads. A file shared at the beginning could be missing until someone scrolled back through the conversation.

## User Impact

Session files now includes older attachments without loading earlier chat pages. Files keep their native previews, and “Show in chat” goes to the source message. A partial-list notice remains when the Gateway really cannot supply the whole list.

## Why This Change Was Made

Files already requests the session’s artifacts. The Gateway collects attachment references in that same transcript pass and reuses its revision-aware cache. There is no new table, migration, history preload, or extra catalog request. A 4 MiB ceiling bounds the extra metadata; if it is reached, the panel retains both the collected references and attachments from the loaded chat. Older Gateways retain their existing fallback.

## Evidence

- In Chromium, with the same paginated chat fixture, the original project brief was missing on `abd8b92cfa` and present on `b63c38fb27`. Both versions made one catalog request. This verifies the Control UI, not a native macOS run.
- 58 focused UI tests, the real Gateway integration test, core and UI type checks, and the UI production build passed. The build reported advisory bundle-budget overages; no budgets were raised.
- In a local synthetic session with 1,204 messages and 27 messages carrying attachments, the catalog RPC took 13.9 ms on the first request after appending history, then 3.7 and 2.6 ms. The response was 6,469 bytes. These are local observations, not a production latency guarantee.

prs.title: fix: finish `database port --to postgres` in minutes instead of hours over a network link
prs.body:
Closes #201249

Prior work: #188397 (merged) made the port copy navigation rows exactly instead of rebuilding them row by row. It left the search rows, which this PR batches.

## What Problem This Solves

Moving an agent store to PostgreSQL with `openclaw database port --to postgres` rebuilds the transcript search rows after the bulk copy, and it sent one INSERT per message. When the PostgreSQL server is not on the same network, each INSERT waits a full round trip, so the port time is set by latency, not by data size. The reporter measured about 21,000 search rows at roughly 92 ms per round trip, and the Gateway has to stay offline for the whole port.

## User Impact

User impact: operators porting a large agent store to a remote PostgreSQL server wait for a few dozen round trips instead of one per message, so the Gateway comes back much sooner. The ported rows are the same, in the same order.

## Why This Change Was Made

The transcript owner already has a batched PostgreSQL write that allocates identities in message order and pairs each identity with its own content. The port was bypassing it with a hand-written per-row statement. It now builds the same statement for a batch of up to 512 rows and runs it over the port's connection, so there is one allocation contract instead of two. To make that possible, the compile-only PostgreSQL Kysely facade in `kysely-sync.ts` is exported for asynchronous callers that run the compiled query themselves. Rows are collected from the source generator one batch at a time, so memory stays bounded.

This does not change the other cost the issue mentions, reading each session's events back from the target before projecting. That is left for a separate change.

## Evidence

Before the change, a 1,100-message session produced 1,100 search-row statements in the new regression test. After it, the same session produces 3 (512, 512 and 76 rows), the message IDs reach the database in transcript order, and each statement stays well under PostgreSQL's 65,535-parameter limit. The test fails on the old code and passes on the new code. For the reporter's 21,000 rows that is about 41 statements instead of 21,000; at 92 ms each that is a few seconds of waiting by arithmetic, not a measurement.

I ran the exact compiled statement against a real PostgreSQL engine (PGlite) with a 1,100-row, three-batch run that included null message IDs, roles and timestamps. Row IDs came out 1 through 1,100 in input order, each row's text, message ID, role and timestamp matched its input, `session_transcript_fts_rows` agreed with `session_transcript_fts`, and the identity sequence ended at 1,100.

<details>
<summary>Commands and what was not run</summary>

- New regression test `src/infra/database-engine/agent-port-projections.test.ts`, two tests, run with vitest 5.0.5: pass on the change, fail on the old `agent-port-projections.ts` (1,100 statements instead of 3). Wall time about 1 s including module import; this is not a `pnpm test` measurement because a full `pnpm install` was not possible in the environment.
- PGlite check of the compiled statement, described above (throwaway test, not committed).
- `oxfmt --check` on the four changed files, `tsc` on the changed files with no errors reported in them, and `git diff --check` pass.
- Existing `session-transcript-projection-rebuild` and `query-compiler` tests pass. Four unrelated `kysely-sync` tests fail only because `tsx` is missing from the scratch dependency set.
- Not run: the PostgreSQL conformance suite (`scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs --engine postgres`) against a live server, `pnpm tsgo`, `pnpm lint` (oxlint did not discover files in this environment), a port over a real WAN link, and CI.

</details>

prs.title: fix(onboard): reject --secret-input-mode ref when the provider API key flag differs from the env var
prs.body:
AI-assisted: yes

Closes #201401

## What Problem This Solves

- Fixes an issue where users running `openclaw onboard --non-interactive --secret-input-mode ref` with a provider API key flag (for example `--anthropic-api-key`) while the provider's environment variable holds a *different* value would silently end up with a reference to the stale environment variable; the explicitly passed key was discarded with no warning, and onboarding reported success.
- **Related:** #201401; the Gateway credential flags already reject this exact mismatch (`src/commands/onboard.ts`), so provider flags now follow the same contract.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Intended outcome:** When `--secret-input-mode ref` is used and both the provider flag and its env var are set to different values, onboarding now fails with the same error shape the Gateway credential flags use, instead of silently keeping the env value. Matching values, env-only, and flag-only (plaintext) flows are unchanged.
- **Out of scope:** No changes to reference serialization, plaintext flag precedence, or the Gateway credential checks themselves.
- **Highest-risk area:** The shared non-interactive resolver used by provider methods, custom-provider onboarding, and reset validation.
- **How is that risk mitigated?** The comparison is added only to the existing ref-mode branch, after the existing malformed-input check (preserving the current malformed-input error precedence), and both values are normalized the same way as today. The error message contains neither value.

## User Impact

- **Success criteria:** `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=A openclaw onboard --non-interactive --accept-risk --secret-input-mode ref --anthropic-api-key B` (A ≠ B) now exits 1 with `--anthropic-api-key does not match ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Set the environment variable to the same value or omit the flag.` and persists no credentials; when A = B the env reference is stored exactly as before.
- **What should reviewers focus on?** `src/commands/onboard-non-interactive/api-keys.ts` (single comparison in the ref-mode branch) and the new regression tests in `src/commands/onboard-non-interactive/api-keys.test.ts` (`stores the env reference when a ref-mode flag matches the env var`, `rejects a ref-mode flag that differs from the provider env var without leaking either value`).

## Evidence

- **Real environment tested:** Isolated worktree of this PR branch, shipped CLI entry point (`node scripts/run-node.mjs`) with local runtime build, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/`OPENCLAW_AGENT_DIR` pointed at temp dirs; synthetic (non-secret) key values.
- **Exact steps or commands run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  # mismatch case (should now fail, before it silently stored the env reference)
  ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-stale-env-key \
    node scripts/run-node.mjs onboard --non-interactive --accept-risk \
    --secret-input-mode ref --anthropic-api-key sk-ant-rotated-flag-key
  # matching case (should keep working, with --skip-health)
  ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-same-key \
    node scripts/run-node.mjs onboard --non-interactive --accept-risk --skip-health \
    --secret-input-mode ref --anthropic-api-key sk-ant-same-key
  # regression tests
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/commands/onboard-non-interactive/api-keys.test.ts
  ```
- **Evidence after fix:**
  ```text
  ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-stale-env-key ... --anthropic-api-key sk-ant-rotated-flag-key
  → exit 1
  --anthropic-api-key does not match ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Set the environment variable to the same value or omit the flag.
  (no credential profile persisted; neither key value appears in the output)
  ```
- **Observed result after fix:** Conflicting ref-mode inputs are rejected before any credential is persisted; the matching case still exits 0 and stores `keyRef: {"source":"env","id":"ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"}` as before. Unit suite `api-keys.test.ts` 14/14 green via validate.sh (oxfmt + oxlint + tsgo:core).
- **Before evidence (optional, visual changes encouraged):** On origin/main @ f5b717d232f the same mismatch command was accepted silently: onboarding proceeded past the API-key stage and stored `anthropic:default` with `keyRef: {"source":"env","id":"ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"}` — the passed `--anthropic-api-key` value was never used.
- **What was not tested:** Live provider authentication (synthetic key values only; no real Anthropic credentials were involved). Gateway health checks beyond `--skip-health` (requires a running gateway; unrelated to this change).
- **Proof tier:** L2
- **Proof limitations:** none
- **Review state:** Awaiting CI + maintainer review; CI lanes pending.

prs.title: fix: keep the conversation visible when switching sessions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Opening a chat for the first time briefly replaced the previous messages with gray placeholders and then an empty conversation. This is the transcript flash visible in the after-video on #201318, not the sidebar list jump that PR fixes.

## User Impact

User impact: switching chats keeps the previous conversation readable, but not interactive, until the selected conversation can be shown. Already-loaded conversations still switch immediately. If a first load takes longer than half a second, the selected chat shows its own loading state.

## Why This Change Was Made

Having message rows in the page does not mean they are visible: the transcript deliberately hides them while it restores the reading position. The handoff now covers both preparation and positioning. It reuses the mounted conversation rather than copying messages between sessions or blocking navigation on history.

## Evidence

Four first visits in the actual desktop Control UI, with distinct synthetic histories, Chromium at 1100 × 760, and 4× CPU slowdown. We checked the pixels in the conversation body on every frame of the 25 fps switch clips (initial app startup excluded). On main (`abd8b92cfa49`), messages disappeared on all four switches for 9–12 frames each: 44/297 frames in total. On the tested change (`c342aa29cbf9`), 0/296 frames lost message text. Each click reached the correct transcript.

The UI typecheck, both focused component/browser tests, and all ten bundled navigation tests passed, including slow startup, retained scroll position, and typing focus. This was not a live Gateway test.

### Clean comparison

Before: on a first visit, the previous messages disappear before the selected conversation appears.

![Before: loading placeholders replace the visible conversation](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/618f5a1c-dae3-4d2f-8783-f17144407c3f)

After: the previous conversation stays readable until the selected chat can show its messages.

![After: message text remains visible during the switch](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/85614709-ed7e-474e-a0d9-994760f46cb1)

### Annotated comparison

![Before: the highlighted conversation area has no readable messages](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/462f7146-4ea2-4a6d-a383-55f8e2ce5415)

![After: the highlighted conversation area keeps the outgoing messages visible](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6c2d18a1-8601-4fb2-a761-d9520b3527fa)

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cd7c8346-3cc3-423c-873a-e76cc1aaa60c

After — the same four switches, without a blank frame:

Reported by @vyctorbrzezowski.

prs.title: fix(talk): load conversation history when starting a fresh call
prs.body:
Root cause: `src/gateway/talk/handlers/session.ts:330-332` loads history only when the call is a voice replacement (`replacement ? readTalkRealtimeInitialItems(...) : []`), so a fresh Gateway-relay call into the same conversation starts the voice provider with no history, unlike browser Talk (`talk.client.create`), which already reads it for every call.

Related: #182681 (separate Android selected-conversation routing fix)

## What Problem This Solves

Starting a fresh realtime Talk call through the Gateway relay omits the conversation's recent history, even when the call targets the correct chat. Stopping and reopening Talk therefore starts the voice provider without the context saved during the previous call. The existing history-loading path runs only for an in-call voice replacement.

## User Impact

Fresh relay calls, including Android Talk, receive the selected conversation's bounded recent history at startup. No APK update, configuration change, or migration is required for this Gateway fix.

This does not fix Android selecting the wrong chat (#182681), or a provider ignoring supplied startup instructions (#199052). In particular, it is not a claim of complete GPT-Live subscription recall without the separate provider fix.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the existing selected-session history reader for fresh calls as well as voice replacements. It retains the same session authorization, history bounds, and quoted-background treatment. Empty sessions still supply no history; the saved transcript is unchanged.

The production change removes a conditional: +1/-3 lines, with no new helper, state, setting, or provider-specific behavior. The regression adds 21 lines to the existing handler suite; documentation describes the startup behavior.

## Evidence

- Gateway proof (isolated source Gateway, `talk.session.create` with the Android relay params, local OpenAI Realtime-compatible endpoint recording the startup instructions): https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201352#issuecomment-6987252694
  - `origin/main` 7ce2d10eced5: the conversation's saved speech is in `chat.history`, but the fresh call's instructions have no history block.
  - Head 554749826ea4: the fresh call's instructions carry the conversation's speech as quoted `<shared_session_history>`; another conversation's speech is absent.
  - Controls, same on both: an empty conversation and a call with no `sessionKey` get identical 1468-byte instructions; an operator without `operator.talk` is refused before any provider connection opens.
- Regression `native-consult-target.test.ts` "reopening Talk": 2 failed on `origin/main` 7ce2d10eced5, 2 passed on this head.

- Reproduced on upstream `1ab0fc863407d45396d00e9afcdbcd98d9351f9d`: both new cases fail because the reopened call's provider instructions contain no shared history.
- The regression exercises production Gateway request dispatch, relay transcript persistence, close, and fresh creation for both `main` and an explicitly selected conversation. With the fix, the earlier keyword reaches the provider; another conversation's keyword does not. It also checks quoted, non-instruction treatment. Existing empty-session and voice-replacement coverage remains in the same suite.
- Focused handler and prompt-prefix suites passed: 125 Gateway tests plus 16 prefix-stability tests, 141 total, in 126.67 seconds wrapper wall time. After removing three duplicate assertions to respect the existing file-size limit, the final 40-test handler file passed again with `pnpm test src/gateway/talk/handlers/native-consult-target.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 93.01 seconds wrapper wall time, including cold compiled-worker preparation. This existing integration suite exercises dispatch, persistent transcripts and call ownership; it is not a new per-test Gateway boot. The new regression cases took 1.14 and 7.64 seconds in that run.
- Targeted Gateway test-graph typecheck, type-aware lint of both changed TypeScript files, formatting of all three changed files, and `git diff --check` passed. No full release build or broad suite is claimed; CI timing is not yet available.
- Independent native source review found no actionable P0–P2 findings. The AutoReview CLI could not connect to its Responses WebSocket endpoint and produced no report; this is not claimed as a successful AutoReview run.

Proof boundary: real Gateway, Talk RPC, transcript and history owners; local Realtime-compatible provider endpoint. No fresh physical Android microphone/speaker or live provider acceptance is claimed. No production Gateway or device was changed.

## Merge danger

Two-way door: a revert restores the old startup context; nothing is written or migrated. Blast radius: Gateway-relay Talk calls (Android, iOS relay) now start with the same bounded, quoted history that browser Talk and voice replacements already get.

Publication preparation independently verified the complete two-file diff, clean working tree, exact one-commit ancestry, and passing `git diff --check`. The tests, build, and device verification above were not independently rerun. No new automated review was performed. Hosted screenshot evidence was explicitly waived by the requester.

Base commit: `954f1a4fea0fd69ff0f951c9ebf7f2af79b86f33`

Contribution by @saariuslystoned; original source commit authored by Bobby Bones.

prs.title: feat(ui): render LaTeX in Control UI markdown
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Control UI Markdown displayed supported LaTeX literally. This renders bounded math while preserving code, escaped input, currency, URLs and sanitized output.

## User Impact

Math is lazy-loaded; ordinary messages request no KaTeX engine, styles or fonts. Equations stay readable as source until ready, and failures keep that fallback. Wide equations scroll inside the message and now show a fade where content continues. Math stays findable in transcript search and readable in paste excerpts and web source previews.

Original contribution by @jjjhenriksen; repair work requested by @RomneyDa. Contributor authorship and coauthor credit are preserved; Allow edits from maintainers remains enabled.

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion with @RomneyDa](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/clawtributor-review-pr-144324)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/41d889a9-23c8-4603-889b-a35ad86acfb6)

- [Rebase discussion and verification with @vyctorbrzezowski](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/ac39fc44-8e46-4656-ba81-f57ba2533d4c)

## Why This Change Was Made

Preserve the existing parser, generation-fenced leaf, shared lazy runtime, MathML and separate sanitizer. One 200-expression allowance covers stable streamed additions and the mutable tail. KaTeX **0.18.2** addresses GHSA-238p-pmpm-9mq7 while retaining `trust: false`. Plain-text consumers of the shared parser (search, paste excerpts, source previews) read math tokens as their TeX source, so math stays searchable and readable outside the rendered view. Wide equations reuse the table fade convention rather than adding a new affordance.

This remains built-in math, not a plugin. Product decision (2026-11-08, @vyctorbrzezowski): use built-in math rendering with KaTeX and prepare this selected PR for merge; merging remains a separate decision. #175507 contains the earlier equivalent implementation, not this latest rebase. KaTeX is the one new dependency (MIT, pinned 0.18.2, loaded only when a message contains math); dense math retains real CPU cost, bounded by the 200-expression message budget.

## Evidence

- **Rebased November 18, 2026:** signed head `9a657d163052cd39f9f9ac5504d6d673994ed942` on main `fe83a7e0afa56fb311f3c43f459abaffd7c5e248`; tree `faf8f8330cfb569109fb505f6f3f87debe08dd18`. The rebase applied without conflicts and preserves Jacqueline’s authorship and all coauthors. No merge or auto-merge was enabled.
- **Focused verification:** [secretless AWS Crabbox run](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_e7026256d55fe5a97a6272d176356287), lease `cbx_8cdcdefd7d4f`, verified IAM endpoint 404. Frozen install, **133 tests in 8 files**, UI typecheck, formatting, lint and test-line ratchet passed. `pnpm ui:boot-manifest:gen` regenerated upstream boot-graph changes; the initial manifest-drift assertion failed, and its generated output was retained verbatim. Remote inspection confirmed that this manifest was the only changed tracked file; its exact bytes and diff were verified before amending the signed commit. This is not a claim that the initial aggregate run passed.
- **Production build and base-relative performance:** `pnpm ui:check-performance:base fe83a7e0afa56fb311f3c43f459abaffd7c5e248` passed after manifest generation: chat boot **+1,841 B gzip**, New Session boot **−147 B**, startup **+17 B**, unchanged request counts. Existing absolute-baseline debt remains; no budget was raised. No new visual behavior was introduced, so the earlier screenshots below are reused, not recaptured.
- **Hosted checks:** fresh CI must evaluate the new head. The November 15 CI failures below remain unresolved historical evidence, not current-head results.

- **Previous-head CI diagnosis (November 15, `5a985a9784f5`):** dependency review, sensitive-change review, security-fast, CodeQL, production build, type checks, lint, and base-relative UI performance passed. [CI run 43739956845](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43739956845) is **not green**. The failed assertions are WebKit model-picker slash/search focus, retained-input earlier-page navigation, and WebKit mobile history loading. Three additional UI E2E shards (2/7, 4/7, 6/7) reached the workflow’s 20-minute step deadline. Other jobs were still running at this observation; this is not a final passing-CI claim.
- **Bounded investigation, no speculative patch:** inspected all six failed-job logs and compared scheduled main runs 43735445742 and 43741025505. Main’s corresponding unit/browser lanes passed, so these failures are not classified as inherited. In a fresh secretless AWS lease, [diagnostic run run_79e7f9d096a9e16619ac10bf8b5323df](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_79e7f9d096a9e16619ac10bf8b5323df) tested the unchanged exact head: `pnpm --dir ui test src/pages/chat/chat-view.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` (**124 passed**), `OPENCLAW_UI_WEBKIT=1 pnpm --dir ui test --project=webkit src/pages/chat/components/chat-model-picker.browser.test.tsx --maxWorkers=1` (**37 passed**), and `pnpm test:ui:e2e ui/src/e2e/chat-history-reading-stability.e2e.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` (**3 passed**, Chromium/WebKit). This was a Node 24 focused replay, not CI’s whole-shard/Bun unit ordering. The failures did not reproduce; passing replay is not a repair or proof of cause. Full-shard timeouts remain unresolved. No CI reruns, timeout changes, weaker assertions, or source changes were used. AWS lease `cbx_0b45fdf9dd41` released. Those hosted failures remain unresolved; that run is prior-head evidence, not a result for the November 18 rebase.

- **Previous rebase 2026-11-15** onto main `89ee0bd382d16ec16183a10e81a8930a92ed1909`. Signed head at that time: `5a985a9784f52c4fe8be7f257a7e147a356d8321`; tree: `9a24c275681aaddfce49d711c223596df12dd2d9`. Preserved original authorship and coauthors. Two mechanical conflicts combined upstream streaming-prefix handling with the math budget and retained both WebKit test entries. Boot-manifest regeneration also captured an upstream link-preview modifier module; generated bytes were retained rather than edited manually.
- **November 15 rebase proof:** secretless [AWS Crabbox run](https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_4b0b2e3f28dc44a20fe1dbcc88827c0f), IAM endpoint 404: frozen install, **133/133 tests in 8 files** (including upstream GitHub-source-footer coverage), UI typecheck, formatting, lint and test-line ratchet passed. The production-build/base-relative performance check ran after regeneration and passed: chat boot **+2,173 B gzip**, startup **−2 B**, no additional requests versus this base. Static baseline debt is not claimed fixed. Lease released. No new visual changes were introduced by this rebase; earlier visual evidence below is reused, not recaptured.

- Rebased 2026-11-12 onto main `f817a8b3eb` as one commit authored by Jacqueline Henriksen, with fengwhang, roboclaw-bot and Vyctor as co-authors (the previous 27-commit history ends at `65a255a2d8e0`; the content is the same as merging that head into this main). On this exact tree (secretless AWS Crabbox): frozen install, test-line ratchet (slack 29), 126/126 math, markdown and preview unit tests, `tsgo:ui`, oxfmt, oxlint, boot-manifest regeneration (no diff) and `ui:check-performance:base` all pass; chat boot JS is +2,440 B gzip versus that base and within its limit.
- Prior published head (2026-11-12): `c373dc51caa39c6d841f5c326b1b3337520d0a5a`; tree: `f102135ebe755e77a3f791bcc238b459969c9dc9`. Earlier on this PR: the named test-line allocation covers the new regressions, and web source previews keep display math (`$$…$$`) in titles and search excerpts, per hosted review.
- **Earlier round (re-review + visual QA):**
  - Hosted review P2 fixed: math was dropped from plain-text projections. Transcript search text, paste-chip excerpts and web source previews now keep the TeX source (`Solve $x^2$ today` → `Solve x^2 today`, not `Solve today`). Four regressions fail on the previous head for exactly that reason and pass now.
  - Visual QA fix: wide display equations scrolled inside the message with no visible cue on overlay-scrollbar platforms, so they looked truncated. They now fade their clipped edge(s) like Markdown tables do (CSS scroll-driven mask, no JavaScript). Equations that fit are never masked, keyboard focus drops the fade so the focus ring stays visible, and engines without scroll timelines keep their native scrollbar. The new browser test fails without the CSS and passes with it in **Chromium and WebKit (6/6 each)**.
  - 374 affected UI tests across 20 files (math, streaming, paste, source previews, chat-thread consumers), UI typecheck, lint, format, production build and `ui:check-performance` (zero violations) passed; test-line ratchet passed with no allocation change. Independent P0–P2 reviews of both changes were scoped-clean.
- **Earlier rounds (unchanged inputs, reused):** Node-safe math element registration with a real red/green Node regression; one 200-expression budget across a whole streamed message; KaTeX 0.18.2 (GHSA-238p-pmpm-9mq7); measured Chat boot allowance kept separate from upstream baselines (all 13 effective limits unchanged); finite-animation settlement in one native-menu geometry test. Not claimed: a real-model Gateway run, or a cause for one historical WebKit overlay-bounds flake (it passed on the matching-runtime replay and later heads). No merge or auto-merge is requested. Fresh hosted CI must evaluate this head.

prs.title: improve(ui): use one filter button for Meetings at every width
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

On desktop, Meetings showed a **Filters** disclosure plus separate **Filter** and **Clear filters** buttons under the search box. That is four controls for one search. Phone already used a cleaner pattern.

## User Impact

Every width now shows a search field (Enter searches) and one filter button. On desktop the button opens a compact popover with Provider, Account, Agent and dates, plus **Clear filters** and **Filter**. Phone keeps its sheet. The button shows as active while extra filters are applied. Desktop keeps the longer hint about what search covers; phone keeps the short one.

## Note

Filtering on every keystroke was considered and rejected. The search is server-side, so it would send one request per key.

## Why This Change Was Made

Search runs on the Gateway, so Enter still submits one query rather than sending a request for every keystroke. The filter button keeps the provider, account, agent and date controls accessible.

## Evidence

- Meetings unit and browser tests (42) passed.
- `meetings.e2e.test.ts` and `transcript-library.e2e.test.ts` (10) passed in Chromium, including a new desktop flow: Enter search, then a popover filter that keeps the query.
