prs.title: fix(config): stat each agent database preflight side once per row
prs.body:
Closes #200267

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway boot with many agents re-stat every candidate database row against every configured target before the gateway is ready — measured by the reporter as 8.8M main-thread file calls at ~470 agents. The preflight check now answers exact configured claims with a path compare and stats each side once per row, removing the quadratic file-call storm.

- Problem: `isConfiguredAgentDatabaseTarget` runs one `targets.some(...)` whose alias branch calls `fs.statSync` on the target and on the row for every non-matching owned target, and the boot preflight calls it once per row.
- Solution: check exact matches first (no filesystem probes), then walk targets with the row's existence stat hoisted out of the loop (missing rows stop at the first existing target).
- What changed: `src/config/sessions/targets.ts` (function body only — signature and callers untouched) plus focused regression tests.
- What did NOT change: ownership rules, alias detection via `isSameOpenClawAgentDatabasePath`, and the second quadratic (fresh-state missing-suffix probes) noted in the issue.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix follows the reporter's suggested shape and keeps the loop: rows still string-compare against every target, so only the repeated file calls are removed, not the scan.

- Best fix: yes for this layer — a per-preflight matcher index (the issue's "further step") is a larger change left out.
- Alternative: caching stat results across rows was rejected because the function has no lifecycle to invalidate it.
- Risk / non-goals: a stat or realpath error the stock loop hit on an earlier target is no longer hit when an exact match answers first; the reporter verified equivalence over 4,000 randomized rows (missing files, symlinks, hard links, symlink loop, ENOTDIR).

## User Impact

Gateway startup on states with many agents stops spending tens of seconds of main-thread file probing in the database readiness phase; the `ready` line arrives sooner with no behavioral change to admission answers.

## Evidence

Real Gateway startup with a 30-agent roster (30 configured agent databases seeded in an isolated state dir; `agents.ownership: "explicit"`), `fs.statSync` instrumented with a counting preload (real runtime, no mocks), before/after on the same fixture:

```text
BEFORE (fix files reverted to origin/main):
  bootstrap completed 6256.9ms (total 8672.0ms)   gateway ready ✓
  statSync calls: 8136 agent-path (9970 total)
AFTER (this revision):
  bootstrap completed 4909.6ms (total 7289.7ms)   gateway ready ✓
  statSync calls: 1055 agent-path (2889 total)
```

The matcher's per-row work is the difference: each candidate row answers via the exact configured claim without probing, so agent-path filesystem work drops from ~271 stats/agent to ~35 stats/agent across the fleet while both runs reach successful readiness.

Synthetic 400-row x 400-agentless-target sweep (the boot admission shape: candidate rows against every earlier candidate path), old vs new shape, `fs.statSync` instrumented with a real `node:sqlite`-free runtime script:

```text
rows=400 targets=400
OLD: stat calls=320000  pathname stats=160000  ms=570.1  hits=0
NEW: stat calls=800  pathname stats=400  ms=6.9  hits=0
AGREE: same answers
```

Focused regressions in `src/config/sessions/targets.test.ts`, each failing on base: an exact claim behind an existing compatible target answers with zero `statSync` calls; a missing row stats the pathname exactly once across 40 owned targets (base re-stats it 40 times); symlink aliases still resolve; an unusable (NUL-byte) earlier target no longer fails an exact claim.

## AI Assistance

This PR is AI-assisted. Used `git grep` on the preflight call sites and the reporter's suggested shape to rework `isConfiguredAgentDatabaseTarget` in `targets.ts`, with `vitest` and a standalone `node` instrumentation script for validation. The implementer understands the code: exact claims short-circuit before any stat and the row's existence check is hoisted out of the target walk. All evidence above is from real local runtime execution.

prs.title: improve(gateway): avoid scanning parked workspaces for run leases
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A Gateway with unavailable startup workspaces keeps scanning those parked lookups whenever a worktree run lease is acquired or released. Lease facts cannot restore a workspace, so this costs CPU and temporary allocations throughout steady state.

## User Impact

Gateways with parked workspace recovery do less background work during ordinary runs. Late workspace restoration, bounded cleanup, restart recovery, readiness, and worker authority remain unchanged. No configuration or schema changes are needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Filter lease-only registry receipts before entering the lookup scan. The subscription remains necessary while startup recovery is unresolved; completed passes already skip scanning. Retaining the existing inner matching order also preserves early exit on batches of real worktree facts.

This follows #183433, which removed per-lookup Map-entry allocations from session notifications. It addresses the remaining registry-receipt path. Production grows by ten lines for the receipt filter; no cache or new lifecycle state is added.

## Evidence

The existing persisted-placement restoration test now acquires and releases a real run lease while recovery is parked. It fails on parent `24c2e742bb0f81a00185c87c33a158583eea0c2b` with two target reads instead of zero, then passes with this fix. All 26 recovery-admission/startup tests pass, including delayed restoration and uncertain publication. Test execution was about six seconds for the 20-test persisted recovery suite on the shared host, plus compiler preparation; the six startup tests also passed.

Acceptance: zero parked-target reads on lease-only receipts; lower CPU/allocation per install with unchanged completed/unsubscribed controls. Five interleaved pairs, 1,000 parked lookups, 50,000 warm installs for timings and a separate 5,000-install allocation window (including collected objects):

| Per lease publication | Base median | Candidate median |
|---|---:|---:|
| Main-thread CPU | 16.434 µs | 1.076 µs |
| Sampled allocation | 69,010 B | 4,264 B |
| Elapsed per 50,000 installs | 822.28 ms | 53.82 ms |
| Completed-pass CPU control | 0.986 µs | 1.009 µs |
| Unsubscribed CPU control | 0.973 µs | 0.977 µs |

Initial A/A controls: 16.249/17.778 µs and 68,930/69,023 B per install. Across the five pairs, parked CPU ranges were 16.370–16.522 µs vs 1.059–1.084 µs; allocation ranges were 68,664–69,237 B vs 4,248–4,289 B. Elapsed p95 across five samples (nearest-rank maximum) was 826.61 ms vs 54.40 ms. Shared-host scheduling affected elapsed spread; CPU uses thread accounting.

Reproduce with `node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/placement-startup-wake-measure.ts --registry-leases`, using the optional historical owner path for base. The Gateway companion runs against a generated fixture with 10,000 sessions, 1,000 local placements, and 62,000 files/1.116 GB. The actual Gateway A/A/B comparison, after its normal startup sweep, measured 20.263/20.133 → 1.186 µs CPU and 69,786/69,679 → 4,385 sampled bytes per install. Readiness was 16.91/10.09/9.33 seconds; these few starts are setup observations, not a startup-speed claim. The fixture has a 461 MB agent DB and runs on macOS/APFS, so this proves the notification path at session/workspace scale, not 35 GiB database or btrfs I/O performance. The callback does no DB or filesystem I/O. No production data or live server was used. A separate allocation-attribution pass measured 64,321 → 134 B/install beneath the bundled startup owner (−99.8%); its more heavily loaded timing windows are kept separate from A/A/B.

Both baseline and candidate runtime artifact builds passed. Codex autoreview of the final staged range against `24c2e742bb0f81a00185c87c33a158583eea0c2b` is scoped-clean through P2. An earlier source/build-instance concern was resolved by the process-wide singleton contract and the positive baseline Gateway measurements.

`pnpm check:changed --staged` passed every gate except the dead-export scan. Its unrelated failures reproduce on the exact parent using `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-deadcode-exports.mts`: `OPENAI_CODEX_CLIENT_VERSION_FLOOR` was introduced by `1680f54504807` (#201130); `watchSelectedAgent` lost its final production caller in `d33473385623a` (#201218). These are inherited main regressions, not ignored check failures. This PR leaves their owners unchanged.

prs.title: fix: let the next update finish a killed update after the machine restarted
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

If `openclaw update` is killed and the machine then restarts, the next `openclaw update` refuses and tells you to run `openclaw update repair`. That happens even though the restart ended every process the killed update had started. The refusal exists because the proof the update relied on, a lease row in a temporary file, is gone after a restart.

## User Impact

On Linux and macOS hosts, an update killed by a crash or power loss before a reboot no longer needs a manual repair. The next `openclaw update` settles what the killed update left and continues. Windows, containers, and updates that were killed while running an older version keep today's refusal.

## Why This Change Was Made

When an update adopts its run, it now also records the boot it runs in: platform, kernel boot ID, Linux PID namespace, and a digest of the machine identity. That is the existing `captureNamespacedStateLeaseProcessOwner().namespace` value. It is stored as an optional `namespace` key on `origin.driver` and on each `origin.previousDrivers` entry. When the next update finds the lease row gone, it settles the killed run only if all of the following hold:

- the run has no `driver:identity-unavailable` step and no managed handoff;
- every recorded driver has a namespace from this same host, with the same non-null machine identity, on the same platform, from a different boot;
- the platform is Linux or macOS, and on Linux both the recorded driver and this process are in the host's initial PID namespace;
- the run's last write predates the current boot. A cloned machine that shares the host name, machine identity and state directory has its own boot, and its live updater keeps writing.

The installation is still claimed the normal way, the claim must land in the same lease store path, and the drivers are checked again under the claim. Every other #200680/#200866 condition is unchanged, including the recorded-exit check and the store identity comparison on the lease path.

Storage: this is additive JSON in `update_runs.origin_json`. There is no table, column, schema version, or migration change. The maintainer approved this field before implementation, as `docs/reference/database-schemas/storage-changes.md` (review checkpoint) asks; it follows the additive driver-metadata precedent in `docs/reference/database-schemas/layout.md` (the `origin.driver` paragraph, now extended).

- The origin and driver schemas are non-strict, so older readers drop the key: `src/infra/update-run-driver-schema.ts:3` (`z.object`) and `src/infra/update-run-schema.ts:225`/`:234` at `v2026.11.5`, and the same on `main`.
- Lease payload schemas are strict (`src/infra/update-managed-service-handoff-schema.ts:11` `processIdentitySchema` and `:137` `currentPayloadSchema`, same at `v2026.11.5`). The namespace never reaches them: `recordedUpdateRunDrivers` now returns plain process identities for every lease, recovery, interruption and backup caller, and the managed-handoff helper entry stays plain.
- The public run record uses a closed `driver` (`packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/update-runs.ts:27`), so `toPublicUpdateRun` strips the key.
- Origin byte budget: with eight maximally escaped drivers, the namespaces would push admission identities and routing out of the 16 KiB origin. The codec now drops namespaces first in that case, so a run without them simply keeps today's repair path.

Update behavior: the installed updater runs first and cannot be patched. On the first update from a published version, the killed run was recorded by old code without a namespace, so nothing changes: it still refuses after a restart until a run recorded by this code is killed. A downgraded or older reader drops the key when parsing, and if it rewrites the run the namespaces are lost, so that run falls back to the refusal. A downgrade never reads the namespace as authority.

Not covered: a reboot in the middle of package publication still refuses through package settlement's own lease-store rule, which this PR does not change. Git-checkout behavior is untouched.

## Evidence

The killed-run process test now starts each restart case from a real child updater killed with SIGKILL. It removes the lease store the way a restart clears the temporary directory, then rewrites the run's recorded driver boot to an earlier one. The current process's namespace and uptime are injected at their readers. The decision code is not mocked. The test also asserts that the killed child recorded its own real boot namespace.

- Red on base `d4195774b99`: both new positive cases (Linux and macOS) refused with "The update lease store no longer holds that update's lease" (`3 failed | 40 passed`; the third failure was a control whose expected refusal I then corrected).
- Green on the fix: both positive cases settle the recovery, roll back the dead run's config change, and proceed.
- Controls that still refuse, each asserting the refusal text, that the update did not proceed, and that the reserved recovery, run status and config bytes are unchanged:
  - the same boot with the lease gone;
  - a run from an older version without a namespace, or with a `null` namespace;
  - a null machine identity, or a different machine identity;
  - a non-initial Linux PID namespace for this process, and for the recorded driver;
  - a managed handoff;
  - a `driver:identity-unavailable` step;
  - one of several drivers without a namespace, or recorded in the current boot;
  - another platform;
  - run activity after this boot began.
- `update-run-abandonment.test.ts`: adoption records the namespace, keeps earlier drivers' namespaces, keeps them out of `recordedUpdateRunDrivers`, and strips them from the public record (checked against the wire schema).
- `update-run-ledger.test.ts`: with eight maximal drivers carrying maximal namespaces, admission identities and routing are kept and the namespaces are dropped.

<details><summary>Commands</summary>

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/update-cli/update-command-killed-run.process.test.ts` on `e4b80179501`: 47 passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/update-run-abandonment.test.ts src/infra/update-run-ledger.test.ts src/infra/update-run-capture-receipts.test.ts src/infra/update-run-ledger.compaction.test.ts`: 73 passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/update-restart-module-outcome.test.ts test/scripts/eager-import-closure.test.ts`: 24 passed
- `pnpm tsgo:all`, `pnpm check:baseline-ratchets --base d4195774b99 --no-merge-base` (all ok, including session-identity and test-lines), `pnpm check:docs`, `git diff --check`
- 17 sibling update, Doctor-maintenance and Gateway update suites (`update-command-migrated`, `update-repair-command`, `update-finalization-lifecycle`, `doctor-update-schema-guard`, `update-status` and others), plus `update-command-install-layout.test.ts`: 437 passed, 1 skipped
- CI on `512cdd5d11e`: all checks pass
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs`: all lanes ok except the dead-export scan, which reports exports in `src/plugins/plugin-metrics.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/session-event-delivery.ts` and `src/sessions/session-controller-model.test-support.ts` that this PR does not touch

</details>

Review: one independent reviewer read the diff without my conclusions. It found no critical or high defects. I applied its findings: the cloned-machine case is now refused by the last-activity check, the claim on the restart path must use the same store path, an unrecognized captured namespace records as unknown instead of failing adoption, the codec comment was corrected, and controls were added. CI then caught that the plain-identity helper pulled zod into Control UI boot bundles; it now lives in the zod-free run record module. CI also showed that `update-command-install-layout.test.ts` built its expected printed run from the stored origin; it now expects the driver without its namespace and asserts that the printed JSON carries none. The `autoreview` helper does not run on this machine, so it was not used.

prs.title: fix: keep recently used session worktrees from idle cleanup
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A session can use an old managed worktree without refreshing its recorded activity. Once the run finishes, idle cleanup can still treat the checkout as unused since creation. Returning to a removed checkout also recreated an empty directory before reporting the removal.

## User Impact

Recently used worktrees retain their idle-retention window. Returning to an already removed worktree keeps its path absent and reports the worktree ID alongside the existing Restore guidance. Previously removed worktrees still require explicit restoration.

## Why This Change Was Made

Actual run boundaries now record activity through the existing registry writer: native/plugin workspace preparation, run-lease acquisition, and final lease release. The persisted timestamp coalesces updates over five minutes across processes, using existing live-row and observed-timestamp conditions. There is no new cache, configuration, schema, or per-tool-call write. Directory creation belongs to workspace preparation after binding validation; the earlier duplicate mkdir is removed.

The explicit worktree acquire service already recorded activity, but ordinary execution did not use it. GC also considers session-owner activity and live custody, so this change does not imply that every historical removal was caused by the timestamp omission.

Production delta: +30 lines, including the shared bounded-write operation and its callers, with two redundant lines deleted. Tests add 67 net lines; the rerunnable synthetic measurement script adds 200 lines.

## Evidence

- An old checkout used yesterday is collected on the base after its run lease ends. The regression passes with the fix, including coalesced short runs, refresh at final release after a long run, and eventual collection after becoming idle again.
- A real Gateway test reproduces the removed path reappearing after chat refusal; it stays absent with this change, and the diagnostic contains the worktree ID.
- An existing full Gateway/model-turn test now ages the record before sending chat and verifies that successful execution refreshes activity without invalidating run custody.
- 165 focused tests pass across workspace preparation, run leases, GC/capacity, snapshot retirement, cron cleanup, embedded attempts, and the two Gateway product tests. Codex autoreview is clean through P2.
- `pnpm check:changed` on the final committed head passes every gate except two unrelated export failures. Those failures reproduce on clean exact parent `0aafe6691b818c24ac00a2172e57819b21632554`: `OPENAI_CODEX_CLIENT_VERSION_FLOOR` was introduced unused in production by `1680f54504807` (#201130); the last barrel consumer of `watchSelectedAgent` was removed by `d33473385623a` (#201218). These are main regressions. Benchmark lint and all other checks pass on this head.
- Synthetic fixture is prepared: 10,000 canonical sessions, a 35 GiB agent DB, and 62,000 files / 1.14 GB checkout. Two baseline A/A controls and five alternating A/B pairs are complete. All candidate runs recorded first use and kept the timestamp unchanged through 20 subsequent short runs; every baseline run left it at 1. Local filesystem is APFS; btrfs qualification is unavailable because the configured remote runner lacks credentials.

Measurement acceptance: recent use must advance activity, the next 20 short runs must keep that timestamp, and coalesced owner cost is compared with A/A noise; the first required durable write is reported separately. Exact-head CI [44350917733](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44350917733) passed for `aace1b071df88f1f157ad48c87bd002458b2253d`, including `openclaw/ci-gate`. Final-head [ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/201333#issuecomment-6984702746) reports zero findings and zero open items. Runtime proof uses an in-process real Gateway/agent runner with a synthetic provider; no standalone shipped-CLI or live external-provider proof is claimed.

### Synthetic owner measurements

Warm filesystem caches; setup/imports excluded. Each sample is a fresh Node 26.12.1 process. Coalesced values are per operation (20 operations per sample). CPU includes process threads, excludes Git/state-broker children; allocation is main-isolate V8 allocation. The first write is necessary new durable work, not a speedup.

| Owner/phase | Arm (n) | Wall median / p95 (ms) | CPU median (ms) | Main allocation median (KiB) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| lease/first-write | base (5) | 31.997 / 48.548 | 33.946 | 5676.8 |
| lease/first-write | candidate (5) | 32.938 / 43.824 | 35.631 | 5966.8 |
| lease/first-write | aa (2) | 32.351 / 32.981 | 34.142 | 4898.7 |
| lease/coalesced | base (5) | 26.173 / 27.106 | 9.713 | 2893.7 |
| lease/coalesced | candidate (5) | 27.652 / 30.125 | 11.301 | 2698.8 |
| lease/coalesced | aa (2) | 26.693 / 27.098 | 9.710 | 2799.9 |
| workspace/first-write | base (5) | 3.184 / 3.856 | 6.769 | 667.4 |
| workspace/first-write | candidate (5) | 5.373 / 5.797 | 24.781 | 1223.2 |
| workspace/first-write | aa (2) | 3.773 / 3.852 | 10.041 | 677.7 |
| workspace/coalesced | base (5) | 1.663 / 1.969 | 4.224 | 885.1 |
| workspace/coalesced | candidate (5) | 1.641 / 2.253 | 3.059 | 927.1 |
| workspace/coalesced | aa (2) | 1.597 / 1.610 | 2.951 | 950.5 |

The first workspace write adds 2.19 ms median wall, 18.01 ms process CPU and 556 KiB main allocation; it occurs at most once per five minutes through these boundaries. Coalesced lease wall/CPU increased 5.7%/16.3%; main allocation decreased 6.7%. Coalesced workspace wall held steady, CPU decreased, and allocation increased 4.7%. This correctness fix explicitly pays for recording use; no claim of an overall speedup. A/A controls and all raw samples are retained locally; five-sample p95 is the maximum sample.

Reproduction: seed with `scripts/perf/agent-startup-inspection.ts seed --state-dir <new-root>/state --gib 35`; prepare using `scripts/perf/worktree-activity-measure.ts --prepare <root>`; then run `<root> <new-result.json>` under `node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs`. For baseline, `OPENCLAW_BENCH_BASELINE_DIR` points to the three owner modules (`registry.ts`, `run-lease.ts`, `workspace-sandbox.ts`) extracted from `0aafe6691b818c24ac00a2172e57819b21632554`.

### CI repair

The first CI run found one PR-caused test fixture failure: the image-admission test used the removed early mkdir as a stop hook. The final test-only follow-up stops through its existing admission callback after evaluating the real image policy. Both image-support cases pass locally; the filesystem spy, mock-order assertion, and unnecessary mock cleanup are removed. Codex autoreview of the repair is clean. Production code and the measured owner files are unchanged from the measured head. The failed run is retained as evidence; fresh exact-head CI and ClawSweeper re-review both completed successfully. No CI rerun or inherited-failure exception was used for this PR-caused fixture failure.

prs.title: fix(release): accept only exact low-risk beta test failures
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The release operator authorized low-risk FRV10/11 test-tooling waivers for 2026.11.10-beta.1, but the existing whole-job grants could also hide a different product failure in the same shard. The strict evidence reader also rejected the native runner's pre-invocation parallelism telemetry.

## User Impact

No shipped product behavior changes. Release qualification can accept only the exact observed MCP fixture listener collision and cron pre-output assertion, while preserving their raw failure conclusions and reasons. This does not make FRV11 pass or waive missing coverage.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the existing strict test-evidence parser and P-owned waiver validator: require one exact failed test step, completed invocation evidence, and the complete ordered failure-signature set. Aggregate causes remain exact. The parser permits only the documented positive-integer pre-invocation telemetry line; unknown telemetry still fails closed.

Grants are limited to version 2026.11.10-beta.1 and the exact Node/Bun job, test, assertion, and stack/source signature observed in FRV11 run 44290065577/1. Changed ports/source lines intentionally do not match. Extra or changed errors, setup errors, incomplete/missing/cancelled coverage remain blocking. UI, QA classifier/actual-tool-execution ambiguity, mixed firstbirth/attachment/subscriber failures, and other possible product defects receive no grant. Existing grants are unchanged.

The extra leaf validation is necessary to avoid a whole-job exemption; there is no second parser, assertion relaxation, timeout padding, or runtime state store. The Darwin tooling workflow explicitly includes the newly transitive parser in its path triggers, preserving its runtime source-closure contract.

## Evidence

- Replayed both complete authenticated original job logs through the production policy validator: exact MCP and cron leaves accepted; the original mixed FRV11 aggregate rejected for its additional UI, UI-E2E cancellation, and fast-core failures. Raw logs remain private.
- Original parser against both real logs: expected red (zero signatures); updated strict parser: exact one signature each. UI remains rejected.
- Focused parser/waiver suites passed; affected state, reuse, and strict-summary consumer suites passed (418 tests across six consumer files, plus 21 waiver tests). Tooling test typecheck, targeted lint, formatter check, docs inventory, and git diff --check passed.
- Independent OpenClaw reviewer, model openai/gpt-6.1-sol, reviewed the full six-file change against 6d815d786f4db0ab8a72541c7a78832b0e148bfe, including enforcement callers and original logs. One P2 test-fixture no-op mutation found and fixed by constructing the altered assertion before log framing; focused tests/typecheck rerun green. No additional production P0–P3 finding. This narrative review lacks helper-owned isolation and structured validation.
- First-head PR CI identified a source-closure regression in `pr-wrapper-source-closure.test.ts`: the parser was missing from the Darwin workflow path exceptions. Reproduced the exact failure locally and added that single exact path; the correction does not broaden runtime permissions or accept additional failures. The corrected closure test passes (red before, green after). The required workflow suites passed: 1,401 tests across eight tooling files, plus the completed 19-test and 35-test non-tooling groups. A first 180-second run ended by command timeout, not a test failure; the completed rerun passed. Independent delta review found no P0–P3 issue and confirmed no wrapper inventory expansion is needed.
- Hosted ClawSweeper identified the same Darwin routing omission and a second P1 omission: the new parser import was absent from the fixed producer and publication source inventories. Reproduced the latter at the real verified inventory wrapper (exact `outside the fixed closure` rejection), added the parser to both inventories, and passed all 218 producer/publication admission tests. A fresh independent delta review found 28/28 exact reachable/allowlisted modules and no further dependency or P0–P3 issue. Tooling typecheck, targeted lint/format, and workflow validation passed (workflow validation required unsetting empty ambient token variables).
- Local ClawSweeper checkout and Codex CLI are unavailable; the bound autoreview tool is unavailable. Hosted review findings are addressed above; the final-head re-review of 2a7509b0567459a5d83ed3c387da9c311615d237 reports zero findings. CI run 44353789783 and its required CI gate passed on that head; required security statuses passed. Native protected squash merge landed 7d0c6307b23ef28a53b7ab11e2bdda9b616a4018 on main at 2026-11-18 17:14:22 UTC. The separate Darwin workflow was still running at merge and is not claimed as passed. No shipped runtime assertions or qualification failure conclusions are altered.

Authorized by Dallin Romney for the narrow final FRV waiver task. No release branch edits, qualification dispatch, or release publication is included.

prs.title: refactor: use task prompts for scheduled reminders
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Scheduling a reminder in an existing conversation shouldn’t require a special action just for the agent’s main conversation. The editor, CLI, and agent tool offered two ways to schedule that work, with different delivery and execution rules.

## User Impact

Use an agent task with `session:<key>` to continue an existing conversation, including the main conversation. Control UI no longer offers **Post to main session** or **Runs in: Main session**. CLI scripts should replace `--system-event` and `--session main` with `--message` and the actual conversation key, for example `--session session:agent:main:main` or `--session session:global` on a global-scope install.

After upgrading, run `openclaw doctor --fix`. Doctor backs up cron state and reports each conversion. It rewrites eligible jobs in place, retaining their ID, schedule, enabled state, run history, scratch, and valid delivery settings. The target is the owning agent’s main conversation, with `session:global` for global scope. If Doctor cannot faithfully continue a job (for example, a headless script that used the old main-session notification behavior, a missing prompt, or an unresolved owner), it pauses the job and explains what to review before enabling it. The model now sees the reminder as a **task prompt**, not as a system notice.

## Why This Change Was Made

An explicit conversation key uses the same queue and execution path regardless of which conversation it names. Immediate hook wakes, channel join and lifecycle notices, and post-run notices from scheduled plugin commands still use the internal notice path where applicable: they report an event to the conversation, rather than being user-authored automation prompts. Backup schedules already run an isolated command and do not need the removed mode.

Expected overlap with the sibling automation cleanups: the shared cron schema and generated validators, Doctor’s cron repair, scheduler routing, CLI and agent tool descriptions, and the Control UI editor and docs. This change does not redesign the remaining modes or wake policy.

## Evidence

- Doctor’s SQLite repair tests passed for a named agent with a custom main key and for global scope (2 tests). They cover backup creation, preserved job ID, disabled state, schedule, last-run state, delivery, prompt, and a no-op second repair.
- Cron protocol validation passed (93 tests); generated-validator parity, core and UI typechecks, formatting, and diff whitespace checks passed. The focused CLI run was interrupted by a source change while the subprocess compiler was building; the full CLI, scheduler, native client, and upgrade suites were not verified here.
- Local Codex autoreview (P1, three passes) found that same-kind payload edits had lost their field updates. The update logic was restored; the follow-up core typecheck passed. The final delta was not independently re-reviewed.
- The real Control UI was exercised in Chromium with a mocked Gateway and a fictional weekly garden-inventory reminder. Both capture checks passed. The before capture used the original worktree UI source, which matched `origin/main` outside translation artifacts. The captures show the Action picker; no live model or channel delivery is demonstrated.

### Clean comparison

![Before: the Action picker offers Post to main session and Run agent task](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/73bc4733-7813-4e9d-add6-eec4c5825c14)

![After: the Action picker offers only Run agent task](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/966c7a94-6ffc-497d-9ff2-0acb7deade4a)

### Annotated comparison

![Before: the legacy system notice action is highlighted](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/36f1d8ed-231e-4ad4-9bad-e31f6417c0cd)

![After: the single remaining agent task action is highlighted](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/af8f0c3a-1200-4327-a0ae-3232be75d2d3)

Co-authored with [Vyctor Brzezowski](https://github.com/vyctorbrzezowski).

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion with @vyctorbrzezowski](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/bfb77f08-1fd2-461f-ada5-4f3ff81fa044)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/45aa2c9e-7319-4a72-8a06-885f132edf55)

## Worked on by

- @vyctorbrzezowski

issues.title: WebUI title generation fails with Kimi K3.1 Pro because the 96-token budget is exhausted

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body:
### Bug Description

Automatic WebUI topic titles are not generated when using Kimi K3.1 Pro through an OpenAI-compatible provider. The main assistant reply succeeds, but the topic remains “Untitled”.

The title-generation calls consistently finish with `finish_reason=length` after exactly 96 output tokens, suggesting that reasoning consumes the entire title-generation budget before visible title text is returned.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Select `moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro`.
2. Open a new WebUI topic.
3. Send a message and wait for the assistant's complete reply.
4. Observe the topic title in the sidebar.

### Expected Behavior

After the first reply, Nanobot generates and displays a short topic title.

### Relevant Logs

```shell
Nanobot's internal model-usage log shows the background title calls ending at the output-token limit:


model=moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro
source=system
stream=true
finish_reason=length
output_tokens=96
error_kind=None
```

### nanobot Version

0.4.1

### Python Version

3.12.12

### Operating System

Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm), Linux x86_64 — rootless Podman container

### Channel / Platform

WebSocket

### LLM Provider

Lyceum

### Model

moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro

### Browser

Firefox

### Connection

_No response_

### Configuration (Optional)

```yaml

```

### Additional Context

I observed this outcome for 21 title-generation calls using the current model ID. Other models generally finish title generation with finish_reason=stop.

issues.title: SSRF hardening: _BLOCKED_NETWORKS misses multicast, reserved, and TEST-NET ranges
issues.body:
`nanobot/security/network.py:14` — `_BLOCKED_NETWORKS` (11 entries) does not include several reserved/special-purpose ranges:

- `224.0.0.0/4` — IPv4 multicast
- `240.0.0.0/4` — reserved, includes `255.255.255.255` (broadcast)
- `198.18.0.0/15` — benchmarking (RFC 2544)
- `192.0.2.0/24`, `198.51.100.0/24`, `203.0.113.0/24` — TEST-NET-1/2/3
- IPv6: `ff00::/8` (multicast), `2001:db8::/32` (documentation)

**Repro** (verified on v0.4.1 / `main` @ `e91906b`):

```python
from nanobot.security.network import resolve_url_target
resolve_url_target("https://255.255.255.255/")   # -> (True, '', ('255.255.255.255',))  allowed
resolve_url_target("https://239.1.1.1/")         # -> allowed
resolve_url_target("https://203.0.113.5/")       # -> allowed (TEST-NET-3)
resolve_url_target("https://198.18.0.1/")        # -> allowed
```

**Impact:** defense-in-depth only — no standalone bypass; these ranges matter only in combination with other issues.

**Suggested fix:** add the missing ranges, or derive blocking from `ipaddress` properties (`is_multicast`, `is_reserved`, `is_global`) instead of a static list.

issues.body:
### Bug Description

Since HKUDS/nanobot#5610, each compaction appends the whole cumulative checkpoint to `memory/history.jsonl`, but `build_dream_prompt` still keeps only the first 1000 characters of each entry. Whatever lands later in a checkpoint never reaches Dream, and the cursor then moves past it for good. On my workspace, 69.8% of conversation journal text has never been shown to Dream. Nothing is logged; `/dream` reports a normal completion.

Code at `eb8546c32`:

1. Cumulative checkpoint appended whole: [`agent/memory.py#L954-L955`](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/blob/eb8546c32111b157759132eefb020545cc196e69/nanobot/agent/memory.py#L954-L955)
2. Per-entry head truncation: [`agent/memory.py#L521`](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/blob/eb8546c32111b157759132eefb020545cc196e69/nanobot/agent/memory.py#L521) → [`utils/helpers.py#L394-L398`](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/blob/eb8546c32111b157759132eefb020545cc196e69/nanobot/utils/helpers.py#L394-L398)
3. Cursor advances past the batch: [`command/builtin.py#L433`](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/blob/eb8546c32111b157759132eefb020545cc196e69/nanobot/command/builtin.py#L433), [`cli/gateway_runtime.py#L655`](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/blob/eb8546c32111b157759132eefb020545cc196e69/nanobot/cli/gateway_runtime.py#L655)

The cap dates from HKUDS/nanobot#5114, when entries were incremental and short; `test_truncates_long_entries_at_1000_chars` pins it.

### Steps to Reproduce

Both files are on [`shakewingo:fix/dream-cumulative-truncation-repro`](https://github.com/shakewingo/nanobot/tree/fix/dream-cumulative-truncation-repro), one commit on top of `eb8546c32`: [`tests/agent/test_dream_cumulative_truncation.py`](https://github.com/shakewingo/nanobot/blob/0d68a3995620afc83c3e4cbf647ab7132682cd35/tests/agent/test_dream_cumulative_truncation.py), [`scripts/dream_history_audit.py`](https://github.com/shakewingo/nanobot/blob/0d68a3995620afc83c3e4cbf647ab7132682cd35/scripts/dream_history_audit.py).

**Deterministic test** (scripted model; real code from `archive()` to `build_dream_prompt()`). The same 40 facts written as incremental checkpoints all reach Dream; written as cumulative checkpoints, only the first 13 do:

```text

AssertionError: history entry lengths [769, 1559, 2349, 3139]; Dream sees only facts [0, 1, ..., 12]
1 failed, 1 passed
```

**Audit any workspace** (standard library only; prints aggregate counts, no entry text or session ids):

```bash
SNAP=$(mktemp -d)
cp ~/.nanobot/workspace/memory/{history.jsonl,.cursor,.dream_cursor} "$SNAP"/
python3 -I scripts/dream_history_audit.py "$SNAP"
```

Every journal entry reaches Dream in full before the cursor passes it. Entries that do not fit in one run wait for the next run instead of being cut.


### Relevant Logs

My workspace, 2026-11-13 (the journal keeps about the last 1000 entries, about three weeks here; Dream had consumed all but the 2 newest):

The oldest entry is always included so the cursor can advance (entry size is already capped at write time). issues.title: Token consolidation never triggers — tiktoken estimation consistently underestimates actual API token count

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body:
### Bug Description

## Problem Description

Nanobot's token consolidation system uses tiktoken (or provider-specific counters) to estimate prompt token usage. This estimation consistently underestimates the actual token count returned by the API. As a result, consolidation never triggers even when the actual token count significantly exceeds the configured context window limit.

## Environment Information

- **nanobot version:** 0.3.0 (latest from main)
- **Deployment:** Termux on Android
- **LLM Model:** xiaomi/mimo-v2.5 via OpenRouter API
- **Context Window Config:** 131,072 tokens
- **Actual API Token Count:** 204,315 tokens (from `_last_usage.prompt_tokens`)
- **Consolidation Status:** Never triggered

## Evidence

The `_last_usage` field returned by the API shows the actual token count:

```python
_last_usage: {
    'prompt_tokens': 204315,
    'completion_tokens': 733,
    'total_tokens': 205048,
    'cached_tokens': 203200,
    'provider_tokens': 205048
}
```

Despite being at 204,315 actual tokens with a configured limit of 131,072, consolidation has never triggered. The session continues to grow without any compaction.

## Root Cause

The consolidation trigger logic in `nanobot/agent/memory.py` uses `estimate_session_prompt_tokens()` which calls `estimate_prompt_tokens_chain()`. This function:

1. First tries `provider.estimate_prompt_tokens` (provider-specific counter)
2. Falls back to `_estimate_prompt_tokens_with_source` which uses tiktoken
3. Final fallback is a byte heuristic

The problem is that tiktoken estimation is consistently lower than the actual API token count. The API already returns the exact token count in `_last_usage.prompt_tokens`, but this data is stored in `nanobot/agent/loop.py` (line 1129) and is not accessible to the consolidation code in `memory.py`.

The consolidation trigger logic:

```python
budget = context_window_tokens - max_tokens - 1024  # safety buffer
target = budget * 0.5  # consolidation ratio
if estimated < budget:  # consolidation idle - no action
    return
# else: run consolidation
```

Since `estimated` (from tiktoken) is consistently lower than `budget`, consolidation never fires.

## Proposed Solution

Modify `estimate_session_prompt_tokens` to check if a recent actual token count exists and use that instead of tiktoken estimation. The actual token count is already available via the API response — nanobot just isn't using it for the consolidation decision.

**Option 1 (Cleanest):** Store `_last_usage.prompt_tokens` in session metadata (similar to how `_last_summary` is stored) so the consolidation code can access it. Then modify `estimate_session_prompt_tokens` to use this actual count when available.

**Option 2 (Minimal change):** Pass `_last_usage` from the agent loop to the consolidation code when calling `maybe_consolidate_by_tokens`. The consolidation logic can then use the actual count instead of estimation.

**Option 3 (Provider-specific):** Modify the provider's `estimate_prompt_tokens` method to return the actual API token count when available, rather than running tiktoken.

## Impact

- Consolidation never triggers, causing sessions to grow unbounded
- Users must manually delete session files or restart nanobot to prevent context overflow
- Affects all users engaging in extended conversations, especially with larger context windows
- The actual API token count is already available but unused for this critical decision

## Additional Context

The tiktoken estimation appears to be roughly 30-50% lower than the actual API token count in testing. This suggests the estimation is not just slightly off, but fundamentally inaccurate for modern models with large context windows.

The fix is straightforward because the actual data already exists in the system — it's just not being used where it matters most.

## Labels

- bug
- memory
- consolidation
- token-estimation

### Steps to Reproduce

Normal usage as context grows

### Expected Behavior

Consolidation triggers before reaching configured context_window_tokens

### Relevant Logs

```shell

```

### Python Version

3.11

Linux

Telegram

### LLM Provider

OpenRouter

```yaml
"maxTokens": 8192,
      "contextWindowTokens": 131072,
```

prs.title: fix(session): replay user images from stored attachments
prs.body:
## Why

When a user asks a follow-up about an attached image, the next model request can contain a local path marker instead of the image. A fresh process then has no image in its model history to answer from.

## What changed

- Keep `media` as the input for the current turn. Save new user images as structured attachment references, and restore them in order when their turn is replayed, with or without a caption.
- Keep source paths available for UI previews, not as substitute image text for the model. Legacy path-only messages keep their original text; a missing stored attachment gets a path-free notice.
- Keep temporary sessions in memory. Text-only models omit historical images with a notice; memory archives use a text marker instead of loading image bytes.

## Scope

This PR targets `main` directly. It does not change how assistant reply text is filtered or address the draft-text issue in #6717.

Either PR can land first. The second will need one mechanical conflict resolution in `Session.get_history`: keep both deletions (the assistant-text sanitizer call from #6717 and the adjacent user-media breadcrumb block from this PR). Applying that resolution in either order reproduced the original combined tree exactly.

## Verification

- An offline Chat Completions test sends two images, deletes one source file, reloads the session in a fresh agent, and checks the image blocks in the next request. It covers both a caption and an image-only turn.
- On this image-only branch: 325 focused tests passed, 1 skipped; Ruff and strict type checks passed on the changed Python modules.

An extension can observe a model request or a whole run, but neither tells it exactly when the runner takes a queued input. Queue indicators and other observers need that handoff even if the next request never starts.

prs.body:
## Why

A user asked for a `message(...)` notification draft as text. When they asked the assistant to repeat it, the draft was gone from the next model request: replay had mistaken the reply for a tool call and removed it.

## What changed

- Replay stored assistant text verbatim, including standalone `message(...)` and `generate_image(...)` examples, literal `[Message Time: ...]` or `[image: ...]` lines, indentation and line endings.
- Stop filtering those strings out of session-list previews. Preview whitespace folding and the length limit stay in place.

## Scope

Real tool calls, timestamp metadata and user attachments are unchanged. User-image persistence and replay are reviewed separately in #6720; this fix does not need that PR. Old path-looking lines that were actually written as assistant text may now appear as literal text, not as attachments.

## Verification

- The history regression checks the exact one-line draft and multiline reply seen on a later turn. A separate regression checks that a literal image-marker line can be a session preview.
- On this issue-only branch: 95 tests passed across session history, runtime context, SQLite storage and SDK streaming. Ruff and strict type checking passed on the changed production code.

Reported and reproduced by [@master1018](https://github.com/master1018).

Resolves [NAN-464](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-464/移除会话重放中遗留的-message-time-前缀剥离)

Resolves [NAN-463](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-463/从-webui-打开并继续原渠道会话)

A conversation started in Telegram or another channel could not be continued from the WebUI. Starting a new WebUI topic lost that context; sending a reply back to the original channel would surprise the people there.

## What changed

- List saved public channel conversations alongside WebUI conversations. Use the channel name as the title and the existing `@handle` to distinguish chats, topics, and channel instances.

Keep the gateway's workspace policy and leave rename, reset, delete, fork, and recovery controls unavailable for channel conversations. Hide private/internal history and label message origin only when it was recorded.

There is no migration, platform backfill, new account linking, or per-user access control. As with the rest of the instance's WebUI, only grant access to trusted operators: saved history can include group messages. Older channel history may lack origin labels or matching tool results.

Reviewed desktop and narrow screenshots.

prs.title: perf(webui): avoid redundant diff bundle assets
prs.body:
## Why

Opening a file diff could download the Markdown parser even when the conversation had no rendered Markdown. The packaged WebUI also shipped a second copy of Shiki's language and theme assets inside the diff worker, even though the worker receives the resolved grammar and theme from the page.

## What changed

- Specialize the production worker build for Pierre's worker context, so Rollup drops the unused language and theme loading paths.
- Give the shared HTML serializer its own chunk. The production build checks that the worker does not regain the Shiki catalogs and that syntax highlighting does not pull in the Markdown vendor chunk, even indirectly.

## Scope

Initial app loading, language support, and Vite's chunk warning limit are unchanged. Large-chunk advisories remain; the goal is to remove unnecessary work, not clear the warnings.

## Blast Radius

The change affects emitted browser and worker assets only. Both the normal Markdown renderer and the worker-backed diff renderer still need the shared serializer or the resolved grammar as appropriate. No gateway, protocol, or persistence changes.

## Verification

- **First HJSON diff: 578 → 419 kB of JS response bodies** (−159 kB). Compared production builds against `965230232` in fresh Chromium contexts on an isolated gateway with the same seeded conversation and no previously rendered Markdown. The diff displayed the expected text and token color without requesting the Markdown parser; switching to a Markdown conversation still rendered formatting.
- The Pierre worker graph fell from 403 scripts / 10.92 MB to 7 scripts / 0.95 MB before compression. This is emitted JS size, not a wheel download measurement.
- `bun run build`, `bun run check:imports`, `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, 204 focused Vitest tests and 20 focused Playwright tests passed. Disabling each optimization separately reproduced its corresponding production build guard failure.

Resolves [NAN-461](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-461/减少-webui-diff-worker-的重复打包与按需下载)

prs.title: fix(webui): reconcile running turns on reconnect
prs.body:
## Why

A browser that misses a turn's terminal frame can keep showing an Agent as running after reconnect. A failed history read or a page without the completion ID cannot repair that state. The Gateway already knows which runs are live; reconnect should not depend on recovering the transcript first.

## What changed

- A trusted WebUI attach returns the live named runs for that chat. The client uses absence to clear only previously confirmed runs, not new or unacknowledged submissions.
- Terminal delivery includes sockets that attached during the history write. Retained recovery data no longer reports a finished run as active in attach, hydration, or the session list.
- Check reconnect convergence without a history completion ID in TLA+ and implementation regressions.

## Scope

Previously confirmed named runs in persistent sessions after a healthy reconnect. The snapshot reports liveness, not success or transcript coverage. It does not infer a result while offline or introduce a fixed completion deadline.

## Blast Radius

Same-version WebUI/Gateway reconnect and run indicators. The attach field is additive and only sent to authenticated WebUI sockets; the paginated transcript and its recovery markers keep their existing semantics.

## Verification

- [TLC reproduction and assumptions](webui/verification/turn-sync/ATTACH-RECONCILIATION.md): all 13 default configurations exhausted without a counterexample. The attach model checks up to two losses without completion evidence from history.
- Client and Gateway regressions cover failed reads, missing IDs, preserving newer work, attaching during both successful and failed terminal writes, and excluding retired runs from the session list.
- Ran the built WebUI in Chromium against an isolated Gateway. Dropped the real `turn_end` frame, then injected either HTTP 503 or a fragment without the completion ID. Both the sidebar ring and the Stop button cleared after reconnect, and the answer was recoverable from the real history.

Contributes to [NAN-279](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-279/为-webui-重连建立一致的同步边界与有界缺口补齐)

prs.title: perf(webui): batch startup recovery and authenticate before React
prs.body:
## Why

Opening WebUI should make a conversation usable quickly, not merely paint a placeholder. **Draft: the recovery and desktop history improvements are real, but the end-to-end target is not met.** In the mixed navigation run, the desktop new-chat command took longer to be acknowledged.

## What changed

- The launcher validates the same WebSocket config without loading the listener or the foreground agent runtime. The gateway batches both restart scans; checkpoints, pending follow-ups, interrupted transcripts and child tasks are still handled before admission.
- The browser starts one same-origin, no-store bootstrap before loading React, translations and chat. The initial static JavaScript needed to start authentication fell from 248 kB to 3.75 kB (gzip). Chat controls remain behind successful authentication.

## Tradeoffs

Keep the draft open until the desktop send regression is understood. Profile chat creation, catalog refresh and the server acknowledgement separately; the existing-chat route also still waits for the full session list. A cached PWA launch and remote/native latency were not measured. No new background service, auth shortcut or data migration is introduced.

## Verification

Windows, production assets, same Python/Chromium. Restored one consistent **2.45 GiB** database snapshot (**1,012 sessions, 340 WebUI chats**) per process. Five paired runs per version with the order alternated; fresh browser contexts, HTTP cache disabled, service worker blocked, normal OS filesystem cache. Browser times start at navigation with the gateway listening. The constrained profile uses 10 Mbit/s down, 150 ms latency, 4× CPU slowdown. No external model was called.

| Median, seconds | Base | PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| Command → first successful HTTP `/` | 10.35 | 10.09 |
| Desktop: new chat can type / `/help` acknowledged | 0.67 / 2.25 | 0.89 / 3.58 |
| Desktop: existing chat text visible | 2.50 | 1.23 |
| Constrained: bootstrap request starts | 1.01 | 0.40 |
| Constrained: new chat can type / `/help` acknowledged | 1.92 / 3.54 | 1.86 / 3.31 |
| Constrained: existing chat text visible | 3.33 | 3.29 |

The command-to-HTTP ranges overlap: **8.75–10.88 s → 5.78–14.28 s**. Separately timing both recovery scans on three fresh restores per version gave **2.60 → 0.19 s** combined; both versions emitted the same number of recovery events and no inbound work. These stage savings did not translate to equivalent launch savings.

A separate first-open check (three paired process starts; the *only* page opened was desktop new chat) also reproduced the send regression: typing **0.243 → 0.258 s**, server acknowledgement **0.751 → 1.543 s**, with command-to-HTTP **11.71 → 6.65 s**. This separates initial navigation from background work left by a previous chat.

All 40 mixed-scenario browser contexts used one bootstrap and had no unexpected HTTP or page errors. The gateway acknowledged each `/help`; every history page returned the same 172 persisted events. Separately checked visible text against the response and verified that a clean, unauthenticated deep link gets a 401, no socket and no composer. Production build, 535 focused Python tests (one skipped), 31 browser fixture cases, and the corrected live component-gallery coverage case passed locally. The production asset manifest is unchanged by that gallery-only correction. No private content, identifiers or credentials are attached.

prs.title: fix(mcp): isolate server startup and retries from chat
prs.body:
## Summary

A slow or unresponsive MCP server no longer blocks ordinary chat or delays tools from healthy servers. The gateway reports slow startup after 10 seconds and cancels an unfinished startup attempt after 60 seconds. Tools that become ready during a turn are available on the next model request. Users do not need to send another message to use them.

This is a draft for design review. The change is not ready to merge.

## Benchmarks

### Latest change: use a tool that becomes ready mid-turn

A real gateway and stdio MCP server processed one user message against a local test model endpoint. The first request arrived before the MCP server was ready. The server finished discovery during that request, and the model made a built-in tool call to continue the same turn. We did not send a follow-up message.

| What we measured | Better result | Previous draft `2065ef90f1` | Current draft `bc62a8a82` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First chat request reaches the model endpoint | Lower; one paired run, not a latency comparison at scale | 1.22 s | 1.25 s |
| Model can call the newly ready MCP tool | Earlier, with a successful tool result | Not available during the current turn | Available on request 2; request 3 received `pong` |
| Ordered definitions on consecutive requests with no further tool change | Identical | Identical where the list was unchanged | Identical on requests 2 and 3; existing definitions stayed in their original order |

The tool list can change when a tool becomes ready. A model provider may reuse less of the previous prompt on that request. The earlier equal-prefix result does not apply to this transition. No provider cache hit rate was measured.

### Previous change: slow startup, timeout, and chat

**Compare:** draft `47edc783fa` vs. draft `2065ef90f1`. Both ran the same gateway workload on macOS arm64 with Python 3.11, real stdio MCP child processes, and a local model endpoint. The endpoint captures model requests and returns test responses. No external model was called.

**Result:** Chat latency was similar in these runs, and the reusable prompt prefix did not change. The slow server still worked. The unresponsive child exited, and the next attempts started after the expected delays.

| What we measured | Better result | `47edc783fa` | `2065ef90f1` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **First chat request reaches the model endpoint** with a 12-second MCP startup in the background. Time starts when the client sends the chat message. | **Lower** | 1.14–1.17 s | 1.06–1.21 s |
| **Slow MCP tool becomes available** with the same 12-second startup. Time starts when the gateway process launches. The tool must return `pong`. | **Lower**, with a successful tool call | 13.41–13.75 s; `pong` | 13.33–13.40 s; `pong` |
| **A child that never answers the handshake exits** while the gateway stays running. Time starts when the gateway process launches. | **Lower**; no child left running after cleanup | Still alive after 63 s; no startup deadline | Exited and reported a timeout at 62.86–63.12 s |
| **Wait before restarting an unresponsive child**, measured from timeout cleanup to the next child launch. | **Match the target**, not faster: 15 s, then 30 s | No retry; the original attempt was still running | 15.12 s, then 30.16 s; no overlapping child processes |
| **Reusable prompt prefix** across two model requests for one user input. The MCP tool becomes ready between the requests. | **Higher** for the same workload; **unchanged** is the goal for this timeout change | 5,259 identical tokens | 5,259 identical tokens; same prefix content |

The first two rows show the range of two paired runs. The chat measurement includes gateway and network overhead; the **1-second** limit applies only to how long the gateway waits for initial MCP discovery. The **10-second** slow notice does not cancel the process. The **60-second** deadline starts cancellation; the timeout is visible after transport cleanup. A healthy sibling tool returned `pong` before and after that timeout.

The cache row counts tokens in the **matching start of two requests**, not extra tokens sent or billed. We normalized temporary checkout and workspace paths and used the same tokenizer on both sides. Ordered tool definitions matched byte for byte across all four compared requests. The next user input called the recovered tool. These measurements do **not** show a live provider's cache hit rate.

<details>
<summary>Earlier benchmarks: discovery, reconnect, and the tool list</summary>

These measurements use different earlier versions or prototypes. Each row identifies its comparison; they are not all comparisons with `main` or new runs on the latest commit. The original PR base was `d3bb330f57`.

| What we measured | Better result | Reference | Earlier PR result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First chat request reaches the model endpoint while a 12-second MCP server starts | **Lower** | Original `main`: 12.64 s | 1.11–1.13 s |
| Healthy MCP tool becomes available next to an unresponsive peer, using the slower configuration order in two runs | **Lower** | Serial background prototype: 2.91–3.17 s | Per-server discovery: 0.43–0.52 s |
| A 12-second stdio MCP tool becomes available after the gateway launches | **Lower**, with a successful tool call | Draft `f02258e39e`: no tool within 16 s | 13.2–13.7 s; returned `pong` |
| Healthy MCP tool becomes available when four unresponsive servers are configured ahead of it | **Lower** | Draft `f02258e39e`: 11.6–11.7 s | 2.45–2.58 s |
| Hot reload replaces a stalled server: time to a successful tool call | **Lower** | Draft `f02258e39e`: 10.05 s | 0.23 s |
| A healthy server reconnects while another server stalls: time to a successful tool call | **Lower** | Draft `f02258e39e`: 10.01 s | 0.22 s |
| Status requests in 60 seconds while Apps is open and a server is still connecting | **Lower** if Apps still shows the result | Old polling schedule: 61 | 21; same schedule for the first 10 s |
| Reusable prefix with a tool added between two requests in the same turn | **Higher** for the same workload | Live tool list: 4,360 matching tokens | Tool list held for the turn: 5,305 matching tokens |
| Total input tokens in request 1 / request 2 in that same cache test | **Lower** if the requests still support the same task | Live tool list: 5,306 / 5,462 | Tool list held for the turn: 5,305 / 5,423 |
| Discovery time for 4,000 synthetic tool definitions through the connector, with no network | **Lower** | Draft `0c367b5a2d`: 36.48 ms | 28.87 ms; same ordered tool definitions |
| Discovery time with an allowlist that selects 40 of the 4,000 definitions | **Lower** | Draft `0c367b5a2d`: 12.85 ms | 6.72 ms; same result |

The healthy-peer test used the same 2.5-second test timeout on both sides. It measures when a tool becomes available, not when a model answers. The reload and reconnect rows are single paired observations. The Apps row uses a virtual clock. The synthetic discovery values are medians of three interleaved batches, not end-to-end latency. The token rows are local estimates, not provider usage or cache hit rate.

</details>

### Verification

- Recovery follow-up (`3022ed495`): cancelling a tool call while its old connection closes no longer stops background recovery. Reload and shutdown drain that cleanup before proceeding. Apps continues polling after ordinary connection failures and reflects recovery without a page refresh.
- This follow-up passed 392 focused Python tests (one Windows-only case skipped on Linux), 20 WebUI component tests, WebUI type checking/build, focused lint, and the Python import-boundary check. A real HTTP MCP fixture verified cancellation, recovery, reload, and shutdown. A real Chromium browser against the built WebUI and an isolated gateway showed a failed stdio MCP recover without refreshing the page. All test MCP children exited. The full CI and native upgrade matrices were not rerun locally.
- The `bc62a8a82` draft passed 266 focused Python tests, the import-boundary check, and Ruff. In a separate real gateway run, a healthy MCP tool returned `pong` while its peer was stalled. A peer configured to delay startup by 12 seconds later connected and returned `pong`. No test MCP child remained after shutdown.

- A real Chromium browser used the authenticated Gateway and the built Apps page. It showed slow startup, recovery, and timeout, and exposed **Reconnect** for the timed-out server.
- The preceding draft passed **403 Python tests**, **347 Python tests with minimum dependencies**, and **19 WebUI tests**. The Python checks cover transport cleanup, hot reload, request formatting, proxy and redirect safeguards, and protected gateway activation. WebUI type checking and build, import boundary checks, and Ruff also passed.
- Earlier real stdio checks verified that a name conflict could not send a tool call to the wrong server. Renaming and reloading restored the tool under the new name. The timeout follow-up did not re-run the full native packaged-upgrade matrix.

## Before this PR

The gateway waits for MCP connection attempts before it starts the agent. Its readiness hook also waits for another attempt before each turn. A configured MCP process that starts but never replies can delay ordinary chat, even when the user does not need an MCP tool. If a process fails quickly, the next message can start it again. Serial discovery also delays other MCP servers.

Keeping chat off the connection path also lets a server finish discovery during a turn. The next model request uses the live tool list. An earlier draft held additions until the next user input to preserve a longer prompt prefix, but that could hide a useful tool for the rest of a long turn.

## How the draft works

1. **Gateway and MCP lifecycle.** The gateway starts one MCP maintenance task after normal startup admission. It gives initial discovery one shared window of up to one second. It does not wait for MCP in each chat, Dream, or heartbeat run. The provider cancels an unfinished startup attempt after 60 seconds and closes its transport before retrying. Failed attempts retry independently of chat after 15, 30, 60, then at most 120 seconds. The delay resets after a successful connection or a configuration change.
2. **Separate discovery from publication.** The connector opens one server and returns one handle for its capabilities and cleanup. It does not write to a tool registry. The provider permits up to four concurrent stdio process launches. The handshake and discovery do not hold a launch slot or the configuration lock. Each configured server has at most one connection attempt, so stalled servers do not delay healthy ones. A failed server does not publish partial tools. OAuth and the WebUI connection test consume the discovery result directly and keep their own deadlines. Each SDK transport still opens and closes in its owning task.
3. **Use live tool definitions during a turn.** Discovery publishes ready tools immediately. The next model request can use them, even for the same user input. Removed tools stop appearing in the next request, and execution still checks the live registry. Built-in tools stay first, and the order stays deterministic when the registry is unchanged. This change does not alter an in-flight model request or trigger an extra one.
4. **Do not redirect a conflicting tool name.** Two server names can generate the same wrapped tool name. The provider removes the ambiguous name rather than replacing its target. It unregisters each tool by object ownership, not a name prefix. An ambiguous name cannot be reassigned during the gateway's lifetime. Non-conflicting names stay unchanged. Rename one server or tool and reload to use its new name.
5. **Report the active connection.** The provider uses the active connection and attempt tables for status. Reload revokes removed or changed connections and cancels obsolete attempts. It can return a pending result while discovery continues, instead of canceling a healthy slow connection. The gateway reports a slow connection after ten seconds without canceling it. The Apps page checks every second during the first ten polls, then every five seconds while open and visible. It continues to check after startup times out or a connection fails so it can show the next attempt.

The gateway owns startup and shutdown. The connector owns the SDK connection and discovery. `MCPProvider` owns routing, publication, and retries. The existing runner reads the live tool list for each request. `AgentLoop`, `AgentRunner`, provider payload formats, OAuth consent, network policy, and rules for replaying tool operations do not change. No new installed dependency, setting, or on-disk cache is added. At `bc62a8a82`, the production diff was **+516 / −641** Python lines and **+61 / −17** WebUI lines against the draft base; test and documentation changes are separate.

### Reuse existing libraries

- The existing `referencing` library resolves JSON Pointers inside the document. nanobot still moves local targets under `$defs` for model compatibility. Resolution does not retrieve files or URLs.
- AnyIO provides stream iteration and context-manager cleanup. A small receive adapter keeps malformed progress notifications out of SDK logs, which can otherwise include the raw payload.
- Tools, resources, and prompts use one loop over the MCP SDK's page requests. The loop checks repeated cursors and completes a list before publishing it. The SDK's session group does not fetch subsequent pages, so this change does not use it for discovery.
- SSE and Streamable HTTP use the same preflight and HTTPX client setup for URL validation, proxy routing and redirects. Each transport keeps its own request headers, timeout settings, and SDK lifecycle.
- Tool results use SDK content types directly. Images and embedded image blobs still become local artifacts. Python's stable list sort preserves the exact built-ins-first tool order without maintaining two intermediate lists.
- Discovery reuses each wrapped tool name for the allowlist, diagnostics, and registration. The allowlist still runs before tool schemas are normalized. The turn-history owner preserves MCP mention metadata directly; its unused WebUI import shim is removed.

## Compatibility and open decisions

- **Background discovery:** The ten-second reload wait limits the response, not the lifetime of discovery. A slow stdio handshake can finish after the reload returns, without changing `toolTimeout`. A startup attempt still running at 60 seconds is canceled. The gateway waits for the connection owner to close its transport, even if shutdown overlaps the timeout. A server that really needs more than 60 seconds to start now times out. Interactive OAuth and explicit connection tests retain their own deadlines.
- **Intentional change for conflicting names:** Older versions could silently replace a tool with another tool under the same name. The draft disables that name instead. The configuration guide explains how to rename and reload. Restart the gateway after removing a conflict if you need to restore the original name. This does not change stored configuration or existing non-conflicting names.
- **Update continuity:** An earlier macOS arm64 run used the published 0.4.1 native wheel and the actual 0.4.1 updater code with an isolated local feed. It completed both jumps to private `0.4.2.dev0` and `0.4.2.dev1` fixtures from this source. In a separate run, an injected restart failure restored 0.4.1, and the restored installation then updated successfully to `0.4.2.dev1`. An MCP process started but never replied on the candidate gateways. Existing chat history, later writes, restart, the next update, and the shutdown of all fixture MCP children passed. This is not public-feed, signature, or all-platform upgrade evidence. No settings schema, stored chat data, install layout, or update protocol changes.

## Related work

This builds on the existing MCP lifecycle owner and readiness recovery from #5343 and #5535. It preserves the transport cleanup ownership addressed by #3640 and the tool replay safeguards from #6537.

Resolves [NAN-450](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-450/mcp-后台连接不阻塞聊天工具就绪后可在当前轮使用).

prs.title: fix: restore absent memory files when reverting commits
prs.body:
When a dream commit recreates a tracked file that was absent from its parent tree, `GitStore.revert()` skips that path instead of restoring its absence. `/dream-restore` can therefore leave the recreated memory in place. If the file has already been removed from the working tree, the all-parent-paths-absent case can also return without recording the deletion in Git.

Restore absent parent paths with `unlink(missing_ok=True)` and include them in the restored set so the existing commit path stages any required deletion. Add regressions for top-level and nested memory files, including an already-missing working-tree file with both a single tracked path and the four memory paths used by the agent.

prs.title: feat(memory): add progressive wiki and drain Dream history
prs.body:
## Summary

Replace this draft's structured lifecycle writer and automatic concept injection with progressive Markdown memory. `SOUL.md`, `USER.md`, and `memory/MEMORY.md` stay resident; detailed knowledge lives in `memory/wiki/` and is read only when relevant.

- Dream maintains canonical facts, a small resident entry point, topic indexes, and relative links using the existing file tools. Wiki pages are knowledge, not registered skills or operating instructions.
- Restricted project sessions can read the agent wiki without gaining write access. Dream can write wiki pages, but the journal and cursor files remain runtime-owned.
- Git records dynamic page additions, edits, deletions, and renames. Restore reconstructs the selected version's parent page set, including snapshots from before the wiki existed. Directory traversal rejects symlinks and Windows junctions.
- Each manual or scheduled invocation starts one Dream task. The runtime supplies the history file path and fixed pending line/cursor range; the prompt describes the complete input to consolidate without prescribing tools or a paging procedure. The cursor advances only after normal task completion. Concurrent Dream invocations are serialized, and history arriving during a run waits for the next one.
- Fix the shutdown busy loop exposed by CI: explicitly remove each drained background-task batch instead of relying on deferred completion callbacks. Work scheduled by those tasks is still drained before resources close.

## Compatibility and limits

No mandatory migration, configuration change, new retrieval engine, or management UI. Existing resident files, journal/cursor formats, SDK memory read/write semantics, and custom Dream guides remain supported. An old custom guide must opt into wiki routing if desired; processed records are not automatically replayed.

History is no longer clipped to 1,000 characters per record or embedded in runtime-sized batches. Dream receives the file and input range, not an outer loop that restarts it every 20 records. Normal model context, tool-output, and iteration limits still apply. If the task fails or reaches an execution limit, the entire input range remains pending; edits already written are retained, not rolled back. The prior draft's writer-specific benchmark results do not apply to this replacement.

## Validation

Local Windows / Python 3.14.6, synthetic temporary workspaces only:

- `python -m pytest tests/agent tests/command tests/utils/test_helpers.py tests/utils/test_token_estimation.py tests/tools/test_filesystem_tools.py tests/tools/test_apply_patch_tool.py -q -n 4 --dist loadfile --tb=short` — 2,432 passed, 5 skipped.
- `python -m pytest tests/webui/test_gateway_webui_smoke.py -q -k real_gateway_goal_single_run_and_stop --tb=short` — 2 passed, 6 deselected; real gateway/WebSocket with a local synthetic model.
- CI's full Ruff command, `basedpyright`, `python -m scripts.check_import_boundaries`, `uv pip check`, and `git diff --check` — passed.
- Earlier checks of unchanged GitStore and CLI contracts: GitStore 26 passed, 7 skipped (Windows symlink privileges unavailable; all four junction cases passed), and Dream/heartbeat/cron CLI tests 23 passed, 141 deselected.

The real AgentLoop/file-tool integration test uses a scripted synthetic provider: one Dream session reads 26 records across multiple tool calls, including three long records whose tails reach the model, writes a wiki page, and leaves a newly appended record pending. Regression tests also cover line coordinates after history retention, Unicode line separators, whole-range failure recovery, and overlapping invocations.

The previous CI run failed during gateway shutdown after the goal smoke assertions. Its tested target snapshot also reproduces the completed-task/callback race in a controlled subprocess; the fixed source exits normally. The regression uses a process deadline because a busy loop also prevents asyncio timeouts from firing, and a second case verifies that newly scheduled background work is not lost.

[Test Suite CI](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/44054633474) passed for this revision: Python 3.11, Python 3.14 with coverage, Windows Python/process/installer checks, Docker, both native acceptance jobs, and the required-check gate. The coverage job passed 11,835 tests (90 skipped), plus 245 serial CLI tests (1 skipped); WebUI/TUI-only jobs were skipped by the path rules. No live-model or real-history acceptance run is claimed. Keep this PR as a draft pending review.

Resolves [NAN-187](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-187/为-dream-增加渐进式-wiki-记忆)
