prs.title: fix(task_tracker): bound the run completion callback and always clean up
prs.body:
## Description

Fixes the **run-cleanup half** of #8173: a chat run whose completion callback hangs or is cancelled never releases its entry in `TaskTracker._runs`, so the run stays `running` forever.

### Root cause

`TaskTracker._producer` clears its `_runs` entry and pushes the end-of-stream sentinel at the end of a `finally` block, *after* awaiting the `on_finished` completion callback. Two paths meant that cleanup never completed:

1. **The callback hangs.** `on_finished` is `ChatManager.mark_chat_finished`, which persists a completion marker under a lock shared with ~24 other manager methods. Lock contention or a stalled repo suspends the producer task *inside its own `finally`*. The task is then not done **and** the entry is still registered, so every status reader reports `running` — workspace reload is blocked and inbound messages are dropped with HTTP 409.
2. **The producer is cancelled mid-callback.** `CancelledError` is a `BaseException`, so it escapes the `except Exception` guard and skips cleanup entirely, leaving subscriber streams without their sentinel.

### The fix

- Run the callback through `asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.shield(...))` bounded by `ON_FINISHED_TIMEOUT`, so a hung callback is logged and given up on rather than holding the run open.
- Move the cleanup into a nested `finally` so it always runs.

**Related Issue:** Relates to #8173

Deliberately *not* `Fixes` — see the scope note below.

### Scope — what this does **not** fix

This addresses the cleanup leak only. The other items from #8173 are **not** implemented here: the post-spawn connection health probe, the idle watchdog, `force` semantics on the reload/disable-enable paths, and in-channel hints for `/new` and `/stop` on backends that do not support them. Those are larger design questions and I would rather land the narrow fix first.

Note that the wedge is now **bounded** by `ON_FINISHED_TIMEOUT` rather than eliminated: the run stays `running` while the callback runs, because `test_attach_or_start_reports_completion_before_becoming_idle` pins that ordering deliberately (it asserts `get_status == "running"` from inside the callback). Reordering the pop ahead of the callback would break that contract.

### What the new tests cover

New `tests/unit/app/test_task_tracker_cleanup.py` (6 tests) covers a hung callback, a callback that raises, a callback that raises `TimeoutError`, a producer cancelled mid-callback, and `request_stop` against a slow callback. Waits are event-based rather than fixed sleeps.

Against unmodified source these fail on behavioural assertions (`run entry survived a hung completion callback`, etc.), not on import or attribute errors.

### Security Considerations

Not applicable — no change to channel auth, credentials, or config handling.

## Evidence

Verification is a real failure on unmodified source followed by the **same command** against the patched tree. Base is `5c56644a` (`main`), patch is `e2b7b8be`.

**1. Unmodified baseline — the new tests genuinely fail.**

```

=========================== short test summary info ============================

FAILED tests/unit/app/test_task_tracker_cleanup.py::test_completion_callback_timeout_is_logged_not_raised
FAILED tests/unit/app/test_task_tracker_cleanup.py::test_cancellation_during_callback_still_clears_the_run
FAILED tests/unit/app/test_task_tracker_cleanup.py::test_request_stop_with_a_slow_callback_does_not_wedge_the_run
4 failed, 1 passed in 8.32s
```

**2. Same command with the patch — all green.**

```

```

**3. Full `tests/unit/app` with the patch — no regression.**

```

```

One caveat worth stating plainly: the baseline run pins the module source with `PYTHONPATH` pointing at a pristine checkout. The venv's editable install points at the patched worktree, so simply `cd`-ing to the unmodified tree would still have imported the patched code and produced a false green — that happened on the first attempt and the baseline above is from the corrected invocation.

prs.title: fix(scroll): recognize url-referenced media in tool-result folding
prs.body:
## Description

When a chat session accumulates enough turns to trigger context compression, historical completed tool results are inspected by `ScrollContextManager._tool_result_fold_candidates()` to collapse long or media-carrying results into compact pointer stubs (`[scroll folded] ...`).

Previously, `_tool_result_has_inline_media()` only checked for `source.get("type") == "base64"` or `source.type == "base64"`. URL-referenced media blocks (`source.type == "url"`), such as video, audio, or image outputs generated by `send_file_to_user` and similar tools, were not recognized as inline media. Consequently, these media tool results failed the `has_media` check and, having short text captions (<= 200 chars), were skipped by `_tool_result_fold_candidates()`.

As a result, uncollapsed media blocks were carried over across turns and re-spliced verbatim into rebuilt request payloads after compression. Subsequent model API requests failed repeatedly with errors such as `400: Video count 2 exceeds limit 1 per request`, permanently hanging the session for that channel.

This change extends `_tool_result_has_inline_media()` to recognize `source.type == "url"` with non-empty URL values for both dictionary-based and object-based sources.

**Related Issue:** Fixes #8474

**Security Considerations:** None.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation
- [ ] Refactoring

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Core / Backend (app, agents, config, providers, utils, local_models)
- [x] Channels (DingTalk, Feishu, QQ, Discord, iMessage, etc.)
- [ ] Console (frontend web UI)
- [ ] Skills
- [ ] CLI
- [ ] Documentation (website)
- [x] Tests
- [ ] CI/CD
- [ ] Scripts / Deploy

## Why the issue happens

In `src/qwenpaw/agents/context/scroll/manager.py`:

```python
    @staticmethod
    def _tool_result_has_inline_media(block: Any) -> bool:
        ...
        for item in output:
            if ScrollContextManager._block_type(item) != "data":
                continue
            source = (
                item.get("source")
                if isinstance(item, dict)
                else getattr(item, "source", None)
            )
            if isinstance(source, dict):
                if source.get("type") == "base64" and source.get("data"):
                    return True
            elif getattr(source, "type", None) == "base64" and getattr(
                source,
                "data",
                None,
            ):
                return True
        return False
```

When a tool output provides a data block with a URL source (`source={"type": "url", "url": "https://..."}`), `_tool_result_has_inline_media` returned `False`.

In `_tool_result_fold_candidates`:

```python
    has_media = self._tool_result_has_inline_media(block)
    if (
        not has_media
        and self._tool_result_text_chars(block) <= _PRE_TRIM_MIN_CHARS
    ):
        continue
```

Because `has_media` was `False` and media tool results generally have little or no text characters (`<= 200`), the block was skipped and never folded. During context compression and payload rebuild, the raw media block remained in the active payload.

## The change

1. In `src/qwenpaw/agents/context/scroll/manager.py`, `_tool_result_has_inline_media` now also checks:
   - For dict sources: `source.get("type") == "url" and source.get("url")`
   - For object sources: `getattr(source, "type", None) == "url" and getattr(source, "url", None)`
2. In `tests/unit/agents/context/test_scroll_manager.py`:
   - Added `test_tool_result_has_inline_media_recognizes_url_sources` to test both base64 and URL sources across dict and object representations as well as negative cases.
   - Added `test_pressure_fold_recognizes_url_media_independently_of_text_length` to verify that tool results carrying URL media bypass the text length restriction and fold into pointer stubs under context pressure.

prs.title: fix(loop): record tool calls appended to one reply message
prs.body:
## Description

`DoomLoopGate` never fired on 2.3.0. agentscope 2.0.10 appends every iteration's blocks to the same assistant message and uses `state.reply_id` as its id, so `_auto_record_from_ctx` — which treated the message id as a per-iteration cursor — recorded only the first snapshot of a reply. With the default `window_size=3`, the warning could fire only when that first snapshot already held 3 identical calls, and the `after=4 / stop` stage was unreachable.

A reply is not always a single message either: when a warning is injected, `check_pending_gates()` appends a user continuation message and the next reasoning step opens a new assistant message that reuses the same `reply_id`. Neither the message id nor a per-message block count can tell which calls were already recorded, so this revision tracks the `id` of every recorded tool-call block for the turn and records only ids it has not seen yet. Every iteration contributes its own calls, and re-checking an unchanged snapshot stays a no-op. (Thanks to @lalaliat for pointing out the message-count gap in review.)

**Related Issue:** Fixes #8700

prs.title: fix(channels): scope WeChat credentials per agent workspace
prs.body:
## Description

Two agents could not hold separate WeChat accounts in one installation.

The custody check hashed every *other* agent's credential scope against the
process-wide `WORKING_DIR`, so an agent without an explicit `bot_token_file`
fell back to that same path. Both agents then produced the same "token file"
and "context tokens" hashes, the second one failed with `ACCOUNT_IN_USE`, and
its channel page could not even fetch a QR code (`409 ACCOUNT_IN_USE`).

`wechat_auth_scopes()` already resolves a missing `bot_token_file` against the
`working_dir` it is given, so the fix is to pass each agent's own workspace:

```python
other_dir = Path(profile.workspace_dir).expanduser()
wechat_auth_scopes(other, working_dir=other_dir)
```

Agents that deliberately share a credential directory still collide, which is
the intended guard: the context-token file lives beside the token, and one
directory means one account.

**Related Issue:** Fixes #____ (replace with the issue number; the linked issue
also covers the upgrade migration that duplicates an inline `bot_token`, and the
single-execution-source limit, which this PR deliberately does not change)

**Security Considerations:** Only the *scope hashing* of other agents' configs
changes; credential storage, custody leases, approval authorization and the
plugin execution source are untouched. Agents with identical credentials still
collide by design.

`bot_token_file` under its workspace):

  http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/config/channels/wechat/qrcode
# before: {"detail":"ACCOUNT_IN_USE"}   after: 200 with qrcode_img

......                                                                   [100%]

- missing `bot_token_file` → the workspace decides, so two workspaces give

both agent ids.

The two adjacent problems are tracked in the issue rather than this PR:
the upgrade migration copying an inline `bot_token` into every agent profile,
and the channel plugin's single execution source (a second agent's channel
cannot run, and its QR fetch returns `500 RUNTIME_SOURCE_MUTATING`, while the

prs.title: fix(media): enforce the inline budget, rescale after a refusal, and report omissions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The downscale pass added in #8632 judged an image by its longest side alone. Three gaps followed from that, and they are fixed together because they meet on the same path.

**1. The byte budget and the side limit are two independent limits.**
A 2000x2000 PNG is well inside the 8192 px side limit and can still weigh 11.46 MiB, so the pass returned it untouched and the formatter rejected the request on bytes right afterwards. Both limits are now checked, and a formatter that provisions its own limits passes them down, so this pass and the cap cannot disagree about what fits.

**2. PNG has no quality knob.**
Every quality step emitted the same bytes and paid for another full deflate. The quality loop is skipped for PNG; only reducing the side makes it smaller.

**3. A rejection could not name the image it rejected.**
The retry log said "some media" while every image in the request was dropped, which left no way to tell which one the provider objected to. Each wire media block now gets a label (position, media type, decoded size) across the Anthropic `source`, OpenAI `image_url` and Gemini `inline_data`/`file_data` spellings, and the log names them.

**4. A rejection that named the media was replayed forever.**
Non-streaming recovery recognised only `413` / body-size wording. A `400 image dimensions exceed the maximum allowed size` fell through to `raise`, and because the offending block stayed in `state.context`, every later turn sent it again and collected the same rejection. The streaming path did strip media, but only for that one request — the identical loop, one turn later.

Both paths now classify a payload refusal, mark the historical copies as omitted once (`mark_media_omitted_after_overflow`) and retry. The stored message keeps its bytes, so the full-resolution file stays retrievable; only request copies are stripped.

**5. When the refusal is about the active turn, shrinking beats deleting.**
If nothing historical can be omitted, the refusal is about the image the user is asking about. Deleting it would be wrong. The request-scoped limits (`max_image_side`, `max_bytes`) are halved once for a single retry and restored afterwards, so the retry sends a smaller rendition while the stored message is untouched.

**6. Dropped media was invisible to the user.**
When media is replaced by a text placeholder the model answers as if the file had never been attached — indistinguishable from "the model ignored my image". The reply now carries `qwenpaw_media_omitted` (`{count, reason}`), which the Console renders as one system line and non-Console channels send as one extra text line.

## Scope

Type: B (state machine / retry), with a D-shaped surface because the notice crosses agents → channels → console.

- `src/qwenpaw/providers/capping_formatter.py` — `MAX_IMAGE_SIDE` moves here, beside the byte cap, so both media limits have one home; new `max_image_side` field (`ge=0`, default 8192).
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/utils/image_resize.py` — two limits decided independently, `max_side` threaded through, quality loop skipped for PNG.
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/model_factory.py` — reads the formatter's limits and passes them down; new `_describe_wire_media_blocks` / `_wire_media_label`.
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/utils/message_request_normalizer.py` — threads `max_bytes` / `max_side` to the resize pass.
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/react_agent.py` — payload-refusal classification on the non-streaming path, one-shot limit tightening with restore, per-response omission notice.
- `src/qwenpaw/app/channels/base.py` — `_media_omitted_notice`, sent with the existing fallback notice so channels without Console rendering see it too.
- `console/src/pages/Chat/fallbackNotice.ts`, `console/src/pages/Chat/index.tsx`, `console/src/locales/{en,zh}.json` — parse and render the notice.

## Self-review

1. **Callers of `downscale_image_bytes`** — `_rescale_source` is the only intermediate, `normalize_messages_for_model_request_async` the only entry point; both are updated, and both keep the old behaviour when the new keyword arguments are omitted (`max_side=MAX_IMAGE_SIDE`, `max_bytes=MAX_INLINE_MEDIA_BYTES`).
2. **`MAX_IMAGE_SIDE` relocation** — `grep -rn MAX_IMAGE_SIDE src/` returns only `capping_formatter.py` (definition) and the modules that import it; no stale constant remains in `image_resize`.
3. **`max_image_side` as a new field** — declared with `ge=0` and the same default as before (8192), so every existing formatter subclass inherits it; `_normalize_messages_for_formatter` reads it with `getattr(..., MAX_IMAGE_SIDE)` so a custom formatter without the field still works.
4. **`_describe_wire_media_blocks`** — used only by `QwenPawAgent._last_wire_media_summary`, which returns `[]` when no formatter is active.
5. **Reversal** — `max_bytes <= 0` keeps its old meaning of "no byte limit" rather than shrinking forever.
6. **Both limits agree** — the resize pass receives `formatter.max_bytes` / `formatter.max_image_side` instead of the module constants, so a provider override cannot make the pass shrink to a different budget than the one enforced a moment later.
7. **Bounded retries** — the shared recovery budget (`remaining = 2`) is unchanged. Limit tightening is one-shot per request: `_qwenpaw_media_limits_tightened` blocks a second shrink, and both `finally` blocks restore the original pair, so an unrelated later request is not silently served smaller images.
8. **Stored history is not rewritten** — the omission pass only writes `qwenpaw_omitted_media_ids` metadata. `test_omissions_survive_resume_and_allow_new_images` verifies the state round-trips and a newly attached image is still sent.
9. **The notice is additive** — with no omission the channel output is byte-identical to the previous string (a single fallback line). An unparsable notice renders nothing rather than an empty system message.
10. **Non-streaming classifier stays narrow** — `is_request_body_too_large` is untouched (still `413` / body-size only); the media branch is a separate condition that additionally requires media on the wire and the existing payload-rejection classifier.

## Test scope

- Targeted: `test_context_overflow_recovery.py` + `test_react_agent_media_strip.py` + `test_media_omitted_notice.py` + `test_message_request_normalizer.py` + `test_image_resize.py` + `tests/unit/app/channels` — **365 passed**
- Adjacent: `tests/unit/agents -k 'media or overflow or omitt'` — **460 passed, 3 skipped**
- Console: `fallbackNotice.test.ts` — **6 passed**; `sdkHostIntegration.test.tsx` + `ChatPage.coverage.test.tsx` — **196 passed**; `tsc -b --noEmit` clean; `prettier --check` clean
- `pre-commit run --files <changed files>` — all hooks passed (black reformatted two test files on the first pass, clean on the re-run)

## Evidence

A 2000x2000 high-entropy PNG, well inside the side limit and far over the byte cap:

```
INPUT   side=2000x2000  bytes=12,015,257  (11.46 MiB)
        longest side 2000 <= 8192 -> the old side-only check returned this unchanged
OUTPUT  bytes=596,065  (0.57 MiB)  media_type=image/png  changed=True
        under 2 MiB cap: True

max_bytes=0 -> unchanged=True  (11.46 MiB)
```

The media labels, one per wire spelling:

```
#1 image/png 1.0 MiB      (Anthropic source)
#1 image/jpeg 1.0 MiB     (OpenAI image_url data URL)
#1 image/webp 1.0 MiB     (Gemini inline_data)
```

The refusal path, measured before and after the change:

```
before  marked=0  max_image_side=8192  qwenpaw_media_omitted=ABSENT
after   marked=8  max_image_side=8192 (history had blocks to omit)

active-turn only:
before  marked=0  side=8192 bytes=2097152
retry   side=4096 bytes=1048576
after   side=8192 bytes=2097152 (restored)
```

Removing the new classifier turns two tests red; removing the streaming omission call turns one red — both restored afterwards.

Refs #8632, #8629

prs.title: fix(loop): record every tool call appended during a reply so the doom-loop gate can fire
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`DoomLoopGate` is enabled in the default mode (`window_size=3`,
`similarity_threshold=0.5`, `stop` after 4 hits) but it has never fired. A reply
that repeats the same tool call with the same arguments — the case in #8712,
where one `Bash` invocation was approved 14 times in 70 seconds — ran until the
user pressed stop twice.

The gate's auto-recording path de-duplicated on the **message** id:

```python
last_msg = context[-1]
if last_msg.id == state.last_recorded_msg_id:
    return
```

Inside a single reply, every assistant message is written with the same
`state.reply_id`: `agentscope` creates one `ReplyContext(reply_id=…)` per reply,
and `AgentState.append_context` either extends the existing message or appends a
new one with that same id. From the second iteration on, `last_msg.id` already
equalled `state.last_recorded_msg_id`, so the function returned before recording
anything and the history never grew past one entry. A three-entry window can
never fill, `_detect_repetition` can never return true, and no stage is reached.

This is not specific to shell calls: no tool, in any reply, could trip the gate.

## Scope

Type: B (state machine / dedup)

One file of production code plus one test file. `agents/tools/shell.py` is not
touched: the earlier revision of this PR changed `_with_shell_guard` to stop
overriding the result state with `ERROR`, on the theory that the tool result
never reached the model. That theory was wrong — the result does reach the
model — so that change is reverted, and this PR fixes the layer that actually
dropped the repetition.

## Self-review

1. Failure — a block with an unexpected shape cannot raise: the scan skips any
   block whose type is not `tool_call`/`tool_use`, and reads fields defensively
   for both block objects and plain dicts.
2. Timeout — not applicable: the gate has no timeout path; it runs synchronously
   inside `check()`.
3. Skipped — a text-only iteration (`has_tool_calls is False`) records nothing;
   an empty or non-list `content` returns early.
4. Concurrency — one iteration that carries several parallel tool calls records
   every block it contains (`test_blocks_of_one_iteration_are_all_recorded`).

## Evidence

Recorded against the real `DoomLoopGate` with synthetic contexts that mirror
what the agent writes:

| context | history after 8 iterations | gate fired |
| --- | --- | --- |
| same message id every iteration (before) | stays at 1 | never |
| same message id, blocks appended (after) | 8 | iteration 4 |

Production logs agree: `qwenpaw.log` since 13 November contains no
`DoomLoopGate` and no `Doom loop` line at all.

The concrete case from #8712 — 14 identical `Bash` calls inside one reply — now
reaches the configured stop stage instead of running to completion.

## Test scope

- Target: `tests/unit/loop/test_doom_loop_auto_record.py` — **7 passed**.
- Red/green: with the `src` change reverted the same file gives **2 failed**
  (including the three-iteration stop case), and **7 passed** once restored.
- Adjacent: `tests/unit/loop` — **99 passed**.
- Adjacent: `tests/unit/modes` + `tests/unit/agents/tools/test_shell_resources.py`
  — **196 passed, 4 skipped** (the skips are the platform-gated resource tests).
- Lint: `pre-commit run --files` — all hooks passed.

Fixes #8712.

prs.title: fix(governance): enforce destructive-command and system-credential guards
prs.body:
## What changed

Fix two governance security gaps:

1. Run the shared destructive-command classifier in the `PolicyGuardedTool` governance path.
   - Catastrophic commands now produce `SAFETY_CHECKS_DESTRUCTIVE_COMMAND`.
   - The default auto-deny configuration blocks them directly.
   - Setting auto-deny to `none` still routes ordinary CRITICAL findings through approval.
   - Relative destructive targets are classified using the effective tool working directory.

2. Protect system credential files by default.
   - Adds sensitive-path coverage for `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/gshadow`, `/etc/sudoers`, `/etc/ssh/`, and related credential files.
   - Existing persisted governance policies gain this protection during path resolution without requiring migration or user configuration.
   - Public account metadata such as `/etc/passwd` remains readable.

## Why

The governance path bypassed `ToolGuardEngine`, so the default
`SAFETY_CHECKS_DESTRUCTIVE_COMMAND` auto-deny rule could never be produced.
Some catastrophic commands could consequently reach sandbox fallback and run
unsandboxed when sandboxing was unavailable.

Separately, root deployments could read `/etc/shadow` without approval because
the default sensitive-path list only covered user-level credential locations
and the global `Read(**)` policy allowed all remaining reads.

  - auto-deny opt-out and restoration

prs.title: fix(security): flag inline Office COM automation in shell commands
prs.body:
## Summary

On Windows with approval level `auto` and the sandbox off, an agent-authored
inline Office COM command runs instead of being stopped.
`PowerPoint.Application`, `Excel.Application`, `Word.Application` and
`Outlook.Application` are single-instance COM servers, so attaching to one
binds to the **user's** already-open app and `Quit()` on that object
terminates the user's document — not a private automation instance.

The command matched no detection rule, so `GovernancePolicy.evaluate`
classified it as `SANDBOX_FALLBACK`, and `ResourceGovernor` rewrites that
decision to `ALLOW` whenever the sandbox is unavailable
(`running unsandboxed`). Nothing sat between the model and the user's
Office process.

This adds a `CRITICAL` rule that matches the COM construction itself, so
the call lands on the approval path instead of the unsandboxed one.

Refs #8002

## What Problem This Solves

A user had PowerPoint open on a real file. With approval level `auto` and
the security sandbox off, the agent emitted an Office COM self-check such as
`New-Object -ComObject PowerPoint.Application` followed by `Quit()`, and the
shell tool ran it. PowerShell attached to the **running** PowerPoint COM
server and `Quit()` closed the user's presentation — with data loss and no
warning, because the decision path never asked.

The root cause is not a missing sandbox rule but the fallback rewrite: an
unmatched shell command is `SANDBOX_FALLBACK`, and when the sandbox is
unusable `ResourceGovernor` turns that into `ALLOW`. Any command no rule
recognises is therefore executed unsandboxed and unguarded.

## Changes

`src/qwenpaw/security/tool_guard/rules/dangerous_shell_commands.yaml` —
new `TOOL_CMD_OFFICE_COM_AUTOMATION` rule (`category: resource_abuse`,
`severity: CRITICAL`) with three patterns:

1. a COM construction verb (`New-Object`, `GetActiveObject`, `GetObject`,
   `CreateObject`, `CreateInstance`, `GetTypeFromProgID`, `Dispatch`,
   `DispatchEx`) followed by an Office `*.Application` ProgID — catches
   `New-Object -ComObject PowerPoint.Application`,
   `[Activator]::CreateInstance([Type]::GetTypeFromProgID("Word.Application"))`,
   `win32com.client.Dispatch("Excel.Application")`
2. the same pairing in the other order, for the split
   `$t = GetTypeFromProgID(...); CreateInstance($t)` spelling
3. `.Quit()` invoked on an attached Office server

## Behaviour

| command | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `New-Object -ComObject PowerPoint.Application; $ppt.Quit()` | `sandbox_fallback` → `ALLOW` (sandbox off) | `ask` |
| `echo hello` | `sandbox_fallback` | `sandbox_fallback` |
| `python render_deck.py --out deck.pptx` | `sandbox_fallback` | `sandbox_fallback` |
| `git commit -m 'document Word.Application'` | `sandbox_fallback` | `sandbox_fallback` |

Mere mentions of the ProgID do not match, so built-in scripts that only
`Close()` a private temp presentation are unaffected (verified: no
occurrence of these ProgIDs or `ComObject`/`win32com` anywhere in `src/`,
`tests/`, `scripts/`, `plugins/` or `e2e/`).

Note the rule escalates to `ask`, not `deny`: `execution_level=off` is
documented as "tool guard completely disabled", so nothing fires there by
design and this change does not alter that.

## Evidence

End-to-end through `GovernancePolicy.evaluate` with the bundled rules
loaded (before → after):

```
$ python - <<'PY'
pol = _create_default_policy()
spec = ToolCallSpec(tool_name="Bash",
    target='New-Object -ComObject PowerPoint.Application; $ppt.Quit()',
    agent_id="a", session_id="s")
for level in ("auto", "smart", "strict", "off"):
    pol.execution_level = level
    d = pol.evaluate(spec)
    print(level, "->", d.action.value, d.source)
PY
# before: auto -> sandbox_fallback  smart -> sandbox_fallback  strict -> ask  off -> sandbox_fallback
auto     -> ask              source=detection_rules
smart    -> ask              source=detection_rules
strict   -> ask              source=STRICT mode
off      -> sandbox_fallback source=sandbox

benign auto     -> sandbox_fallback source=sandbox
benign smart    -> sandbox_fallback source=sandbox
benign off      -> sandbox_fallback source=sandbox
```

Full validation:

```
$ pytest tests/unit/governance tests/unit/security/tool_guard   # 842 passed
$ pytest tests/unit -k "tool_guard or governance or detector"   # 874 passed
$ black --line-length=79 / flake8 / pylint (10.00)              # clean
```

prs.title: feat(plugins): expose the semantic colour roles to plugin themes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

#8071 asks for a plugin theme extension point. #8422 landed the first slice:
six roles (`bg`, `surface`, `surface-raised`, `border`, `text`,
`text-secondary`). Those cover the page frame, but not the semantic colour
surface a theme actually has to touch — a plugin that wants its own accent,
status colours, or the lower-contrast text and border tiers still has to reach
into raw `--app-*` names, which this closed API deliberately rejects.

This PR widens the closed set to the 31 semantic colour roles that
`console/src/styles/tokens.css` already defines and the console already
consumes, and keeps the compatibility story honest:

- the original six roles keep their current minimum SDK version, so plugins
  that already call `overrideTokens` are unaffected;
- the new roles sit behind `sdk.version >= 1.2.0` plus a `themeTokens`
  capability, so a plugin cannot silently depend on a role that an older host
  does not know.

Group 2 from #8071 (fifteen shape and layer roles: radius, shadow,
focus-ring, scrollbar, fill) stays out of this PR and is left for a separate
discussion, as requested.

## Evidence

Every role below is already read by the console. No component was changed and
no new colour was invented — this only opens roles that exist.

| family | role | representative consumer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| surface | `surface-subtle` | `layouts/index.module.less:324` |
| surface | `surface-sunken` | `components/RenderableCodeBlock/index.module.less:122` |
| surface | `shell-bg` | `layouts/dockableSidebar.module.less:13` |
| text | `text-tertiary` | `layouts/dockableSidebar.module.less:36` |
| text | `text-quaternary` | `layouts/index.module.less:254` |
| border | `border-subtle` | `layouts/index.module.less:53` |
| border | `border-strong` | `layouts/sidebarA.module.less:99` |
| accent | `accent` | `App.tsx:421` |
| accent | `accent-hover` | `App.tsx:422` |
| accent | `accent-soft` | `App.tsx:423` |
| status | `success-bg` | `components/LoopInput/index.module.less:57` |
| status | `warning-border` | `components/Chat/ToolCards/shared/offloadBanner.module.less:11` |
| status | `error-text` | `tauri/BackendLoadingPage.module.less:52` |

Both schemes are exercised rather than assumed: `themeTokens.test.ts` asserts
each role lands in the `:root` block with its light value and in the
`html.dark-mode` block with its dark value.

## Self-review

1. Overlapping registrations — `install.test.ts` keeps the existing
   "stacks per token and falls back on dispose" case, and the new semantic
   roles go through the same stacking path.
2. Switching scheme or preset while an override is active —
   `themeTokens.integration.test.ts` keeps "wins over the preset's inline
   `--app-surface` in both schemes" and "restores the preset when the plugin is
   unloaded".
3. Cleanup — "removes the element once every override is gone" and
   `disposeAll(pluginId)` both still clear the new roles.
4. Invalid input — a role missing one scheme and a genuinely unknown name both
   still throw; the unknown-name case now uses `not-a-role` so it does not
   accidentally test a role that became valid in this PR.
5. Backward compatibility — `sdk.version: 1.0.0` stays valid for the original
   six roles; `1.1.0` with `themeTokens` is rejected with a clear message;
   `1.2.0` with `themeTokens` is accepted.

## Test scope

- Console: `src/plugins` — 34 files, 462 passed, including the five
  capability-gate cases and the seven `pluginSdk` cases.
- Python: `tests/unit/app/routers` 161 passed and
  `test_plugins_router_lifecycle.py` 115 passed, including the new
  `test_frontend_list_reports_declared_sdk`; `tests/unit/plugins` passed with
  `test_theme_tokens_capability_gates_on_sdk_version`.
- `tsc -b --noEmit`, eslint, prettier and pre-commit on the touched files.
- Browser: `python scripts/verify_theme_tokens.py` from `console/` (values in
  the follow-up section below).

## Coordination with #8764

#8764 also moves `SDK_VERSION` to `1.2.0` and touches
`src/qwenpaw/plugins/frontend/index.d.ts`. This PR needs the same version slot.
Whichever lands first, the other rebases onto it — the two changes are additive
and share only that version line, so the rebase is mechanical. If #8764 lands
first, this PR moves to 1.2.1; the gate reads `>= 1.2.0`, so the bump changes
no behaviour.


## Review follow-up

Three rounds are folded into `cc5551c3`.

**One compatibility decision on both list paths.** The loader rejects an
incompatible SDK declaration before a plugin loads, but `/frontend_plugin`'s
disk fallback forwarded the manifest verbatim, so the console became the only
judge. `1.2.0rc1` and `1.2.0.dev1` are below 1.2.0 under PEP 440 and may not
carry `themeTokens`, yet the console's numeric comparison read them as 1.2.0
and accepted the extended roles. Both paths now call `_sdk_declaration()`,
which runs `validate_sdk()` and reports "not declared" when the declaration is
invalid. A pre-release without `themeTokens` is still forwarded unchanged, and
the six original roles need no declaration at all. Covered by
`test_frontend_list_rejects_incompatible_prerelease_on_disk[1.2.0rc1|1.2.0.dev1]`,
`test_frontend_list_keeps_a_prerelease_without_extended_capabilities` and
`test_frontend_list_applies_the_same_check_when_loaded`.

**The gate covers undeclared usage.** `validate_sdk` used to run only when a
plugin declared `themeTokens`, so a plugin could use a new role while declaring
nothing at all. `/frontend_plugin` now carries `sdk_version` and
`sdk_capabilities`, and `chat.theme.overrideTokens` consults that declaration
for every extended role: no declaration, an older version, or a missing
capability each throw with the role, the plugin, what is required and what was
declared. A manifest that cannot be read is treated as undeclared, so the check
fails closed. The original six roles keep their 1.0.0 minimum and need no
declaration.

**Components demonstrate it through the public API.** `themeVerify/main.tsx`
registers through `chat.theme.overrideTokens()` and disposes the handle it
returns; the internal store is not touched on the success path. Playwright
reads `getComputedStyle` for nine roles in both schemes — `bg`, `surface`,
`border`, `text`, `accent`, `error-text`, `success-bg`, `warning-border`,
`info-text` — plus the card, button and text probes: 23 expectations, no
failures. The harness also writes the user preset inline on `<html>` the way
`App.tsx` does, applies an override, changes the preset while it is active and
then disposes: the override keeps winning during the change, and after dispose
the page shows the *new* preset (`rgb(42, 42, 42)`), not the earlier one.
Stacked registrations still walk back across two disposes, and the same public
call with an undeclared plugin throws in the browser too.

Third-party scope is documented in `plugins/frontend/README.md`: this is a
colour surface, not a full UI theme. Only the listed roles participate, and
layout, spacing, typography, iconography, chart palettes and markup that
hardcodes `rgb()`/`rgba()` do not follow the override.

prs.title: fix(pawapp): disable proxy buffering on chat and tool-call SSE streams
prs.body:
## Description

Follow-up to #8522, which added `X-Accel-Buffering: no` to the `/api/console/chat` SSE responses. Two more SSE endpoints that the Console consumes still lack it:

- `POST /chat/stream` in `pawapp/app.py` (used by the pawapp SDK host)
- `GET /tool-calls/{session_id}/{tool_call_id}/stream` in `app/routers/tool_calls.py` (used by `console/src/api/modules/toolCalls.ts`)

Behind nginx with the default `proxy_buffering on`, their events are held until the buffer fills or the response ends, so the stream arrives late or all at once — the same symptom as #8516.

This sends `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `X-Accel-Buffering: no` on both responses, matching `backup.py`, `portability_imports.py`, `project_directory.py`, `skills_stream.py` and `workspace.py`.

prs.title: perf(runtime): sort tool schemas to stabilize LLM prefix cache
prs.body:
## Description

Stabilizes the LLM prefix (KV) cache by making the largest prefix segment of the request deterministic.

**`ToolRegistry.filter()` now returns descriptors in sorted name order.**
Tool schemas are serialized before messages in the LLM request and represent the single largest prefix segment (~3,000–8,000 tokens). The previous dict insertion order was stable within a process but not deterministic across restarts or plugin load-order changes (e.g., plugin registration timing). A defensive `.sort(key=lambda d: d.name)` guarantees identical schema ordering regardless of registration timing.

The second source of instability from #6952 — interleaved env_context fields — was independently addressed upstream by #7346 (request-specific fields moved behind the reusable prefix, current date last). This PR adds regression tests (`TestBuildEnvContextOrdering`) that lock that ordering in, so future contributors cannot silently reintroduce the interleaving.

Remaining smaller sources of cache invalidation (continuation summary shifts under scroll compression, `[scroll folded]` tool-result replacement) are intentional design trade-offs documented in the Scroll memory architecture.

**Related Issue:** Closes #6952

**Security Considerations:** N/A — purely reorders existing prompt segments.

- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Documentation
- [x] Refactoring

The sort key is unique: `ToolRegistry.register()` rejects duplicate descriptor names, so `out.sort(key=lambda d: d.name)` is deterministic and stable. prs.body:
## Description

When `disable_thinking=True` reaches the OpenAI Responses adapter, inherited `reasoning` settings are removed. The adapter previously restored `reasoning.effort=none` only for a hard-coded list of model names, even when another model's declared `ThinkingControl` supports turning reasoning off.

prs.title: fix(skills): refine pool cards and builtin update status
prs.body:
Following an update to the skill pool, legacy built-in skills were incorrectly flagged as "outdated," causing the notification dot to persist. This update refines the status-detection logic and optimizes the information hierarchy and action layout within the skill cards.
- Functions such as "Auto-sync," "Auto-update," "Broadcast," and "Delete" have been consolidated into the card menu; "Auto-sync" and "Auto-update" can now be toggled independently.
- Skill descriptions are now limited to two lines, with the full text accessible via hover. Top-margin spacing has been reduced, text readability improved, the "last updated" timestamp moved to the right, and the help icon (question mark) positioned directly next to the skill name.
- A distinction is now made between "outdated" versions and "legacy built-in" skills; previously installed copies are retained, accompanied by relevant explanatory notes.
- The notification dot now appears only when an update is available for an outdated version; no update prompt is shown if the installed version is current or newer.
- Multilingual text has been synchronized, with layouts adapted for both desktop and mobile platforms.

issues.title: [Bug]: Dashboard Cost Overview bars are scaled to the largest figure, so the Monthly bar is always full
issues.body:
### Affected component

web dashboard

### Severity

S3 - minor issue

### Current behavior

The Overview tab's Cost Overview card shows three rows (Session, Daily, Monthly), each with an amount and a bar. The Daily and Monthly amounts are right, but the bars don't measure anything against a budget:

- Each bar's width is `value / maxCost`, where `maxCost` is the largest of the three amounts ([`Dashboard.tsx` L440-L445](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/dfe8ab35bd682e3510fe81856f27c0926742cd25/web/src/pages/Dashboard.tsx#L440-L445), [L572](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/dfe8ab35bd682e3510fe81856f27c0926742cd25/web/src/pages/Dashboard.tsx#L572)). The month's spend includes the day's, so with the default window the Monthly bar is full (apart from a few hours around the start of a UTC month), and Daily is drawn as a share of the month. A full Monthly bar reads as "monthly limit reached" even when far less of `[cost].monthly_limit_usd` has been spent. In my case it was full at about 55% of the configured monthly limit.
- The "Session" amount isn't a session total. The dashboard fetches the summary for the window selected on the Cost tab ([L1740](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/dfe8ab35bd682e3510fe81856f27c0926742cd25/web/src/pages/Dashboard.tsx#L1740), [L1774](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/dfe8ab35bd682e3510fe81856f27c0926742cd25/web/src/pages/Dashboard.tsx#L1774)), and on that path `session_cost_usd` is the total of the records in the window, the whole ledger for "All time" ([`tracker.rs` L746-L767](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/dfe8ab35bd682e3510fe81856f27c0926742cd25/crates/zeroclaw-config/src/cost/tracker.rs#L746-L767)). With the default window ("today") it is roughly the day's spend again (the local day; Daily is the UTC day, as is the daily limit). With "All time" it is the all-time total, which is never less than the month's, so its bar is full.

The limits that do govern spending (`daily_limit_usd`, `monthly_limit_usd`, `warn_at_percent` and the enforcement settings, [`schema.rs` L7471-L7492](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/dfe8ab35bd682e3510fe81856f27c0926742cd25/crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs#L7471-L7492)) aren't part of the `/api/cost` response ([`api.rs` L1296-L1319](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/dfe8ab35bd682e3510fe81856f27c0926742cd25/crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api.rs#L1296-L1319)), so the card has nothing else to scale to.

### Expected behavior

The bars show how much of each configured limit has been used:

- **Daily:** `daily_cost_usd / daily_limit_usd`.
- **Monthly:** `monthly_cost_usd / monthly_limit_usd`.
- Both are capped at a full bar when over the limit, and change colour at `warn_at_percent`.
- **Session:** drop this row, or rename it to the selected window (e.g. "Today", "All time") without a bar. Its amount is the selected window's total, and there is no session limit to measure it against. If it is dropped, the window total could move to the Cost tab, which at present shows only per-agent and per-model spend for the window. (The card's "Total tokens" and "Requests" lines are window totals too.)

This needs the limits (and probably `warn_at_percent` and whether cost tracking is enabled) in the `/api/cost` response, or from another source the card can read. Open points for maintainers:

- Where the limits should come from: `/api/cost`, or a second request to the config read path. `/api/cost` admits only paired bearers and admin sessions, which can also read the config, so the difference is one request versus two, not access.
- What to show when cost tracking or enforcement is off, or when a limit is unset (see #12512): plain amounts without bars, or bars against the limits anyway.

### Steps to reproduce

```text
1. With some spend recorded this month, open the dashboard's Overview tab.
2. Cost Overview: the Monthly bar is full, whatever share of
   [cost].monthly_limit_usd has been spent.
3. On the Cost tab, choose "All time", then go back to Overview: the Session
   amount is now the all-time total, and its bar is full. In my case both the
   Session and Monthly bars were full.
```

### Impact

Misleading budget display: a full bar suggests the monthly limit has been reached, and the real share of the limits isn't shown anywhere on the card.

### Logs / stack traces

_No response_

### ZeroClaw version

v0.9.0 (with some open web PRs merged locally; none touches the cost card). The code references above are from current `master` (`dfe8ab35b`).

### Rust version

_No response_

### Operating system

Linux server (amd64); desktop browser

### Regression?

Unknown

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.body:
### Documentation location

docs/book/src/channels/email.md, "Tools-only: enable it, don't bind it"

### Documentation issue type

missing documentation

### Problem

The tools-only section says that enabling an email alias registers `email_search` and `email_read`, and that binding it to an agent is what starts the IMAP listener. So it tells you to leave the alias out of every agent's `channels` list, and it covers the legacy fallback when no agent declares any bindings.

It doesn't mention approval routes, which also start the listener. `ActiveChannelAliases::contains` in `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs` also accepts any channel named by an approval route:

- a `request_route` or `escalation_route` in `[sop.approval.policies.*]`
- the `approval_route.approver_channel` of an enabled agent's risk profile

A route can name a bare channel type such as `email`. When exactly one email alias is enabled, the route resolves to that alias. An operator who follows the section but routes approvals through email still gets the IMAP listener for that alias. Outbound behavior is unaffected; this is about unwanted inbound listener activity.

### Expected documentation

Add approval routes to the exclusions in the tools-only section. To keep an alias tools-only, leave it out of:

- every agent's `channels` list
- SOP approval `request_route` and `escalation_route`
- the risk-profile `approver_channel` of every enabled agent, including a bare `email` route when only one email alias is enabled

Optionally, add a sentence on what the listener does for an alias that only an approval route names: it stays live to deliver approval replies, but it isn't assigned to an agent for ordinary traffic.

### Related issue, PR, RFC, or discussion

Follow-up to #12003 (merged as 71e68a0d63), from @Audacity88's review suggestion: https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/12003#pullrequestreview-5703250355

issues.body:
### Summary

Recalculate canonical `size:*` and `risk:*` labels whenever a pull request's reviewed diff changes, while preserving explicit maintainer overrides and avoiding elevated execution of untrusted PR code.

### Problem statement

PR size and risk labels currently require manual maintenance even though they influence review depth, routing, and contributor expectations. Labels can become stale after new commits, conflict repairs, or scope reductions, so reviewers may be looking at metadata that no longer describes the current diff.

The maintainer label contract already defines canonical size thresholds, high-risk paths, recalculation on pushed PR updates, and `risk:manual` as the override that freezes automated risk replacement. What is missing is the implementation and evidence needed to enable it safely.

#665 previously proposed merge-queue support and automatic PR sizing, but its implementation in #680 closed without merging. The current repository therefore still has no workflow that calculates or applies PR size or risk labels. This issue carries the unlanded size goal forward under the newer #6808 label contract and adds the separately staged risk-classification work.

This is separate from the report-only Project dashboard planner in #8914. Project fields own issue planning state; `risk:*` and `size:*` remain PR labels. It is also narrower than #9330: AI-assisted review may recommend labels later, but this issue owns deterministic calculation and label application.

### Proposed solution

Add a staged PR-label workflow that runs when a pull request is opened, reopened, or synchronized.

#### Phase 1: deterministic size labels

- Calculate effective changed lines from GitHub PR metadata using the thresholds documented in `docs/book/src/maintainers/labels.md`.
- Define and test the existing docs-only and lockfile-heavy normalization rules rather than leaving them implicit.
- Apply exactly one canonical `size:XS`, `size:S`, `size:M`, `size:L`, or `size:XL` label.
- Remove a prior automated size label only when the newly calculated value differs.
- Recalculate after every pushed PR update so the label describes the current reviewed diff.

#### Phase 2: report-only risk classification

- Evaluate the documented high-risk path set and explicit workflow/toolchain escalation rules.
- Produce an auditable job summary containing the proposed risk label and the evidence that selected it.
- Compare report-only results with maintainer-applied labels before enabling mutation.
- Treat uncertain or conflicting signals conservatively and surface them for maintainer review.

#### Phase 3: risk label mutation

- Enable automatic replacement only after maintainers approve the report-only results and exact classification rules.
- Apply exactly one canonical `risk:low`, `risk:medium`, or `risk:high` label.
- If `risk:manual` is present, do not add, remove, or replace the PR's current `risk:*` label until a maintainer removes the override.
- Never lower a maintainer-frozen classification.

The label-writing job must use GitHub API metadata only. It must not check out, import, source, build, or execute pull-request code under `pull_request_target` or any other elevated write context. Permissions should be limited to repository-content reads and pull-request/issue label writes.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- No ProjectV2 field mutation; that remains the separate #6808 Project-writer slice.
- No automatic `type:*`, component, status, contributor-tier, stale, or resolution labels.
- No AI model dependency for the deterministic classifier.
- No final review decision, approval, merge, closure, or CODEOWNERS override.
- No automatic removal of `risk:manual`.
- No execution of untrusted fork code with elevated permissions.

### Alternatives considered

**Keep both labels manual:** This preserves judgment but leaves labels stale after ordinary PR updates and consumes repeated maintainer attention.

**Implement both families as immediate mutations:** Size is sufficiently mechanical, but risk includes semantic and rollback considerations. A report-only risk phase gives maintainers evidence before automation can overwrite live metadata.

**Fold this into #9330:** AI-assisted review may recommend risk and size, but deterministic label maintenance should remain usable without an AI reviewer and should have a smaller permission surface.

**Fold this into the Project writer:** Project status and PR classification have different owners, triggers, permissions, and failure modes. Keeping them separate avoids coupling issue-planning automation to fast-changing PR metadata.

### Acceptance criteria

- Opening, reopening, or synchronizing a PR recalculates its size classification.
- Exactly one canonical `size:*` label describes the current effective diff.
- Docs-only and lockfile-heavy normalization rules are explicit and covered by tests.
- Risk classification runs report-only first and records the rule evidence behind its recommendation.
- Maintainers approve the exact risk rules before automatic risk mutation is enabled.
- Once enabled, automatic risk classification applies exactly one canonical `risk:*` label unless `risk:manual` is present.
- `risk:manual` prevents automated risk additions, removals, and replacements until a maintainer removes it.
- Re-running the workflow without a classification change does not create label churn.
- Fork pull requests are supported without checking out or executing untrusted code in an elevated write context.
- Workflow permissions are limited to the minimum label-read/write surface.
- Tests cover threshold boundaries, normalization, high-risk paths, manual override, stale-label replacement, idempotency, and malformed or incomplete GitHub API data.
- Maintainer docs describe triggers, calculation rules, override behavior, failure handling, and rollback.

### Architecture impact

Expected surfaces are a small classification helper with unit tests, a GitHub Actions workflow or existing workflow integration, and the maintainer label/CI documentation. The classifier should consume GitHub API diff metadata and repository-owned policy constants rather than duplicate label rules across shell and workflow YAML.

The implementation should remain independent of ProjectV2 automation and optional AI pre-review. Those systems may consume the resulting labels but should not become required dependencies.

### Risk and rollback

The primary risks are incorrect review-depth metadata, label churn, and unsafe permissions on fork pull requests. Mitigate them with deterministic tests, report-only risk evaluation, `risk:manual`, API-only elevated execution, minimal permissions, and idempotent writes.

Rollback is to disable the workflow or its risk-mutation phase. Existing labels remain ordinary GitHub metadata and can be corrected manually under the current maintainer policy.

### Expected routing

Should attach to an existing roadmap/tracker issue.

### Next decision surface

Track this as the risk/size automation implementation slice under #6808. Before Phase 3, maintainers should review the report-only comparison and approve the exact risk mutation rules.

### Breaking change?

No.

### Data hygiene checks

- [x] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [x] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

### Related

- #665
- #680
- #6808
- #7365
- #8914
- #9330

issues.body:
### Task

Settle how the release size gate handles the next release. The x86_64 Linux `zeroclaw` binary, built with the standard distribution features, is about 0.7 MB (about 1%) under the 64 MiB hard limit that fails a release build. Decide whether to raise the limit with a recorded headroom policy, shrink the binary, or replace the absolute limit (for example with per-target limits or a growth limit against the previous release), and land that before the v0.8.6 release build.

### Context

**The gate.** Every build leg of `.github/workflows/release-stable-manual.yml` runs `scripts/ci/check_binary_size.sh` in its "Check binary size" step with `BINARY_SIZE_HARD_LIMIT: "67108864"` (64 MiB). A leg over the limit fails. Only the experimental Android leg is `continue-on-error`, and `publish` needs the build job, so one oversized x86_64 Linux binary stops the release from publishing.

**History.** At v0.8.2 the then 50 MB limit was tripped by `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` at 53,154,008 bytes. #8342 (2026-06-26) raised it to 64 MiB to "restore headroom for the 0.8.x line", attributing the growth to organic source growth with no feature or dependency change.

**Measurements.** Sizes of the `zeroclaw` binary for the two x86_64 Linux targets. The two release rows come from the "Check binary size" step of each release run. The last row comes from a manual Cross-Platform Build dispatched on the head of #11306, which merges current master and changes no Rust code; its bytes were read from the binaries the run uploaded.

| Build | Run and commit | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| v0.8.4 release, 2026-08-02 | [30764737521](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/30764737521), `a56c345d51` | 58,323,704 | 58,400,272 |
| v0.8.5 release, 2026-09-05 | [33946673896](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/33946673896), `cb2b20a9fe` | 61,537,880 | 61,572,272 |
| master plus #11306, 2026-10-06 | [37408271392](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/37408271392), `40cb7be43e` | 66,344,920 | 66,409,584 |
| Hard limit | `BINARY_SIZE_HARD_LIMIT` | 67,108,864 | 67,108,864 |

Headroom on the last row is 763,944 bytes for gnu and 699,280 bytes for musl. The binary grew by about 3.2 MB between v0.8.4 and v0.8.5 and by about 4.8 MB in the month since, so at the recent rate the next few weeks of merges cross the limit.

Comparability: the manual workflow resolves the same feature selection (`cargo generate features --selection dist --target <triple>`) and builds with the same `cargo build --release --locked --no-default-features --features ...` command and pinned toolchain (1.98.0) as the current release workflow. Its Linux legs run on `ubuntu-latest` rather than the release workflow's `ubuntu-22.04`, and the earlier release rows used whatever toolchain was pinned at the time, so treat the trend as approximate and the last row as a close estimate of the next release build.

Other targets have more room. On the manual run: `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` 55,920,128, `arm-unknown-linux-gnueabihf` 52,534,300, `armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf` 52,223,004, and `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` 48,227,120. That run's macOS legs hit the workflow's 40-minute job limit; at v0.8.5, `x86_64-apple-darwin` was 51,919,432.

The advisory thresholds in `check_binary_size.sh` (a warning above 15 MB and a "target" warning above 5 MB) fire on every release build at these sizes, so they no longer signal anything.

Related: #10998 (binary-size evidence and optional-tool gating), #11306 (local size measurement and comparison tool), #11221 (gates SaaS and coding-CLI tools behind features but keeps them in the standard distribution, so it does not shrink this binary), and FND-001 section 7 (binary size tracked and reported).

### Acceptance criteria

- A decision recorded on this issue: raise the limit (new value and the headroom policy that sets it), shrink the x86_64 binary below the current limit with margin, or replace the absolute limit with another gate.
- The v0.8.6 release build's x86_64 Linux legs pass the size gate without an ad hoc override during the release.
- If the limit changes, its rationale is recorded where the gate is defined, and the advisory thresholds in `check_binary_size.sh` either mean something at current sizes or are removed.
- If the binary shrinks, before and after measurements are attached with target, profile, features, and artifact identity.

### Likely files or areas

- `.github/workflows/release-stable-manual.yml` (the "Check binary size" step)
- `scripts/ci/check_binary_size.sh`
- `Cargo.toml` (`default`, `[package.metadata.zeroclaw] dist_extra_features`)
- `docs/book/src/maintainers/release-runbook.md`

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

Release maintainers; maintainer triage required.

### Risk notes

Raising the limit again without a policy repeats #8342 and leaves the next trip to whoever cuts a release. Shrinking the binary by removing features from the distribution falls under the replacement-first policy (RFC #6165) and needs its own review. Either way, a failing size gate blocks publishing, so this should be settled before the release build starts.

issues.body:
### Summary

Implement `Channel::listener_health()` for the Signal channel, so `/health` reflects whether its signal-cli event stream is actually connected and delivering, and let `/api/channels` fill the `listening` readiness row from that signal for any channel that reports it, not only webhook channels.

### Problem statement

The Signal channel listens on signal-cli's SSE endpoint (`/api/v1/events`). When the connection fails or returns an error status, `listen()` logs it and retries in its own loop with backoff ([`signal.rs` L695](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/89bd18484bf4a262e43223d011306a8add031e29/crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/signal.rs#L695)), so it does not return. Signal does not implement `listener_health()`, so the supervisor records the channel as `ok` before `listen()` and on every health tick while it runs ([`mark_listener_health`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/89bd18484bf4a262e43223d011306a8add031e29/crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs#L7670), the `None` case). With signal-cli down or unreachable, `/health` therefore reports `channel:signal.<alias>` as `ok`. The listener's HTTP client also sets only a connect timeout, so a request that never gets a response, or a stream that stays open but stops delivering, is also reported as `ok`, like a working idle stream.

On the dashboard, the channel card's `listening` row is computed only for webhook channels ([`channel_readiness`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/89bd18484bf4a262e43223d011306a8add031e29/crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api.rs#L1562)). An enabled, bound Signal channel shows `listening` as "not checked" (API value `unknown`) with the note "Live readiness is not checked for `signal` channels yet." That is the honest answer #6985 chose, but it stays that way even for channels that do report listener health, such as Telegram (#10005) and WASM plugin channels (#11348).

### Proposed solution

Building on #6985 and #8732 (channel-owned readiness) and #10005 (passive listener health, no active probing on a timer):

1. **Signal implements `listener_health()`** from what its listener already observes, recording the time of each successful connect and of every received chunk, and starting again from `Pending` whenever `listen()` is entered:
   - `Pending` until the first connect attempt completes, but `Unhealthy` if an attempt is still waiting for a response after the staleness limit;
   - `Healthy` while the last successful connect or chunk is within the staleness limit and no connect attempt has failed since;
   - `Unhealthy` after a failed connect or error status, or when nothing has arrived for longer than the limit.

   signal-cli writes a `:` keepalive comment on the event stream every 15 seconds (configurable with `--sse-keepalive-interval` since v0.14.9), so chunks arrive even when there are no messages. Time the listener spends processing an event before reading the next chunk should not count as silence (or the limit must cover it). The limit should be generous, for example about three keepalive intervals, which also lets a routine reconnect (the listener waits 2s before retrying) finish without reporting `Unhealthy`; an operator who raises the keepalive interval above the limit would see the channel as unhealthy, so the limit should be documented or configurable. This reports the ZeroClaw-to-signal-cli event stream, not signal-cli's own connection to the Signal service.
2. **`/api/channels` fills `listening` from the health registry** for channels that report listener health. For those channels, a fresh `ok` maps to `ready`; a fresh `starting` maps to `unknown` with a note that the listener is starting; `error`, anything stale or no entry maps to `missing`, as webhook does today. The existing "Live readiness is not checked…" note is replaced for those channels (only authentication then remains unchecked). Webhook, which also maps `starting` to `missing`, keeps its current mapping. Two details for the implementation:
   - The registry records `ok` both for a reported `Healthy` and for the `None` fallback, so readiness needs to tell the two apart, for example with an additive field on the component's health entry saying whether the status came from the channel's own signal (it would appear in the health snapshot served by `/api/status`, `/api/health`, RPC and the daemon state file, and in the generated OpenAPI schema; the public `/health` lists its fields explicitly), or with a channel-owned capability lookup like `zeroclaw_channels::listing::qr_pairing_channel`. Errors the supervisor records when `listen()` exits would count as `missing` for a reporting channel.
   - The readiness freshness limit (`CHANNEL_LISTENER_HEALTH_MAX_AGE_SECS`, 30s) equals the supervisor's heartbeat (30s), so a healthy listener can briefly read stale; it should allow a margin, for example twice the heartbeat. The same edge exists today for webhook channels, which share the constant and would get the same margin.

   Channels that report nothing stay `unknown` with the existing note.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- Active probing (`health_check()`) on a timer or per dashboard request.
- Recovering a listener that reports `Unhealthy` (tracked for Telegram in #11608, which proposes restarting it and/or adding request timeouts). For Signal, an idle timeout inside `listen()` that drops a silent stream and reconnects would be a small follow-up.
- `listener_health()` for other channels; email and others could follow the same pattern separately.
- The `authenticated` readiness row. With it still `unknown`, a Signal card summarizes as `unknown`/`degraded` when listening is `ready` and `error`/`down` when it is `missing`.

### Alternatives considered

- Calling Signal's existing `health_check()` (`GET /api/v1/check`) from the readiness request: simple, but it is an active call per request, #10005 kept active probes out of recurring health paths, and it only shows that signal-cli's HTTP server is up, not that the listener's event stream is connected.
- Leaving Signal on the default: keeps `/health` reporting `ok` for a Signal channel that cannot reach signal-cli.

### Acceptance criteria

- With signal-cli unreachable, `/health` reports the Signal channel as `error` at the next supervisor health tick after a connect attempt has failed or has waited longer than the staleness limit (`starting` before that), and returns to `ok` at the next tick after the stream connects.
- A stream that stays open but receives nothing, keepalives included, for longer than the limit is reported `Unhealthy`.
- For a channel that reports listener health, `/api/channels` shows `listening: ready` when its entry is `ok` and fresh, `unknown` while it is `starting`, and `missing` when it is `error`, stale or absent; channels without a listener-health signal stay `unknown`.
- Unit tests for the Signal state transitions and staleness, and an API-boundary test for the readiness row, as #8732 did.

### Architecture impact

- `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/signal.rs`: recorded times and `listener_health()`.
- Either the health registry in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/health` and `mark_listener_health` (an added field on the component's health entry, which the generated OpenAPI schema in `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/openapi.rs` then includes), or `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/listing.rs` (a capability lookup).
- `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api.rs`: `channel_readiness` and the readiness freshness limit.

No config change unless the staleness limit is made configurable; `listener_health()` already exists on the trait with a default.

### Risk and rollback

Low to medium. It changes what `/health` and the channel card report for Signal, and the readiness logic shared by all channels: Telegram and plugin channel cards would have their `listening` row filled in and could now summarize as `error`/`down` when their listener reports unhealthy. Rollback is reverting the PR(s). #11556 (open) also touches `signal.rs`, including `listen()`, so whichever lands second needs a rebase.

### Expected routing

Ordinary feature triage

### Next decision surface

Whether the readiness change should be in the same PR as Signal's `listener_health()` or a separate one, and how readiness should tell a channel-reported status from the default. I can open a PR once the shape is agreed.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [X] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`; merge only after the dependencies below.
- **What changed and why:** Activate canonical registry admission and backend consumers, promote V4 configuration to V5, materialize complete models for routing/fallback/switching, and wire secret-safe registry editing. Registry types, native protocols, chat transport and reflection are prepared in #12454, #12455, #12456 and #12457.
- **Scope boundary:** V5 admission, persistence/editor wiring, canonical model construction and backend consumer/lifecycle cutover. Activation and affected consumers remain together so no intermediate revision clears profiles that active consumers still read. Zerocode and Web follow separately.
- **Blast radius:** Config persistence and secret handling; provider construction; agent/session lifecycle; memory, speech and decision consumers; channel/gateway/RPC dispatch.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related to #9809. Stack part 9; reference implementation `921b8ee993a0b2439a0c2c41cb84337270942a06`. Depends on #12457.

### What this does, simply

The preceding layers prepare independent registry types, native capability protocols, chat transport and generic reflection. This layer activates those components: V4 input is promoted at the V5 admission boundary, backend consumers resolve exact model references, and routing, fallback and switching build complete target bindings. Configuration activation and dependent consumers stay together to avoid a partially switched runtime. This remaining cutover is still large; the preparatory layers make their own architectural boundaries independently reviewable.

## Testing (required)


### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `Yes` — the migration or interactive workflow below supplements passing current-head CI.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** Requested surface: `cli`. Not exercised interactively at this revision.

- **Expected on this branch (after):** V4 configuration becomes V5 connections/models; internal consumers resolve exact model keys; switching/fallback materializes all target configuration and a failed update preserves the previous binding.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Master stores provider-owned profiles and consumer-specific capability settings, and has no canonical decoupled registry.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Earlier green runs are historical only. Current-head workspace CI is required after the review fixes; no current-head all-green claim is made.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** The separate PR-risk reporter failed its head-bound evidence capture. Live CLI/migration verification remains pending; passing CI does not establish the two old-configuration migration restrictions identified in review. Original #9809 CI does not validate intermediate stack revisions.
- **Commands run and tail output:** At `7457ad9664`, `cargo check --offline -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-providers -p zeroclaw-memory -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-gateway --all-targets` passed. Expanded config unit suite passed 2,085 tests, including the final fallback and timeout regressions. `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `git diff --check` and the changed-line docs quality gate passed. Existing Rust-toolchain deprecation/unused-dependency warnings were not changed.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Addressed previous-head split dependency errors (retained embedding factory, complete timeout helpers, deferred dispatch-dependent sampling, and secret-test trait import). New-head execution remains pending. Compared the integrated provider and UI trees byte-for-byte with the saved pre-split snapshot. Preserved the frozen V4 fixture. Corrected previous-head CI failures caused by unnecessary TOML rewriting; the existing comment-preservation and atomic-save assertions remain intact. New-head execution is pending. Inspected ownership, imports and the incremental diff against the parent. Runtime/network behavior has not been re-executed locally.
- **Visual interface evidence:** Pending: CLI Quickstart and configuration command output require exact-head verification before interface sign-off.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `f280f09627d3049431f51232f21fb2f9b84e79a2`; source formatting only.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** No interactive action performed; current-head CI passed, while manual runtime checks remain pending.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Local Cargo build/test/clippy were intentionally skipped at the author’s request to use GitHub CI instead of repeated heavy local compilation.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? Yes; existing capability selection is represented in the new registry. Existing admission boundaries remain in force.
- New external network calls? Yes; native capability adapters use the selected connection and protocol. No additional allowlist bypass is introduced.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? Yes; connection credentials and sensitive headers use the existing encrypted persistence and masked edit contracts.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? Yes; shared extraction policy is selected per materialized model.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: Migration, registry editing and provider selection cross configuration trust boundaries. Preserve ciphertext, use masked compare-and-swap edits, validate references before installation, and keep the previous binding when construction fails. Provider output remains subject to runtime tool admission.

## Compatibility (required)

The terminal setup and configuration screens need to edit the same connections and models that the backend resolves. No provider inference request was made.

- The adapter uses ZeroClaw's MCP client and the configured web-search proxy. It returns source links and excerpts, caps provider error text, and reports connection failures with a retry-or-switch hint.
- **Scope and blast radius** DuckDuckGo remains the default for fresh and upgraded installs. The new route is available when the compiled tool is enabled and selected and the user has configured Parallel.
- **Linked issues** Related #12480, which tracks the project decision about the default provider.

### What this does, simply

If you choose Parallel for web search, ZeroClaw sends the query to Parallel's keyless MCP endpoint and returns links and excerpts to the agent. There is no account or API key to set up. Anonymous usage is rate limited.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes.
- **Interface exercised** CLI config and the built-in web search provider.
- **Setup** Use a fresh config with no `ZEROCLAW_web_search__search_provider` override.

```sh
env -u ZEROCLAW_web_search__search_provider cargo run --locked -p zeroclaw --bin zeroclaw --features tools-external -- --config-dir "$(mktemp -d)" config get web_search.search_provider --json
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-tools --features tools-external --lib web_search
```

The CLI should report `duckduckgo` on both `master` and this branch. On this branch, the focused tests also show that an explicit `parallel` routes to the Parallel adapter and that the adapter returns a result through the configured proxy. The Parallel route is absent on `master`.

### How I tested

- **Tested revision** `2191fdf` on macOS arm64. [Quality Gate](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/43974139666) covers the repository's Rust and documentation checks.
- **Local results** `cargo +1.98.0 fmt --all -- --check`, `git diff --check`, and the documentation style and local-link checks passed. The added external docs link returned HTTP 200.
  - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-config --lib web_search` returned `1 passed; 0 failed`.
  - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-config --test migration` returned `106 passed; 0 failed`.
  - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-tools --features tools-external --lib web_search` returned `160 passed; 0 failed`, including proxy routing, response limits, and transport errors.
  - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --features tools-external --lib web_search_tool` returned `1 passed; 0 failed` and verified rate-limited registration. The same command filtered to `minimal_assembly_exposes_eleven` returned `1 passed; 0 failed`.
  - `cargo +1.98.0 clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-tools --features zeroclaw-tools/tools-external --all-targets -- -D warnings` passed. Rust 1.99.1 emitted deprecation warnings for existing atomic calls in the test builds.
- **Beyond CI** I built `zeroclaw` with the `tools-external` feature. `config get web_search.search_provider --json` showed `"value": "duckduckgo"` in a fresh config directory. After `config set web_search.search_provider parallel --no-interactive`, a separate process read `"value": "parallel"`. The CLI build emitted a macOS debug linker warning about the compact unwind table.
- I also passed the explicit Parallel config to the built-in tool. It returned three linked results for a public query with no key. I did not probe the public quota.
- **Visual interface evidence** Exact plain-text output from the smoke check. It called `WebSearchTool::execute` with the explicit config and printed the tool result.

```text
Empty web search config: duckduckgo
Explicit web search config: parallel
Search results for: Rust standard library Vec documentation (via Parallel)
1. std::vec - Rust
   https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/vec/
```

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- **New permissions, capabilities, or filesystem access scope?** No.
- **New external network calls?** Yes. Explicitly selecting Parallel causes the web search tool to send queries to `https://mcp.parallel.ai/mcp?tools=web_search` through the configured search proxy. Existing tool selection, enablement, and approval controls still apply.
- **Secrets, tokens, or credentials handling changed?** No.
- **PII, real identities, or personal data added to the diff?** No.
- **Untrusted model-visible text introduced?** Yes. The adapter validates source URLs and bounds returned excerpts and provider errors.

## Compatibility (required)

- **Backward compatible?** Yes. DuckDuckGo remains the default and existing provider selections are preserved.
- **Config, environment, or CLI surface changed?** Yes. The existing `web_search.search_provider` setting accepts `parallel`. Users can upgrade with their current configuration. To opt in, run `zeroclaw config set web_search.search_provider parallel --no-interactive`.
- **Rust, MSRV, or toolchain floor changed?** No.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback** Set `web_search.search_provider` back to your previous provider with `zeroclaw config set web_search.search_provider duckduckgo --no-interactive` (substitute your previous provider if different), then restart any running service that reads this config. Update any service environment override to match.
- **Config toggle** Set `enabled = false` under `[web_search]` to turn off the tool.
- **Observable failure symptoms** Search errors can include `search_status=unavailable, http=429` or `transport=timeout`.
